News.title: BBC warns some channels and radio stations ‘may well’ have to CLOSE – as staff left ‘in tears’ at £2.6million cuts
News.content:
Next

SOME channels and radio stations “may well” have to close, the BBC’s director general has warned.

It comes as part of a series of cost-saving measures by the corporation, including a series of recent job cuts.

Speaking on BBC One’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg, Matt Brittin said the BBC “wouldn’t guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever”.



The company’s current financial situation has led the director general to admit that these decisions are now required to be considered sooner than they first hoped.



He explained these considerations stem from how audiences are viewing content.

A large migration of viewers to on demand services has meant the BBC has had to re-evaluate its larger broadcasting model.

Brittin, who was appointed director general in March this year, highlighted that vast differences in viewing numbers for live broadcasts compared to streaming means questions must be raised about the future of its on demand output.



He said: “When’s the right time to migrate that service fully to being on-demand? And part of my job is to safeguard value for money for the licence fee payer.”

Brittin continued that the BBC should go “in different ways to reach audiences and we’re locked into yesterday’s model of how people consume content, and actually the audience is always already living in tomorrow’s world”.

A number of programmes have recently been axed amid cost-saving measures put in place at the corporation, with the BBC looking to save £500million.

It follows the announcement that 41 jobs within the sports department would be axed to help save £2.6million.



Warnings of compulsory redundancies were issued to employees, with one staff member at the meeting saying that people were “crying in the office” prior to the announcement, as reported by The Telegraph.

While five new positions are set to be created, the department will see a net loss of 36 roles in total.

This came after the news that lunchtime and overnight sports bulletins, which run on BBC’s 24-hour News channel, are to be scrapped leading to a further seven redundancies.

The BBC has lost a number of live coverage events over the past 10 years, including Formula 1, England’s Six Nations matches and the Open.

News.title: Woman sexually assaulted & then slapped by young man after confronting him on Tube as cops release CCTV
News.content:
ATTACK PROBE Woman sexually assaulted & then slapped by young man after confronting him on Tube as cops release CCTV







Next

A WOMAN has reportedly been sexually assaulted and slapped in the face on the Tube.

The attack is said to have taken place at 8.30pm on July 4 while the victim was walking through Baker Street Underground station in London.



When she confronted the attacker, she was allegedly struck across the face.

Cops have now released a CCTV image of the suspect in the hope of tracking him down.



The police are urging anyone who recognises the man in the picture to come forward.

Information can also be submitted anonymously to Crimestoppers.



It comes as a man was left fighting for his life at Liverpool Street station in Central London earlier this month.

Cops arrived at the scene to find the man with life-threatening head injuries lying on the platform.

Trump added: “That would be ‘SUPER’!



“Everyone last night agreed, also.”

News.title: Childcare worker, 35, slapped with over 400 charges after ‘abusing 150 children’ at five nurseries
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

‘ABUSE’ HELL Childcare worker, 35, slapped with over 400 charges after ‘abusing 150 children’ at five nurseries







Next

A CHILDCARE worker has been slapped with over 400 charges after allegedly abusing 150 children at five nurseries.

Hamish Tait, 35, has been accused of sexual assault, producing child abuse material, and inappropriate filming over the span of more than 15 years.



The suspect reportedly worked at or attended 62 early childhood education facilities, including five nurseries, between 2009 and 2025, according to local cops.

The additional charges laid on Friday include 105 counts of producing child abuse material, one count of carrying out a sexual act with a child under 10, five counts of filming a person engaged in a private act in circumstances of aggravation, and four counts of possessing child abuse material.



A probe, named Operation Moonbi, into Tait was launched in 2025 after the National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children in the US flagged child abuse material he allegedly uploaded.

Electronic devices at Tait’s home in Sydney were seized during a police raid.



Local authorities allege these computers contained child abuse material.

It took investigators one whole year to analyse 2.4 million electronic files stored on his devices.



Detective Acting Inspector Emmanuel Tsardoulias previously said the victim identification work was “painstaking and detailed”.

He said: “Our victim ID team is tenacious, committed and will stop at nothing to identify children or victims of child exploitation.”

Police also conducted 12 search warrants during the probe.

At least 136 alleged victims have been contacted by authorities.

Authorities have also published a website listing all the places Tait worked at.



The childcare worker has been remanded in custody since he was arrested and charged in July 2025.

He is yet to enter a plea for the charges.

The suspect is next due in court on October 8.

News.title: Incredible plan for 370ft ‘sci-fi’ superyacht with suspended glass-bottom infinity pool & spaceship-style command centre
News.content:
Next

INCREDIBLE plans for a glamorous superyacht starring a spaceship-style command centre and suspended glass-bottom infinity pool have been unveiled.

Concept vessel HIVE shall stretch across a sprawling 377ft of glass, wood and cream and feature a stunning underwater lounge and panoramic views.



Revealed at Monaco’s Yacht Festival, lovers of luxury will be making a beeline for the new honeycombe designed ship.

Renderings show a cavernous central atrium lined with curved wooden balconies stacked on top of each other, a bit like cells in a honeycomb.



Suspended between smooth curves of wood and cream hangs a crystal clear infinty pool – a blue gem at the heart of the vessel, fitted out with ContraWave technology.

Running through the middle of the yacht, the 66ft pool appears to float in mid-air.

Sweeping views of the sea abound as lucky passengers lounge on the wood-pannelled decks, enmeshed in luscious green ferns.

At the centre of a low-lit concert hall stands a majestic black grand piano as a glittering chandelier dangles overhead.



Inside the command centre, captains appear to be running an intergalactic spaceship rather than a superyacht.

Panaromic wrap-around screen show live views of the sea alongside navigation data.

A retractable glass roof offers vast views of the night sky while an underwater lounge boasts the opportunity to see fish up close.



To relax on a balmy holiday trip, passengers can pick up a book from the glass-encased library and kick back in the on-deck garden.

The “hive” concept was hatched after discussions kept circling back to the idea of a central space for people to come together before splitting off into their own rooms.

The concept was developed by a team from Studio De Voogt, led by senior designer Jan Schaffers, working alongside Feadship’s naval architects and engineers.

Parisian salons of the 1930S inspired the design as a hub for late-night gossip and conversation.

Designer Jan Schaffers said the space highlighted “the idea that experiences can change people”.



Despite the sci-fi look construction team Feadship insisted the superyacht can be built from tech that lready exists or is in active development.

The yacht would be powered by three 900kW generators fuelled by hydrotreated vegetable oil as well as fuel cells and a 5MWh battery bank.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Shunning the use of conventional rudders the HIVE vessel would use high-tech propellers to thrust in any direction.

A scale model of the ship is being housed inside the House of Feadship during the Monaco Yacht Show – running until September 26.

News.title: Jealous killer, 61, who was caught on CCTV stalking estranged wife, 49, before slashing her throat is jailed
News.content:
Next

A JEALOUS killer who was caught on CCTV stalking his estranged wife from “bar to bar” before slashing her throat has been jailed for life.

Raymond Williams, 61, murdered Tania Williams, 49, after he saw her talking to another man while on a night out in Norwich, Norfolk.



Neighbours reported hearing screams and a female voice saying: “What are you going to do? Kill me?”, before Tania was discovered dead.

The mum-of-four was found lying on the ground in a “pool of blood” close to her home in Thorpe St Andrew at around 11.40pm on January 17.



She was tragically declared dead at the scene, before armed officers descended on Williams’ accommodation and arrested him two hours later.

Williams denied murdering Tania, but a jury returned a unanimous guilty verdict following a 17-day trial.

And Williams was today jailed for life with a minimum of 27 years.

In a statement read in court, Tania’s family said: “We never imagined that one day we would receive a call telling us that Tania had been murdered.



“Even now, we struggle to accept that she is no longer here with us and that her life was taken in such a devastating way.

“The people we were before that phone call feel different from who we are now.

“Something in our family has changed forever, and there will always be an emptiness where Tania should be.”

In CCTV footage shown in court, Williams is seen prowling from “bar to bar” to track his estranged wife down across the city centre.

He eventually finds the mum-of-four in Revolucion de Cuba, on Queen Street, before the pair both walk out of the bar and down the street.



She appears to distance herself from him as they stroll down the road and heads off to catch a bus home.

Meanwhile, Williams is seen jogging down Wensum Street towards where his white Vauxhall Corsa was parked on Fishergate.

Security footage then shows this car parked on Yarmouth Road as he “laid in wait” for Tania.



She is then seen on CCTV getting off her bus and walking towards her home in Catherine Gardens.

At 11.30pm, neighbours heard petrified screams in the area and a female voice saying: “What are you going to do? Kill me?”

Tania died at the scene despite the best efforts of her neighbours and paramedics.

Area coroner Johanna Thompson previously said the security officer was identified by her son following the horror.

Two hours after finding her, armed police arrested Williams at his accommodation, where he was dressed completely differently.



He had disposed of everything he was wearing earlier in the evening in a bid to avoid forensic detection.

CCTV had captured Williams acting suspiciously around bins in nearby alleyways.

Footage showed him taking off his watch, which had been given to him by Tania, and dropping it down a drain.

Williams, who previously served as a Norfolk police community support officer, was found guilty of her murder.

Norwich Crown Court heard he had been “consumed with jealousy”.



Tania’s heartbroken family hailed her “bubbly personality” in a touching tribute.

It read: “My mother Tania was a woman of great faith – believing in Christ; she was also a woman who was passionate about her four children.

“Tania was undoubtedly beautiful, she was honest but mostly was always giving to others, the list about her bubbly personality truly goes on.

“Our family wants to continue to honour her and her generous nature even in her passing, which stems from deep rooted faith and kindness.

“Even though her life was cut short; she still lived a full life – leaving many beautiful memories with her children and family behind.



“Her children want to keep their memories of her alive by honouring her passions and fulfil any dreams she didn’t get to do here on earth.”

Senior Investigating Officer Detective Inspector Sam Pontin described the investigation as “thorough and complex”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He added: “Thanks to the strength of the evidence presented, the jury was able to reach its verdict and hold Williams accountable for his actions.

“While no verdict can undo the pain caused by Tania’s death, I hope today’s outcome provides her family with some measure of justice.”

News.title: Watch moment I was robbed by knife thug on bike in broad daylight – he tried to do a DEAL with me in busy street
News.content:
Next

AS a court reporter based in the Old Bailey I encounter criminals daily, but being a victim was not something I had ever thought about – until on day earlier this year.

I was on my way home on 11 April when 19-year-old Mohammed Daidai rode up to me on an e-bike near London Paddington, and just moments later he had his hand on my neck.





He drew me in and forcibly snatched my headphones to put them on himself.

In that split second I dashed for the pavement and went on the other side of a parked car for cover.

Brazenly, rather than making a run for it, the balaclava-clad robber then tried to barter my mobile for my headphones – saying he would give them back if I showed him my phone.

Seeing as there was enough distance between us that he couldn’t reach me at arm’s length I begrudgingly waved my handset in the air for a brief moment.

But the picky teenager said: “I don’t want your Samsung, I’ve got a better phone,” before showing off his iPhone unprompted.

He then asked what else I had on me, and asked if I carried cash. I told him: “Who carries cash?”

At this point a woman in a black Mercedes drove up alongside us and rolled down the window to ask if I was going to “move the car” that I was using for cover.

Bizarrely I then had to explain that I was being robbed, to which the driver said: “Sorry to interrupt,” and drove off without looking back.





This was probably not the way Mr Daidai had expected this robbery to go and he appeared as confused as I was.

I took the opportunity to demand my headphones back, as I had held up my bargain and showed him my phone, whether or not he wanted it.

I then told him I was a journalist and that I would see him in court for this matter.

Mr Daidai scarcely believed me and said: “You are lucky I didn’t take more off you,” before riding off.

I remember being in a state of shock and gave myself a minute to collect my thoughts before calling the police, though I had no expectation they would do anything about it.

So it came as a great surprise when I received a call back just half an hour later to say Mr Daidai had been arrested and cops had recovered my undamaged headphones.

Five months down the line, I found myself in the witness box at Southwark Crown Court, looking into the eyes of my robber as I said: “I told you so.”

Daidai, wearing a black sports jacket, had been held in custody since his arrest after cops realised he should have been behind bars for possessing a “large kitchen knife”.



Reading my own statement in court last Friday, I said: “Experiencing crime as a victim without the sanitised lens of the court is fundamentally scary and primal.

“Having covered many similar cases I said I couldn’t be sure Daidai didn’t have a knife and genuinely feared I might be stabbed.

“But once I saw the teenager from the other side of the bonnet I remember thinking to myself: ‘What is this kid doing trying to rob me in broad daylight?’

“Mr Daidai made repeated attempts to make me present my mobile phone, saying he needed it for ‘directions’, even after he said he didn’t want my Samsung and that he had a better phone than me.

“I felt indignant and annoyed, and so I told him no, I am not handing my phone over, because you already have my headphones.

“I told him I was a journalist and that I would see him in court for this matter. I have done so now.

“As journalists we generally avoid being the subject of a story, so it’s extra unfortunate that my role in this one is as a victim of crime.

“At its core, this case is a tragically familiar tale heard within these corridors: A young man throws his life away for quick money, too insignificant a sum to be interesting for the papers.”



Defending Daidai, John Clifton said letters provided by his mother and sister, who sat in court, offer a “different perspective of the person that is the subject of these charges.”

But, sentencing, Judge Mukul Chawla told Daidai: “You are now 19 years of age, you are quickly building a list of convictions which will inevitably, if you continue to do so, subject you to further time in custody, and that will be a complete waste of your life.

“But if that is the decision you choose to make, then that is entirely up to you.

“You could avoid that by staying off drugs, but that is your choice.

“You know what the problem is and you know how you can avoid that particular problem.”

Daidai did not react as he was sentenced to 15 months’ imprisonment, suspended for two years.

Judge Chawla also ordered 40 days of rehabilitation activities, adding: “You do have a future if you choose to use it, but that is very much a matter for you.”

Yet I, too, share limited confidence that this is the last the court will see of Mr Daidai, as almost one in three criminals in England and Wales commit another crime once freed.

Nearly one in six jailed for less than 12 months go on to reoffend – as was the case for Daidai, who served five months in prison while awaiting sentence.

I know I represent a sliver of victims who get to confront their muggers – as an overwhelming 92.5 per cent of reported robberies end without a single charge being pressed, Home Office figures show.



So I meant it when I told the court: “I count my lucky stars knowing I have been fortunate enough to walk away from a robbery with no injuries, to have my stolen headphones returned undamaged, and to have this day in court so I can tell my robber: I told you so.”

News.title: Razor-blade ‘spurs’, catastrophic injuries & £14k bets in cruel ‘grudge matches’… horror rise of UK’s cockfighting rings
News.content:
Next

WITH razor blades attached to their heels, the cockerels square up for a violent fight – cheered on by a baying mob fuelled by blood lust.

The birds suffer “catastrophic injuries” during these bouts, which are exploding in popularity across the UK – and The Sun can reveal cruel gangs are hosting “home and away fixtures” and “grudge matches” inspired by football and boxing.





Crowds of up to 60 people, including toddlers, attend these sinister spectacles where bets of up to £14,000 are placed by the cockerels owners, in addition to thousands from those watching around the cockpit.

The RSPCA tells The Sun cockfighting is a “very lucrative” business for the crooks involved and individual fertilised eggs or offspring from the “purebred bloodlines” of champion fighters sell for up to £10,000 a time.

The ‘sport’ is increasing in popularity with the charity receiving 202 reports of cockfighting since 2021 – but they suspect numbers could be far higher due to fight rings being highly secretive, underground operations.

This week eight men appeared in court charged with keeping premises in Bradford allegedly used for cockfighting, arranging illegal cock fights and causing harm to animals.

The accused, aged between 22 and 60, are yet to enter pleas and hail from areas ranging from Lancashire to Cheshire, Staffordshire, West Yorkshire and the West Midlands.

Two further men are due to face charges including Muhammad Ifraz Amin, 38, of Great Sankley, who is accused of 21 offences and will soon be arrested by police after failing to attend court.





Their alleged criminal activities join other high profile cases – including locations found with multiple fighting pits and “makeshift gyms” where cockerels were “mutilated” and one travellers’ site where 242 birds alongside cockfight knives were seized.

“The life expectancy of these birds is very low. Even the winning bird may not survive. They can suffer catastrophic injuries,” says Will Rippon, Chief Inspector of the RPSCA’s Special Operations Unit.

“There can be lots of blood from injuries. In some fights they end up covered in blood. If one shot opens a main artery it will be very bloody.

“The birds physically suffer horrendous injuries from the fights but also mental and emotional suffering.

“Then there are injuries to the birds’ eyes, heads, beaks, spurs, bodies, legs and wings – all of this is illegal, unnecessary and cruel suffering.”

Cockfighting has been illegal in England and Wales since 1835 yet there remains a feverish appetite for it – with bouts taking place across the UK, especially in the north of England.

The bouts, which can be attended by between a handful and 60-plus people, typically take place in garden sheds, garages, private homes, waste ground, rural farms and travellers sites.

Entertainment and money are the main motivators, with Will telling us he’s aware of one fight where £14,000 was bet by a cockerel’s owner – in additional “hundreds of pounds” in bets from spectators.

It’s becoming so popular that gangs of up to 10 people are joining forces to produce cockfighting teams and engage in “home and away matches” across the UK.

Each team consists of multiple fighting cockerels due to the high fatality rate. Teams have their own name, ‘home venue’ and even participate in “grudge matches”.



Will says: “Historically, to get a very good, top of the range fighting bird you would need to have a large breeding stock, which is logistically difficult and expensive.

“Now if you’re connected you can get a very high-end bird to bring to these fights a lot more easily and can stand a good chance of winning.

“Large enterprises form to get good bloodlines and good breeding practices set up. To fight for a season, they need to have hens and a lot of people working to look after the birds.

“If they want to have the really high-end birds, they have to put time in. The more time and care they take, the better the birds will fight.”

Cockfighting is split into two categories – ‘naked heel’, where their rear claw, known as the ‘spur’, is often sharpened, and ‘spurred’, where they attach a metal cuff with “razor blades, short metal spikes and other sharp weapons” to the heel.

The latter is typically more gruesome. It can last from seconds to 10 minutes, while ‘naked heel’ bouts can last up to an hour. Sometimes they have multiple rounds, like in a boxing match, which last up to eight minutes each.

In some cockfights, it’s a battle to the death. In others, there are referees and sometimes the owner forfeits the match to save their bird being slaughtered.

Highlighting the threat to the cockerels’ lives, a bird is considered a ‘champion’ if it has won three fights and a ‘grand champion’ for five wins.

Descendants of those victors are bought for huge sums. One fertilised egg or offspring from that winning “bloodline” – similar to in dog fighting – is sold for up to £10,000 a time.

Will says: “People go to great lengths to get birds with certain bloodlines that are particularly game and produce good fighting stock – based on their aggression and technique.



“They will pay up to £10,000 for a good, well-bred and tested bird. When they turn up to big fights they want to win, it’s like boxing, it’s all about bravado.”

Some illegally smuggle “good fighting stock” with “very good bloodlines” from outside the UK, Will says, typically from countries where the ‘sport’ is legal – like Thailand and the Philippines.

This presents its own risks, because without health certifications and other checks, there are risks of avian flu and other diseases ravaging UK livestock or even transmitting to humans.

Will explains the overseas trade is “very lucrative”, with individual birds selling for up to £9,000 due to being considered “the best in the world”.

Prized birds are known as being “game” – cockerels that are naturally more aggressive and want to continue fighting even after injuries.

Many of the birds undergo training, according to Russ Middleton, 62, Head of Intelligence at the League Against Cruel Sports (LACS).

“I’m aware of cockerel ‘treadmills’ and large round hamster wheels,” the former police detective tells us. “They put them inside and let them run to build stamina and strength.

“They also attach weights to their legs and have them spar against other fighting cockerels. They wear ‘muffs’, which cover their spurs or claws, so they can practice without major injury.”



It’s also known that trainers use “dummy cockerels”, which Will says are “incredibly lifelike” stuffed toys for the birds to fight against.

Russ says some trainers surgically remove the comb and wattles – the flaps of skin on the bird’s head, neck and earlobes – to reduce the areas where they can sustain injuries that could end a fight early.

When it comes to ‘spurred’ fights – where sharp items are connected to a metal cuff that is fitted to the bird’s heel – their lives are especially in danger and bouts can last just seconds.

“Some attach razors, small blades or short metal spikes but the new trend is using the spurs (the rear claw) of dead birds after making them sharper and more pointy,” Will says.

Some involved in the ‘sport’ are known to create and collect grim trophies to celebrate victories and their commitment to cockfighting.

“They make trophies with the spurs and blades from the bird,” Russ says. “They can be put in wooden frames with glass covers or turned into jewellery.

“I’ve seen quite large, almost unwearably large, gold rings with these fighting items or spurs, other times it’s a cockerel standing on a ring.”

The clashes typically take place in purposely dug out pits. In some ‘venues’ there are as many as three to allow for multiple fights to take place – potentially at the same time.

The arenas are lined with carpet and another material on the ground to catch the blood and the perimeter is made from “6ft doors, wood, hay bales or rubber matts”.



Will says the fights are often meeting points to discuss further criminal activity and attendees range from “toddlers to kids of all ages, teenagers and adults”.

Watching in the wings of the arena as the fights happen are black market traders, who peddle prescription-only veterinary medicines to treat the injured birds.

“Some owners carry their own vet kits to patch-up the injured cockerels themselves or buy it there,” Russ says. “They will have medicines, antibiotics and all sorts of medical supplies.”

This black market trade, which also exists on social media, is due to owners knowing vets may report them if they suspect a bird is involved in cockfighting.

The main challenge for investigators is that is ‘sport’ is highly secretive. The RSPCA and LACS urge anyone with any information to inform them immediately.

Red flags can include unusual activity at a location like numerous people and vehicles appearing, the sound of cockerels and loud or excitable voices. It can happen in both rural and urban areas.

They ask the public to be especially vigilant as we approach the new cockfighting season, which spans November until early summer.

Those found guilty of these crimes face fines and prison sentences of up to five years – but due to its prevalence it seems many are undeterred.

Russ adds: “Cockfighting is highly unpleasant and deeply distressing to watch. It’s dreadfully cruel and all in the name of so-called ‘entertainment’ or ‘sport’. It must be stopped.”



For more information visit the RSPCA or the League Against Cruel Sports. You can report suspected animal crimes here and here.

News.title: Noah Woods left playground through gap in fence, inquest hears
News.content:
Three-year-old Noah Woods, who was found dead in a pond following a huge search in Suffolk, had left a play area "through a gap in the fence", an inquest has heard.

A major search was carried out in the village of Brantham after the toddler went missing on 15 September. His body was found the next day in nearby water by police divers.

Assistant coroner Jyoti Gill said it was a "very sad and tragic death" as she opened and adjourned the inquest in Ipswich.

A tribute issued by Noah's family called him a "happy, cheeky, playful" boy who loved to laugh, with his mother urging other parents to "hold their children a little tighter and cherish every moment".

Suffolk Coroner's Court heard from police that Noah had left the playground, walked into a memorial garden and left that through an open gate. He then ran down a path on a new housing estate towards nearby Decoy Pond.

Det Ch Insp Matt Connick from Suffolk Police told the court that CCTV showed Noah in the play area being looked after by a relative, which was "part of a normal routine".

The detective said Noah "left through a gap in the fence leading to the memorial garden where he left through an open gate".

After he had left the play area, he was closely followed by the relative trying to catch up with him, Connick added.

The inquest heard the relative had shouted out to Noah, who lived in neighbouring East Bergholt, but he went out of sight shortly afterwards.

Another man was said to have joined the search and then police were called.

At the time of the search, volunteers were told that Noah was non-verbal and partially deaf.

A statement from Brantham Parish Council, which maintains the play area at Merriam Close, said it was "deeply saddened by Noah's death and our thoughts remain with his family and all those affected at this extremely difficult time".

"The parish council understands that there was a break in the internal fencing, being constructed to separate the play area from the memorial garden, however the whole of the area at Merriam Close, including the play area and memorial garden are completely enclosed by appropriate perimeter fencing," it said.

"The council will co-operate fully with any investigation and, while inquiries are ongoing, does not consider it appropriate to comment further."

News.title: Some BBC channels and radio stations may well have to close, director general says
News.content:
Brittin took over as BBC director general in May after a decade as president of Google in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

Asked by Kuenssberg if he would allow a programme to be made and presented by AI, Brittin replied: "I would do, within guardrails."

He added: "We want to experiment with this technology and understand what it can and can't do, but I'm here because I believe in human creativity.

"I don't think anything we do should be replaced by AI. I think there are lots of places where AI can help us make the licence fee go further, but also help us in our decision-making and creativity. But it's not a substitute for humans."

He also warned of the danger of a handful of tech companies having too much control over information in the future.

"We're also in this moment where AI is in takeoff. So I think there's a danger that six companies will control access to information in future and the creation of information and misinformation," he said.

"Six companies, none of them European, let alone British. In that world, here's the BBC. It's the most trusted organisation by over half a billion people."

Asked if he trusted big tech companies he replied: "There's a lot of platforms out there, so I wouldn't trust any platform innately.

"And I think what you do is you keep under review how those things work and whether your content can show up in the right place and fulfil its mission.

"I think the BBC and our apps and services should be the antidote to the algorithm. Everywhere else you go is driven by some commercial interest."

The interview will be available on BBC Sounds and YouTube on Saturday 26 September, then on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg on BBC One and iPlayer at 09:00 BST on 27 September.

News.title: Daniel Thomas pleads not guilty after dinghy slashed
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has pleaded not guilty to criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the Channel with a knife.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, was arrested after the livestreamed video on Tuesday.

Thomas, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court in Hampshire via videolink, is also charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone.

He pleaded not guilty to both charges and was remanded in custody until his next court appearance at Portsmouth Crown Court on 29 September.

News.title: NHS to suspend staff suspected of snooping on patient records
News.content:
NHS staff in England suspected of looking at patient records without a valid reason will be immediately suspended as part of a "zero-tolerance crackdown" on snooping.

Those under suspicion will also be locked out of NHS computer systems, preventing any further viewing of confidential records, including from home.

NHS England chief executive Sir Jim Mackey has written to every trust, ordering the measures to be introduced immediately to strengthen protection against data breaches.

The move follows a series of high-profile incidents involving the records of Nottingham and Southport attack victims and a child who was injured in a crocodile enclosure in Cambridgeshire.

This week, Bristol Foundation NHS Trust said it had launched an internal investigation after it emerged the medical records of an 18-year-old had been accessed years after his death.

The boy's mother, Paula McGowan, told the BBC she was "deeply concerned and hurt" and called for the NHS to do more to deal with the problem.

News.title: Watch: Robbie Williams' surprise singalong after Peru gig cancelled
News.content:
Robbie Williams gave an impromptu performance outside a hotel in Peru's capital Lima, after his concert at a stadium in the city was cancelled.

Authorities announced that the Arena 1 Park gig could not go ahead, citing failures by the venue to comply with safety regulations.

Robbie told fans outside his hotel he was "broken-hearted" and held a brief singalong with the cheering crowds.

News.title: Met should probe handling of 'Putney Pusher' case, police watchdog says
News.content:
The police watchdog has said the Metropolitan Police's professional standards unit should investigate the force's handling of a case after the death of a man suspected of being the "Putney Pusher".

Nicholas Brandram was found dead at his London home on 15 September. His family said he took his own life after the "immense pressure" of a police investigation.

The 44-year-old was under suspicion of being the jogger who pushed a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge in west London in May 2017.

The Met police made a mandatory referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) following the banker's death.

The family of Nicholas Brandram said a Metropolitan Police investigation into its handling of the case should be "thorough, independent and unflinching in establishing what went wrong".

His sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker said in a statement: "We have been clear about the litany of failings that need to be examined, and we expect those questions to be answered."

They called for the investigation to be a "priority", adding that they wanted no other family "to endure what ours is going through".

In a statement, the IOPC said: "After carefully considering the referral, we have decided that an investigation is required and that the Met's Directorate of Professional Standards should conduct it.

"We have recommended the review considers matters including the necessity and proportionality of arrest, what engagement was there with the media and considerations made in relation to Mr Brandram's welfare and the relevant policy."

News.title: Jeffrey Donaldson victim describes 'profound impact' of child sex abuse
News.content:
The victims of child sex offender Jeffrey Donaldson have described the impact the abuse had on them.

Donaldson was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

The former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader appeared at Newry Crown Court for a hearing prior to his sentencing in October. He is seeking to appeal his convictions.

The prosecution barrister told the court that one of the women said her childhood had been stolen, while the second said the abuse affected her every day.

In her submission to the pre-sentencing hearing, Rosemary Walsh KC outlined what she described as the "salient facts" that were heard during the course of the trial.

She also described the impact the offending had on both victims, whom were described during the trial as Complainants A and B.

She said both complainants often wondered what life would have been like if they hadn't experienced the abuse.

In her victim impact statement, Complainant A described the "profound impact" the abuse had on her.

Walsh said the complainant believed her childhood had been "stolen" and that she felt an "enormous amount of anger that is always simmering away under the surface".

Walsh said the abuse Complainant B had suffered affected her "every day and every relationship", and that she had to fight on a daily basis the wish that she would die.

The prosecution barrister also outlined further aggravating and mitigating factors.

She said, in sentencing, the youth of the victims had to be taken account, as well as the "multitude of offences", which "spanned a considerable period of time", and the fact there were two victims.

Donaldson's defence barrister Keiron Vaughan KC told the court that the 63-year-old was "of previous good character" and that there had been no offending of this type over the last 18 years.

"In that period of time, Mr Donaldson has or did achieve significant things in his life," he said.

"I readily accept that these convictions obliterate all those achievements that he has made in his life, and that's certainly something he will have to live with."

Vaughan said he acknowledged the court would impose a "lengthy custodial sentence", but that he had complete confidence that the court would treat Donaldson in the same way it would any other defendant of a similar age and in similar circumstances.

Addressing Donaldson directly, Judge Paul Ramsey said: "Mr Donaldson, I will be sentencing you as soon as I can next month."

His wife, Eleanor Donaldson, 60, faced a trial of the facts on mental health grounds, meaning she was not required to participate in the proceedings.

She was accused of five related charges, including four counts of aiding and abetting.

She was found to have done the acts of which she was accused â a verdict which she is to appeal.

Eleanor Donaldson cannot be given a prison sentence, she could, however, be given a treatment order or an absolute discharge.

She was not required to participate in the proceedings.

However, Judge Ramsey told her defence barrister Ian Turkington KC that in dealing with her, he "would like to be able to speak directly to her" and therefore requested that she appear via video link if she is deemed medically fit to do so.

News.title: Just how hot and dry was your summer? Use our postcode lookup to find out
News.content:
Where does the data come from?

This lookup uses data from the HadUK Grid dataset (opens in new tab), which is produced by the Met Office Hadley Centre. HadUK Grid is one of the main products used by scientists to monitor and research the UKâs changing climate.

The data for 2026 is provisional, with fewer observations feeding into calculations due to lags in data availability. As such, the precise values could change slightly in future as more data comes available. The historical averages are calculated over a 30-year period from 1991-2020, which matches the standard period used by the UNâs World Meteorological Organization.

The HadUK dataset displays temperature and rainfall data across a uniform grid covering the entire landmass of the UK. The data does not cover the Channel Islands. Every value on the grid is an estimate for the centre point of a 1km by 1km grid box, the most detailed climate data publicly available for the UK. The values are created using observations from land-based weather stations across the country, and by taking into account additional factors such as altitude, terrain and distance from the coast to scientifically âfill in the gapsâ between weather stations.

What do we mean by your area?

Weâve matched every active postcode in the UK to its nearest 1km by 1km grid cell in the HadUK dataset.

The results displayed for your area represent a mean average of that grid cell and the surrounding grid cells to your location. For most areas, this represents a 5km square centred on your postcode. Along irregular coastlines and on small islands, the nearest grid cells are chosen to match the shape of the coastline or island, but no cells are further than 7km away.

This approach aims to avoid sharp jumps between neighbouring locations which may occasionally arise due to uncertainties in the data, while still making use of the most detailed dataset available to capture local weather conditions across the UK's varied geography.

What does your areaâs weather data represent?

The average temperature represents the mean average of the selection of grid cells across the month or season.

The maximum temperature is the mean average of the daily maximums recorded across all nearest grid cells for the month or season; the minimum temperature is the mean average of the daily minimums.

The rainfall is the total amount of rain for the month or season, averaged across the selection of grid cells.

To calculate the number of days above the heatwave threshold, we first averaged the daily maximum temperature for each grid cell with its nearest grid cells on every day. Using the Met Officeâs heatwave thresholds (opens in new tab), we determined how many maximum daily temperatures exceeded the threshold for your location, based on the centre of your grid cell. Your areaâs heatwave threshold may be approximate if your postcode is near a county boundary.

This is not the same as the number of days spent in an official heatwave, where the threshold has to be met or exceeded for at least three consecutive days.

Acknowledgements

Methodology support from Dan Hollis, Amy Doherty and Oli Claydon, UK Met Office.

News.title: Giant veg records smashed despite 'bonkers' summer
News.content:
Seven giant vegetables are believed to have smashed Guinness World Records as competitive growers showed off their supersized produce at competition.

The provisional records were set on Friday at the National Giant Vegetables Championship, part of the Malvern Autumn Show at the Three Counties Showground in Worcestershire.

Among the potential record holders was a 26.02kg (4st 1.8lb) beetroot, a 7.808kg (1st 3.2lb) sunflower head and a cucumber plant measuring more than 7.5m (24.6ft).

The achievements came despite a challenging summer for growers, with record-breaker Graham Barratt - who presented the giant cucumber plant - describing the weather as "bonkers".

Organisers said the seven records would need to be verified, with confirmation expected on Saturday.

News.title: Council is letting staff down with fire and rehire plans, says worker
News.content:
A council worker has accused Glasgow City Council of letting staff down after it announced fire and rehire plans due to a stalemate over equal pay proposals.

The council has threatened to sack more than 23,000 members of staff and then rehire them on new contracts after negotiations broke down with unions.

The talks were about the council's plans to replace a pay system found to discriminate against mostly women workers. The changes would see the majority of staff unaffected or better off, but they would cut pay for 11% of staff.

Speaking on the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast, one worker described the situation as "heartbreaking".

Joanne, a support for learning worker from Glasgow, said the local authority "had a cheek to say they care about their employees" after she read the council's message saying it was dismissing all staff.

She was told two weeks ago that she would be one of the workers facing a pay cut under the new system, leaving her "distraught". She will lose about Â£300 per year.

She said: "I came away from my work crying - really, really upset. I couldn't believe that after 25 years' service to Glasgow City Council, I am getting let down yet again."

She continued: "I am working with the most vulnerable children in society. I would put it to Glasgow City Council: please come and do my job for one day - one day only.

"It is so wrong, and I can't afford to lose money."

News.title: Victims 'grossly failed' by sex offender bail decision
News.content:
Victims and their families were "grossly failed" by the court system that bailed a sex offender and repeatedly allowed him to return to his home overlooking the playground he targeted, London's victims' commissioner said.

Zafer Dogan, 32, of Enfield, north London, was jailed on Thursday for two years and four months for taking thousands of pictures of children and using AI software to "nudify" them.

Andrea Simon said the case showed "the justice system did not centre victims" and called for a multi-agency review.

The Ministry of Justice said while the Crown Prosecution Service had the right to challenge them, final bail decisions were "made by the independent judiciary".

The ministry added: "The protection of victims, witnesses, and the public must always be considered when deciding whether or not an offender should be released on bail."

Dogan had pleaded guilty to three counts of making indecent images of a child, which included 900 category C images, 294 category B images and 653 category A images, which are the most serious.

He also admitted possessing extreme pornography, possessing a prohibited image of a child, creating purported intimate images of an adult, obstructing a constable in the execution of their duty and a further two counts of making indecent photographs of a child.

According to the police, he had taken more than 5,000 pictures, many from his bedroom window.

Despite protests from the police and prosecutors, he had previously been bailed back to his flat, forcing one family who had fallen victim to his crimes to move into temporary accommodation.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today, Simon said: "I think victims and their families were grossly failed by the decision to allow this paedophile to return to an address where he was overlooking a playground near to his victims.

"The case [shows that] the justice system just does not centre victims. To know that the police and prosecutors opposed bail multiple times, but nevertheless, he was returned to the community, is an indication that the capacity pressures on prisons are not being balanced with the impacts that that's having on victims' lives.

"We seem to be lurching from one crisis to another, and victim safety and their rights seem to be put to one side, as the justice system struggles."

News.title: Cyber attack on police force may have 'compromised' staff information
News.content:
A cyber attack on a police force in Wales may have resulted in staff information being "accessed or compromised".

Dyfed-Powys Police said the hack had caused disruption to some non-emergency systems but no personal data relating to members of the public was believed to have been accessed.

The force said the incident was identified on 14 September, and an investigation is under way.

The Information Commissioner's Office, external (ICO) has been notified, with a spokesperson saying: "We can confirm we have received a breach report from Dyfed-Powys Police and we are assessing the information provided."

Dyfed-Powys Police said it remained fully operational and its response to emergency incidents had not been affected.

It said online and email contact services were unavailable for a period following the attack, but these had now been restored and 999 and 101 service had not been affected.

The force said it was receiving support from cyber-security specialists and its systems had been subject to "precautionary measures" while specialist teams investigated the incident and worked to restore services safely.

A spokesperson said: "At this stage, our investigation has found no evidence that members of the public's personal data has been accessed or compromised as a result of this incident.

"We are, however, continuing to investigate whether any information relating to our staff may have been accessed or compromised, and are taking all appropriate steps to protect that information, and will provide appropriate advice to colleagues if required."

They added they "understood the potential concern this may cause" and wanted to "reassure the public that we have and will continue to take all necessary steps to protect our information and maintain the security of our systems".

The force said it would provide further updates when it was in a position to do so.

The ongoing investigation is being managed by Tarian, the Regional Organised Crime Unit (ROCU) for southern Wales, and force systems are being monitored.

The IOC spokesperson said anyone worried about their personal information can visit the ICO website for advice and support.

"We advise checking regularly for updates from the organisation impacted and following their advice if they confirm that an individual's personal information has been compromised," they added.

The area served by Dyfed-Powys Police includes Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion, Pembrokeshire and Powys, and equates to more than 500,000 people - a number that rises significantly with tourists each year.

The force has 1,349 police officers, as well as 1,063 police staff, police community support officers (PCSO) and special constables, according to an information request in March 2026.

News.title: No action taken against Iranian man who tried to enter nuclear base
News.content:
No action is to be taken against an Iranian man who tried to enter the Faslane nuclear submarine base earlier this year.

The 34-year-old was arrested at HM Naval Base Clyde near Helensburgh, Argyll and Bute, on 19 March, along with a 31-year-old Romanian woman.

The Crown Office said it had carefully considered the case and decided there should be no further proceedings against the man.

It had previously said in March that no proceedings would be brought against the Romanian woman.

News.title: Mum's heartbreak over LA killing and granddaughter's location
News.content:
The mother of a Scottish law graduate killed in Los Angeles says the lack of information from US authorities since her daughter's death has been heartbreaking.

June Bunyan's dismembered body was found in her apartment in September last year.

Her husband Jonathan Renteria has been charged with murder, mutilation and child cruelty. He has pleaded not guilty.

Jill Bunyan, June's mum, says she is in legal limbo and is still not certain who is caring for her baby granddaughter.

News.title: Men charged over £10m village ketamine haul
News.content:
Three men have been charged after police seized what is believed to be the UK's second-largest haul of ketamine.

West Yorkshire Police said 500kg (1,102lb) of the drug, worth an estimated Â£10m, was found at a property on Rose Avenue in the the Upton area of Pontefract. The largest find was worth an estimated Â£17m and was found in Merseyside in 2025.

The force said 20 black bin bags were found during the West Yorkshire operation, led by the Regional Organised Crime Unit.

Curtis Binns, 32, Paul Turner, 40, both from Upton and Christopher Willis, 42, from Wolverhampton, have been charged with drugs offences and are due to appear at Leeds Magistrates' Court later.

Police said Binns, 32, of Sunny Avenue, had been charged with possession of a Class B drug with intent to supply and money laundering.

Turner, of Common Lane, had been charged with possession of a Class B drug with intent to supply while Willis had been charged with supplying a Class B drug.

Ketamine is commonly used as a horse tranquiliser.

When abused, the drug can cause serious health problems including permanent bladder damage that can require lifelong treatment.

News.title: One person taken to hospital after barracks fire
News.content:
A person has been taken to hospital after a fire broke out in an accommodation block at Catterick Garrison military barracks.

North Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service said multiple crews were sent at 19:48 BST on Thursday where the blaze was found to be "well alight".

The service said the person was taken to hospital with smoke inhalation while fire crews remained on scene until 02:43 BST.

It said on-site personnel kept a watching brief overnight and a fire investigation was due to take place.

Sir Elton John, Charli XCX and Troye Sivan are set to perform at London's new Apple Music Hall.

Apple confirmed the opening of the state-of-the-art live performance space, located within Battersea Power Station, earlier this week.

Accommodating up to 600 people, the venue opens on Monday, 28 September, with Sir Elton performing on its launch night.

A total of seven further events will run at the space until December, featuring Baby Keem on 2 October, Skye Newman on 7 October and Troye Sivan on 13 October.

They will be followed by Arlo Parks on 22 October, Burna Boy on 29 October, Chase and Status on 26 November, and Charli on 2 December.

Apple said the venue has been designed intentionally to “close the gap between intimacy and production value and allow for an unprecedented level of creative control”.

open image in gallery Apple Music Hall in Battersea Power Station ( Apple Music/AP )

It said: “Every seat feels close to the performer, yet the infrastructure offers what an artist requires for an arena tour, with a 38ft-wide stage that can be reconfigured for traditional front-facing sets or more in-the-round experiences.”

The venue is also equipped with a 48-speaker spatial sound system positioned all around the audience, so when an artist performs in spatial it allows fans to hear that performance in an “immersive environment”.

Apple has also partnered with independent UK promoter Communion One to support bookings and promotion for Apple Music Hall.

Communion One managing director Mazin Tappuni said: “Apple Music Hall is a fantastic venue, like nothing fans will have ever seen before. The production quality is world class, livestreaming to fans across the world, from a live room where every square foot has the artist and their fans in mind.”

Live events at Apple Music Hall will be powered by UK founded ticketing platform Dice which Apple said was “committed to fair and innovative solutions for fans to access their favourite shows”.

open image in gallery Sir Elton John and Charli XCX are set to perform at London's new Apple Music Hall ( Getty )

Dice chief commercial officer Andrew Foggin said: “The thought and attention to detail that has gone into every aspect of the venue is clear to see, and is in total alignment with our ethos of ensuring fans have the best possible experience when discovering and attending shows.”

Performances at Apple Music Hall will be livestreamed globally so fans outside London can tune in to the one-time-only shows.

Tickets for the first three shows go on sale at 9am on Monday, 28 September. Visit applemusichall.com for more details.

News.title: Princess Kate hosts secret tea party for Three Peaks Challenge participants
News.content:
The Princess of Wales invited fellow Three Peaks Challenge adventurers for tea at Windsor Castle.

Kate previously completed the challenge in a surprise feat of endurance to raise money for the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity and “explore life beyond diagnosis”.

The princess, who announced in January 2025 she was in remission from cancer, is captured in a social media video posted Friday (25 September) sitting down with her guests including 11-year-old Ted Haslam, a wheelchair user who also completed the challenge.

In a written message accompanying the post, the Princess of Wales said: “Listening to their experiences of the challenge and their reasons for taking it on was a powerful reminder that recovery is rarely a journey we make alone, and of the importance of the people who walk alongside us along the way.”

Ed Sheeran’s shows at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been canceled, The Independent has confirmed.

The concerts were scheduled to take place this evening and Saturday at the home of Robert Kraft’s New England Patriots.

Staff at the stadium told The Independent the concert had been canceled due to bad weather as a huge nor’easter storm approaches the area.

The news comes amid major controversy surrounding Sheeran’s ongoing U.S. tour.

Earlier this month, rapper Macklemore announced he had been fired as the British singer-songwriter’s support act over his pro-Palestine comments at an earlier concert. The “Thrift Shop” musician claimed that billionaire Kraft — who owns Gillette Stadium — personally called Sheeran to say he would not be allowed to perform at the venue.

open image in gallery Ed Sheeran’s shows at Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium have been canceled due to bad weather conditions ( Getty Images for iHeartRadio )

open image in gallery Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft is central to the controversy surrounding Ed Sheeran’s tour as he called the singer personally to tell him that Macklemore would not be allowed to play at his venue ( Getty )

Sheeran later responded by stating he would not be drawn into a public debate about the Gaza war and that it was “the promoter’s decision” to remove Macklemore.

The fallout continued when Sheeran’s other opening acts withdrew, while protesters gathered outside his first solo concert last week.

During that show, Sheeran broke down in tears while reading a prepared statement from an autocue, declaring: “I’ve had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes. I’m so, so sorry. I don’t want to disappoint fans. I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore.

“What happened in Israel, and at the music festival on October 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate. My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilian loss and loss of children’s lives. And the systemic injustice we’re seeing unfolding in the West Bank cannot be overlooked.”

He also said that he went ahead with the show despite backlash and the exodus of his opening acts to honour his commitment to his fans, adding that it is “completely central to who” he is.

open image in gallery Macklemore said Kraft called Sheeran personally to inform him that he would not be allowed to play at Gillette Stadium over his pro-Palestine comments ( AFP/Getty )

Following his dismissal, Macklemore challenged Kraft to match his $1 million donation to organizations aiding Palestinians, saying: “Whatever we disagree about, perhaps we can agree on this: Palestinian lives are worth protecting. A Palestinian life is no less valuable than any other life on this earth.”

Kraft later responded in a statement shared to X, suggesting he was doubling Macklemore’s donation.

“I have dedicated much of my life to building bridges between all people,” Kraft wrote. “I believe deeply that all lives are worth protecting. Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid the region in fighting this humanitarian crisis.

“Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges.”

The cancellation of the Massachusetts concerts — which were to be held just outside Boston — comes as a nor’easter is set to slam the East Coast over the weekend, dumping heavy rain and unleashing hurricane-force winds on residents living in North Carolina all the way up to Maine.

“This storm may be remembered for its destructive coastal flooding and severe beach erosion, especially along eastern Long Island and the Massachusetts coast,” AccuWeather Chief Meteorologist Jon Porter said.

Strong wind gusts topping 40 mph from North Carolina to New York are pushing ocean and bay waters toward shore, and meteorologists say flooding will be at its worst through Friday in the mid-Atlantic region.

Some urban areas like Boston may even see flash flooding, forecasters warned.

California crews working on an infrastructure project were surprised this month when they uncovered the fossilized bones of a large, hoofed mammal that walked the region’s ancient floodplains over 40 million years ago.

The bones include several ribs, a femur and other limb bones and fragments that could have belonged to a brontothere, which is also known as a “thunder beast,” according to paleontologist Dr. Joseph El Adli, who made the discovery during routine monitoring of the a City of Oceanside project.

Leaf-eating brontotheres rivaled an elephant in size and often carried a Y-shaped horn on its nose, the city noted Wednesday.

Alternatively, Adli believes the bones could also be from an herbivorous amynodont: a hornless, hippo-shaped “swamp rhino” that had tusks where its canine teeth should be.

Both North American species come from the order Perissodactyla, which are “odd-toed” hoofed mammals. An order groups together closely related animal families.

open image in gallery Southern California crews just uncovered bones that could be from this ancient mammal ( Roger Witter/NPS )

The workers found the fossils 12 feet deep in the Santiago Formation, a layer of thick rock strewn across northwestern San Diego County.

The formation dates back to the Eocene, which refers to the epoch after the dinosaurs, when mammals were evolving into large forms.

Previous fossils in the city have been dated to the same time.

“Based on the known age of the surrounding rock and the types of organisms found within the unit, paleontologists estimate that the fossils are between 40 and 45 million years old, falling within the Uintan North American Land Mammal Age,” the city said in a news release.

open image in gallery Workers found the fossils 12 feet deep, and the findings included a femur and other limb bones ( City of Oceanside - Government/Facebook )

The bones were exposed from beneath several tons of mudstone over a week before they were placed in a plaster field jacket for safe transportion to an off-site, climate-controlled laboratory.

The bones will be removed from the plaster jacket, cleaned, hardened using museum-grade glues and resins and studied over the coming weeks, before they are sent to a museum.

“Further examination of the bones once they have been fully removed from the rock that encases them should allow paleontologists to narrow down the precise identity of the Oceanside fossil discovery,” the city noted.

open image in gallery The bones will be removed from the plaster jacket and rock encasing them and then hardened using glues and resin ( City of Oceanside - Government/Facebook )

Workers are also looking for more bones - including a skull - that could help determine what exactly they came from.

Several blocks are still closed, according to the city. The location of the find is not being shared to safeguard the integrity of the site.

Bronotheres and amynodonts have previously been found throughout North America, including Oregon’s Hancock Mammal Quarry. Skulls from the mammals are on display at the John Day Fossil Beds National Monument visitor center in Kimberly.

President Donald Trump said on Friday morning that Chinese leader Xi Jinping agrees with him about renaming AI to “super intelligence.”

The president posted on Truth Social the day after he hosted Xi for a state dinner at the White House.

“Very productive meeting with President Xi for both the U.S.A. and China,” the president wrote. “Tremendous things will be happening. Like almost everyone else, he seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named Artificial Intelligence to a far more accurate and important name, SUPER INTELLIGENCE. That would be ‘SUPER!’”

Trump has thus far rebuffed calls for Congress to place new regulations on AI, saying, “The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades.”

In response, Trump has attempted to rebrand AI as “super intelligence,” instructing the State Department to rebrand AI under the new banner and that artificial intelligence be referred to as “super intelligence” or SI in all government documents and posts.

During the official visit, Xi seemed to take a more cautious tone to AI than Trump, saying in his initial public address said that the United States and the People’s Republic of China “have the capability and responsibility to develop AI for good, and ensure that AI is always under human control, and serves the well-being of the people.”

open image in gallery President Donald Trump said that China’s President Xi Jinping agrees with him about renaming AI ‘Super Inteligence’ ( AP )

Numerous executives of AI and technology companies attended the state dinner on Thursday evening, including NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman, Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos.

The president has taken a relatively lax approach to AI regulation. He enlisted venture capitalist David Sacks to serve as chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

Some Republicans expressed concern about the coziness with technology companies.

“Maybe they'd like to come over here and testify while they're here,” Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), a critic of the technology industry, told reporters before the dinner on Thursday.

But it comes at a time when many Americans and people across the globe have raised the alarm about the risks AI poses. On Thursday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that an autonomous artificial agent created by OpenAI hacked a government website that contained the health information of Australians.

Albanese said when the agent sought information from the country’s portfal for Medicare, the nation’s health insurance program, and was refused, “it effectively hacked into that medical portal and got that information anyway.”

open image in gallery NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was one of many technology CEOs at the state dinner on Thursday ( AP )

In addition, earlier this month, Jacob Coxon, a former AI researcher at Anthropic, raised alarms when he announced his resignation, saying “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

The president has responded by saying that such alarms are overblown and said, “This is more of a Hoax than even that of RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA, UKRAINE, UKRAINE, UKRAINE, UKRAINE, and Climate Change!”

But some have flagged that “super intelligence” already has a sinister definition meaning AI that could actually surpass human intelligence.

The president and many Republicans argue that the United States should not attempt to restrain AI lest the United States lose the arms race to China.

Still, many Americans, including many of the president’s supporters, fear the risks AI poses and many oppose the construction of data centers that power AI because of the increased electricity costs, the risks to water the noise associated with them.

A civil rights organization has filed a lawsuit against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Los Angeles today, seeking the release of official agency records concerning the deployment of the WRAP, a full-body restraint system used on detainees in immigration custody and during transport and removal operations.

Informally called "the burrito" or "the bag," the WRAP is repeatedly used on immigrants during long deportation flights and for extended periods, according to the American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California.

open image in gallery Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents detain a man as part of a Targeted Enforcement Operation in the Corona neighborhood of the Queens borough of New York City ( Reuters )

"Individuals subjected to the device have reported difficulty breathing, chest pressure, loss of sensation and serious injuries, while medical and use-of-force experts have warned that prolonged or improper use of full-body restraints can create significant risks of positional asphyxia, circulatory distress and death," states the lawsuit filed in Los Angeles federal court.

The ACLU asserts that accounts indicate ICE staff have employed the WRAP as a form of punishment for undocumented people who spoke out against their deportation or tried to contact legal counsel.

Such reports "are particularly troubling given longstanding questions about the policies and safeguards" regulating ICE's deployment of the equipment, according to the court complaint.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump seen with his advisor, Stephen Miller, largely seen as the architect of the administration’s immigration policy ( Reuters )

A message seeking comment sent to ICE was not immediately answered after standard business hours.

In November 2024, as part of its annual report to Congress, the Department of Homeland Security's civil rights oversight office opened a complaint alleging ICE "inappropriately" used the WRAP and failed to operate the equipment in accordance with manufacturer guidelines, "which caused breathing difficulty and pain, failed to consider medical and psychological conditions prior to use and lacked sufficient monitoring," according to the 21-page legal filing.

The ACLU also maintains that the current ICE Air Operations Handbook "provides little substantive guidance concerning when, how or under what safeguards the device may be deployed."

The lawsuit, brought under the Freedom of Information Act, seeks agency records to clarify the scope and manner of ICE's use of the WRAP, the operational standards governing its deployment, and official oversight regarding safety and legal compliance.

open image in gallery Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents walk outside the Ventura County Government Center in Ventura, California, on July 27 ( AFP/Getty )

"The requested records are necessary to evaluate whether ICE's practices comport with constitutional requirements, medically accepted standards and the agency's own policies and obligations," the ACLU stated.

When deployed during deportation operations, detainees were immobilized for long stretches in poses creating heightened risks of breathing difficulties and circulatory complications, the lawsuit alleges, noting medical experts have warned that extended restraint in seated or forward-leaning positions increases asphyxiation risks, particularly for individuals with heart or lung conditions.

"Individuals described an inability to breathe, chest pressure and loss of sensation while restrained," the suit says.

The lawsuit notes an October 2025 report in which the Associated Press identified 12 fatal incidents over the past decade "where local police or jailers around the U.S. used the WRAP and autopsies determined `restraint' played a role in the death."

As the U.S.-created Board of Peace moves forward with plans to rebuild Gaza, it has publicly stated there is no future role for the U.N. agency that has provided support to displaced Palestinians for decades.

However, the former head of the organization says that behind closed doors, board members and other representatives have demonstrated greater willingness to engage with the agency than public statements suggest.

Israel has sought the removal of the agency, known as UNRWA, from Gaza, repeatedly claiming that it has been infiltrated by Hamas militants.

The International Court of Justice has noted that these claims have not been substantiated.

Despite this stance, UNRWA remains the primary aid distributor in the territory, maintaining an essential role in delivering health and educational services.

Philippe Lazzarini, who headed UNRWA until earlier this year, said in his first interview since stepping down that members of the Palestinian technocratic committee have expressed a desire to work alongside the agency.

Minutes from meetings obtained by another U.N. official confirm that UNRWA and the committee have held discussions regarding joint efforts in Gaza.

A Board of Peace official confirmed that representatives from the board have met on several occasions with UNRWA leadership.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

While the organization's overarching mandate in its current form is coming to an end, its operations "may persist if they are serving Gazans well," the official added, speaking on the condition of anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the media.

Israel's Foreign Ministry offered no comment on the matter.

Nearly a year after the ceasefire, reconstruction work in Gaza has not begun.

Israel continues to deny entry to the Palestinian committee designated by the Board of Peace to govern the strip, insisting that Hamas must disarm first.

The committee maintains that it requires physical access to the territory to execute its plans.

This standing dynamic leaves UNRWA on the ground in Gaza with an operational staff significantly larger than any other U.N. entity or non-governmental organization.

Although Israeli military action impacted the agency's ability to coordinate the entrance and distribution of aid, its core services have persisted.

"They want to get rid of the agency, but on the other hand they know that if you get completely rid of the agency today, it might have a further ... devastating impact on the population," said Lazzarini, whose last day in office was March 31.

Lazzarini noted that UNRWA supports approximately half of Gaza's public health system.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

The agency retains roughly 11,000 Palestinian employees in Gaza. According to UNRWA, these workers conduct around 14,000 medical consultations daily, operate waste and water management infrastructure for more than a million people, run math and digital literacy classes for over 280,000 children, and manage temporary learning centers for 60,000 more.

Emphasizing the necessity of field staff for aid delivery, Lazzarini noted, "If you want the vaccine to end up in the mouths of the children, you still need the workforce, the presence of an agency like ours."

In public announcements, UNRWA has been excluded from the Board of Peace's strategies for Gaza. During a briefing to the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, board officials cited various U.N. entities as partners, omitting UNRWA.

However, Lazzarini stated that the Palestinian committee expected to govern Gaza has privately acknowledged UNRWA's necessary role in planning.

Two senior U.N. officials alongside the board official confirmed that the board has met multiple times with UNRWA following the ceasefire agreement.

Speaking anonymously because they were not authorized to brief reporters, the officials verified at least three meetings between UNRWA representatives and the Palestinian committee this year, including two held during Lazzarini's leadership.

Shortly before finishing his tenure, Lazzarini spoke with Ali Shaath, the head of the Palestinian committee.

"Basically, he said, ‘I don’t know how I can succeed without you’," Lazzarini said. Neither Shaath nor a committee spokesperson responded to requests for comment.

An internal U.N. summary of a January 26 meeting in Cairo, conducted without UNRWA present, stated that Shaath praised the agency, expressed a clear intent to see its operations restored, and noted that the committee's governing apparatus would rely heavily on its work.

A senior U.N. official added that the Tony Blair Institute, a partner of the Board of Peace, sought assistance from UNRWA and held discussions with its staff. In response, the institute stated that it collaborates with various U.N. entities and non-governmental organizations in Gaza "to understand the situation on the ground, the needs of the population and the practical requirements for improving conditions."

At a donor conference for UNRWA on June 30, the agency's current acting head, Christian Saunders, described the organization as "vital" to the board's efforts to implement the ceasefire framework.

Conversely, the Board of Peace representative offered a different characterization, stating that the meetings were aimed at reviewing UNRWA's operations to structure programs that are "far more efficient and accountable."

"UNRWA’s days are over," the official remarked, adding that personnel "will remain if they pass vetting and are delivering on their mandate and not advancing ideology or Hamas interests."

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

Lazzarini characterized the situation as an "absurd contradiction" where the Board of Peace disavows UNRWA while U.N. member nations "expect it to deliver."

"We continue to emphasize that UNRWA is indispensable," Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi told reporters on Thursday, following a meeting of over 50 nations regarding the agency at U.N. headquarters.

UNRWA was originally established to assist Palestinians who fled or were expelled during the 1948 war surrounding the creation of Israel.

In January 2024, Israel asserted without providing public documentation that hundreds of agency staff were members of militant groups and that over a dozen took part in the October 7 attack.

Lazzarini noted that he was never provided written evidence to support the claims despite requests made to Israel and member nations, but stated he does not regret terminating the accused personnel.

"I did because it was in the best interest of the agency and the population we were helping," Lazzarini said, adding that he subsequently experienced "extraordinary vicious, heinous attacks on social media" and was confronted directly on the street "in Geneva and in New York" by "pro-Israeli groups."

Reflecting on his experiences during the conflict, he recalled accounts from Palestinians released from Israeli custody who described being required to wear diapers in detention and spending days sitting in their own waste. He also described meeting a displaced father in a school yard with four children who slept with his shoes near his head to prepare for rapid evacuation during shelling.

His book, "A Witness to Gaza: What Cannot Be Erased," is set to be published in French in October, with an English edition planned afterward.

News.content:
