Sports.title: Top European leagues heighten pressure on Infantino with call for major changes at Fifa
Sports.content:
The Premier League has joined forces with La Liga, Serie A and the Bundesliga to call for urgent governance reform at Fifa after the World Cup sell-off debacle (FFE) as Gianni Infantino prepares to seek a fourth term as president.

Their strongly worded statement is the latest indication that Infantino’s willingness to hold an external governance review does not go far enough, after the Guardian revealed that several Fifa Council members had rejected that proposal.

In a thinly veiled attack on Infantino the four biggest European leagues accused the Fifa president of promoting “exploitative ideas” which threaten the foundations of the global game. They also reference the Folarin Balogun affair by calling for more checks and balances to ensure that “individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference”.

There has been considerable tension between the leading European leagues and Fifa for some time, particularly over the increasingly congested match calendar, which has been exacerbated by the development of new competitions such as the Club World Cup.

The lobby group European Leagues filed a legal complaint to the European Commission against Fifa two years ago, accusing it of abusive practices, which has since been extended to include the women’s game.

“Football’s longstanding foundations have, in recent years, been threatened by a fundamental governance problem, whereby Fifa’s president has actively promoted exploitative ideas rather than safeguarding against them,” the statement read. “And while football’s stakeholders ultimately forced the withdrawal of the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, the conditions that led to FFE remain.

“The Fifa president has now acknowledged the need for reform, but it is not enough for surface-level, process changes to be explored in the aftermath of FFE. Fundamental governance reform is essential to restore clear constitutional boundaries within Fifa, including confidence that individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference.

“The future of Fifa matters to everyone who cares about football, because our sport cannot grow globally if its foundations are undermined.”

In addition to condemning Infantino the leagues also called for three governance changes to be endorsed by the next president: the creation of a permanent decision-making body within Fifa including representatives of national associations, leagues, clubs and players; a commitment to publish the reasoning behind major decisions in advance; and the separation of Fifa’s regulatory functions from its commercial operations.

A Fifa governance that concentrates unchecked regulatory, commercial and political power in a single office, while relegating affected stakeholders to mere advisory status, is not fit for purpose,” the statement added.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“At this crucial time for our sport, we encourage candidates for the Fifa presidency to endorse these principles and, within the first 100 days of the next presidential mandate, to convene an independently chaired governance convention representing member associations and the wider football community, mandated to report publicly within six months.

“All candidates for the Fifa presidency should publish their own reform programme, debate its contents and adhere to fair election rules. Fifa’s financial, legal, communications and marketing resources, as well as its football development funds, must remain strictly neutral and never create an electoral advantage for any candidate.”

The deadline for presidential candidates declaring their intention to stand is 18 November, before the election in March.

Infantino is the only declaration to date, with the Guardian reporting this week that there are growing concerns within European football that he will end up being re-elected unopposed.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino regrets not being ‘more involved’ with Balogun decision
Sports.content:
US men’s national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino says he regrets not being “more involved” in the situation surrounding US forward Folarin Balogun at this summer’s World Cup.

Balogun was given a red card after a challenge against Bosnia and Herzegovina defender Tarik Muharemović, which by rule is accompanied with a one-game suspension. Balogun’s ban for the next game against Belgium was suspended after the US Soccer Federation and US president Donald Trump lobbied Fifa, with Trump saying that he personally placed a call to Fifa president Gianni Infantino to ask the ruling be reviewed. Infantino maintains that the decision to reinstate Balogun was made independently by Fifa’s disciplinary committee.

The entire affair cast a pall over what had been an otherwise positive tournament for the US to that point. Belgium’s players and coaches said in the wake of it that it provided extra motivation ahead of the match. Balogun himself later spoke of having felt uncomfortable with the attention the situation placed upon him.

Speaking with broadcaster Andrés Cantor, Pochettino said he was not involved in the decision – though in retrospect, he may have preferred to be.

“Maybe I regret not having been more involved,” Pochettino said in the Spanish-language interview for Fútbol de Primera. “In the situation that later generated all of the negativity afterwards. Maybe I regret not having been more inside of that decision making process. I wasn’t involved in that decision, to overturn the red card. As a football person, I understand everything … Beyond whether we were right or not [about the call on the field], I think nobody understood how it happened.”

The US were thoroughly outclassed by Belgium in the 4-1 loss, beaten badly in every phase of play. In his remarks to Cantor, Pochettino suggested that the backlash surrounding the Balogun situation actively contributed to the loss.

“As a football person,” said Pochettino, “where many times we have that emotional intelligence – [we know] that energy can change things. I think that energy changed the minute that happened. And by then, the game is played under different parameters, and that match was never a match where I believe the tactics, strategy, or selection of players would have changed the course of what happened during the game.”

Pochettino also suggested that the group who participated in US Soccer’s efforts to get Balogun on the field against Belgium may have been too large for his liking.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“That’s something we’ve talked about internally,” said Pochettino. “I think that these types of things have to be managed under a much more limited structure, a structure where decisions have to be made by very few people, where very few people manage these types of things. [Those decisions] should be strictly sporting and common sense, beyond whether a rule or a committee can say one thing or another.”

Pochettino’s USMNT will face Peru in Orlando on Saturday before facing Chile, Mexico and Canada across the rest of this extended international window.

Sports.title: De la Fuente brings insatiable Spain to England knowing World Cup is not enough
Sports.content:
“I’m going to tell you a story,” Luis de la Fuente said. “As soon as the game finished on 19 July, before anyone had cooled down at all, just two or three minutes after the final, one of the players – and you’ll have to forgive me for not telling you which one, but it was one of those who has been with us for the longest time – came up to me and said: ‘Mister, now what? What’s left to win?’ And I said: ‘Bloody hell, the game against England at Wembley on 26 September.’”

It was a Friday afternoon at Las Rozas and Spain’s coach had just named his first squad since that day in New Jersey. It was a familiar one, full of history makers. Of the 26 from the World Cup, only four had been left out and there was an explanation for each: Marcos Llorente has announced his international retirement; Joan García is injured; Borja Iglesias, who always felt the likeliest to leave first, is not fully fit; and Gavi is suspended for Wembley, although he could have faced Croatia and Czechia.

Fermín López is back after missing the World Cup through injury and is joined in the squad by Josep Martínez, Dean Huijsen and Roberto Fernández. Pedro Porro then pulled out, replaced by Iván Fresneda.

“How could there not be continuity with players who are champions of everything?” De la Fuente asked. Well, of course. It is not even as if the season has been going long enough for anyone else to make a claim on a place, although there were three strong candidates for that spare striker’s role, Sergio Camello and Carlos Espí competing with Espanyol’s Fernández. There certainly hadn’t been time for anyone to build a case stronger than those who came back from the US with the trophy. All the more so with De la Fuente, loyal to his players and making a virtue of continuity.

Even the new face in the squad, the Inter goalkeeper Martínez, has been here before. In fact, officially he has a cap, from when Spain’s under-21s – managed by De la Fuente – stepped in for the senior side just before the pandemic-postponed Euros in the summer of 2021. And when he was questioned about Unai Simón potentially losing his status as No 1, he replied: “Unai was recognised as the best goalkeeper at the World Cup, he broke every record, etc. Maybe, just maybe, he has to be given some continuity.”

View image in fullscreen Such is the bond between Luis de la Fuente and his players that Marc Cucurella has his face tattooed on his arm. Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty Images

Which is not to say there will not be changes of personnel at some point, the Spain coach says. There are plenty of players “knocking at the door”, he explained, before saying it was up to them to walk through the door and into the house. For now, though, there is little new to say or to see, naturally enough. A status report on Spain as they arrive at Wembley could pretty much be reduced to four words: yep, still world champions.

But that’s the point. They are still European champions too. Oh, and they have won the Nations League. At grounds around Spain, although not at the Camp Nou, which eight of the squad call home, supporters have paid homage to the champions. In their own small towns all across the country, footballers have been feted. Ferran Torres threw the first pitch at Yankee Stadium and appeared on just about every TV show in the US. His image, celebrating the winner at the MetLife, is plastered on the wall by the dressing room at their Las Rozas HQ. They will walk out at Wembley with an extra star on their shirt; those stars have already been added to badges all around Spain’s HQ.

They should enjoy this – and there is a genuine sense of occasion at going to Wembley for their first game as world champions, as if that were part of the celebrations too – but they go there to compete as well. That at least is the intention, and the challenge. In a way, they are being invited to forget the unforgettable, not just at the Euros in two years’ time but now. The coach admitted he does not like this new international break comprising four games in 11 days, but whereas others may not take the Nations League so seriously, he does like it, does want to win it. The Nations League was the beginning of a new Spain era after all, the first trophy – won in 2023 – for a generation that had always lived eclipsed by their predecessors. When they reached their second final in June 2025 and lost it, on penalties to Portugal, it hurt.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Spain’s players, including their captain, Rodri, met fans at their final training session before leaving for England. Photograph: Dennis Agyeman/AFP7/Shutterstock

Spain may be world and European champions, reason to relax, but they perhaps uniquely still have an objective: if they are to match that generation, they have one more major tournament to win. Besides, De la Fuente says, competing is just what they do. The word he keeps using is “insatiable”. He means them, but it fits him too.

He joined the Spain setup 13 years ago on a three-month contract with the under-19s for the Euros. He had been unemployed for more than a year. He took over the senior side in 2022, having been a European champion at under-19 and under-21 level, and has reached every final. This week his contract was extended to 2032: not reward for services rendered, but services pending, those two things coming together in a conversation in New Jersey.

“This team won’t stop; it wants more and more, to be the best,” De la Fuente said. “I will tell them that too. What we did at the World Cup is not enough to keep us winning games or to beat England. You have to be better. That’s our culture and our mentality, our attitude, so I have no doubts and no worries. We know Spain are the team to beat, we know that it makes things harder, but it motivates us and we’re ready for it. Success is not winning; it is being in a position where you can win. And I would back these players, always. You can follow them to the end of the world.”

Sports.title: Pocognoli deserves time but Scottish FA must also prove their credentials
Sports.content:
If time is the commodity most cherished by a manager, Sébastien Pocognoli’s decision to lead Scotland is no surprise. Host nation status for Euro 2028 means it will be exceptionally difficult for them not to qualify for the tournament.

In the Nations League, starting on Saturday in Slovenia, Pocognoli can experiment without fear of serious consequence. The 39-year-old has taken over a national team that represents a country which had not only – and partly unfairly – grown weary of Steve Clarke but screamed for a brave new dawn. The public wants what the public gets. They are unlikely to turn on Pocognoli, even if the start to his international management career proves bumpy. The Belgian has cannily called up a batch of untried and young players for his opening set of fixtures. Not all will be cut out for international football – Clarke’s mainstays remain crucial – yet the head coach will gain kudos for giving opportunity. An improvement in talent identification, including sourcing more players who qualify for Scotland through family bloodlines, is now a priority. Pocognoli’s salary, understood to be seven figures at base level, underlines the Scottish Football Association’s sense that they have sourced a difference maker from the out-of-work market.

After a playing career spent mostly in his native Belgium. Pocognoli was central to a European football fairytale. The Union Saint-Gilloise title win in 2025 was their first in nine decades. USG’s fortunes had been transformed after the involvement of Tony Bloom and his favoured analytics tool, Jamestown. While it would be unjust to dismiss the influence of Pocognoli, an underlying theme where Bloom’s secret sauce is prominent is that the overall system may be more relevant than the individual in the dugout. Key decisions, including tactical style, at USG were made by the sporting director.

Craig Mulholland has been appointed as the Scottish FA’s chief football officer with a role as varied as the title is vague. After background roles at Rangers and Nottingham Forest, Mulholland’s credentials for this post are questionable. Somebody from another country may have marked Scottish football’s homework differently. Mulholland talks the talk. The rest remains to be seen.

Alongside urging Scottish clubs to field more homegrown youngsters – he is destined to have varying results on that front – and hiring a batch of underwhelming age-group coaches, Mulholland has been at Pocognoli’s side since his August appointment. Mulholland spoke of data as central to the manager search, having employed a sports intelligence agency not only to assist with that but to present to clubs at a recent summit. As Pocognoli will attest, analytics cannot prevail via half measures.

Mulholland’s assertion that “people doing an international job for the first time are more successful than those doing it for the second time” was striking. This lacked appropriate context. Luis de la Fuente, Gareth Southgate and Didier Deschamps inherited outstanding players despite technically being rookies. It also missed the point; Scotland have become regular tournament participants. What the country needs is a coach who can negotiate the brick wall hit by Clarke at two European Championships and a World Cup.

View image in fullscreen Scott McKenna reacts to Vinícius Júnior’s goal for Brazil, which in effect ended Scotland’s disappointing 2026 World Cup. Photograph: Marta Lavandier/AP

For Pocognoli, this is a shot at redemption. His post-USG stint at Monaco lasted only 38 games before he was sacked. The period was not entirely disastrous, with Pocognoli guiding the team to the Champions League’s knockout phase. At both clubs, his development of young players has been praised. Scotland hope the skill is transferable during short international periods.

Pocognoli’s strength, which may well translate successfully to the international game, was in coaching. He is likable, honourable and will take senior players with him. The group have enjoyed the intensity of sessions and clarity of message during a camp in La Manga this week. “The basic principle is to attack together and squeeze the pitch,” Pocognoli says. “When we need to defend, we have to defend like brothers. When we lose the ball, we try to regain it as soon as possible. That for me is the base.”

Pocognoli is without Scott McTominay for this Nations League window as the midfielder recovers from a heart procedure. Scotland remain weak in the goalkeeping and centre-back departments. Much stock is being placed on Oli McBurnie seizing an international second chance. Pocognoli’s typical formation is 3-4-3.

Clarke embarrassed the Scottish FA during a recent dinner appearance in Edinburgh, where comments about strong-arming his employers into handing him a four-year contract before the World Cup were made public. The episode did not reflect well on Clarke either, albeit football people looking out for themselves is hardly a new concept.

Ian Maxwell, the Scottish FA’s chief executive, purred about evolution when introducing Pocognoli. “I think in a lot of aspects, Scottish football needs to modernise itself,” he said. “We need to think differently about how we do things across a range of areas”. It was impossible to take this sentiment seriously given Maxwell’s haughty dismissal of those who questioned whether the Clarke extension was wise. Within months, the message was one of change. Maxwell, suddenly an advocate of innovation, has been in office since 2018.

Pocognoli’s unveiling was overshadowed by the Scottish FA belatedly getting around to publicly withdrawing support for Gianni Infantino continuing as Fifa president. This was clumsy, as in keeping with so much that happened before and during a miserable World Cup. Mike Mulraney, the Scottish FA’s president and the head of Fifa’s finance committee, remains conspicuous by his silence. Pocognoli has been hired by unconvincing people.

Scotland’s last trip to Ljubljana, in 2017, concluded with failure to reach the following year’s World Cup confirmed and Gordon Strachan using genetic limitations as a feeble excuse for his own shortcomings. The majority of the intervening years, seven of them under Clarke, have seen Scotland become a relevant international force once more. Whether Pocognoli can build on that foundation or leave supporters believing they should have been careful what to wish for will be a subject of great intrigue.

Sports.title: Kieron Dyer making waves at Southend after leaving ‘hooligan’ days and ‘deathbed’ behind
Sports.content:
Kieron Dyer is recounting a tale from his time in Japan at the 2002 World Cup. “You have a lot of time on your hands,” he begins from behind his desk at Southend United’s training ground.

Dyer, a chess fan, was looking for an opponent in the England squad. “Sol Campbell was a deep thinker, and I asked if he played. He said yes, and I told him I’d pummel him. I’m not joking, we played for an hour and he’d moved two pieces. If that was how much he was thinking so early …” Dyer belly laughs. “I was like: ‘Sol, I’m not sitting here for five hours playing chess with you, mate!’”

Dyer admits he lost to Campbell by default. He then speaks proudly of his youth playing chess at school, at Boys’ Brigade and for Suffolk: “The only person I couldn’t beat was Mr Sharples – if you’re reading, I want a rematch.” His rating on Chess.com – the app “everyone who plays is on” – is an impressive 1380 and he is trying to find Arsenal’s Eberechi Eze on it.

Kieron Dyer on his love of chess – and why he lost to Sol Campbell at the 2002 World Cup

Chess is an unexpected passion, another layer peeled back and more proof that public perception and real-life personality can be far removed. Young Dyer had a well-earned reputation for being party-prone, hitting headlines for, among other things, holidaying in Ayia Napa and high-stakes gambling on England trips.

“Twenty-year-old Kieron Dyer was a hooligan. Let’s not get it wrong,” he says in a brutally honest self-appraisal. But he always ignored the external noise. “If the people who know you know that you’ve got a kind heart and spirit, that’s all it needs.”

Dyer’s chess aptitude and the pleasure he takes from thinking in patterns, tactical tweaks and in-game judgment calls are good indications as to why he, aged 47, has made his foray into management.

View image in fullscreen Dyer is hands-on as a manager, moving goalframes himself before training. Photograph: Andy Hall/The Guardian

He began coaching soon after retiring in 2013, first with Ipswich’s academy and under-23 teams, then on Paul Cook’s first team staff at Chesterfield. The top job had not been on his radar, but last season he found himself clashing, in a loving way, with Cook, who encouraged him to test the water.

Dyer’s tenure has begun swimmingly, one defeat in nine leaving Southend second in the National League. The aim, with the club financially stable two years after Justin Rees’s consortium completed its takeover, is a Football League return.

Guardian Sport’s conversation with Dyer is politely interrupted by regular door knocks. His squad must complete an online wellness check on waking and are required to report to Southend’s management office by 9am to sign in. Tardiness is not tolerated.

“If you’re late for a meeting, you don’t come into the meeting,” Dyer says. “And if you’re late for training you go home. A £10 or £20 fine doesn’t mean anything – it has to hurt.” It is a tactic he has borrowed from his former teammate Craig Bellamy, who himself took it from Vincent Kompany. “I always say coaches are thieves. You steal things from other people that fit how you want to build your culture.”

At 8.15am the small office Dyer shares with his assistant Adem Atay is packed with seven staff. The mood is jovial; rewatching clips from the weekend’s 6-1 win at Gateshead makes happy viewing.

View image in fullscreen Dyer has taken ideas from other managers on the type of culture he wants in his Southend squad. Photograph: Andy Hall/The Guardian

“I’m watching Real Madrid here,” Dyer jokes before purring at Southend’s fourth goal. Particular pleasure is taken in a freeze frame showing five of his players in the penalty area and two more lurking outside it.

Suddenly Dyer lunges at the screen, gesticulating wildly. “Complete the run. Don’t stop. You’re stretching them,” he bellows. He knows the run was not completed but his appetite for improvement is obvious.

Yet he is also aware just how difficult a game football is. Perfection is impossible, and in a later team meeting he tells his squad to ignore external mutterings that, having been six up at half-time, they should have scored more. Dyer knows maintaining intensity in such games is tough, particularly at the back end of a three-game week involving 1,200 miles on a coach. “No negatives from the game,” he concludes.

View image in fullscreen Even after a 6-1 away win, Dyer and his coaching staff can still find elements players can improve on. Photograph: Andy Hall/The Guardian

The Gateshead trip returned Dyer to Newcastle, whom he joined for £6m in 1999. Leaving for West Ham eight years later, he had won 32 of his 33 England caps and played in the Champions League. He had also fought with his teammate Lee Bowyer on the St James’ Park pitch, nearly retired out of frustration at a misdiagnosed hamstring injury, and been turned upon by supporters for supposedly refusing to play on the right for Sir Bobby Robson at Middlesbrough in 2004. Robson was sacked shortly after.

“A lot of people don’t realise our relationship was more than a manager and player,” he says of Robson. “Honestly, it was like father and son. We used to bicker at each other, hug each other, kiss each other.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The reality of what was portrayed as a major fall-out was more nuanced. Dyer had seen others push back on playing out of position and get their way: “Because of what happened to me as a kid I was thinking: ‘I won’t be taken advantage of.’”

Dyer is referring to being sexually abused by his now deceased great-uncle Kenny during his pre-teens, something he wrote candidly about in his autobiography, Old Too Soon, Smart Too Late.

With training approaching, Dyer is outside on his own, wheeling goalframes into position, meticulously placing discs on the grass. He enjoys the solitude, describing himself as “very guarded”. Atay, who worked with Dyer at Ipswich, confirms that on their shared car journeys one of them drives while the other sleeps. Dyer says: “I’m just: football club, home. I don’t go out; I don’t really have a life outside of football. I’m happy with it.”

And yet, once the session begins, introverted Dyer becomes extroverted Dyer. He enthusiastically explains a trio of complex drills, splitting 24 players into six teams. He encourages; he admonishes; he joins in.

The electric pace may be long gone – Dyer has so much metal in his legs that for a time he carried his own X-rays to speed up his passage through airport security – but the touch and deftness of pass remain.

Post-training the losing team must spin a wheel of misfortune; punishments include burpees, collecting equipment and a week without pool and darts. “That one devastates them,” Dyer says. “I particularly enjoy it when they have to make the staff hot chocolate.”

View image in fullscreen Southend’s wheel of misfortune claims another victim, with Zavier Massiah-Edwards having to pay £10 for getting a quiz question wrong. Photograph: Andy Hall/The Guardian

Dyer’s day is thereafter peppered with meetings, phone calls and planning. He still speaks regularly to Cook and turns for advice to people such as the former England caretaker manager Peter Taylor, a frequent visitor to training, Bellamy and Tony Mowbray.

He can draw on myriad experiences, within and outside the game, too, most recently life-saving surgery. In 2015 Dyer was diagnosed with primary sclerosing cholangitis. By 2023 he required a liver transplant. During an overnight stay in a Chesterfield hotel, Dyer woke in agony and went by taxi to Addenbrooke’s hospital in Cambridge, 130 miles away. Three months later he was still waiting. “That was mentally challenging,” he says. “They sent me home for my own sanity.”

Within two days Dyer was recalled for surgery, the operation taking place three years ago last Saturday. “Being on your deathbed certainly humbles you,” Dyer says. “Not many people get second chances.”

Sports.title: David Beckham takes £39m dividend as World Cup deals drive record profits
Sports.content:
David Beckham has taken a $51m (£39m) dividend from his business empire after a series of deals with brands for the Fifa World Cup.

Beckham appeared in about a dozen ad campaigns across this summer’s tournament in the US, working with brands including Lenovo, McDonald’s, Bank of America, Verizon and the PepsiCo crisps brand Lay’s.

The World Cup work helped to fuel a record year for DRJB Holdings, the commercial company for Beckham’s brands business, where revenues surged by a fifth to $110.5m last year, up from $92.3m in 2024.

Pre-tax profits also climbed to a record $65.7m, a 46% increase on 2024.

DRJB Holdings – which is made up of three divisions, the largest of which is DB Ventures, which covers most of his partnerships with brands such as Hugo Boss – paid out $51.1m to shareholders last year, compared with $53m the previous year.

View image in fullscreen David Beckham in a US advert for Stella Artois during the Fifa World Cup 26. Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty

The former England captain, who retired from professional football in 2013, sold a 55% stake in his businesses in 2022 to the US group Authentic Brands for £200m, meaning he took home 45% of last year’s total dividend.

However, the Companies House filing, which will be published next week, showed a further $61.6m was paid in special dividends this year. This meant Beckham was paid out about $51m.

Before this year’s World Cup the company secured partnerships including a multiyear deal with Bank of America: he became an ambassador for its global sports programme.

The 51-year-old also launched menswear collections for Hugo Boss, an eponymous range of spectacles for Safilo and a limited-edition Predator football boot with Adidas.

He also struck a new deal for Beckham & Friends Live, a show on Paramount+ that was broadcast around the Uefa Champions League.

Beckham featured in a Stella Artois campaign alongside the actor and producer Theo James to mark the beer’s partnership for the second season of Netflix series The Gentlemen.

DRJB Holdings is jointly owned by Authentic Brands Group and Footwork Productions, controlled by David Beckham.

View image in fullscreen Beckham with his new star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in Los Angeles in June. Photograph: Chris Pizzello/AP

Corey Salter, the chief executive of entertainment at Authentic Brands, said Beckham was “one of the most powerful global brands in sport, lifestyle, entertainment and much more”.

Slater added: “What these results show is that behind the Beckham brand is a strong and highly effective team within Authentic, set up with the financial discipline and strong fundamentals to continue to grow profitably through 2026 and beyond.”

DRJB Holdings includes the Seven Global division, which contains licensing agreements with companies such as Adidas. The remainder of the business is Studio 99, the production company that made the four-part Netflix documentary Beckham that was released in 2023. It also produced Victoria Beckham’s Netflix documentary, which was released last year.

David Beckham is also an investor in businesses including the supplement specialist IM8, which he co-founded in 2024, and the honey-based fruit snack firm BeeUp.

Sports.title: Socceroos denied famous win as late Brazil goal cancels out Irankunda stunner
Sports.content:
It was a Friday night in which the stars descended on Townsville. There was Bruno Guimarães, Raphinha and Vinícius Júnior in the Brazilian XI, with Endrick leading the line and Estêvão out on the flank, all instructed by Carlo Ancelotti in the dugout. But on this evening, their limelight was stolen by Australia’s star boy Nestory Irankunda.

His magnificent 68th-minute free kick may have been cancelled out at the death by Rayan’s header, ensuring Australia and Brazil shared a 1-1 draw at Queensland Country Bank Stadium, but on a night in which some of the planet’s biggest and best were on hand, Irankunda stood up to be counted.

It was a moment that almost everyone in the sold-out stadium of 25,440 probably felt coming; the kind of joint premonition that comes with watching a special talent. When Paul Okon-Engstler won a free kick about 25 yards out from goal, you knew it was a set piece screaming out to be hit. And when Irankunda stood over it, you definitely knew that’s what he was about to do; the 20-year-old is many things, but lacking in confidence isn’t one of them.

And then, he delivered. A perfectly placed free kick dipped over the Brazilian wall, leaving goalkeeper Hugo Souza with naught to do but watch wistfully as it nestled in the back of the net.

Out came the back flips as he raced towards the corner flag, a wry grin spreading over the face of Tony Popovic in the dugout. The most precocious of Australia’s talents certainly has a long way to go in his game but when he’s doing stuff like that, it again reiterates just how good he’s going to be for the Socceroos.

View image in fullscreen Nestory Irankunda celebrates scoring for the Socceroos against Brazil in Townsville. Photograph: Matt Taylor/AAP

It sparked a late flurry of activity from Brazil, hurling themselves forward in an attempt to avoid the potential embarrassment of falling to a perceived lesser-footballing nation in Australia. And they were rewarded with the last kick of the game when a corner was swung in from the left by Raphinha and on to the head of Rayan, whose effort was sent goalward with enough power to ensure that, even if Patrick Beach got a touch on it, he couldn’t prevent it from ricocheting off the crossbar and crossing the goalline.

“I think it’s maybe a sign of progress if we are a bit disappointed, and I think the dressing room’s a bit quiet,” Popovic said. “I think that’s a good sign. Yes, of course, you’re delighted that you get a point in a game like this against Brazil. But when you have the lead up until the last kick of the game, then of course you walk off a little bit deflated. Once that settles down, I’m sure we can look at the performance as a whole and be very happy. But, you know, I’m actually glad there’s disappointment, because I have it as well.”

We’d seen flashes of the Brazil promoters of this two-game series – Queensland state government reminders of their role in organising the fixture have been everywhere this week – to that point. A brilliantly composed finish from rising 19-year-old Estêvão had the ball in the back of the net on the stroke of half-time, only for the VAR to rightly call it back for a foul by Bruno Guimarães on Harry Souttar in the buildup. A burst of acceleration by Vinícius Júnior set the scene for Estêvão to have an early shot deflected away soon after. Raphinha, in the form of his life for Barcelona, created space outside the box before dragging a shot wide just past the hour mark.

View image in fullscreen Rayan celebrates scoring an equaliser for Brazil against Australia in Townsville. Photograph: Jono Searle/AAP

“It doesn’t feel like a defeat because it’s a draw,” said Ancelotti. “We could have won; we had our chances. We have to be patient. We fought back after conceding the goal and secured a deserved draw. These are tests we have to go through, give players opportunities and move on. It was a test. The next one is another test too.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Football Desk Australia 

“It’s no surprise. They defend very hard, very well. We played well, but these things can happen. The match against Australia didn’t surprise me.”

But in football, there’s always an opposition, although on this evening, it’s also probably accurate to say that both Brazil and Australia had two: the 11 men opposite them, and the ice-rink of a surface at Queensland Country Bank Stadium that only degraded as the night went on – despite it being 20 days since it was last used for a North Queensland Cowboys NRL and NRLW double-header.

It was evident from the brief moments of hesitation or deliberately cautious movement that neither group of players were truly confident in the surface beneath them, but this still didn’t stop several of them from falling to the turf as the night progressed. Just how this was allowed to happen – especially in light of that aforementioned Queensland state government grandiosity – beggared belief. “[The pitch] was not good,” said Ancelotti. “The pitch … it was difficult to play on a pitch like this. And we hope to have a better pitch for the next game.”

But credit, too, goes to the Socceroos. There were certainly moments of defensive heroics and dogged determination that we’ve come to expect from them under Popovic. But there were also periods of assertiveness in possession, times when they defended higher up the pitch, and when players showed the gumption to run at their man and take him on.

Sports.title: Man City found guilty on 114 charges of Premier League financial breaches
Sports.content:
Manchester City have been found guilty on almost all of the charges relating to breaches of the Premier League’s financial regulations.

City were first charged with 115 breaches of these rules in February 2023.

3 Man City's long-standing case finally looks to be reaching its conclusion Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

But the Citizens have now been found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges.

The sanctions have not been decided, with all possibilities remaining on the table.

talkSPORT understands City will appeal once it is confirmed the charges have gone against them

A Premier League spokesperson told talkSPORT that the league process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality.

As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the Club’s statement of February 2023.

In 2023, the club said it was 'surprised' by the charges and it 'welcomes the review of this matter by an independent commission, to impartially consider the comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of its position'.

A Premier League spokesperson has now said: "The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."

What do Man City's charges relate to?

City were first charged following an investigation into alleged breaches between 2009 and 2018.

The investigation began after German newspaper Der Spiegel published leaked financial documents from City in November 2018.

The case was referred to an independent commission to adjudicate over the charges.

3 Manchester City have dominated English football over the last 15 years, but their achievements could now be tarnished Credit: Getty

According to the Times, Premier League clubs were informed of the outcome of Man City's charges after a meeting on Thursday.

City have won a total of eight Prem titles, four FA Cups, seven League Cups and one Champions League under the ownership of Sheikh Mansour - who bought the club in 2008.

Six of those honours have come since the charges were brought forward.

What now for Manchester City?

Reacting to the huge news live on air, talkSPORT's Ben Jacobs confirmed Man City will only appeal once the Premier League have decided on their punishment.

Jacobs told talkSPORT: "The independent panel ruling on Manchester City's 115 charges have found the club guilty on all but one.

"Now, when we say all but one, we don't necessarily mean 114 out of 115 because these charges, broadly speaking, are in different kinds of buckets that were then repeated year on year on year.

3 Enzo Maresca is tasked with overseeing his Man City squad in the wake of huge news Credit: Getty

"But the vast majority of the charges against Manchester City are deemed to be enforceable and, as a consequence, the independent panel are now moving from guilt to sanctions, and it's an ongoing process.

"Manchester City are waiting to see, following being found guilty, what the exact punishment is going to be and then from there, they are expected to appeal. A Manchester City spokesman has told talkSPORT that the Premier League process remains ongoing with 'significant elements still to be completed'.

Jacobs added: "City still point to the fact that, originally, UEFA had found them guilty of certain elements, and they were able to overturn that case as well."

When will Man City learn their punishment?

While news of City's charges has sent shockwaves across English football, Jacobs revealed it could be months before we discover their exact punishment.

He pointed to Everton's initial 10 point deduction for breaching the Premier League's profit and sustainability rules in the 2021/22 season, which was then implemented during the 2023/24 campaign, with the penalty reduced to six points upon appeal..

Jacobs explained: "Due to the strict confidentiality, the sanctions can be passed down to the club or, alternatively, the guilt can be found first.

"And then the process still has to understand what exactly the final punishment will be. We saw this with slightly smaller cases like Everton and Nottingham Forest, where the Premier League pushed for, in those cases, a certain points deduction and it got scaled back.

"My expectation is there'll still be an element of back and forth and it could take several weeks, if not months, to get a final resolution.

If City appeal, it's going to be longer.

"Could they go to the Premier League in light of the vast majority of these charges being upheld and ask for a more amicable settlement? Possibly as well, But I'm not expecting this to resolve itself in its full entirety in a matter of days or during the international break, maybe even not during this season as well."

This is a developing story and is being updated.

For the latest updates, breaking news alerts, and comprehensive analysis, refresh this page or follow our real-time news coverage by watching and listening to talkSPORT live.

For broader context, explore related coverage on our homepage for the top trending stories. For the latest talkSPORT videos, download the app.

talkSPORT cares about getting it right, not just getting it first and because this is a developing situation, details will change. We will be updating this page constantly with verified info, expert takes, and official statements.

Stay tuned for further developments as this story continues to break.

Sports.title: Danny Ings set for immediate debut after agreeing shock deal to join League One side
Sports.content:
Danny Ings set for immediate debut after agreeing shock deal to join League One side

Wycombe Wanderers have confirmed the signing of former Liverpool and West Ham United striker Danny Ings.

The 34-year-old has been without a club since leaving Sheffield United over the summer.



3 Former Premier League striker Ings left West Ham in 2025 and has recently been at Sheffield United Credit: Getty

And the League One side have won the race to land the experienced hitman, who was linked with a move to Leicester City earlier in the year.

Wycombe statement

"Former England international Danny Ings has joined Wycombe Wanderers," a statement read on the club's official website.

Ings has also signed in time to make his debut for Wycombe this weekend against Reading.



"And he could feature in the League One clash with Reading at Adams Park on Saturday," the club continued.

"The 34-year-old striker is a free agent after leaving Sheffield United in the summer and arrives in Wycombe with a wealth of experience including 240 appearances in the top flight with Burnley alongside Chairboys coach Sam Vokes, as well as Southampton, West Ham, Aston Villa and Liverpool.



"He’s netted more than 120 professional goals, including one for England in a friendly against Wales in 2020, and has trained with the Chairboys over the past week before putting pen to paper on a deal this morning.

"His move remains subject to EFL and FA approval, and he’ll wear squad number 28."



“We are excited to welcome Danny Ings to Wycombe Wanderers," Director of Football Strategy and Data Intelligence Tom Stockwell said.

"Danny is an attacking player with top quality and a huge amount of experience at the top of the game. We believe Danny can help the team on and off the pitch.

3 Wycombe's new striker could make his Chairboys debut this weekend Credit: Getty

"He joined up with the team Friday last week and has trained with the group since, so we know he’s fit and sharp, and ready to have an immediate impact."



Wycombe v Reading goes ahead

Reading's trip to Adams Park will go ahead as planned after Reading turned down the chance to postpone the fixture.

Andy Rinomhota, Jeriel Dorsett and Charlie Savage all received international call-ups from from Zimbabwe, Montserrat and Wales, respectively, earlier this month.

And EFL rules state that clubs are eligible to request a postponement if three or more of their players are selected for international duty.

The Royals had the chance to delay the clash, but opted to proceed with the fixture.



3 Reading's meeting with Wycombe goes ahead as scheduled Credit: Getty

"First of all, congratulations to the three lads who received international call-ups," Reading head coach Leam Richardson said.

"It’s a fantastic achievement for them and a proud moment for the club.

"We considered the circumstances carefully and, on this occasion, felt it was right to play the game.



"Football is a squad game and we have confidence in the players available to us, while keeping the fixture in place also helps us avoid adding another game to an already busy schedule.

"It’s better for the supporters too. Saturday afternoon is the ideal time to play football whenever circumstances allow, so we were pleased to keep this one in place."

Sports.title: Premier League and LaLiga lead calls for FIFA reform as pressure grows on Gianni Infantino
Sports.content:
Premier League and LaLiga lead calls for FIFA reform as pressure grows on Gianni Infantino

Four of Europe's 'Big Five' leagues have banded together to hit out at FIFA president Gianni Infantino.

Infantino has come in for criticism in recent weeks following his plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup.

2 Infantino is under mounting pressure from Europe's biggest leagues Credit: AFP

European football's governing body UEFA considered legal action against the FIFA supremo, which saw the idea temporarily shelved.

Earlier this week, Infantino was open to an external review of the plan while adding he should be allowed to continue to operate as FIFA president ahead of the election in March 2027.

However, the Premier League, LaLiga, Bundesliga and Serie A chiefs have since called for "a new governance structure for our sport's global governing body that is transparent, objective, proportionate and inclusive".

What does the statement say?

Richard Masters, chief executive of the Premier League, Javier Tebas, president LaLiga, Marc Lenz, CEO Bundesliga, and Luigi De Siervo, CEO of Serie A have all co-signed the statement in question.

"Football's longstanding foundations have, in recent years, been threatened by a fundamental governance problem, whereby FIFA's president has actively promoted exploitative ideas rather than safeguarding against them," the respective Leagues say.

"And while football's stakeholders ultimately forced the withdrawal of the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, the conditions that led to FFE remain."

'Political interference'

The statement continued: "The FIFA president has now acknowledged the need for reform, but it is not enough for surface-level, process changes to be explored in the aftermath of FFE - fundamental governance reform is essential to restore clear constitutional boundaries within FIFA, including confidence that individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference."

The last point in particular refers to US president Donald Trump's input in USMNT striker's Folarin Balogun 2026 World Cup suspension being overturned for the last-16 tie with Belgium.

2 The leagues aren't best pleased about political interference surrounding key decisions Credit: Getty

The letter continued: "The future of FIFA matters to everyone who cares about football, because our sport cannot grow globally if its foundations are undermined.

"FIFA's governance problem goes far beyond the role of one individual. The wider question is whether FIFA's president should simultaneously wield such regulatory, commercial and political power without effective checks and balances, including the agreement of affected stakeholders.

"More than a decade ago, following criminal proceedings involving senior football officials, FIFA's own reform process sought to address these issues - yet, once again, football has suffered one of the biggest abuses of power in FIFA's history.

"We are speaking up together, as founding members of European Leagues and the World Leagues Association, because we understand how FIFA's relentless expansionism affects everyone.

"And ahead of the presidential elections next year, the leagues have called on candidates to 'publish their own reform programme'.

"Now is the moment to decide not only who will lead FIFA, but also how FIFA should be led.

"Leagues have a crucial role to play in this process, and we want to ensure that the voice of every league is heard."

Sports.title: Jobe Bellingham warned over errors that are preventing first senior England call-up
Sports.content:
Jobe Bellingham warned over errors that are preventing first senior England call-up

Jobe Bellingham needs to get to a point where he's properly consistent for Borussia Dortmund before he's called up by England.

That is the opinion of European football expert Andy Brassell, who believes errors in big games have kept the younger brother of Jude in the Three Lions' Under-21 squad.



3 Jobe will have ambitions of joining brother Jude in the senior England squad Credit: Getty

Jobe has featured in all four of Dortmund's Bundesliga games this season, playing 90 minutes in each of the first three matches.

He came off the bench to assist the club's winner in the 1-0 victory over Stuttgart that moved BVB two points clear of Bayern Munich.

His form led to reports that the 21-year-old was in serious contention to earn a senior England call-up in Thomas Tuchel's September squad.



However, the younger Bellingham is remaining in the U21 ranks for now despite his upturn in form during his second season in Germany.

How close is Jobe Bellingham to senior England call-up?

Brassell explained to talkSPORT.com: "I think it's still a bit uneven.



"I saw him in the Franz Beckenbauer Super Cup the week before the start of the season [a 2-1 defeat to Bayern Munich].

"He had bits during that game when he was great and he had other bits of it where he looked like he was drowning.



"Against the likes of [Michael] Olise, it was really hard for him.

"Certainly, his turning the ball over in the run-up to the second goal is something that had already been flagged in that game."

3 Jobe remains an integral part of Lee Carsley’s U21 side Credit: Getty

"He's been really improved in the Bundesliga since then," Brassell continued on the former Sunderland star.

"I think there's something there; there's no doubt about that, but I also feel it's better conditions under which for him to develop this season.



"They do have more options, they do have more legs in midfield.

"Joey Veerman has come in from PSV, and there are people around Dortmund who think he will supplant Jobe Bellinam and Jobe will find himself on the bench. I don't think it's that simple.

"I think Veerman, despite being older, is someone who is developing in terms of a higher league as well.

"I think that will be quite tough for him and that will take time. They can take the pressure off each other a little bit."

3 Jobe Bellingham has played a key part of Dortmund topping the Bundesliga after four rounds Credit: Getty



"What we have is a Dortmund side that's faster, stronger, more athletic, and he plays into absolutely all of that."

'Enough errors in big games'

Jobe had a baptism of fire after completing a £31million switch to Dortmund after helping Sunderland seal Premier League promotion.

He initially struggled to cement his spot in the starting XI and manager Niko Kovac claimed he wasn't 'doing himself any favours'.

Off-field struggles were part of that, with Jobe’s father, Mark, holding a heated discussion with the club's former sporting director, Sebastien Kehl, on the opening day of last season.



Bellingham, who was then linked with a loan move away, ultimately stayed put and has battled back to earn his manager's trust.

"He's very much a Niko Kovac type of player," Brassell added to talkSPORT.

"But I think there are enough errors in big games that it feels to me that for a while, I don't think we can start talking about England yet; he needs to get to a point where he's properly consistent for Dortmund.

"And at the moment we would be rewarding potential rather than production, I think."

Sports.title: Arsenal Invincible insists squad never cared about record – there were no extra bonuses
Sports.content:
Arsenal Invincible insists squad never cared about record – there were no extra bonuses

Ray Parlour revealed Arsenal's Invincibles squad's focus was never on remaining unbeaten.

In 2004, the Gunners won 26 times and lost none across the 38-game season, beating Chelsea to the title by 11 points.



2 Arsenal's 03/04 team remains the only side to go unbeaten for an entire Premier League season Credit: AFP and licensors

It was an iconic team that consisted of players like Jens Lehmann, Ashley Cole, Martin Keown, Patrick Vieira, Dennis Bergkamp, Thierry Henry and were managed by a legendary manager in Arsene Wenger.

However, the incredible feat was never an original aim for the north London side, as Parlour told talkSPORT Breakfast.

He said: "I think the press really ramped [the idea of going Invincible] up with eight games to go, that's when they realised that they haven’t been beaten yet.



"The players were only interested in winning the league, to go unbeaten was just a bonus - we didn’t get anything extra from doing it.

"22 years later, and it’s still not been done again. The good thing about the team I was in was we had really good players to come on. People like [Nwankwo] Kanu, [Sylvain] Wiltord, they would come on and score you a goal."



Parlour went on to compare the Invincible squad with Mikel Arteta's current side following their heavy 3-0 defeat to Brighton, insisting something would have been salvaged by his winners.

"We would have come back even if we were down 2-0. We would never give up as a team, which was a real bonus for everyone involved in it.



"The hardest games were the last four, we won the league at White Hart Lane with a 2-2 draw, we also had Birmingham, Fulham, Portsmouth and Leicester.

"On paper, we should be winning them pretty comfortably but it doesn’t work like that, and we got battered."

2 Parlour was a key figure in Arsenal's all conquering side that remained unbeaten across an entire season en route to winning the league Credit: Getty Images - Getty

A unique legacy in the Premier League

Since Arsenal, a few teams have come agonisingly close to replicating the feat, including Chelsea in 2004/05, and Liverpool in 2018/19 - both suffering only one defeat.



Incredibly, the Merseyside-based team still finished second that year despite winning 97 points.

Arsenal, though, actually remained unbeaten for 49 Premier League games until they were finally beaten 2-0 by Manchester United.

Critics have insisted it can't really be deemed Invincible as they were knocked out of the FA Cup by Manchester United, the League Cup by Middlesbrough, and the Champions League by Chelsea.

The Invincible dream, however, is over for another season at least, with Brighton ensuring that.



The only teams who are still able to complete an invincible run this season are Liverpool, Manchester City, Brentford, Everton, and Leeds.

Sports.title: When will Erling Haaland score 100 Norway goals? Striker already broken Ronaldo and Zlatan records
Sports.content:
When will Erling Haaland score 100 Norway goals? Striker already broken Ronaldo and Zlatan records

A new-look Erling Haaland. Same old story.

The neatly cropped Manchester City and Norway striker has made another electric start to the season by scoring the 300th goal of his club career.

3 Haaland surpassed both Ronaldo and Zlatan Ibrahimovic for goals scored for their country and is well on course to score 100 for Norway Credit: Getty

Already one of the Premier League's greatest players, Haaland took just 384 appearances to reach the milestone, at a faster rate than both Kylian Mbappe (398) and Cristiano Ronaldo (499).

The 26-year-old is now looking to topple France and Portugal's captains again on the international front.

What is Haaland's goal record for Norway?

Haaland enjoyed a stunning debut World Cup campaign, scoring seven times en route to Norway's run to the quarter-finals.

And in the Nations League, he scored twice against Denmark to make it 64 goals in 56 international appearances, at a rate of 1.143 goals per game.

The first 55 of those strikes had not come at a major tournament, with Norway having not qualified for any during his tenure until now.

However, through the World Cup, Haaland scored in each of his last 14 competitive games for Norway until he blanked against England.

The final appearance of that epic run was his brace to eliminate Carlo Ancelotti's Brazil in the round of 16 at the start of July.

When will Haaland score 100 goals for Norway?

With his two against Denmark in the 3-2 win, he surpassed Ronaldo Nazario and Zlatan Ibrahimovic's 62 goals for Brazil and Sweden respectively and, at the rate Haaland is currently scoring for Norway, he's set to bring up a century of goals in around 32 more matches.

3 Haaland was inspirational for Norway at the World Cup Credit: Getty

3 In the Nations League, he has continued to score goals and is a contender to win the Ballon d'Or Credit: Getty

Erling Haaland's career statistics 2015-17: Bryne - 0 goals in 16 apps 2017-19: Molde - 20 goals in 50 apps 2019-20: Red Bull Salzburg - 29 goals in 27 apps 2020-22: Borussia Dortmund - 86 goals in 89 apps 2022-Present: Manchester City - 169 goals in 205 apps 2019-Present: Norway - 64 goals in 56 caps Total: 368 goals in 443 apps

That would mean Haaland would reach the 100-goal milestone at around 88 international caps - dwarfing some of his rivals' tallies.

Assuming he avoids injuries and continues to average around 10 appearances for Norway per calendar year, it would only take him until around mid-2029 to early 2030 to hit triple figures.

At that rate, Haaland would still only be around 28 to 29 years old when he reaches 100 goals on the international stage.

Of course, much could also depend on the quality of opponents that Norway could come up against over the next three-and-a-half years.

Stale Solbakken's men, who have moved up 12 places to 19th in the FIFA rankings, also face Portugal and Wales, including the reverse fixture in Denmark, in the Nations League Group D.

Haaland, as it stands, has six goals in 11 caps against top-15 FIFA opponents (0.55 goals/game) - that shoots up to 16 in 18 games against teams ranked between 16–50 (0.89 goals/game), and he has a whopping 42 goals in 27 appearances against countries ranked lower than 50th (1.56 goals/game).

How does Haaland compare to Ronaldo, Kane, Mbappe and Lukaku

Five-time Ballon d'Or winner Ronaldo is currently the all-time leading scorer in the history of the sport with 979 goals for club and country.

Having played as a winger in the early phases of his career, it took the now-41-year-old until his 165th cap to reach 100 goals. He is now closing in on 1000 career goals, which is something Haaland has also been backed to replicate.

Ronaldo, who turns 42 in February and is set to retire next summer, was boasting a ratio of 0.61 goals per game at the time of his century.

Belgium's Romelu Lukaku, 33, is just seven goals away from scoring 100 goals, while 33-year-old Harry Kane has a chance to close the gap against Spain, Croatia and the Czech Republic in the international break.

Sports.title: David Raya is not the Premier League’s best goalkeeper – summer signing is miles clear
Sports.content:
David Raya is not the Premier League’s best goalkeeper – summer signing is miles clear

Forget Arsenal's David Raya, Aston Villa newbie Zion Suzuki is the best goalkeeper in the Premier League.

At least that's according to talkSPORT supremo Adrian Durham.

4 Suzuki's heroics against Tottenham helped Aston Villa to a 3-2 win Credit: AFP

Despite many tipping World Cup winner Raya to be amongst the best goalkeepers in Europe, Durham isn't having it.

The Spaniard has won the Premier League Golden Glove in each of the last three seasons, while also being named in UEFA's Champions League Team of the Season for the 2025/26 campaign.

But legendary broadcaster Durham has insisted the 31-year-old is not a patch on Suzuki.

Villa signed the Japan international from Serie A side Parma as a replacement for Emiliano Martinez, who left Villa Park for Chelsea last month.

While the Villans have made a sub-par start to the season - collecting just four points from the opening five games following last week's 3-2 win at Tottenham - Suzuki has quickly made an impression on supporters.

And he's certainly caught the eye of Durham, who believes the 24-year-old is the best in his position in the league.

Speaking on Fiery Fridays as part of talkSPORT Daily podcast, Durham delivered his goalkeeping opinion to Angelina Kelly and Alex Crook.

What did Durham say about Raya?

"Lazy people will say [Arsenal's] David Raya [in the best goalkeeper]," Durham began on this week's episode.

"People who watch football will say Zion Suzuki at Aston Villa, who was also probably the best goalkeeper at the World Cup.

"Now I can hear Arsenal fans crying right now, dry your eyes!

4 Raya is bidding to become the first player to win four consecutive Premier League Golden Glove awards Credit: Getty

4 Legendary talkSPORT broadcaster Durham believes Raya's performances are overhyped

"People bang on about his spectacular saves, when you break them down, are they actually that good?"

Durham brought his receipts this week as he continued: "I'll give you an example, when they played Chelsea and beat them 2-1, Estevao came on.

"He cut him from the right and had this shot with his left foot.

"David Raya tipped it over and everybody's going 'Ooh' and everybody's going 'Aah'.

"It was like they're at some sort of magic show.

"You know the classic Arsenal overreaction where everything any Arsenal player ever does has to be the greatest thing in the world ever."

What did Durham say about Suzuki?

Turning his attention to Suzuki, Durham then purred: "In the meantime, Suzuki makes incredible save after save after save to keep Villa at 0-0 [against Tottenham] at the weekend and they go on to win the game.

4 Suzuki has conceded five goals from his opening four Premier League games - keeping one clean sheet Credit: Getty

"He's 6ft 3in, he's a proper bulky presence, brilliant frame for a goalkeeper.

"His distribution off both feet, pinpoint, any distance, absolutely phenomenal.

"So about time people stop banging on about David Raya, the Spanish [Jordan] Pickford.

"Focus on the best 'keeper in the Premier League."

Villa will look to build upon their first league victory of the campaign when they face Brentford following the extended international break.

Sports.title: Jurgen Klopp rejects Virgil van Dijk’s ‘disgrace’ claim over controversial Germany goal
Sports.content:
Virgil van Dijk raged that Germany's goal against the Netherlands was a 'disgrace' - but Jurgen Klopp insisted the correct call was made.

Felix Nmecha fired Germany in front in the 32nd minute, but Cody Gakpo rescued a point in stoppage time for the Oranje in Thursday's UEFA Nations League 1-1 draw.

3 Van Dijk and the rest of his Netherlands teammates were furious that Germany's goal was allowed to stand

However, tempers flared following Nmecha's strike in Amsterdam, which came after Brian Brobbey suffered a suspected hamstring injury.

Despite the Dutch striker being in pain, Germany opted to play on and subsequently put the ball in the back of the net.

This prompted a furious response from the Netherlands players, with Van Dijk branding the decision to allow the goal to stand a 'disgrace'.

What did Jurgen Klopp say?

Discussing Van Dijk's furious reaction to the opener being allowed to stand, Klopp, who returned to management in July, saw the incident differently to his former Liverpool captain.

He said in his post-match press conference: "It certainly wasn't a disgrace. The goal was completely legitimate. I don't have a guilty conscience.

"And I would have one if it weren't legitimate. I would have taken it anyway, but I would have had a guilty conscience. I don't have one."

Klopp then added: "I would have told my players that they had to keep playing.

"They [Netherlands] didn't. And we took full advantage of it with a really excellent move. Great cross, great run. Felix was where he needed to be - and he smashed the ball in.

"It certainly wasn't a disgrace, but when emotions are running high, you can say anything in the heat of the moment."

What else was said about Germany's opener?

Joshua Kimmich backed his manager's comments, and felt that Van Dijk didn't give a 'considered response' to the incident.

3 Kimmich has pinned the blame on the referee for not stopping the game in the lead up to Nmecha's goal

"I played a pass to Philipp [Treu], he crossed the ball, and we scored a goal," the Bayern Munich and Germany captain said.

"The referee stops the game, especially when a player has a head injury.

"It is the referee's responsibility to determine whether the player is seriously injured.

"I didn't hear a whistle, so the game continued completely correctly."

Which Germany players are out injured?

Brobbey wasn't the only player to suffer an injury in a hotly-contested Nations League clash.

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz will return to Arsenal to undergo an MRI scan on a hamstring issue.

3 Havertz faces a potential spell on the sidelines owing to a hamstring issue suffered on international duty Credit: Getty

Bayern Munich star Jamal Musiala is also set to leave the Germany camp owing to a thigh issue.

Florian Wirtz and Jonathan Burkardt are now set to join the team sooner than initially expected.

“At the moment, both are on the MRI [scans]," Klopp said of both Havertz and Musiala.

"Of course, that’s not great now. I just hope this is nothing bad.

"The boys are probably out for us, but hopefully then also relatively quickly available again."

Sports.title: Manchester City found guilty on 114 Premier League rule break charges - and could be kicked out of the top flight or face huge points deduction
Sports.content:
Manchester City found guilty on 114 Premier League rule break charges - and could be kicked out of the top flight or face huge points deduction

Manchester City have been found guilty of all but one of their 115 rule-break charges concerning the Premier League’s financial regulations.

The competition accused the club of widespread financial cheating over an era of sustained success - with an independent panel hearing concluding in 2024.

There has since been a frustrating wait for a verdict but sources have disclosed that clubs have been informed that the panel has now reached a decision - and there is a belief it's a win for the top flight. It is understood that the Premier League have triumphed on the vast majority of charges.

The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties, and even relegation.

Points deductions could even be applied onto previous seasons, raising the chance that City will be stripped of their Premier League titles.

It is inevitable that they will appeal.

Manchester City have been found guilty of all but one of their 115 Premier League rule-break charges

The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties, and even relegation

A Manchester City spokesperson said: 'The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the Club’s statement of February 2023.

'The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.'

Man City, who have always strongly denied wrongdoing, were charged in February 2023 by the Premier League with a hearing concluding in December 2024.

Their statement that February insisted that they were 'surprised' by the charges.

The Premier League accused Man City of multiple breaches of financial rules and of failing to co-operate with a subsequent investigation. The alleged rule breaking was claimed to have taken place over a 14-year period.

A three-man panel was tasked with considering the evidence, with the initial expectation a verdict would have been reached on the case within months. It has since taken three-and-a-half years.

The original 115 charges were extended to a total of 130 after an administration issue in what is the most expensive and wide-ranging case in English football history.

Manchester United legend Rio Ferdinand was quick to stick the boot in on social media, writing on X: 'Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet.'

The charges stretch from the years 2009 to 2023, encompassing much of the Pep Guardiola era

He was part of the United team who were famously pipped to the title by City on the final day of the 2011-12 season.

City remained steadfast in maintaining their innocence over more than 115 alleged breaches across eight years, some including the start of the Pep Guardiola era.

The club were accused of failing to report accurate financial information for nine seasons stretching from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as failing to provide full details of former manager Roberto Mancini’s pay between 2009-10 and 2012-13.

They were also alleged to have failed to provide full details of money paid to players between 2010-11 and 2015-16 and failing to co-operate with the probe from 2018 to 2023.

Between the years mentioned, Manchester City won eight Premier League titles, a Champions League, four FA Cups, and seven EFL Cups.

In 2022 Guardiola said he would quit the club if he felt the club's hierarchy had ever lied to him. The next year, he said he would not walk out on his deal, even if he was relegated to League One.

Guardiola always insisted he was 'fully convinced' that the club is innocent and said in May: 'I trust them, I trust them. Because I spoke with them and I trust how they behave and how they did.'

City vehemently denied any breaches of financial rules but the investigation started in December 2018 after German website Der Spiegel published documents from a Football Leaks cache which had originated from Portuguese hacker Rui Pinto.

The club have maintained that they are innocent throughout the process and are expected to appeal

It alleged that City had overstated sponsorship income with money paid from the club's owners instead of sponsors linked to Abu Dhabi.

Roberto Mancini's wages were said to have doubled via a secret contract with an Abu Dhabi club when he was at Man City, while they were also alleged to have broken rules over approaching young players.

The Mail on Sunday has led the way on reporting the story. In July 2021, they reported on emails that appeared to suggest that Man City had millions funnelled into the club by Abu Dhabi to help inflate their income.

Back in February 2020, the club were banned from the Champions League and fined £25million after they were found to have seriously misled European footballing governing body UEFA and broken financial fair play rules.

This was then lifted by the Court of Arbitration for Sport which also reduced the club's fine to £9m.

City spent £440million over the summer, equalling the British transfer record by signing Enzo Fernandez for £125m, and their former chairman David Bernstein claimed that 'makes a mockery' of the Premier League's regulation of the top division.

Writing in the Sunday Times, Bernstein said: 'The fact they have done this (transfer spend) against the background of the 115 Premier League charges is extraordinary and makes a mockery of regulation in England's top division, supposedly the best-run league in the world.'

It was a bumper summer for City after the exit of Guardiola. They also signed Elliot Anderson (£116m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (£86m), Iliman Ndiaye (£60m), Allan and Geronimo Rulli.

Enzo Maresca insisted that he was not worried about the situation when he became their manager in the summer

Other marquee signings down the years have included Jack Grealish for £100m, Erling Haaland for £51.2m, Josko Gvardiol for £77.6m, and Riyad Mahrez for £60m.

Four Premier League sides had reserved the right to seek compensation in the event City were found guilty.

Speaking to the BBC in August, Premier Leagume chief executive Richard Masters described the case as 'hugely complex' as he defended the length of time taken to reach a conclusion.

'I do accept it is taking longer than expected and I understand that people want to find out as soon as possible what's going on, but I simply can't provide that,' he said.

'The process is the process,' he said. 'It will resolve itself. But as you know, I literally can't say a thing about it. There's only one available option, which is to allow the process to reach its natural conclusion. I can't talk about the substance of the case. I can't talk about the timing of the case. Our rules are very clear about that. I understand that people are frustrated but it will take as long as it takes.'

When Enzo Maresca, Guardiola's former assistant, took the managerial reins in the summer, he insisted that he wasn't worried about the situation.

He said: 'No, no, to be honest (they're not a concern.

'The only thing I can say is that three years ago, the treble season, I was here. And there were the same words about this kind of problem,” Maresca explained.

City spent £440m on players this summer, including a British record-equalling £125m on Enzo Fernandez to secure him from Chelsea

'In three years, it’s still the same, so nothing happened. I don’t have anything to say because it’s something that is there.'

The club have made a stunning start to the season, sitting top of the Premier League with five wins from as many games.

It is perhaps merciful that this decision has arrived towards the start of a three-week international break rather than during the cut and thrust of the domestic season.

The Premier League's latest domestic broadcast deal has seen the amount paid per game fall by around £2.5m.

Some have wondered if that is an indicator that fans are getting fed up of various litigations, with Nottingham Forest, Everton and Leicester City docked points in recent times.

Sports.title: Rio Ferdinand calls for Man City to be STRIPPED of title as football world reels after bombshell guilty verdict

Rio Ferdinand calls for Man City to be STRIPPED of title as football world reels after bombshell guilty verdict

It meant City won the league ahead of local rivals United on goal difference, with Ferdinand in the United team that lost out that day.

Rio Ferdinand has suggested he is in for another Premier League medal after Manchester City were found guilty on 114 of 115 financial charges

The former defender was referring to the dramatic title won by City when Sergio Arguero scored late against QPR

And the former defender has taken to social media, essentially demanding that City are stripped of the title they won that year.

'Another premier league medal to be added to the cabinet,' the 47-year-old wrote on social media.

He would leave United at the end of the 2013-14 season, in which City won the Premier League again – though Liverpool finished second.

The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties, and even relegation.

Points deductions could even be applied onto previous seasons, raising the chance that City will be stripped of their Premier League titles.
