Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua £150m fight is finally CONFIRMED - in Cardiff at 2am on a Friday night in December - and Netflix reveal price it will cost to watch
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua £150m fight is finally CONFIRMED - in Cardiff at 2am on a Friday night in December - and Netflix reveal price it will cost to watch

Anthony Joshua's long-awaited fight with Tyson Fury has finally been confirmed for December 11 at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium – and it will save Joshua around £7.5million in tax.

It is understood each man will pocket around £75m for arguably the biggest bout to be staged on British soil after Joshua’s team, led by Eddie Hearn, succeeded in forcing the promotion’s Saudi backers to scrap plans to stage the showdown in New York.

Hearn initially pushed for Wembley Stadium, but the combination of a roof over the Principality Stadium and the Welsh government’s willingness to bend their late-night curfew swung the fight towards Cardiff. The ring walk is expected to take place around 2am to suit a US-based audience, in line with the demands of Netflix, which will broadcast the heavyweight showdown.

Although the delivery of the fight in Wales will be positioned as a victory for British fight fans, pragmatism around tax was also a key consideration in Hearn’s argument against Madison Square Garden in New York.

As Daily Mail Sport revealed earlier this month, the two fighters would have been taxed around 30 per cent of their purses in America, compared to 20 per cent in the UK, with Joshua particularly unhappy about the prospect of an extra £7.5m being added to his bill. The two-time world champion instead demanded that his contract be honoured, which stipulated a British-based fight.

Boxing supremo Turki Alalshikh said: 'Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury Vs Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans.

'The time for talking is over. Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua. Years in the making. One night to settle it. December 11th. LIVE on Netflix.'

Netflix today confirmed the fight would be available 'at no additional cost' to subscribers. Their general membership pricing starts at £7.99 a month in the UK.

Bookmaker Betfair make Fury the early favourite to win, pricing him at 8/15. Joshua is priced at 13/8.

Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua has been announced for Friday, December 11

The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects

Joshua tweeted: 'I am inspiring a generation', alongside an emoji of the British flag.

His promoter Eddie Hearn, who fought relentlessly to keep the fight in the UK, wrote: 'WE DID IT. Forever indebted to the U.K. public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn’t have got this over the line without you.'

Fury's name appearing first on the card for the Battle of Britain will be an early win for the Gypsy King in his constant PR war with Joshua.

The pair had originally been pencilled in to fight on November 20 at Madison Square Garden in New York, but a determined push from Joshua and Hearn saw the contracts re-negotiated to bring the fight back to British soil.

Hearn had been adamant that British fans deserved the opportunity to watch two of the country's biggest sporting stars go head-to-head at home, and fought hard to make that happen.

Fury, too, wanted the fight in the UK, but had been prepared to accept a move to America because of his concerns that the bout could once again slip away.

Now those fears, after ten years of frustration, have been put to bed. The fight will take place in Cardiff, with the later-than-usual start time expected to mean ring walks at around 2am UK time as organisers attempt to satisfy the American audience watching on Netflix.

Wembley had been the preferred venue for the showdown, but the major stumbling block was securing the necessary late-night permit.

With Netflix and Turki Alalshikh keen for the event to cater to viewers in the United States, organisers required a start time significantly later than would normally be permitted at Wembley.

Cardiff, however, was able to secure the required permit - clearing the final obstacle to bringing the fight back to Britain.

Cardiff's Principality Stadium has come out on top to host the fight after weeks of negotiations

The scale of the occasion is already being felt in the Welsh capital, with hotels in Cardiff now understood to be sold out as supporters scramble to secure accommodation for one of the biggest fights in British boxing.

For Joshua, the move represents the culmination of a push to ensure the fight was staged in the UK.

The former two-times world champion and Hearn had been clear that, after years of watching British heavyweight stars travel overseas for major fights, Joshua-Fury belonged in front of their home crowd.

Fury was willing to compromise on the location if necessary, however, with his priority being to finally get the fight over the line.

The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects.

Joshua won Olympic gold at London 2012 before turning professional, while Fury had already made his professional debut in 2008 and was building an unbeaten record of his own.

For years, the prospect of the two eventually sharing a ring became one of British boxing's great hypothetical match-ups.

Fury's stunning victory over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015 elevated him to the summit of the heavyweight division, while Joshua was rapidly closing in on world-title status himself.

FURY VS JOSHUA - BIG FIGHT ODDS Fury to win - 8/15 Draw - 16/1 Joshua to win- 13/8 Victory method: Tyson Fury by Points or Decision - 16/5 Fury by TKO/KO/DQ - 13/10 Anthony Joshua by Dec/Tech Dec - 15/2 Joshua TKO/KO/DQ - 13/5 Fight to go the distance: Yes - 13/8 No - 4/9 Odds courtesy of Betfair

Joshua claimed the IBF heavyweight title by stopping Charles Martin in 2016 before adding the WBA and IBO belts to his collection. By 2017, Joshua-Fury had evolved from a fantasy fight into a genuine target. But the negotiations repeatedly broke down.

The closest it came to fruition was in 2021, when the two camps appeared to be on the brink of agreeing a two-fight deal.

The proposed showdown was publicly discussed and appeared to be edging towards reality, only for Fury to become contractually obligated to face Deontay Wilder after an arbitration ruling.

That fight ultimately took place, with Fury beating Wilder for a third time, while Joshua embarked on his own defining chapter against Oleksandr Usyk.

Joshua lost his WBA, IBF and WBO titles to Usyk in 2021 before suffering a second defeat to the Ukrainian in their 2022 rematch. Once again, Joshua-Fury seemed to drift further away. Then came another tantalising opportunity.

Negotiations accelerated in late 2022, with both camps discussing a potential December showdown, but the fight again failed to materialise. Fury moved on to other opponents while Joshua began rebuilding his career following the two defeats by Usyk.

The emergence of Alalshikh and the rapid expansion of Saudi Arabia's influence over boxing created a fresh route to making the fight. And this time, the years of disappointment are finally over. The contracts have been signed. Joshua-Fury is no longer a fight being negotiated, teased or promised. It will take place in Cardiff on December 11.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua's torture training! Boxer uses ancient Cossack warriors' stretching machine to prepare himself to fight Tyson Fury in a painful-looking workout routine
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua has been summoning the strength of an ancient warrior as he prepares for his long-awaited bout with Tyson Fury on a stretching machine.

Boxing's biggest battle of the year is expected to take place at Cardiff's Principality Stadium in early December, after a venue war that saw it move from Madison Square Garden in New York.

Despite the superfight being shrouded in uncertainty for much of the year, both Joshua and Fury have been knuckling down in the gym in preparation for their showdown.

Away from the usual training drills associated with boxing, it appears that Joshua is trying something new in order to get the best out of himself when he faces the Gypsy King.

The two-time heavyweight world champion has posted a video to Instagram of him using a Pravilo machine, a stretching machine used by warriors in medieval times.

The machine is a training and conditioning device that originates from Slavic and Russian traditions. It is best-known for being used by historical Cossack warriors for over 1,000 years.

Anthony Josshua has posted a video of him using the ancient warrior Pravilo machine

And if the video posted by Joshua is anything to go by, it can be somewhat of a torturous bit of equipment, based on how it stretches out each limb of the human body.

The 36-year-old can be seen being pulled into a starfish position by the modern version of the machine, which he keeps in his new training gym in Dubai.

Earlier this year, Daily Mail Sport revealed Joshua had in fact quit the UK to move to Dubai – even as thousands tried to flee amid rising panic due to the conflict in the Middle East.

The post on Instagram – which is captioned 'When the instructor says, relax and breathe' – also shows the 251.0lb (113.9kg) frame of Joshua being easily rotated 180 degrees, displaying the strength of his core.

Joshua will be returning to the Welsh capital where he has won twice previously, beating Carlos Takam and Joseph Parker in 2017 and 2018 respectively.

Wembley had looked an ideal venue for the fight, but the strict 11pm curfew has been a sticking point, despite London mayor Sadiq Khan saying he wanted to ensure allowances were made to host the fight.

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury could now be set to fight in Cardiff, Wales in December

Boxing dealmaker Turki Al-Sheikh has been insistent on a start time of 2am.

The streaming giant Netflix has yet to sign off on Cardiff, but American sportswriter Dan Rafael last week reported he had asked Netflix if they would approve, with a source telling him: 'I think they're OK.'

A spokesperson for the Welsh Rugby Union said: 'We'd be delighted to host this fight.

'We are very keen to attract more boxing to the stadium, which has a rich history in the sport, enhanced by its closable roof, unrivalled sight lines and unique city-centre location.'

Sports.title: Chris Eubank Jr fires brutal dig at fierce rival Conor Benn after Brit's devastating second round defeat by Ryan Garcia in Las Vegas
Sports.content:
Chris Eubank Jr brutally mocked his fierce rival Conor Benn after the Brit suffered a devastating defeat by Ryan Garcia.

Benn, 29, was crushed via a second-round stoppage in Las Vegas as they fought for Garcia's WBC welterweight crown.

Benn was dropped by a right hook in round two, and although he managed to beat the count, he struggled to fend off Garcia's subsequent attack, leading to referee Thomas Taylor bringing the fight to a stop, shattering the Brit's world title dream.

It was Benn's first fight at welterweight for four years after he had taken on Eubank Jr at middleweight, meaning he had to cut weight ahead of the fight, something his great rival had to do for their bitter showdowns.

And, Eubank Jr seemed to enjoy his foe's struggles having gone through something similar.

Taking to X shortly after the fight concluded, he posted: 'Welcome to the "fighting after cutting too much weight" club… Enjoy.'

Chris Eubank Jr aimed a brutal dig at Conor Benn after his defeat to Ryan Garcia on Saturday

Benn suffered a heavy defeat by Garcia and his long-time rival Eubank Jr seemed to enjoy it

Eubank Jr had previously posted a photo with Garcia ahead of the fight with the caption: 'Get the job done kid.'

For his two fights against Benn last year, Eubank Jr had to cut down to 160lbs.

He missed that weight for the first bout, before he came under the limit for the second.

Meanwhile, Garcia's triumph over Benn, who was taken to hospital as a precaution, was the Mexican-American's first defence of his WBC crown.

Speaking afterwards, he insisted he hadn't been at full fitness, but outlined his ambitions going forward.

'I have always had the right hand,' he said. 'But I carried a lot of injuries, so I couldn’t really show it.

'I know people question my Mexican heritage because I don’t speak Spanish. But I always feel my people with me and I do it for them. Teofimo Lopez can get it next.

'I want to clean the division out. I want Devin Haney’s a** again, too.'

Sports.title: Why Conor Benn's 85-second humiliation against Ryan Garcia was the inevitable consequence of his fast-tracked career - and how the Brit became a sacrificial pawn in boxing's power struggle, writes JEFF POWELL
Sports.content:
The Wizard Of Oz is now a spectacular fantasy production encompassing the inside of the giant globe called The Sphere which looms large over the Las Vegas Strip.

Where the yellow brick road leads for Conor Benn after his one round, one minute and 25 seconds destruction by the fastest gun in Sin City is a question to which nobody had the answer as he was being ferried to hospital for precautionary checks. And may not have for some time to come.

There is no clear pathway back to the heights to which he was thrust all too prematurely and without justification this Saturday night.

Benn had no place being in the same ring as world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia, who is emerging as the golden goose saviour of American and Mexican boxing. Nor had he done anything like enough in his patchwork career thus far to qualify for the honour of topping the bill at an arena as grand as the T-Mobile in as hallowed a home of boxing as Las Vegas.

This was a match made far away from fight heaven, deep in the casino vaults. Benn Jr leaves here millions of dollars the richer but with not so much as a scintilla of evidence that he will ever be able to mix it with the royalty of the ring, in which King Ry sits upon the throne. He has the payoff but not the legacy he craved.

For the second time in as many months English sport comes home from America with its tail between its legs. Only this clinical beat-down of an inferior boxer was aeons more humiliating than the retreat of our footballers from the World Cup. His defeat more comprehensive than that by Argentina.

Conor Benn was beaten inside two rounds by Ryan Garcia in their welterweight championship fight

Benn's humiliating defeat came after he thrust all too prematurely and without justification into the title fight

Benn had no place in being in the same ring as world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia

Little did Benn know, in his delusion of self grandeur, that in return for securing his family’s financial future he was used as a sacrificial pawn in the power struggle for control of big-time boxing between the houses of Queensberry and Matchroom against the arrival of UFC promoter Dana White on their doorstep.

Garcia, younger of the two by a year but a decade wiser, knew. He tried to cushion Benn’s fall from grace by calling him a ‘good dude who I hope can come back from this.’

But as a man who likes to tell it as it is he felt compelled to add: ‘ I knew exactly how the fight would go. Rushing in against me from the start is not a good idea. Not the way to go. You need patience in this game.’

When it was pointed out to him that Benn has not stopped an opponent for more than four years he added: ‘I must be honest. I did not feel any power in his punches.’

Not that there were many of them. Benn’s charge from the first bell was suicidal against the best, fastest and hardest counter puncher in the world. He ran headlong into a hail of Garcia’s trademark left hooks. To note that he lost the first round is as understated as saying that Goliath had a bad day at the office against David. And when in the second Garcia brought into play the right hand which is now almost as deadly as the left Benn was gone in 85 seconds.

Gone crawling on the canvas and still so unsteady when reeled to his feet that the referee let him continue only so far as the next battering.

Garcia observed: ‘It could have been stopped after the first knock down. I looked into his eyes down there and they were glazed over. He was already gone.’

He echoed the pre-fight fears of many of us that Benn could be in critical jeopardy if this went on too long, saying: ‘It would not have been good for Conor if this lasted any further.’

Benn appears to have been a sacrificial pawn in the power struggle for control of big-time boxing between Queensberry and Matchroom against the arrival of UFC promoter Dana White

Has he lived to fight another day? Dana White sounded less than totally convinced: ‘I’ve told Conor to go on holiday with his family and call me when he’s ready to come back. Then we can try to find the right fight for him.’

That would not be at welter after his ‘hellish’ struggle to cut his poundage. But if he can be hammered into oblivion by a 147-pounder what will become of him if he goes back up two divisions to middleweight?

No such doubts hang over Garcia. Having been saluted to the reverberating rafters of the T-Mobile by his half-brother Mexicans in the delirium of their Independence weekend celebrations, this Californian will resume his American love affair in more world title fights against the likes of Devin Haney and Teofimo Lopez.

He, not Conor Benn in his wildest dreams, is the face and the future of boxing over here.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia destroys Conor Benn with brutal second-round TKO to retain WBC welterweight title in Las Vegas showdown
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia sealed a stunning second-round TKO win over Conor Benn in Las Vegas on Saturday night, retaining his WBC welterweight title in the process.

Benn ran blindly to the slaughter - in a fight which was always a lunge too far - and was left groveling on hands and knees at the feet of the new face of American and Mexican boxing.

Garcia took just four minutes and 25 seconds to devastate and humiliate the upstart son of Nigel the great.

Benn’s predictable sally forth from the first bell was as pointless, desperate and doomed to disaster as The Charge of the Light Brigade.

He was stopped in his tracks by the barrage of left hooks which have taken Garcia to the welterweight championship of the world, over which he will reign for as long as he likes.

The first round was but a prelude to the carnage to come in the 85 seconds which the first round lasted. A punishment doubled by the dynamite which also explodes from Garcia's right fist.

Ryan Garcia sealed a stunning second-round TKO win over Conor Benn in Las Vegas

Garcia took just four minutes and 25 seconds to devastate and humiliate the British star

The 28-year-old retained his WBC welterweight title after the devastating display in Sin City

Conor was reduced to crawling on the canvas by a two-fisted assault to which he had no answer. When he staggered drunkenly to his feet referee Thomas Taylor looked long and hard into his glazed eyes before letting him carry on.

The kill was mercifully swift. A combination of lefts and rights which the third man in the ring could no longer ignore.

This is a warning which his handlers must not forget. This was fight too much, too soon. As Garcia had warned he done nothing to deserve the tilt at the WBC belt his father had worn with such pride.

Nor his elevation the top of a bill in the T-Mobile arena nor in this Mecca of boxing Whether he will ever be ready to mix with the company of prize-ring loyalty is doubtful.

He was not only outclassed, out-sped an out-thought but was treated to punching of almighty power with which his dad could not gift him.

The last 24 hours before the first bell had been consumed by doom-casts about Benn’s drastic weight draining to reach the welter limit of 147 lbs.

Followed by extraordinary claims that he had put on more than two stones following Friday’s weigh-in which, if authentic, would have catapulted him into the ring three divisions even heavier than the super-middleweights.

The truth would out as his robe slipped off. But if he had gorged himself between stepping on the scales and the first bell that might done him much good. Such drastic shifts in poundage are as debilitating as dehydration.

If this was another of the mind games played by Benn and Garcia throughout the wind up and build up it seemed doubtful that any of that would have a material effect on the fight itself. Would anyone in this hardest of all games risk being beaten by indigestion.

Conor was reduced to crawling on the canvas by an assault to which he had no answer

The referee swiftly waved off the bout after a barrage of punches from the American star

The substantive issue was Garcia’s boxing class and knock out power versus Benn’s frenzy and punch resistance.

For the high-paying fans – Benn’s long-haulers from the old country and Garcia’s Gen Z armies of groups from his two nations of identification the US and Mexico – what mattered most was that both delivered the barn-burner of a fight they promised.

Quite beautifully those three congregations fell silent together in commemoration of one boxer who never gave in, never gave up, never delivered a disappointing fight, never offended anyone, never betrayed a friend.

The giant screens in the 02 went into black and white mode for a nostalgic picture of Ricky Hatton who died too young as the previous British fighter to top the bill in what was until recently the fight capital of the world. Over to you Master Benn.

Garcia came to the ring to the strains of a patriotic Mexican song, wrapped in that country’s flag and to rapturous acclaim from the baying Amex majority in the house.

Unabashed and as expected Benn went instantly on the offensive only to be met by barrage of Garcia’s trademark left hooks.

Less than three minutes later it was all over.

Sports.title: Conor Benn shows off remarkable weight transformation after piling on 32 pounds in just HOURS, having been 'dragged to the pits of hell' during excruciating weight cut ahead of mega-fight with Ryan Garcia
Sports.content:
Conor Benn shows off remarkable weight transformation after piling on 32 pounds in just HOURS, having been 'dragged to the pits of hell' during excruciating weight cut ahead of mega-fight with Ryan Garcia

Conor Benn has shown off a dramatic 32lb weight gain just hours after coming in one pound under the 147lb welterweight limit ahead of his bout with USA's Ryan Garcia.

The 29-year-old Briton came in at 146lb (66kg) at Friday's weigh-in for Saturday's fight, half a pound heavier than champion Garcia.

Just 12 hours later, Benn revealed on social media that he had added 32lb, taking him to 12st 10lb (80.73kg).

Speaking at a ceremonial event in front of fans later on Friday, Benn already appeared noticeably bigger, with his face and shoulders having filled out.

'Did it look hard? How did I look?' he asked. 'We'll see tomorrow night how good I really feel.'

Benn had previously said he could weigh as much as 12st 7lb (80kg) by the time he stepped into the ring on Saturday evening (around 4am Sunday, UK time).

‼️ Conor Benn has rehydrated to 178.4 pounds already.



📈 He is up 32.4 pounds (including clothes etc) in just 10 hours! 😱 pic.twitter.com/m6netuS2c1 — EverythingBoxing | Darshan Desai (@EverythingBoxi2) September 12, 2026

Benn revealed on social media that he had added an incredible 32lb hours after the weigh-in

The 29-year-old Briton had come in at 146lb (66kg) at Friday's weigh-in for Saturday's fight, half a pound heavier than champion Garcia before quickly adding it back on

Speaking at a ceremonial event in front of fans later on Friday (above), Benn already appeared noticeably bigger, with his face and shoulders having filled out

He has not fought at welterweight for more than four years, having moved up through the divisions before competing at middleweight during his two-fight rivalry with Chris Eubank Jr.

Now, for the biggest fight of his career, taking on Garcia for the World Boxing Council (WBC) title under the bright lights in Las Vegas, he has had to come all the way back down.

'It feels like I've been dragged down to the pits of hell, had a fight with Satan and God brought me back to life,' he told BBC Sport earlier this week.

'Making weight has been the hardest thing I've done. I haven't made weight for four and a half years so it's going to be hard.'

Whether the weight cut affects Benn's strength and power on Saturday night will be one of the central questions of his WBC world title fight.

Garcia has suggested Benn's move back down could leave him vulnerable, but Benn was dismissive of that concern when he spoke to Daily Mail Sport earlier in the week.

'You think I've been up at middleweight, mixed it with someone who's competed at super middleweight? You think I'm worried about what a lightweight can do to me?' he told this publication.

'You think I'm concerned in the slightest about this guy? I'm not concerned about one little thing he brings to the table… that silly left hook of his is useless. He can bring whatever he wants. It don't concern me.'

USA's Garcia claimed the WBC title with a dominant points victory over Mario Barrios in February and is making the first defence of his belt against Benn on Saturday

Benn's unusual route to this fight has been shaped by his rivalry with Eubank.

Their first meeting at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in April 2025 was the culmination of years of animosity between the two families, with Benn and Eubank Jr inheriting a rivalry that began with their fathers in 1990.

The fight itself was fought at a catchweight above 160lb, with Benn stepping up significantly from his previous division. Eubank won a close decision, leaving Benn to reflect on a performance in which he felt the occasion and the emotion had affected him.

Seven months later, the pair met again at the same venue. This time Benn won the decision, dropping Eubank twice in the final round in a dramatic conclusion to their second fight. It left them level at one victory apiece and appeared to finally close the door on one of British boxing's most talked-about rivalries.

Benn insisted the atmosphere this week is nothing like those two nights when asked whether his hatred for Garcia compared.

'This is nothing like the Eubank fight,' he said. 'The Eubank fight, there was nothing pleasant or friendly or fake about the Eubank fight. There was a lot more raw emotion in that fight and I let that get the better of me the first time. That won't happen here.'

Garcia has won 25 of his 28 professional fights, including 20 by knockout, with two defeats and one no-contest. He claimed the WBC title with a dominant points victory over Mario Barrios in February and is making the first defence of his belt against Benn. Benn has 25 wins, 14 by knockout, and one defeat.

Benn said of his rival: 'He just carries on like a spoiled brat, like a big child who throws his toys out of the pram. I'm not worried about him in the slightest. If anything, I'm gonna have a bit of fun with him. He's a little bit sensitive, highly emotional, and a little bit insecure.'

There is also an uncomfortable shared history between the two men when it comes to drugs testing.

Benn's original 2022 fight with Eubank was cancelled after he returned two adverse findings for clomifene, something he has consistently denied intentionally taking. Garcia subsequently returned an adverse finding for ostarine following his 2024 victory over Devin Haney, which he also denied intentionally taking.

Both men were asked at the fight's press conference whether they had concerns that the other could use performance-enhancing drugs ahead of Saturday's contest.

Neither appeared keen to make it a central issue, with the focus instead returning to the fight itself.

Benn defeated Chris Eubank Jr by unanimous decision to take revenge in their rematch at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium last November

Garcia has also questioned whether Benn's career has prepared him for this level of opposition, arguing that the Briton is taking a step too far by challenging for the world title.

Benn's response was typically blunt. 'How is this too far? He quit against Tank Davis. He got outclassed by Rolly (Romero), and then got a world title shot with Barrios,' he said.

'Then there is me. Stepping up to fight the contenders up at middleweight, fight of the year up at middleweight, avenging my loss. Two big stadium shows. Just come off beating a two-time former world champion and having to make 147, which again I ain't made in four years in six weeks.

'What's he talking about? Ultimately, who cares what he thinks? I don't listen to quitters anyway.'

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia was banned for racial slurs, hit with a $1m doping fine and U-turned on his support for Donald Trump... but America's controversial rock-and-roll boxer is out to save his sport by beating Britain's Conor Benn
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia was banned for racial slurs, hit with a $1m doping fine and U-turned on his support for Donald Trump... but America's controversial rock-and-roll boxer is out to save his sport by beating Britain's Conor Benn

A dazzling talent just reaching his prime will enter the T-Mobile Arena here this Saturday night with the hopes of a fighting nation resting on his shoulders.

Conor Benn, not so much. British boxing is enjoying a boom, not least with its dominance in the marquee heavyweight division.

The young man the son of Nigel is challenging for the world welterweight crown carries the burden of restoring America to its historic pre-eminence in the prize-ring.

Not just by adding to an unusually low head count of their champions but by resuscitating the excitement, the stardust, the impudence, the controversy, the brilliance and the fascination of the public over here with the hardest game of all.

Ryan Garcia is the only poster boy left to them following the retirement of Floyd Mayweather. Vitally, he has all it takes to bring a new generation of fans clamouring to his fights.

At 28 he has the matinee idol looks of a young Elvis Presley which brings the girls squealing into the crowds. A rock and roll bad-boy reputation which chimes with the lads. Showmanship within the ring and charisma outside the ropes.

Ryan Garcia will take on Conor Benn on Saturday night with the American carrying the hopes of a fighting nation on his shoulders

Garcia has reconciled with Andrea Celina Velarde (left), the beautiful mother of two of his three children (above)

Benn has arrived in Las Vegas with the aim of taking the WBC welterweight belt from Garcia

Glamorous blondes vie for his favours. Even though he is resisting those temptations now he has scrapped divorce proceedings and reconciled with Andrea Celina Velarde, the beautiful mother of two of his three children.

And, boy, can he box. The speed of hand and foot. The knock-out punching power. The taunting evasion. And, yes, the conceit which on occasion gets him into trouble.

The two defeats scarring his 28-fight record – against two of America’s other world champions Gervonta Davis and Rolly Romero – came when he was at his most arrogant and complacent.

The no-decision verdict which negated his stand-out victory over Devin Haney was imposed for failing a post-fight drug test for performance-enhancing Ostarine.

Like Benn he protested his innocence: ‘I’ve never knowingly taken drugs.’ His relatives revealed he had been struggling with his mental health and against alcohol. But unlike Conor he preferred taking his punishment – a $1million fine and a 12-month ban – rather than financing a protracted court case which would also have kept him under lengthy suspension.

Not that King Ry - he wears a gold crown for his ring entrances - is prone to compromising his regally unvarnished opinions. Garcia was a vociferous backer of Donald Trump in his first presidential election campaign. But given his Mexican roots he criticised Trump’s second-term deportation policy. Finally he renounced his support, denouncing the Trump administration’s handling of the Epstein Files.

A devout Christian, he called rapper Eminem a satanist and posted on Twitter: ’I don’t support the LGBTQ+. F*** you guys. Rot in hell.’

He called for a boycott of the Olympics for ‘disrespecting Jesus Christ' with the section of the opening ceremony of France 2024 in which drag queens imitating Greek gods were widely supposed to be parodying the Last Supper.

Garcia scrapped divorce proceedings with influencer Andrea in August 2025

Garcia turned down WBC offers to help with his mental health difficulties but progress has been deemed to be made, leading to him fighting and beating Mario Barris in February

The rock-and-roller came out in him when he was arrested for causing $150,000- worth of damage while trashing a room and a corridor at the ritzy Waldorf Astoria hotel in Beverly Hills. That risked a short prison term, which has not been applied.

Another suspension was imposed. This one from competing in fights sanctioned by the WBC for racist slurs live on the internet against the black community and muslims. President Mauricio Sulaiman reported that Garcia had turned down a number of offers from the WBC to help Garcia with his mental health difficulties.

Sulaiman relented last November, saying he recognised the progress made in that regard by the fighter’s large family.

Promptly, this February, Garcia defeated the highly rated Mario Barrios to claim the WBC welterweight belt, inflicting a first round knockdown on his way to a unanimous decision.

The braggadocio bubbles to the surface before fights. As soon as this weekend’s bout was announced he told Benn to his face: ‘You box like amateur trash. You're just a flashy trash can. I’m going to throw you out with trash.’

All the ingredients are there for the making of a turbulent, troubled super-star son of this angry and violent 21st century. All wrapped up in the rare skills and brave heart of a potentially great fighter.

Some indication of whether all that will be enough for him to kindle another golden age in US boxing may be seen in how he deals with Benn. The huge scale of that task is evident in this, my overwhelmingly American list of the 20 greatest boxers of all time, with Lennox Lewis the Brit who came closest to inclusion...

Sports.title: Battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars: Conor Benn takes on troubled Ryan Garcia after burning Eddie Hearn with $10MILLION payday in his sights - but here's why Briton's fate rests solely in the hands of his narcissistic American rival
Sports.content:
‘Who ya like buddy?’ It’s the most asked question in casino-ville as the hours tick down to this Saturday’s world title fight between two angry young men.

One, America’s extravagantly gifted but troubled world welterweight champion. The other, the ever-persistent English challenger who never stops throwing punches whether they connect or not. As if in manic obsession with defeating not only opponents but also his demons and a sceptical outside world.

So, Ryan Garcia or Conor Benn?

When the denizens of this neon gambling Strip in the Nevada desert ask that question they don’t’ want to know which of these two combatants you like personally more than the other. It is their way of trying to find out who you might be betting on to prevail in the atmospheric T-Mobile Arena.

Their inquiries are even more numerous than usual on such occasions as this. Because neither the Americans nor the Mexicans who are thronging here in support of their blood brother by heredity know very much about Benn. Other than the fact he is the son of a fabled icon of the British ring.

On his two previous US visits Benn Jr made hard work of beating men who looked more like nightclub bouncers than professional boxers. Of his exploits back home only the pair of fights against Chris Eubank Jr evoked any interest whatsoever on either side of this border.

What they are aware of is the two positive tests for performance enhancing drugs and the protracted legal battle to technically clear his name which kept him out of the ring for months. Just as they know about Garcia’s conviction and suspension for a similar finding.

Conor Benn is locked in the battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars in Las Vegas

Benn is lining up a $10m payday after burning his bridges with promoter Eddie Hearn

So, what’s to like?

There can be no doubting Benn’s work ethic. He trains like a dervish to manufacture the maximum possible out of however much natural-born ability he inherited from Nigel the Dark Destroyer. Nor does he ever give up. Eubank Jr had to go beyond the normal limits of even this battle-hardened business to inflict the only defeat of Conor’s career thus far. A loss he avenged, albeit in partly contrived and contentious circumstances.

Eubank the Younger was perilously drained in the rematch by a clause in the contract which prevented him rehydrating fully after struggling to cut poundage to meet the agreed catchweight.

What goes around comes around. If not in a full measure of the irony. Benn has had to sweat and strain down by almost a stone from middleweight to make the welterweight championship limit of 147 lbs. As he puts it: ‘Five weeks in hell.’

To say his body looks shredded is putting it mildly. But he has not been subjected to rehydration limitations following his Friday morning visit to the scales.

Eubank was handsomely rewarded to put his health on the line, and now Benn has been lured into similar jeopardy by the fortune – some reports say ten million dollars – he is receiving from UFC boss Dana White to be one of the first poster boys for his venture into boxing.

Benn tells it otherwise: ‘I’m doing this because I relish challenges. Have always wanted to strap on the same green WBC belt my dad was so proud to wear. To start getting the world titles that will leave a legacy for my kids. And to prove wrong everyone who doesn’t give me a chance of winning. That puts all the pressure on him, not me.’

Hearn backed the British fighter during his controversial doping ban saga

Ryan Garcia stands in his way of the WBC title, who is the more talented of the fighters

WEIGH-IN VERDICT: After all the brouhaha Conor Benn made the weight with a full pound to spare After what he described as 'five weeks of hell' dieting down by two divisions he scaled 146 lbs in readiness to challenge world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia here this Saturday night. He did so with a told-you so smile. Throughout the speculation as to whether he could shed the best part of a stone in his training camp journey from middleweight Benn had assured one and all that he would be comfortable at his long-ago weight. Good as his word he came in only half a pound heavier than Garcia. Although he is leaner of hip the muscle is still there on arms and torso. Complete with a six pack as a reminder of his constant work ethic. The slightly taller part/Mexican great white hope of American boxing does look more natural at the weight. But Benn does not appear stressed from all his exertions. Even so Garcia is still a solid odds on favourite in the Vegas betting

Whether or not Benn can take in sufficient liquids and pasta before entering the ring, the dangers to him are greater than those with which Eubank struggled. Garcia, one year the younger at 28 but the riper in championships experience, has authentic one-hit-knockout power.

Benn goes into his first world championship fight reliant on the cumulative effect of his non-stop output. The problem with this is that King Ry is probably the best counterpuncher in the world right now and Benn’s headlong style will likely suit him nicely, thank you.

To complicate the evaluation, both have blotted their copybooks as people. Garcia, the handsome heartthrob, burnished his bad-boy rock-star image by trashing a five-star hotel room. He also needed his family’s help with overcoming mental problems aggravated by a passing fancy for social drugs and booze.

Benn invited mockery for claiming initially that he failed his drugs tests because of eating enough eggs to fill the shelves of all the Tescos in London. Then, in order to collect his bonanza from Mister UFC, he unceremoniously dumped his long-time promoter Eddie Hearn who had bankrolled his hefty legal costs and loaned him half a million quid to help sustain his flamboyant lifestyle through that crisis.

Not much to like there.

So, when it comes to the fight, who ya like? The answer is not Conor Benn’s to give. Because the real question is which Ryan Garcia turns up.

If it is the narcissist whose arrogant complacency has cost him a couple of big fights, it may not be totally beyond the bounds of possibility that Conor could pull off one of the major upsets by a British boxer abroad.

If it is King Ry fully prepared and ready to unfurl all the majesty then we can only hope the son of Nigel is not seriously hurt.

Sports.title: Antonelli angry at "unnecessary" Azerbaijan GP qualifying crash
Sports.content:
Formula 1 world championship leader Kimi Antonelli says he needs to "do a much better job" after an "unnecessary" qualifying crash in Baku left him 16th on the grid.

Antonelli made an unforced error in Q1 when he tagged the inside wall in Turn 1 left-hander to start his second flying lap, sustaining terminal suspension damage that forced him to park his Mercedes W17.

Antonelli's first lap had already qualified him for Q2, but with the Italian unable to take part, he is facing a comeback in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix on Saturday from 16th on the grid.

To add insult to injury, Mercedes proved the class of the field in Baku as team-mate George Russell demolished the competition to take pole by eight tenths, meaning Antonelli likely cost himself a front-row start.

"It was just a misjudgement with the grip changing so much," Antonelli explained. "An unnecessary one in Q1, and it's a very good reminder that like this, things don't go my way, so I need to do a much better job.

"I had a lot more headwind compared to the lap before, so the front just was much stronger, and I turned in roughly in the same spot, but obviously the car turned more and I clipped the wall."

Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT images via Getty Images

With Antonelli missing a large chunk of Thursday practice due to a hydraulic issue, the 20-year-old had already been on the back foot all weekend, so he acknowledged he "wasn't 100% there" and Russell would have been tough to beat.

"George has been doing an incredible job this weekend," Antonelli admitted. "He's been feeling very good with the car, so for sure he has made the difference. I have to be honest with that, but also the car has been very, very quick."

The last time Antonelli started from the rear of the grid, the Italian put in a drive for the ages with a spectacular comeback to win the Italian GP in Monza.

But while Baku's 6km street circuit also offers overtaking potential on its long straight, Antonelli cautioned a Monza repeat would be much more difficult to pull off.

"A good start, stay out of trouble, and then try to set a really good pace," Antonelli summed up his Saturday plans. "Obviously, it's going to be a bit harder than Monza because it's a bit harder to overtake here, but I believe we can still do a good race.

"I have nothing to lose, and I just need to do the best race I can. With experience, you learn how to move forward. Of course, this weekend has been a bit off with everything, but tomorrow I think we can do a good race."

Sports.title: F1 Azerbaijan GP: Russell dominates to pole after Antonelli crashes out in qualifying
Sports.content:
Mercedes driver George Russell has beaten Charles Leclerc to take a dominant pole at Formula 1's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, while team-mate and title favourite Kimi Antonelli is set for a comeback race from 16th after crashing in Q1.

At the 6km Baku City Circuit, Antonelli tagged the barriers on the inside of the Turn 1 left-hander during Q1 and was unable to limp back home in his Mercedes W17 with terminal front-left suspension damage. Antonelli had already set a time quick enough to advance to Q2, but was out of the session and is set to start 16th at best.

Team-mate Russell, who had already proven rapid all weekend, capitalised to take a dominant pole ahead of Leclerc and Oscar Piastri - the Briton's fifth pole of the campaign.

McLaren sprung an early surprise in Q3 when Piastri and Lando Norris jumped early pacesetter Russell to top the first barrage of qualifying runs. Off the back of a messy brace of practices, the papaya squad had yet to string together optimal qualifying laps, with Norris even suspecting something was wrong in his car in Q1.

But Piastri's 1m43.571s lap proved an achievable target for Russell to beat, with the Briton going half a second faster on his second run to set a rapid 1m43.037s, which none of his competitors could find an answer for.

On the final run, Russell took yet another five-tenths chunk out of his own benchmark to set a dominant 1m42.526s pole lap.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT images via Getty Images

Ferrari employed a different run plan by delaying its first run, which yielded Leclerc provisional second, and the Monegasque found another tenth that secured second on the grid ahead of Piastri, albeit a sobering eight tenths behind Russell.

Isack Hadjar celebrated his return from injury with fourth on the grid, while Norris slipped up on his final attempt and settled for fifth ahead of Hamilton. Pierre Gasly secured seventh for Alpine as Max Verstappen could only manage eighth after having to slow down for yellow flags caused by Norris on his final lap.

Carlos Sainz made full use of Williams' upgraded FW48 to claim ninth, as Franco Colapinto qualified 10th following an erratic Q3 session.

Russell topped Q2 with a late 1m43.462s effort, two tenths ahead of Verstappen as it promised to set up a tight pole shoot-out.

The battle for the final Q3 spots was as close as it has been all season with Williams now in the hunt, and Sainz capitalised to go ninth and claim a rare Q3 berth. The dramatic rate of track evolution meant drivers were fuelled up for multiple laps to try and peak on their final run In the dying seconds, Alpine's Colapinto snatched 10th away from Haas driver Oliver Bearman, joining his team-mate Gasly in the next segment.

Racing Bulls was the biggest victim in Q2 with Liam Lawson out in 12th, followed by the second Williams of Alex Albon and Esteban Ocon in the remaining Haas. Arvid Lindblad could only muster 15th to continue what has been a messy weekend so far for the Briton, off the back of an FP2 crash which team principal Alan Permane ascribed to "rookie enthusiasm".

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

Russell also led the way in Q1 after Antonelli disappeared, demoting Verstappen at the end of the session with a 1m43.615s lap. In the background, Williams comfortably made it through with both of its upgraded cars.

On a high-speed track exposing its power unit deficit, Audi paid the price of Williams' progress as Gabriel Bortoleto and Nico Hulkenberg were both eliminated in 17th and 18th. The four cars from Cadillac and Aston Martin were also punched out, with Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll already facing a back-of-the-grid penalty for Honda power unit changes.

Sports.title: F1 Azerbaijan GP: Verstappen beats Russell and Hamilton to top FP3
Sports.content:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen has surprisingly topped third and final practice for Formula 1's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, pipping Mercedes driver George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton on Baku's tricky street circuit.

Verstappen took command at the very end of the one-hour session as teams switched to qualifying runs, defying Mercedes' favourite status in Baku by catching a big slipstream to go fastest.

FP3, held in less representative conditions than qualifying later on Friday afternoon, got off to a quiet start, with the Alpines leading the early running some way off Thursday's FP2 pace. The big-hitters started flexing their collective muscle 15 minutes into the session with Charles Leclerc's second attempt on softs - yielding a 1m45.564s - demoting Ferrari team-mate Hamilton's effort.

As drivers tried to hone their slipstreaming timing for qualifying, with the Baku City Circuit's giant 2km straight making a tow a crucial element of a competitive lap, Red Bull's Verstappen lunged to first place, only to be deposed by Hamilton's 1m45.093s moments later.

Conditions appeared to be gustier than on Friday as race control deployed a brief virtual safety car for a tree branch which was swept onto the track. The wind also made cars less predictable to drive. Verstappen reported a Red Bull which was "jumping like a kangaroo" before going deep into the Turn 15 runoff, one of several drivers to make good use of Baku's escape roads.

Aston Martin's Lance Stroll was not so lucky as he tagged the wall in Turn 1, damaging his front-left suspension which prompted the Canadian to park the car.

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Liam Fabre

Mercedes, which was ominously quick on Thursday, started mixing it up at the halfway mark with Antonelli pipping Leclerc by half a tenth courtesy of a 1m45.046s lap, before Russell claimed top spot with a 1m44.715s lap - both on medium tyres rather than softs.

The Silver Arrows then showed their hands on the softest tyre compound as Russell put down a 1m44.177s marker with 15 minutes to go. As Russell shaved off some time with his subsequent 1m44.021s tour, Antonelli conceded 0.252s to his team-mate.

Verstappen benefitted from a huge slipstream to split the Mercedes cars in second, flattering the real performance of the Red Bull on a weekend set to be dominated by the championship leaders, and the Dutchman ultimately set a 1m43.922s lap to top the session.

Russell could have likely gone quicker still, however, but locked up the fronts into Turn 1 before going straight on in Turn 7, managing to bring the car to a halt without tapping the wall.

With a last-minute effort Hamilton pipped Antonelli to third, followed by Leclerc and Alpine's Pierre Gasly. McLaren's low-profile weekend continued with Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris in seventh and eighth respectively despite the team's upgrades to improve its low-speed cornering.

The returning Isack Hadjar claimed ninth for Red Bull ahead of the second Alpine car of Franco Colapinto.

Sports.title: Why "dangerous" Hamilton-Lawson incident in Azerbaijan GP practice hasn't led to change
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton was reprimanded for impeding Liam Lawson during Thursday's second practice in FP2 but this wasn't the end of the matter.

Even before a single car had turned a wheel on the Baku City Circuit, concerns had been raised about how cars running slowly to harvest or conserve electrical energy through the final corners could represent a hazard to those on a push lap.

In previous years, even those cars not trying to set a timed lap would travel reasonably quickly through Turns 16-19, a left-hander followed by two kinks leading onto the main straight. But the need to preserve electrical power for the straight means there are now huge disparities in speed between those pushing through this area and those just about to open a full-send lap.

The incident between Hamilton and Lawson was a textbook example of what the drivers had feared: Hamilton was on an out-lap, and had been warned Lawson was approaching on a flying lap. Hamilton thought he had enough margin but was caught out because, in the present generation of cars, the amount of electrical boost available is governed by software.

In this case, the driver cannot command full power until the car arrives at a predetermined point on the main straight – otherwise the battery would begin to deplete and enter the ‘ramp-down' phase too early, costing top speed.

"I could see him, I thought the gap was enough, I got to full throttle," Hamilton said after FP2. "Literally as I got into [Turn] 18, the car just died. Swamped up the gap massively and that could happen to anyone."

The need to preserve battery levels for the long straight has made the preceding corners potentially dangerous Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

At the time, Lawson, who had to swerve to avoid the slow-moving Ferrari, took to the radio to emote vociferously: ""Oh my god, that is so f****** dangerous," he complained.

Once the adrenaline had subsided, Lawson agreed with Hamilton.

"There's not really a lot you can do when you look at it," he said. "Lewis comes out of [Turn] 16 in his full throttle, he's got two or three seconds to me which is normally plenty of gap but the speed difference is just so big. He's not deploying anything, I'm deploying everything and you have 60, 70, 80 km/h speed difference, which is bad.

"The problem is if he gets out of the way before 18 and slows down, if there's another car behind me then the speed difference is enormous. So it's something we have to look at overnight.

"If there's something we can do, it's going to have to be before 16 honestly because once you come out of that corner and you're committed."

Ahead of the weekend, race director Rui Marques set out clear guidelines in his regular briefing document for how drivers should tackle this section.

"Cars on out-laps or slow laps should keep extreme left (i.e. not "offline" in middle of track) from exit T16 through to entry T18," said the competition notes.

Drivers on out-laps are instructed to stay on the "extreme left" of the track after Turn 16 Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

"We consider that teams/drivers can and should manage traffic gaps before T18 (going as slowly as required being on the extreme left) to ensure that they can transit between the apex of T18 and apex of T19 without impeding an approaching car that is trying to set a competitive lap time.

"Cars on out-laps or slow laps should keep "extreme" right exit T19 until they achieve relevant speed to open the following lap."

Among the reasons for Hamilton receiving a reprimand after the FP2 incident was that he had failed to obey the instruction to stay on the extreme left. But he felt that a better solution was required – perhaps to enable drivers to have access to more power through that section.

"We'll talk about it in the drivers briefing, about what we could do," he said.

"What they should do is on a single lap, when we're doing a pushing lap, we get max power out of the last corner. When you come through 19 [the final kink before the straight section], it resets, and then you have a little bit more power than the other car.

"There should just be nobody going slow ever through 18 and 19. Even if you're on a slow lap, you still have to go flat out through 18 and 19 with full power. That would mean no one's ever going slow through that section."

Autosport understands that this was indeed discussed during Thursday night's drivers' briefing, but was ultimately vetoed by the teams. The scenario is similar to that in the season-opening Australian Grand Prix weekend, when Turn 9 on the Albert Park circuit was described by the drivers as "sketchy" under the new technical regulations, because it came at the end of one of five straightline mode (SLM) zones where the cars' active aerodynamics are deployed.

Ahead of FP3, the FIA announced it was removing that SLM zone, only to have to revert to the original format after pushback from the teams. There, as in Azerbaijan this weekend, the rationale was understood to be technical and performance-related: removing that SLM zone would undo all the work the teams had done to plan their energy management.

As such, the race director's original "keep left" instructions will stand for FP3 and qualifying in Baku.

Sports.title: Imola or Qatar and Abu Dhabi? What’s really going on with the end of the 2026 F1 season
Sports.content:
As Formula 1 enters the final phase of the season, with three triple-headers on paper, the question remains where the 2026 season will end. In theory, the Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix are still scheduled to take place, and F1 strongly emphasises that, as things stand, this also remains plan A.

At the same time, F1 has to be prepared for a scenario in which those races have to be cancelled because of all the continued unrest in the Middle East, and so the green light has been given behind the scenes to work on a plan B. Unsurprisingly, that plan B is the Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari.

Sources within F1 told Autosport that the organisers in Imola have now been given the green light to build the grandstands and make preparations as if the race in Emilia-Romagna will take place.

This does not mean it will actually happen – Qatar and Abu Dhabi still constitute plan A – but Formula One Management (FOM) has to press ahead with an alternative in order to guarantee a season finale after the Las Vegas Grand Prix in any scenario.

Building the grandstands and continuing all preparations without final confirmation of a race logically brings financial risks, but sources in the paddock say F1 is covering all those risks. This means F1 is fully paying for the preparations – including the construction of the temporary grandstands – and that Imola will not face any financial risk regardless of the outcome.

In the scenario that the Imola option ultimately proves unnecessary, this approach will cost F1 money, but the sport has no choice. After all, if the situation in the Middle East escalates further a month before the scheduled races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, F1 cannot afford not to have a plan B ready to go.

This also underlines that F1 wants to wait as long as possible before making a final decision, while it should not be forgotten how financially attractive the final two race weekends in the Middle East are.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali initially said a decision would be made in mid-September, but the situation has changed since then.

Several team principals currently point to mid-October as the new timeframe for clarity, although F1 stresses that there is no hard deadline. From a logistical perspective, there is still relatively little urgency at this stage, as long as Imola is fully ready to step in on the first weekend of December.

The teams have also been informed of this reality and are not particularly concerned for now, several team principals stressed during Thursday’s press conference in Baku.

“I believe that Stefano was targeting to tell us in mid-October, right? So, we all know what the situation is”, Haas team boss Ayao Komatsu said.

“I believe that Imola is getting ready in case we have to do it. I think the challenges are, for instance, things like European motorhome structure, etcetera. All those people who look after them, they have a winter job, so we need to find alternative people to do that.

“But I’m sure we all, as a family, community, will make sure if we have to do that, that will happen. But hopefully, as a baseline, we can go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi. That would be really good.”

Audi team principal Mattia Binotto shares the same view and confirms that F1 teams should normally be informed by F1 around mid-October.

Mattia Binotto, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Joe Portlock / LAT Images via Getty Images

“As we discussed during the F1 Commission last Monday, mid-October is the last call for such a decision.”

Binotto does not see the potentially low temperatures as an obstacle to a possible season finale in Imola.

“The main challenges are more organisation and logistics, I would think. From a technical point, often we may say wintertime, snow tyres, but at the end, as a matter of fact, the average temperature in Imola in that time of the year is hotter than Las Vegas by the time we’ve got the race in Las Vegas.

“So I don’t think that’s a true concern. It’s more from the organisation and the logistics, really. And again, mid-October, hopefully we may do the right decision.”

Sports.title: Cadillac makes three major tech hires including former Red Bull design chief
Sports.content:
The Cadillac F1 Team has snapped up engineering trio Craig Skinner, Eric Blandin and Tim Lean as it aims to accelerate its development.

Former Red Bull chief designer Skinner, the architect of Red Bull's championship winning RB19, joins as Cadillac's chief development engineer. Autosport understands Skinner was close to a move to Alpine, but is instead taking up the US-owned team's offer.

Former Aston Martin deputy tech chief Eric Blandin becomes the team's head of aerodynamics. Experienced aerodynamicist Tim Lean joins as Chief Engineer - Aerodynamics Modelling and Simulation, following stints at McLaren, Red Bull and Ferrari, reporting to Blandin.

Cadillac made its debut this season as an 11th expansion team, set up by former Manor man Graeme Lowdon with veteran grand prix winners Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas as its drivers.

The team made a respectable debut with its MAC-26 car powered by Ferrari engines, but with management keen to step up its development pace Cadillac CEO Dan Towriss moved to replace Lowdon during the summer break with former Alpine executive Marcin Budkowski.

Having been mired in various operational and build quality issues, Budkowski first job is to further strengthen the team's procedures and tap into co-owner General motors' existing resources.

Craig Skinner, former Red Bull Racing Chief Designer Photo by: Red Bull Content Pool

Meanwhile, the US-owned squad has now also moved to shore up its technical leadership group with three big-name signings as the team prepares its 2027 sophomore campaign.

Given the long lead time and gardening leave periods involved, Cadillac announced the three would "all join the team in the next few months."

“These appointments represent a vital step in the technical evolution of the team,” said Marcin Budkowski, Team Principal, Cadillac Formula 1 Team. “Bringing together experienced leadership across development, aerodynamics and modelling will help us create a stronger integrated technical organization and improve performance on track. Craig, Eric and Tim bring race and championship-winning experience to Cadillac F1 in areas that are central to our long-term development.”

Cadillac recently set up shop in a brand-new UK headquarters in Silverstone, while working on a new state-of-the-art base in Fishers, Indiana.

The signing of Skinner, Blandin and Lean appears to be a clear sign the Cadillac team is full steam ahead despite lingering doubts of part of its ownership group amid a wider investigation into Mark Walter, owner of the TWG Global group which is the team's majority owner.

Sports.title: Chadwick joins exclusive list after Williams F1 test
Sports.content:
Jamie Chadwick became the latest female to drive a Formula 1 car after completing a Testing of Previous Cars programme for Williams at Portimao.

The 28-year-old completed 32 laps in Portugal on Monday aboard the FW47 from last year, as part of her development driver duties for the British outfit.

It meant she became the second female to drive an F1 car this year after Doriane Pin completed a Mercedes test, and the first to do so for Williams since Susie Wolff in 2015.

The test has added to a glittering career for Chadwick, who has claimed three W Series titles, race wins in Indy NXT and the European Le Mans Series, plus a role as test driver for the Genesis Hypercar programme.

Chadwick, who has been affiliated with Williams since 2019, said: "It was a phenomenal day and an incredible experience.

“Few things can prepare you for driving a Formula 1 car at speed around a track like Portimao.

Jamie Chadwick, Williams Photo by: Williams

“But it was everything I imagined and 10 times more. I’m incredibly grateful to the Atlassian Williams F1 Team for this opportunity.

“I remember being young and watching Susie Wolff step into a Williams F1 car and how much that inspired my own journey.

“I’d love to be able to do the same for the next generation, and the experience I gained today will make a real difference both to my own racing and to what I can pass on to the drivers coming through.

“I’m so grateful and incredibly happy with how the day went. It’s an experience I’ll remember for a very long time - I’d go as far as saying it’s been the best day of my life so far."

The test also comes ahead of the return of the Portuguese Grand Prix at Portimao next year, with the Algarve circuit previously featuring on the calendar twice in 2020 and 2021.

“Jamie Chadwick is an inspiration for millions of women and girls who has broken records at every level,” said Williams team boss James Vowles.

Jamie Chadwick, Williams Photo by: Williams

“She has thoroughly earned this F1 test opportunity with Atlassian Williams F1 Team.

"Jamie gathered important data for the team as F1 prepares to return to Portimao next year.

“Her feedback and performance were impressive as we knew they would be. This clearly shows there is a path for women to compete at the top level.

“I look forward to seeing how Jamie uses this experience to advance her own driving and advise our young drivers on what it takes to drive an F1 car.”

Sports.title: F1 Azerbaijan GP: Russell tops FP2 from Antonelli as Lindblad crashes
Sports.content:
Mercedes driver George Russell ended Thursday's practice running at Formula 1's Azerbaijan Grand Prix on top after comfortably leading FP2.

Russell held off Mercedes team-mate and championship leader Kimi Antonelli as the Silver Arrows enjoyed a comfortable cushion through the fast streets in Baku.

With the race taking place on Saturday to observe a national holiday on Sunday, the on-track proceedings got underway on Thursday. On the high-speed 6km street circuit stretching along the Caspian Sea, the red flag came out after 20 minutes for a crash by Racing Bulls rookie Arvid Lindblad, who tagged the protruding Turn 9 wall at the narrow castle section, part of the UNESCO heritage site the circuit loops around.

The session resumed at the halfway mark following some debris cleaning, but in Oliver Bearman's case the second half of FP2 was short-lived, with the Haas driver reporting a power unit failure coming out of the pits.

It took until a paddock wide move towards soft-tyre one-lap runs for drivers to challenge Verstappen's early medium-tyre benchmark. Ferrari's Charles Leclerc first dipped below the Dutchman's time after 25 minutes with a 1m44.473s, before FP1 leader Russell convincingly took over command with a 1m43.759s, seven tenths quicker than the Ferrari.

But Mercedes had more ion that tank still as it looks ominously quick on the power-hungry Baku city circuit. Russell took another generous bite of his best time to set a 1m43.347s lap, with Antonelli slotting into second, five tenths behind, after sitting out a chunk of first practice with a mechanical issue.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

Verstappen moved past Leclerc into third, yet still over eighth tenths in arrears of Russell as Mercedes ended the day with a 1-2 result. Hamilton was two tenths behind Leclerc in fifth, followed by the first McLaren car in the hands of Lando Norris.

McLaren, which is introducing a sizeable upgrade package aimed at improving low-speed performance, was still optimising its updates car as Norris followed 1.5s behind without setting a representative qualifying simulation. Pierre Gasly split the two McLarens in seventh ahead of Oscar Piastri, with Isack Hadjar and Esteban Ocon rounding out the top 10.

Alongside the on-track issues for Lindblad and Bearman, there was more trouble for Aston Martin and Honda as Fernando Alonso only managed nine laps before being consigned to the garage with a suspected oil leak in the power unit.

Sports.title: Verstappen says engine problem cost him half a second to Hadjar | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen revealed a problem with his power unit left him at a disadvantage in qualifying for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

The Red Bull driver was quickest in the final practice session at the Baku City Circuit . However he fell to eighth in qualifying, four places behind his team mate Isack Hadjar

Verstappen’s final qualifying run was spoiled when Lando Norris went off in front of him, triggering yellow flags. But Verstappen said that was only “the last thing that happened” in a qualifying session which had already gone badly wrong.

“The whole qualifying, I’m just lacking top speed,” he told Sky. “I’m half a second a lap off just on top speed, even compared to my team mate. The engine was just not working. So that’s one problem.

“Then in Q3, in my middle lap, just trying to start the lap, the battery didn’t charge. So you start a lap with half a battery, so you have to abort, then you lose temperature because you don’t have enough power, basically. And that then snowballs into the final lap.

“I started the lap, but again, no top speed, a yellow flag in my lap, not enough tyre temperature, and then that’s where you are.”

Verstappen was second-fastest in Q1 and Q2 but he was slower in Q3 than in both the earlier sessions. “We were in a really good place the whole weekend and we had a disaster of a qualifying because of a lot of issues,” he concluded.

Sports.title: Sainz summoned over second yellow flag infringement after qualifying | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Williams’ best grand prix qualifying result of the season so far is under threat as the stewards have summoned Carlos Sainz Jnr over an incident.

Sainz is being investigated for failing to slow for yellow flags during qualifying. He passed yellow flags when Lando Norris went off ahead of him during Q3, though Norris’s car drove away before Sainz reached the scene of the incident.

He has already been reprimanded today for the same infringement. The stewards found he failed to respond correctly to yellow flags during final practice.

Stewards’ verdict on Sainz’s final practice infringement

The stewards did not issue a grid drop to Sainz over his infringement in practice after taking into account how briefly the yellow flag was displayed for.

“A single yellow was displayed in marshalling sector six shortly before [Sainz] entered the sector,” the stewards ruled. “Sainz explained that, approaching turn four, he briefly noticed a light signal in his peripheral vision but was not certain that it was yellow. He therefore asked the team by radio whether a yellow flag was being displayed.

“The onboard video also showed that a yellow warning light was flashing on Sainz’s steering wheel, indicating the yellow sector. Sainz explained that in the circumstances he had not been able to pay attention to this warning.

“Approaching turn four, Sainz braked slightly earlier than on the reference lap, but subsequently applied less brake pressure. At the exit of turn four he accelerated more moderately than on the reference lap. Overall, he lost approximately 0.10 seconds in the relevant sector.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“From the exit of turn four Sainz was able to see the green light marking the end of the yellow sector. Sainz acknowledged that, having seen the green light, he should have understood that he was still travelling within a yellow sector. Nevertheless, on the straight approaching the green light he accelerated up to the limiter while still within the yellow sector.

“The stewards considered the fact that the single yellow was displayed only shortly before Sainz entered marshalling sector six as a mitigating circumstance. However, taking into account the visible yellow indication, the warning displayed on the steering wheel, the telemetry and, in particular, Sainz’s acceleration while still within the yellow sector after the green light had become visible, the stewards were not satisfied that Sainz had sufficiently reduced speed and exercised the required caution for a single yellow.

“The stewards therefore determine that Sainz failed to sufficiently reduce speed under the single yellow.

“The standard penalty under the Penalty Guidelines for such an infringement is a drop of five grid positions. However, the stewards considered that there were mitigating circumstances, in particular the very short period between the single yellow being displayed and Sainz entering the relevant marshalling sector. The stewards also considered the penalties applied in comparable cases, where a driving reprimand has consistently been imposed in circumstances warranting mitigation from the standard penalty. The stewards therefore considered a driving reprimand appropriate and consistent with those precedents.”
