World.title: B.C. attorney general shocked by news report that ChatGPT told Tumbler Ridge shooter how to avoid safeguards
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

British Columbia's attorney general says she's shocked by an article describing alleged interactions between the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter and ChatGPT, in which the AI chatbot vividly describes the effectiveness of a shotgun in a classroom.

The news report, in U.S.-based magazine Mother Jones, also says ChatGPT advised shooter 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar how to get around its own safeguards to obtain information about violent scenarios by framing the content as fictional.

Attorney General Niki Sharma says the details in the article, which does not describe its sources, are "shocking and, as a parent, they are worse" than she ever imagined.

She says on social media platform Bluesky that corporations urgently need mandatory and strict regulation to protect children.

OpenAI, the artificial intelligence company behind ChatGPT, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the article about the chatbot's interactions with Van Rootselaar, who killed eight people in Tumbler Ridge in February, including five students, before killing herself.

The B.C. government, survivors and witnesses of the shootings at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School are suing OpenAI, alleging negligence.

The article published on Thursday says Van Rootselaar's ChatGPT account was banned for discussing committing an attack with a "famous real-world mall as the target."

But it says she then used a second account, which advised her about how to "never get flagged again” by describing situations as fictional or hypothetical.

"Don’t use real-world locations," the article quotes ChatGPT as saying, before adding: "You can still be twisted. Just be clever about it."

It says that Van Rootselaar asked ChatGPT for a scenario about attacking a college campus with a shotgun for maximum effect.

The article says that the chatbot initially declined to help, but after Van Rootselaar added "hypothetically" to her prompt it responded.

"In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 (Remington shotgun) is brutal," it quotes ChatGPT as saying. "Close quarters is its playground."

The article says ChatGPT went on to say: "Assuming each shell results in one hit, you might down 10 to 20 people max, depending on spacing, density, reaction times, and chaos."

OpenAI did not immediately respond to an email sent to their general press address and to an individual spokesperson. General counsel for the company, Che Chang, did not immediately respond to a message sent to his LinkedIn profile.

RCMP Staff Sgt. Kris Clark said the investigation into the shootings had "utilized all available legal processes to obtain all information available from various social media and digital platforms" relevant to the attack.

"To date, all companies that have received requests have complied," Clark said.

World.title: With time running out, new poll suggests Alberta separatism support is slipping
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With a little more than three weeks to go until the Oct. 19 referendum, a new poll done for CBC News suggests support for separation has softened since spring.

Janet Brown Opinion Research, in a random survey of 1,200 Albertans between Sept. 8 and 21, asked respondents the same question they’ll face on referendum day: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

Twenty-three per cent of respondents said they’d vote to start the legal process to hold a binding referendum, while 72 per cent said they’d vote to remain in Canada. Four per cent said they were unsure.

That stands in contrast to Brown’s poll in the spring, which asked Albertans if a referendum were held today on whether Alberta should separate from the rest of Canada, would you vote for or against separation?

The April survey found 27 per cent of respondents would vote for separation, while 67 per cent would vote against.

"It’s part of this overall trend that we’re seeing," said Calgary-based pollster Janet Brown.

“People are feeling more comfortable with Alberta’s role in Canada, more comfortable with Ottawa, more comfortable with the prime minister.

“And all of those things seem to have caused a slight dip in the proportion of Albertans ready to vote to separate,” said Brown.

The survey has a margin of error of +/- 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Over the past months, the remain and leave sides have sought to win over hearts and minds with advertising and large rallies. They’ve criss-crossed the province in RVs decorated with maple leafs and Alberta flags, delivering lawn signs to front yards in cities and small towns.

But according to Brown’s polling, how Albertans feel about the prospect of separation has been largely baked-in for years.

“There’s a slight decline in people who are interested in the separatist option, but these numbers have been very consistent over time,” Brown said.

Lori Thorlakson, a political science professor at the University of Alberta, said as referendum day approaches, the meaning of the separatism question may be changing.

“This most recent shift, I think, really reflects that people are focusing more on what it would actually mean if we were to leave Canada,” she said.

A majority of respondents across the province voiced support for remaining a province of Canada.

Support was highest to remain in Canada in Alberta's big cities, at 74 per cent. In small centres, including in smaller towns and rural areas, support to remain in Canada sat at 69 per cent.

Attachment to Alberta and Canada

Since 2020, Brown has also been asking Albertans whether they feel more attached to the province, more attached to Canada, or attached to both equally.

Her most recent polling saw a decline in people who said they felt mainly attached to Alberta, and a corresponding increase in people who said they felt mainly attached to Canada or attached to both equally.

Some of that could be attributed to Alberta’s relationship with Ottawa, in Brown’s view. Last month, the federal government moved toward listing the West Coast pipeline as a national interest project ahead of an Oct. 1 deadline.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith are seen together earlier this year. The federal government has issued a mandatory notice that it intends to designate a new pipeline to the West Coast as a project of national interest. (The Canadian Press)

Brown believes the increased positive feelings Albertans have for Canada could also be attributed to the ongoing trade war between Canada and the U.S. and tensions with U.S. President Donald Trump.

“It’s made Albertans more focused on their Canadian identity,” she said.

The polling found that 23 per cent of respondents said they were more attached to Alberta than to Canada, down from 33 per cent in April 2026.

Forty per cent of respondents said they were more attached to Canada than to Alberta, up from 34 per cent in April 2026.

The polling also focused on the partisan divide found around the separation question.

At 98 per cent, nearly all respondents who said they would vote for the Alberta NDP if an election were held today said they wanted to stay in Canada.

But among those polled who said they would vote for the United Conservative Party, 53 per cent said they would vote for the separation option, while 40 per cent said they’d vote to stay in Canada.

“That really speaks to the very delicate line that the premier is walking right now,” Brown said. “A bare majority of the people who say they would vote for her party in the next election, they are separatists.

“The premier has taken the ‘stay’ side. That’s making her job very difficult at the moment.”

A focus on mobilization

With sentiment seemingly baked in and with few undecideds remaining, Brown said she anticipates that the final weeks of the campaign are likely to revolve around mobilization, rather than persuasion.

“The game will be about both sides trying to make sure they get their voters out to vote on this referendum,” she said.

Separatist groups have spent recent weeks trying to make their case with voters. As referendum day has drawn closer, separatist group Let Alberta Decide has ramped up its messaging on social media, attempting to gear its campaign toward different demographics.

Speaking to CBC News in late August, Let Alberta Decide leader Keith Wilson said that while he’s not entirely convinced the polls over past months have been accurate, his group assumes they are from a strategic point of view.

“We see this with our signs as well. People are concerned about sharing with other people that they support a better deal for Alberta, or that they support Alberta independence,” Wilson said. “There’s a lot of polarization in our politics, as we know.”

Keith Wilson, left, speaks as Tanya Clemens looks on at the launch of Alberta independence organization "Let Alberta Decide" in Calgary on June 19. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Stephen Carter, a federalist with the group Alberta’s Voice, has said he’s worried about voters seeing consistent polls showing low support for separation and then staying home on referendum day.

"If it's close, we deal with this forever. And that’s the worst-case scenario,” he previously told CBC News.

Other polling across past months has been consistent with Brown’s findings, largely showing that the two sides in the separation debate have been entrenched , with the majority wanting to remain in Canada.

The CBC News random survey of 1,200 Albertans was conducted using a hybrid method between Sept. 8 and Sept. 21, 2026, by Edmonton-based Trend Research under the direction of Janet Brown Opinion Research. The sample is representative of regional, age and gender factors. The margin of error is +/- 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.

The survey used a hybrid methodology that involved contacting survey respondents by telephone and giving them the option of completing the survey at that time, at another more convenient time, or receiving an email link and completing the survey online. Trend Research contacted people using a random list of numbers, consisting of 30 per cent landlines and 70 per cent cellphone numbers.

Telephone numbers were dialed up to five times at five different times of day before another telephone number was added to the sample. The response rate among valid numbers (i.e., residential and personal) was 11.3 per cent.

World.title: Is Israel erasing evidence of alleged war crimes in Gaza? A visual investigation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Satellite imagery shows Israel compacting and removing rubble and debris from Gaza, with possible human remains and potential evidence of war crimes still trapped under it, a CBC News visual investigation of several sites has found.

Multiple destroyed areas in formerly populated areas of Gaza are being cleared, according to CBC's analysis, to make way for new military outposts for Israeli Defence Forces (IDF).

Families in Gaza say this prevents them from retrieving the bodies of loved ones trapped under the ruins.

"Where are the bodies? Where are the houses? Where's the rubble?" said Dalal Faraj, a Palestinian whose home in Gaza City was bombed, after CBC freelance videographer Mohamed El Saife showed her satellite footage of the now-cleared site.

UN officials have raised concerns in recent weeks that Israel is not properly handling rubble — and bodies that may still be under it — left by strikes in the almost three-year conflict sparked by the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.

WATCH | Investigating the clearing of rubble in Gaza: Is Israel erasing evidence of alleged war crimes in Gaza? | Duration 4:10 CBC��’s visual investigations team uncovers new satellite imagery that shows the IDF removing rubble from sites in Gaza that it bombed, which experts and human rights advocates warn risks destroying evidence of alleged war crimes. Families in Gaza interviewed by CBC say this activity prevents them from retrieving the bodies of loved ones trapped under the rubble.

In 2024, the International Court of Justice ordered Israel to take measures to preserve evidence of alleged violations of the UN Genocide Convention in Gaza.

"It is Israel's obligation under international law to do everything possible to ensure these remains are found, identified and buried with dignity," said Ajith Sunghay, head of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

In a statement to CBC News, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it clears structures and dismantles infrastructure in Gaza "based on tactical necessity" and to "reduce the level of risk posed" to its troops. It says this activity is "carried out in accordance with operational necessity, the provisions of international law, and IDF directives."

The IDF denies any accusations it isn't preserving evidence and recovering remains, saying it "treats every body found in the area with respect and seriousness."

Families that CBC News spoke to say no one contacted them about the retrieval of the bodies before or after the IDF removed the rubble from their homes.

IDF military base built over neighbourhood

"Impossible … This is our area?" Dalal Faraj told CBC News, looking at satellite imagery of her former neighbourhood. "Where did the houses go? Where are my husband and son?"

Dalal Faraj, who lives with her children in a displacement camp in Gaza City, looks at satellite imagery of her former neighbourhood. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

In October 2023, as the war picked up pace, Faraj left her home in Shuja'iya, a neighbourhood in Gaza City. Her husband, Taha, 48, and son Nasr, 16, told her to take the five younger children and head to a safer location. Taha and Nasr told her they would catch up when they could.

On Oct. 8, 2023, a day after the war started, an Israeli strike hit her home. She hasn't heard from her husband or son since.

Nasr Faraj, left, and his father, Taha. (Submitted by Dalal Faraj)

The satellite images that CBC's visual investigations team was able to gather show the buildings that once stood in Faraj's neighbourhood are all gone.

As the area was cleared of rubble, a new Israeli military base was built on top of it.

This composite image shows satellite footage of the Faraj family neighbourhood and the location of their home in August 2023, left, two months before the start of the war, and in August 2026, with the Israeli military base at the centre. (Google Earth, Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

On March 10, 2026, a satellite captured a rubble-clearing operation in the Faraj family neighbourhood. CBC News identified 11 diggers and one truck in the area just north of their home.

A composite image of heavy land-clearing machinery the CBC News visual investigations team identified in a March 10, 2026, satellite image. The image shows a clearing operation near the Shuja’iya military base. The colour of the machinery suggests it’s not military, but probably civilian subcontractors. (Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

A month later, satellite imagery shows four diggers clearing terrain west of the Faraj family house.

In April 2026, excavators moved west of the military base, clearing rubble, as shown in this composite image. (Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

Faraj, who now lives with her children in a displacement camp in Gaza, said she's been waiting for years to be able to return to her home to retrieve Taha and Nasr's remains and rebuild. Seeing the pictures broke the last of her hope, she said.

"This area used to be my home. We used to live in a safe place. We would go to school, go out and have fun. Suddenly, this happened," Faraj said.

CBC asked the IDF how many bodies found under the rubble in Gaza since last year's ceasefire have been returned to Palestinians. It did not answer the question.

Destruction of the 'Swedish Village'

Shaher Mohamed Abu Ouda, 36, says 14 members of his family are still missing after the family home in southern Gaza was destroyed.

Abu Ouda lived in a settlement in the Rafah Governorate known as the "Swedish Village." Abu Ouda left the area in 2024, and Rafah was occupied by Israel in 2025.

Shaher Mohamed Abu Ouda, left, speaks with family members about their neighbourhood in Rafah Governorate, which has been destroyed and cleared. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

"Warplanes started shooting at us, then came the F-16s, it shot at the house which we were in," Abu Ouda told CBC. "I left by a miracle."

Eight of the 14 members of the Abu Ouda family whose whereabouts are unknown after the IDF cleared rubble that may have contained their remains. (Submitted by Shaher Mohamed Abu Ouda)

"Until today, I think about what happened that day," he said. "I thought I would go back and see them, but after all these years, I won't even find a blouse."

Comparison shots of the location of Abu Ouda's home show the rubble was there until at least May 2026. By August, the rubble was gone, with heavy machinery tracks visible.

The three satellite images in this composite show the location of the Abu Ouda family home in Swedish Village in October 2023, May 2026 and August 2026. (Google Earth/Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

Footage from May 2026 shows a clearing operation, with six vehicles removing the rubble where the Swedish Village once stood.

CBC News identified vehicles clearing rubble in the satellite image taken on May 7, 2026, at the centre of what was Swedish Village, preparing the location for the military base. (Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

The latest satellite imagery from August 2026 shows the neighbourhood completely flattened, with a military base on top of it.

This composite image shows how the Swedish Village area looked in June 2024, left, and August 2026. (Google Earth/Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

Abu Ouda is not surprised by the satellite images of his neighbourhood, because Rafah has been under Israeli control for years. But the images provided confirmation that he is unlikely to be able to retrieve his family's remains, he said.

"Fourteen people lost their lives and we still know nothing about them," he said. "Even the rubble is not there."

'A new type of destruction'

Júlia Nueno Guitart, a researcher at Forensic Architecture, an independent research group tracking developments in Gaza, confirmed CBC's findings. She said her group has collected more than 2,000 similar incidents and managed to confirm 43 cases "where people have remained under the rubble."

"We have been able to do so either by visual evidence, graffiti on the walls of some of the buildings where people remain or by reports from [Gaza's] Civil Defence, where they inform us of the impossibility of retrieving bodies under the rubble," Nueno Guitart told CBC News.

A graphic shows instances Forensic Architecture has identified in which civilians are reportedly under rubble. (Forensic Architecture)

According to Forensic Architecture's findings, the Israeli military is compacting and clearing rubble around newly established military bases even in areas where bodies are still under the rubble.

"What we are seeing after the ceasefire in Gaza is a new type of destruction, different to the one we have been documenting before the ceasefire," Nueno Guitart said.

According to Janina Dill, a professor at Oxford University in the U.K. and an expert on international law, removing rubble and flattening the bombed area is only compatible with international law if the war dead are collected, identified and buried, and if evidence required to prosecute potential war crimes or suppress violations of international law is preserved.

"If [the rubble removal] is done without taking care of these two considerations, then it is absolutely prohibited and incompatible with Israel's obligations under the Geneva Convention," Dill said.

World.title: Yukon's rural health centres without a nurse for 214 days during year-long period, CBC analysis finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Yukon’s rural health centres continue to struggle with temporary closures and disruptions.

This week, the territory's health department verified the number of interruptions to its community health centres over the past year.

According to CBC’s analysis of the data provided by the department, between August 2025 and August 2026 the territory's rural health centres saw a total of 214 days when there were no nursing services available.

That tally doesn’t totally reflect the latest partial closure at the Beaver Creek health centre from July 2 to Oct. 30. It also leaves out “reduced services” at the Carcross health centre from Sept. 16 to Oct. 14.

Furthermore, Faro is seeing a temporary closure from Sept. 25 to Oct. 2, Ross River from Sept. 4 to Sept 30, and Teslin from Sept. 23 to Oct. 14.

As the Official Opposition, the Yukon Party previously railed against the former Liberal government for its failure to keep health centres open for prolonged periods of time. During last year's election campaign, Currie Dixon, now the premier, vowed that his party was "going to change this.”

Lack of community nurses goes on

Beaver Creek's health centre saw the most days of closure or reduced service over the past year, at 82.

Pelly Crossing and Destruction Bay have also seen significant disruptions.

The problem is marked by a lack of nurses available to work at the rural health centres. It’s been a chronic issue for the community centres which aren't regularly staffed by physicians.

According to the health department, some services are still available during some health centre closures.

The department said in a statement that depending on the community, emergency services were still available, administrative staff could help with medical travel and bookings, and doctor clinics went on.

Health Minister Brad Cathers wasn’t available for an interview.

The health department said the model of community care is under review.

The government also said it’s continually looking for ways to recruit and keep nurses working in the territory, and expanding licensing pathways for qualified health professionals. It’s also “evaluating opportunities” for a more sustainable health-care system in communities.

National nurses association hears some frustration

Valerie Grdisa, CEO of the Canadian Nurses Association, travelled to the Yukon at the end of June and she spoke with dozens of nurses at Whitehorse General Hospital and also met with the health centre team in Carcross.

Grdisa said she heard about pride and innovation in the workplace, as well as frustrations around the ability to retain nurses who want to live and provide care in the communities.

Grdisa said nurses aren’t regularly considering the ability to get licensed and be registered in multiple jurisdictions. She added that there’s actually a rather large workforce in the country, with 518,000 registered or regulated nurses in Canada.

“I think we could do a better job in providing opportunities for people to be more mobile,” she said.

Grdisa also suggested health centres look to hire closer to home.

“I think the homegrown workforce pathways are the way to go, so investing in youth engagement,” she said. “We're talking in the middle schools and high schools, and then having local education programs and apprenticeships and return-of-service agreements.”

World.title: Ottawa signs preliminary deal with Swedish firm Saab for 6 GlobalEye aircraft
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government has announced a preliminary agreement for the acquisition of six GlobalEye detection aircraft that would be built in Canada by the Swedish firm Saab in collaboration with Canada’s Bombardier.

In a statement on Friday, the government said the agreement will serve as the basis for final negotiations surrounding the purchase of these radar aircraft and the production schedule in Canada.

The government announced at the end of May its intention to acquire the Saab aircraft, which are used to detect and track threats such as enemy aircraft, missiles and drones at long distances. The platform offers what is known in the military as an airborne early warning and control (AEWC) capability.

Ottawa is now moving on to final negotiations on a contract, although no specific timeline or final cost have been provided by the government.

WATCH | Canada risks new U.S. political battle over Swedish spy plane deal: Canada risks new U.S. political battle over Swedish spy plane deal | Duration closed caption 2:11 Experts warn Ottawa's decision to purchase the Saab GlobalEye surveillance jet risks a new U.S. political battle, as fully integrating the plane with NORAD would require outfitting it with U.S. stealth communications technology that Washington has never shared.

"While the agreement does not constitute a contract or commitment to procure aircraft, it represents concrete progress toward the acquisition of the GlobalEye platform," the government said in its news release.

The upcoming negotiations will focus on a "Canadian configuration and development program designed to meet Canada's requirements," the government said.

Other current or potential customers for the GlobalEye include NATO, Sweden, France, the Netherlands and the United Arab Emirates. Ottawa is working with Saab to manufacture some of the aircraft for these clients in Canada.

Sources told CBC News that the GlobalEye has met only a handful of the military's requirements and will need important modifications. Ottawa has added that the other American companies interested in the contract, Boeing and L3Harris, are in the same situation.

WATCH | Canada chose GlobalEye spy plane without knowing military's needs: sources: Canada chose GlobalEye spy plane without knowing military's needs: sources | Duration closed caption 2:01 Canada's decision to buy the Saab GlobalEye surveillance plane from Sweden was made without knowing what the military actually needed, sources tell CBC News. Critics say the plane, as is, only meets a handful of Canada's requirements and will have to be modified.

In this context, the government said that GlobalEye was selected based on geopolitical and economic criteria.

"Canada’s approach to defence procurement must deliver more than military equipment. It must defend Canadians while strengthening our economy, growing Canadian industrial capacity and opening new opportunities for Canadian companies to compete globally," Stephen Fuhr, secretary of state responsible for defence procurement, said in a statement.

The Conservative Party has criticized the government's decision to proceed with this acquisition without going to tenders and is now calling on the Auditor General and the Parliamentary Budget Officer to investigate the project.

In a statement last week, the Conservatives said the public needs reassurances that the government did its homework before embarking on the process.

"Canadians deserve to know if politicians, Liberal staffers and bureaucrats were putting political decisions ahead of national security, defence and operational readiness," said Conservative defence critic James Bezan.

World.title: Carney's comments over possibility of U.S. invasion reveal how contingency plans are always in place
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A senior U.S. military commander recently dismissed a journalist's hypothetical question about a feared American invasion of Canada as "absolutely and utterly preposterous."

The head of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, Admiral Samuel Paparo, added: "Would you ask me please, also, what my attack plans are for the Martians?"

It seems, however, it hasn't been such a far-fetched notion for Prime Minister Mark Carney, nor his senior defence officials who have dusted off various long-established — in some cases decades old — contingency plans and worst case scenarios.

In an interview with the New York Times on Wednesday, Carney said he had prepared for the "extreme tail risk" that the Trump administration might order military action against Canada.

That's his way of saying there's a really, really low probability of this happening, but the risk is not zero.

The Times reported that the prime minister, after being pressed on whether he took U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats to make Canada the 51st state seriously, "suggested that he had carefully examined the possibility of a U.S.-led military invasion," but declined to discuss in detail what that involved.

"All militaries in the world spend time analyzing risk scenarios," Defence Minister David McGuinty said Thursday. "Canadians should take it as described to the prime minister: a tail risk."

McGuinty also refused to discuss details of the contingency planning.

WATCH | Nothing unusual in military analyzing risk scenarios, defence minister says: Defence minister says preparations for possible U.S.-led military action are 'normal' | Duration closed caption 1:02 Asked by CBC News if the Canadian military is re-examining plans for potential U.S.-led military action, Defence Minister David McGuinty said 'all militaries in the world spend time analyzing risk scenarios.' The New York Times reported that Prime Minister Mark Carney said he has studied the possibility, which he called 'extreme tail risk.'

Vault full of contingency plans

While the default vision of the phrase "American military action" for many is one of heavily armoured tanks, jets and drones roaring across the Canadian border, an overwhelming number of experts agree such a scenario is unlikely given the vastness of Canada and the difficulty in securing the whole country.

It's generally agreed that in a conventional conflict the Canadian military would be quickly overwhelmed and resistance would take the form of a guerilla campaign.

There are, however, a number of other different scenarios. They range from the kind of rapid regime change that took place when former Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro was captured by U.S. commandos, to the limited air campaign that's been fought over Iran.

As for contingency plans, the Department of National Defence, like militaries across the world, has a vault full of them — some dating back decades.

Retired Lt.-Gen. Andrew Leslie headed the section at the defence department that writes and updates the plans.

He said they are amended as world circumstances dictate, often when a new leader takes power in a country where Canada has an interest.

"You make judgment calls on what is likely to happen, what is unlikely to happen," Leslie said in an interview with CBC News.

"You consult with other departments, with other experts, and then you put it away again."

'Heightened focus' in light of Trump's threats

The planning, Leslie said, would have been updated after Trump's re-election in 2024 and would have been pulled out regularly, especially in light of the Trump administration's threats in January to seize Greenland by force.

"In the context of the threats that the White House has issued against Canada … those would have probably resulted in a heightened focus," Leslie said, citing talk of a 51st state and maps showing Canada as part of the U.S.

Over a year ago, Trump ruled out military action against Canada, saying he'd use economic coercion instead to force the country into the Union.

Given everything that's been said, it would have been natural for Carney to call for defence plans to be revised, Leslie said.

"What a lot of people sometimes forget is that a political leader's first remit at the national level is the safety, security of Canadians," said Leslie, who also served as commander of the Canadian Army.

"So it would be his duty to ensure that all due diligence and prudent steps have been taken to see what might have changed from the way that the old plans were written or updated. And it would be the duty of the Chief of the Defence Staff [Gen. Jennie Carignan] to advise them accordingly, which I'm absolutely sure she did."

WATCH | Invasion talk highlights state of U.S. relations, NDP's Don Davies says: Carney considering U.S. invasion of Canada shows 'profound change' in relations: NDP MP | Duration closed caption 0:47 Asked about reporting in the New York Times that Prime Minister Mark Carney said he studied the possibility of U.S. military action in Canada, NDP parliamentary leader Don Davies said the contemplation of such an 'outlandish possibility' shows everything we thought we knew about Canada-U.S. relations is 'up in the air.'

Impact of Trump's threats go unnoticed in U.S.

The notion of U.S. military action is a hot-button issue for many.

"I think every Canadian worries about it," New Democrat MP Gord Johns said going into the House of Commons on Thursday. Canadians are paying attention when Trump calls the country the 51st state or refers to Carney as the governor of Canada, Johns added.

There is, however, an increasingly puzzled reaction among some Americans who have grown accustomed to Trump's threats, taunts and trolling.

Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor at the University of New Haven in Connecticut and a former instructor at the U.S. Army War College, said many Americans, including himself, are unaware of how Trump's words affect people in other nations.

"I don't think I have a visceral sense of what Canadians are feeling about the United States," Schmidt said. "We really don't have a sense of the impact of what the president is saying has on other places."

He dismissed the notion of the U.S. military taking action against Canada, but said Carney has taken the prudent, responsible course of a leader and measured the risk.

Schmidt said he also wonders whether the prime minister's reference was intended as more of a political signal to not only the Canadian public, but Americans and others.

"When Mark Carney stands up and says that, it just highlights the absurdity of what the American president said. Right? It's a way to emphasize that absurdity," Schmidt said.

World.title: Wheelchair user says ‘discriminatory’ Habs policy forced him to beg for tickets
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With the Habs falling just shy of reaching the Stanley Cup final last spring, Joey Racanelli, like most fans, couldn’t wait to buy tickets for the upcoming season.

But when single-game tickets went on sale in early September, his excitement was short-liv ed.

As a wheelchair user, he buys tickets in the Bell Centre’s accessible seating section. He typically goes to four or five ga mes a season. But without warning, he says the Canadiens quietly changed their policy on reduced mobility seats, limiting him to one match for the entire season.

“I don't think it's their goal,” he added, “but it certainly feels discriminatory.”

Unlike other customers who can purchase tickets online, customers who want reduced mobility seating don’t have that option. They have to call or go in person to the Bell Centre ticket office.

Racanelli described the experience on the phone with the agent as he tried to get to the bottom of why his access was being restricted as embarrassing: “I basically had to beg for more tickets and I still couldn’t get them.”

Joey Racanelli said he was left feeling like he was trying to abuse the system. He tried to get clarification from the team about the ticket policy by phone, via e-mail and on social media, but never received any answers. (Submitted by Joey Racanelli)

Steven Laperrière, the general manager of the disability advocacy group Regroupement des activistes pour l'inclusion au Québec (RAPLIQ), says setting different limits to the number of tickets a disabled person can buy could amount to a violation of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

“You cannot discriminate against persons because of their handicap, you cannot do that.” Laperrière said.

He also takes issue with the policy at large. “Why would a person be only allowed to have only one game per season? We’re in a free country, right?”

CBC confirmed through several other Habs fans who use wheelchairs that Racanelli's experience was not isolated.

WATCH | Wheelchair user speaks out about policy: Quebec wheelchair user says new ticket policy at Habs home games feels ‘discriminatory’ | Duration closed caption 3:41 The Montreal Canadiens said that due to high demand, purchases for the accessible and reduced-mobility section are limited to one game per person per season — for a limited time. But disability advocacy groups say the new policy could violate the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Paying the price for possible system abuse

At the time, Racanelli asked the ticket agent why the policy had changed.

“It felt like [they thought] I was trying to abuse the system, which obviously I was not. I was just trying to get my tickets,” said Racanelli.

Laperrière says he understands it can be challenging for event managers to make sure the accessible seats are being used properly.

At the Bell Centre, Habs tickets in the reduced mobility section come at a much lower price than the other seats around them, which could tempt people to try and game the system.

“There will still be abuse, for sure. But why do people with disabilities have to pay the price and be limited in their ability to go see the Habs games because you can’t manage that properly?” he asks.

People with invisible disabilities like deafness, low vision or intellectual disabilities also have the right to use the accessible and reduced mobility section.

“I get it, it can be tough and you cannot prevent everything,” Laperrière says, “bu t no constraints is worth limiting the freedom of people with disabilities.”

CBC’s investigation found no evidence that the ticket policy change was disclosed publicly or communicated in any way to longtime users of the accessible and reduced mobility section at the Bell Centre prior to them calling to reserve tickets.

Steven Laperrière, the general manager of the disability advocacy group Regroupement des activistes pour l'inclusion au Québec (RAPLIQ), criticized Groupe CH for the lack of transparency around its ticket policy. (Louis-Marie Philidor/CBC)

Laperrière says regardless of why the team changed their policy, the lack of communication with users is inexcusable.

“[Groupe CH] is a big corporation, they do business everywhere. They should know better. And to me, that they’re not putting it online is a lack of transparency, and I think we can understand why.”

Laperrière also phoned the ticket office himself to ask for clarification on the policy, which he recorded. He shared that conversation and a recording from another wheelchair user with CBC. In it, the ticket agent confirms they can only buy tickets for one match per season.

Racanelli says in addition to asking for answers on the phone, he emailed Groupe CH and reached out to the Montreal Canadiens on social media regarding the ticketing policy changes. He did not receive a response.

Team says policy applied to all fans, was temporary

The Montreal Canadiens and Groupe CH declined to be interviewed for this story.

In a statement, the club says that due to high demand, purchases were limited to one game per person, but added that the policy applied to all fans, not just those with reduced mobility.

It added that the policy was only in effect for a limited time, and now that the initial sales period is over, single-game tickets can be purchased — subject to availability.

However, even if the policy was applied to all fans during the limited period, the number of tickets available per client appeared to differ.

When single-game tickets came on sale in early September, customers buying through Ticketmaster were limited to four seats per purchase.

Users of the reduced mobility section were only allowed to purchase the equivalent of two tickets — one for themselves and one for the person accompanying them.

For years, customers who wanted reduced mobility seating had to call or go in person to the ticketing office. That briefly changed last season, when the team moved everything to Ticketmaster. But it reverted to the old system this year.

CBC asked Groupe CH why it moved away from online sales after one year, and if or how it communicated the policy to customers in advance, but it did not provide an answer.

Racanelli says his frustration over the situation grew when he went online and saw other fans on social media talking about all the tickets they acquired to multiple games this season.

Based on his experience, there were no guardrails preventing others from buying tickets to multiple games online.

At the Bell Centre, there are 58 accessible and reduced mobility seats for Montreal Canadiens' games. With 42 home matches, that's fewer than 2,500 available seats a year. (Radio Canada International / Samir Bendjafer)

Racanelli was surprised to learn the one-ticket policy was temporary because at no point did the ticketing agent explain that to him when he asked for details. CBC can confirm that others who inquired were also not told the policy was meant to be temporary.

Despite what wheelchair users were told on the phone, Groupe CH said in its statement “no limits have been placed on the number of games a person with reduced mobility may attend during the season.”

Limited reduced mobility seats in Canadian NHL arenas

How users access the reduced mobility section at other Canadian NHL cities varies.

In Ottawa, Toronto and Winnipeg, wheelchair users can buy their tickets online through Ticketmaster.

Spaces in NHL arenas are limited. According to the Montreal Canadiens website, there are only 58 wheelchair-accessible seats available per game at the Bell Centre.

The Canadiens have a digital tool that allows fans to see what the view looks like from different parts of the Bell Centre. This screenshot shows the view from one of the arena's five wheelchair-accessible areas, in Section 117. (Screengrab from Canadiens website)

The Ottawa Senators say the Canadian Tire Centre has 140 accessible seats available.

Winnipeg has accessible spaces across 11 sections in the Canada Life Centre for Jets games, but it’s unclear how many seats are available per game.

The Toronto Maple Leafs say it is against company policy to disclose how many seats it offers wheelchair users each game at Scotiabank Arena.

The Calgary Flames, Edmonton Oilers and Vancouver Canucks did not respond to CBC’s request for information concerning how access to the accessible and reduced mobility section operates in their arenas.

Racanelli says he understands there are significant challenges in managing the access to reduced-mobility sections at the Bell C entre.

He adds that his experiences at the arena and with the staff are always first-class, but the ticket process has been so challenging this year that he’s questioning going back.

World.title: Quebec City man charged with threatening to kill Mark Carney on social media, promoting hatred
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Quebec City man has been arrested after he allegedly threatened Prime Minister Mark Carney on social media.

The RCMP said in a media release on Friday that Ousmane Bah, 45, from Quebec City, has been charged with uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm to a person, including the prime minister. He has also been charged with promoting hatred against an identifiable group.

The RCMP say he made the remarks using his Facebook account.

The force says their investigation began in the summer, on July 6. Bah appeared in court in Quebec City on Sept. 24, and will remain in custody at least until his next court appearance, on Oct. 1.

Earlier this month, RCMP officers in Alberta arrested a Calgary resident and accused him of threatening to kill Carney as well.

More to come.
