Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The fees are set in US dollars. The official programme page asks US$2,000 for an individual and US$3,000 for a family. Applicants must expect income of at least US$50,000 over the 12 months.

The Remote Employment Act states the same sums in Barbados dollars: BDS$4,000 (US$2,000), BDS$6,000 (US$3,000) and BDS$100,000 (US$50,000).

Applications are filed online with photographs, passport pages and proof of family relationships. The programme says approval typically takes seven business days. The non-refundable fee is then due within 28 days.

The act requires valid health insurance for the whole year. It defines family to include a spouse or partner and children or stepchildren under 26. A stamp lasts 12 months only, so staying on means applying again.

Holders are deemed non-resident for income tax, so their foreign earnings are not taxed in Barbados. They still pay 17.5 percent value added tax (VAT), the island’s sales tax, on local purchases. They may not take a job with a Barbadian employer.

Applications passed 5,000 by July 2024, according to Barbados Today. The Ministry of Tourism says Cabinet approved renewal of the programme on 26 October 2023 until 31 December 2026. As of 25 September 2026, no published decision extends it further.

Work permits and the Immigration Department

Anyone who is not a national must register with immigration before starting a local job. The Immigration Department handles work permits under section 17 of the Immigration Act.

The employer, or sponsor, applies on the worker’s behalf. Short-term permits last up to 11 months. Long-term permits last up to three years, and the employer must show that no Barbadian or resident can fill the post.

Long-term applications use Forms C-1 and C-2 and a medical form. Advisers add qualifications, references and police certificates to the list. Entrepreneurs must also show company registration and proof that investment funds were transferred in line with Central Bank rules.

The application fee is BDS$300 (US$150), paid on submission. A final fee follows approval and varies with the job category and length of the permit. Under the fee regulations it is charged monthly and paid in advance for the whole period.

The department publishes no processing standard. A 2019 guide by a Caribbean law firm cited about three months from filing. Qualifying nationals of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM), the regional bloc, have a separate route for skilled workers.

Special entry permits, permanent residence and the 2026 bills

Wealthy foreigners and retirees often look at the Special Entry and Reside Permit. The Immigration Department lists it as the Special Entry Permit. Invest Barbados, the state investment agency, targets it at people over 60 with assets of US$5 million or more.

Invest Barbados also says applicants should invest US$2 million or more in property or another qualifying asset. People under 60 can seek a temporary permit. Holders may come and go, and a work permit costs extra.

The official checklist asks for Form B, police certificates, title deeds and land tax bills. It also wants proof of financial resources and health insurance valid in Barbados. The application fee is BDS$300 (US$150), and the checklist does not state the final permit fee.

Private advisers quote permit fees of about US$3,500 to US$5,000, but their age bands differ. Some also describe a separate category for owners of a home worth at least US$300,000. Treat these as market claims, not published rules.

Permanent resident status under section 5 of the Immigration Act is narrow. The department’s checklist covers foreign husbands of Barbadian women and certain children of Barbadian mothers. Most other foreigners seeking to settle apply for immigrant status on Form A.

For immigrant status, people setting up a business must show proof of funds brought into Barbados. Applicants over 60 must show means of support, income and property. Neither page sets a minimum number of years on the island.

That framework may change under an Immigration Bill and a Barbados Citizenship Bill, both dated 21 April 2026. The House of Assembly read them a first time on 29 April. The draft would open permanent residence to spouses of citizens and to retired people with sufficient financial resources.

The draft also adds a points test, requiring at least 10 points across age, Barbadian descent, education, skills, experience and financial resources. A joint select committee of Parliament laid its final report on both bills on 11 August 2026. As of 25 September 2026, Parliament’s archive still listed them at the House of Assembly stage.

What it costs: rent by parish, groceries, utilities and cars

Rent is the hardest cost to pin down. Barbados has no official rent index, so every figure comes from agents or crowd-sourced sites.

A timber house with a corrugated roof in Barbados (Photo: Berit from Redhill/Surrey, UK, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Location matters most. Rent depends heavily on the parish, one of 11 districts. St Michael holds Bridgetown, Christ Church covers the south coast, and St James and St Peter form the west coast.

On 25 September 2026 the lowest-priced long-term listings at Terra Caribbean were US$900 a month. They were a studio and a three-bedroom house in Christ Church and a one-bedroom flat in St James. The other two- and three-bedroom homes on its first page asked US$1,250 to US$1,800.

Terra Caribbean says it has the island’s most extensive rental portfolio. Its 2025 sales report found Christ Church drew 42 percent of home sales, while St James dominated the luxury segment. Expect west-coast villas and beachfront flats to cost several times the entry-level figures.

Numbeo, a crowd-sourced price site, put a one-bedroom in central Bridgetown at BDS$2,367 (about US$1,183) a month in August 2026. A three-bedroom there cost BDS$4,267 (about US$2,133). Its page notes only six contributors in 12 months.

Numbeo’s August 2026 figures put a litre of milk at BDS$8.14 (about US$4.07), roughly US$15 a US gallon. A dozen eggs cost BDS$12.67 (about US$6.34). A pound of chicken fillets cost BDS$8.77 (about US$4.39), and a cheap restaurant meal BDS$40 (US$20).

Electricity bills carry a monthly fuel charge on top of the base tariff. Barbados Light & Power set it at 37.53 Barbados cents per kilowatt hour (about US$0.19) for September 2026. Numbeo users put basic utilities for a mid-sized flat near BDS$390 (US$195) a month.

Petrol has retailed at BDS$4.27 a litre (about US$2.14) since midnight on Sunday 13 September 2026, according to government figures. That equals roughly US$8.08 per US gallon. A bus ride on the state Transport Board costs a flat BDS$3.50 (US$1.75), exact fare only.

Cars are expensive. A 2021 US Commerce Department guide lists a 45 percent import duty on motor vehicles, plus excise tax and an environmental levy. Numbeo users price a new Toyota Corolla at about BDS$70,000 (US$35,000).

Electric vehicles get relief. The budget of 16 March 2026 announced an extension of their VAT and excise holiday to 31 March 2029, according to KPMG. A 10 percent import duty still applies.

Healthcare, schools and banking

The Queen Elizabeth Hospital (QEH) in Bridgetown is the main public hospital. It provides free hospital treatment to citizens and permanent residents. Others may be charged, although urgent treatment is always given first.

That means Welcome Stamp holders, work-permit holders and special-permit holders should budget for private health insurance. The Welcome Stamp and the special entry permit both require it. Get quotes before you move, because premiums vary with age and cover.

The US State Department calls medical care good for the region but warns that very serious injuries often need evacuation. It recommends medical evacuation insurance. The emergency numbers are 211 for police, 511 for ambulance and 311 for fire.

Non-Barbadian pupils need a student visa, according to The Codrington School. Codrington describes itself as the island’s only international school and teaches the International Baccalaureate (IB).

Its 2026–27 fees for students from outside Barbados and CARICOM start at US$12,000 a year in the first primary years. They reach US$23,350 in the upper years. An application fee of US$400 and an admission fee listed at US$2,500 to US$6,000 come on top.

The Central Bank of Barbados lists six commercial banks: CIBC Caribbean, First Citizens, RBC Royal Bank, Republic Bank, Scotiabank and Sagicor Bank. Each sets its own account-opening checks.

Barbados still runs exchange controls through the central bank. Keep records of every transfer you bring in. The Immigration Department asks investors for bank statements showing funds arrived in line with Central Bank rules.

The pegged dollar and taxes on residents

The two-to-one peg makes budgeting simple for anyone paid in US dollars. The central bank backs it with foreign reserves, and it has held for more than 50 years. US dollars are accepted across the island.

Tax follows residence and domicile, not nationality. You become resident by spending more than 182 days in Barbados in a calendar year, according to PwC. Keeping a home there and giving notice that you will stay at least two consecutive tax years also makes you ordinarily resident.

The 2026 budget cut personal income tax rates from income year 2026, says the Barbados Revenue Authority (BRA). After a personal allowance of BDS$25,000 (US$12,500), income up to BDS$75,000 (US$37,500) is taxed at 11.5 percent. Income above that is taxed at 27.5 percent.

On a salary of BDS$75,000 (US$37,500), EY calculates annual income tax of BDS$5,750 (US$2,875). Non-domiciled residents pay tax on local income, and on foreign income only when they bring it in, says Invest Barbados.

Welcome Stamp holders sit outside this system for their remote income. Anyone who turns a stay into residence should take local tax advice before the 183rd day.

Daily life: hurricanes, driving on the left and a young republic

A state Transport Board bus in St Andrew. Traffic drives on the left (Photo: Postdlf, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Barbados covers 430 square kilometres, almost two and a half times the area of Washington, DC. With about 283,000 people, that is roughly 660 people per square kilometre.

Barbados became a parliamentary republic on 30 November 2021, replacing the British monarch as head of state. Jeffrey Bostic was sworn in as its second president on 30 November 2025. The prime minister leads the government.

Mia Mottley of the Barbados Labour Party (BLP) has been prime minister since 2018. Her party won all 30 seats in the House of Assembly on 11 February 2026, Reuters reported. It was the BLP’s third clean sweep in a row.

The Atlantic hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November. In its 6 August 2026 update, the US weather agency NOAA forecast a 75 percent chance of a below-normal season. A forecast is not a guarantee.

Hurricane Beryl passed about 150 kilometres south of the island on 1 July 2024. United Nations economists put its effects at BDS$193 million (about US$96.5 million). The Fisheries Division says more than 200 fishing boats were damaged or lost.

Traffic drives on the left, and roundabouts are common. Since 15 October 2025 visitors no longer need a visitor driving permit, the BRA says. Car rentals instead carry a levy of BDS$5 (US$2.50) a day, capped at BDS$35 (US$17.50).

The US State Department rates Barbados at Level 1, its lowest advisory, and says petty crime is common in tourist areas. The UK Foreign Office notes a rise in gang-related gun murders, some in public places.

Sources: Immigration rules come from the Barbados Immigration Department, the Remote Employment Act, the Welcome Stamp programme and Invest Barbados; tax from the Barbados Revenue Authority; currency and banks from the Central Bank of Barbados; hospital rules from the Queen Elizabeth Hospital; with travel, election, weather and price data from the US State Department, UK Foreign Office, Barbados Parliament, Reuters, NOAA, the United Nations, Barbados Light & Power, Terra Caribbean, The Codrington School and Numbeo. All accessed 25 September 2026.

What Is Not Known

Whether the Welcome Stamp runs beyond 31 December 2026 is not known. The last published Cabinet decision, of 26 October 2023, renewed it only to that date. The official page still takes applications, so anyone whose stamp would run into 2027 should ask the programme office before paying.

When the Immigration Bill and the Barbados Citizenship Bill will pass, and in what form, is not known. Parliament’s archive lists both at the House of Assembly stage. The points table, fees and transition rules could all change before they become law.

The final fees and thresholds for the special entry permit are not published by the Immigration Department. Advisers quote figures between US$3,500 and US$5,000 and do not agree on which applies to whom. Only the BDS$300 (US$150) application fee is official.

What rent really costs is not measured. Barbados has no official rent index, agency listings are only snapshots, and the best-known crowd-sourced figures rest on six contributors. No reliable parish-by-parish average exists.

How long a work permit takes is not published. Estimates range from weeks to about three months. Nor is it clearly published how long a resident may drive on a foreign licence, now that the visitor permit has gone.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does the Barbados Welcome Stamp cost in 2026?

The official programme page sets the fee at US$2,000 for an individual and US$3,000 for a family. Applicants must expect at least US$50,000 in income over the 12 months, earned outside Barbados. Approval typically takes seven business days, and the non-refundable fee is due within 28 days of approval.

Can I work for a Barbados company on the Welcome Stamp?

No, the Welcome Stamp covers remote work for employers or clients outside Barbados only. A local job needs a work permit, which the employer applies for through the Immigration Department. The application fee is BDS$300, or US$150, and a final fee follows approval.

How long can Americans stay in Barbados without a visa?

The US State Department says American citizens need no visa for stays of up to six months, with a valid passport and proof of onward travel. The immigration officer on arrival sets the exact stay. Visitors may not work, and longer stays require an extension from the Immigration Department.

Is healthcare free for foreigners in Barbados?

No, the Queen Elizabeth Hospital gives free hospital treatment to citizens and permanent residents of Barbados. Others may be charged, though urgent care is always given first. Welcome Stamp holders and special entry permit holders must carry health insurance, and the US State Department recommends evacuation cover.

How much is rent in Barbados?

There is no official rent index. On 25 September 2026 the lowest-priced long-term listings at Terra Caribbean were US$900 a month, including a studio in Christ Church and a one-bedroom in St James. Numbeo users put a central Bridgetown one-bedroom at about US$1,183 a month, from a small sample.

What currency does Barbados use?

The Barbados dollar, fixed at BDS$2 to US$1 by the Central Bank of Barbados since 5 July 1975. US dollars are widely accepted. Every Barbados dollar price converts to US dollars by halving it.

World.title: Investing in the Bahamas as a Foreigner 2026: Property, Funds and the Zero-Tax Frame
World.content:
GUIDES · BAHAMAS

Key Facts — What it is A standing guide for non-Bahamians putting money into Bahamian property, funds or residence, and into the rules that govern each.

— Who it’s for Home buyers, land investors, fund promoters and would-be residents, mostly from the US, Canada, the UK and Europe.

— What it costs No income, capital-gains or inheritance tax, but 10% VAT on a foreigner’s property purchase and annual real property tax.

— The rules Foreign buyers need an Investments Board certificate or permit, and the Central Bank records foreign money so it can leave again.

— The catch Hurricanes, an economy tied to US visitors, and property-tax rules for foreign owners that changed on 1 July 2026.

— What is still open Whether new taxes follow to cut public debt, and how strictly the new foreign-owner property tax is enforced.

Investing in the Bahamas means no tax on income or gains. The real costs come at the door: transfer VAT, property tax, permits and insurance.

Investing in the Bahamas starts with a simple promise: no personal income, capital-gains or inheritance tax. The price of entry is paid elsewhere, through transfer VAT, property tax, paperwork and exposure to hurricanes and American tourism.

The Bahamas is an archipelago of about 403,000 people, according to World Bank data for 2025. That is slightly more than Iceland’s 392,000 on the same data, spread across many islands.

Output per person was about US$39,455 in 2024, less than half the US level of about US$86,170. The whole economy measured about US$15.8 billion that year, on the same World Bank data.

The zero-tax frame, and what you still pay

The Bahamas levies no personal income, capital-gains, inheritance or gift tax, according to PwC’s tax summary reviewed in July 2026. There are no personal income tax returns to file.

The state lives instead on value added tax (VAT), a sales tax charged at each stage of supply. The Department of Inland Revenue sets the standard rate at 10%. A reduced 5% rate covers listed items such as some medicines.

Unprepared grocery food has been free of VAT since 1 April 2026, the government’s May 2026 budget statement said. In the 2025/26 period it reviewed, VAT raised about US$1.1 billion, or 43.8% of all government revenue.

The zero-tax frame covers Bahamian tax only. The United States taxes its citizens on worldwide income wherever they live. Other home countries apply their own residence and exit rules.

Large multinational groups are the main exception. The Domestic Minimum Top-Up Tax Act, 2024 sets a minimum effective tax rate of 15% for groups under the OECD’s global rules.

The low-tax model draws outside scrutiny. The Council of the European Union listed the Bahamas as a non-cooperative tax jurisdiction on 4 October 2022. The reason given was a failure to enforce economic-substance rules for zero-tax companies.

It was removed on 20 February 2024 after progress on enforcement. In the EU’s 17 February 2026 review, it sat among cooperative jurisdictions with no pending commitments. The next review is due in October 2026.

The Bahamian dollar peg and exchange control

The Bahamian dollar has been fixed at par with the US dollar since 1973, according to the Central Bank of The Bahamas. On 25 September 2026, open.er-api.com quoted exactly 1.00 Bahamian dollar per US dollar.

The central bank itself buys US dollars from commercial banks at the same one-for-one rate. Bahamian law sets fees and thresholds in Bahamian dollars, so this guide quotes them directly in US$.

The peg is protected by exchange control, run by the central bank’s Exchange Control Department. A non-resident who brings in foreign currency to buy property registers that investment, a status called Approved Investment Status.

That status guarantees the right, on application, to repatriate sale proceeds and rental income, the central bank says. The investor must document that the money came from abroad.

Since October 2019, residential deals involving non-residents no longer need prior central-bank approval. Commercial banks may sell foreign currency to repatriate residential sale proceeds, but non-resident-owned companies may not buy property with Bahamian-dollar loans.

From 1 April 2024, non-residents buying non-residential or mixed-use property with foreign money can also close without the central bank. Development projects and purchases using local financing still need its approval.

Buying property under the landholding law

The Atlantis resort towers on Paradise Island, across Nassau Harbour from the cruise port, in March 2024. Large foreign-led projects need cabinet-level approval (Photo: Kiran891, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only â every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesMarkets, currencies and the economy › RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. × Markets today The currency Rates & inflation Economy outlook Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Foreign ownership of land is governed by the International Persons Landholding Act of 1993. The Investments Board of the Bahamas Investment Authority administers it through two routes: a Certificate of Registration or a permit.

A non-Bahamian buying a first home for personal use registers the purchase after closing. The exception is undeveloped land that would leave the buyer holding two or more contiguous acres, which needs a permit.

A permit is also required for a second property or any purchase for investment or commercial use. It must be granted before closing, or the purchase is void under the Act.

Each document costs US$1,000, according to law firm Lennox Paton’s chapter for the Legal 500 guide. Since July 2024, a permit lapses if the buyer misses a 180-day deadline. By then the VAT must be paid, the Chief Valuation Officer notified and property tax paid.

Since July 2025, an unused permit can be extended for 180 days, at most twice, by filing a notice and paying a fee. Large developments also go to the National Economic Council, usually made up of the prime minister, other ministers and senior officials.

Transfer VAT is the largest closing cost. Non-Bahamian buyers pay 10% of the value, so a US$1 million house carries US$100,000 in VAT. Mortgages attract 1% of the sum secured.

Bahamian buyers of homes pay tiered rates from 2.5% to 10%. Since 1 July 2025, a provisional VAT invoice from the Department of Inland Revenue must be obtained before any conveyance is signed.

The assessed VAT must be paid within 180 days of signing, and the deed recorded within the same period. Unpaid transfer VAT ranks ahead of mortgages and other claims on the property.

Real property tax after the July 2026 reform

Owners pay annual real property tax, based on market value, use and the owner’s status. Bahamians are exempt on vacant land and on property in the Family Islands, the islands outside New Providence.

On 1 July 2026, the Real Property Tax (Amendment) Act created a new class called foreign owner-occupied property. It covers non-Bahamians with a residence permit, annual work permit or Home Owner Resident Permit who live in the home.

The occupation can be permanent or seasonal. This replaced the old test of spending 180 days a year in the country, the May 2026 budget statement said.

That class pays 0.625% on value up to US$1 million and 1% above, capped at US$200,000 a year. On those rates, a US$2 million home would owe about US$16,250 a year.

Bahamians and permanent residents with the right to work pay the owner-occupied rate on the home they live in. The first US$300,000 of value is exempt, with 0.625% on the next US$200,000 and 1% above, capped at US$150,000 a year.

Most foreign-owned homes outside the new class, such as rentals, are treated as commercial property. The Department of Inland Revenue lists 0.75% on the first US$500,000, 1% on the next US$1.5 million and 1.5% above.

Foreign-owned vacant land pays US$100 on the first US$7,000 of value and 2% on the rest, on the same schedule. Bills must be paid by 31 December to avoid an extra 5% interest charge.

Arrears are costly. Under the 2026 amendment, the Treasurer may sell a property after more than 12 months of unpaid tax. The budget statement said foreign-owned collections had fallen short.

Investment funds, digital assets and the FTX episode

Funds and securities are supervised by the Securities Commission of The Bahamas (SCB), a statutory regulator set up in 1995. It administers the Investment Funds Act, 2019, the Securities Industry Act, 2024 and the digital-asset law.

Every fund operating in or from the Bahamas must be licensed or registered, as a professional, standard, SMART or master fund. A professional fund may be sold only to eligible investors.

Eligible individuals include those worth more than US$1 million, or those earning over US$200,000 in each of the last two years. Banks, insurers, regulated funds and securities firms also qualify.

SMART stands for Specific Mandate Alternative Regulatory Test. A financial institution or adviser proposes a fund structure for the SCB to approve. Funds built on that template must then follow its written rules.

Digital assets came under the Digital Assets and Registered Exchanges Act, 2020, known as the DARE Act. FTX Digital Markets, the Bahamian arm of the FTX crypto exchange, was incorporated in July 2021 and registered under it.

On 10 November 2022, the SCB froze FTX Digital Markets’ assets, suspended its registration and sought a court-appointed provisional liquidator. The regulator says this was the first action taken anywhere against an FTX entity.

Two days later, the SCB moved the firm’s digital assets into digital wallets under its exclusive control. FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried was arrested in the Bahamas on 12 December 2022 at the request of the US government.

A New York jury convicted him of fraud and conspiracy in November 2023. On 28 March 2024, a US federal judge sentenced him to 25 years in prison.

Parliament replaced the law with DARE 2024, announced by the SCB on 30 July 2024. It adds rules for staking, advice and derivatives, sets reserve and redemption rules for stablecoins and bans algorithmic stablecoins.

The lesson for a foreign investor is that a licence is not a guarantee. Check a firm’s registration with the SCB and ask where client assets are held and by whom.

Residency by investment: the US$1 million threshold

Permanent residence lets a foreigner live in the Bahamas for life unless it is revoked, and may include the right to work. It does not include the right to vote, the government’s residency page says.

Since 1 January 2025, economic permanent residence requires an investment of at least US$1 million, up from US$750,000. It can be Bahamian real estate or zero-coupon bonds from the Central Bank, held for at least ten years.

The change came through the Immigration (Amendment) (No. 2) Act, 2024. Property received by deed of gift no longer counts. Applicants must prove the investment with a tax assessment number or central-bank confirmation.

Buying at the threshold opens an application, not an automatic right. Some government pages still cite an older US$1.5 million figure for faster review. Confirm the current rule with the Department of Immigration.

Permanent residents register property purchases instead of seeking a permit. Those with the right to work also qualify for the owner-occupied property-tax rate under the July 2026 amendment.

Politics, US tourism and hurricane risk

Parliament Square in Nassau, home of the Bahamian Parliament, with its statue of Queen Victoria, photographed in 1996 (Photo: Larry Syverson, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

As of 25 September 2026, Prime Minister Philip Davis leads a second consecutive government of the Progressive Liberal Party (PLP). His party won 33 of 41 seats in the early general election of Tuesday, 12 May 2026.

The Free National Movement (FNM) took the other eight seats. Official results showed 139,026 votes counted and turnout of 66.4%, the Nassau Guardian reported, and Davis was sworn in on 14 May.

Finance Minister Michael Halkitis presented the first budget of the new term on 27 May 2026. It projects US$4.4 billion in revenue and a US$223.1 million surplus. It raises revenue from the largest businesses and immigration applicants, and it reforms property tax for foreign owners.

The economy runs on visitors. The Bahamas received a record 12.5 million visitors in 2025, about 31 per resident, the Ministry of Tourism reported. Cruise passengers made up 86.5% of arrivals.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) counts around 80% of tourists as coming from the United States. Spending by overnight visitors alone equals about 28% of GDP, so a US slowdown quickly reaches rents and hotel values.

The IMF forecasts growth of 2.2% in 2026 after 2.8% in 2025, easing towards 1.5% later. It put central government debt near 74% of GDP and has suggested income taxes and a higher VAT to reduce it.

Wrecked and damaged homes on the Abaco Islands, seen from a US Customs and Border Protection aircraft on 5 September 2019, days after Hurricane Dorian (Photo: Kris Grogan/CBP, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

Hurricanes are the other structural risk. Hurricane Dorian struck Abaco and Grand Bahama as a Category 5 storm from 1 to 3 September 2019. It left 67 confirmed deaths, with 282 people still missing weeks later.

The Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) put the damage and losses at US$3.4 billion, over a quarter of GDP. It compared this to the US losing the combined output of California, Texas and Florida.

Housing alone suffered nearly US$1.5 billion in physical damage. In October 2025, Hurricane Melissa forced evacuations from some sparsely populated islands, though the IMF judged its economic impact modest.

Insure from the day you sign. Under English common-law rules, which the Bahamas follows, risk passes to the buyer at exchange of contracts, Lennox Paton notes. The buyer’s interest should be noted on the policy.

Practical steps before investing in the Bahamas

First, hire a Bahamian attorney before signing anything. Title must run in an unbroken chain to a good root. Deeds to foreign owners since November 1983 should carry their permits or certificates.

Second, wire the purchase money from abroad, ideally into your attorney’s foreign-currency client account. Keep the bank records, because they prove your right to take the money out again.

Third, decide whether you need a certificate or a permit, and obtain any permit before closing. Budget 10% of the price for VAT and agree in the contract who pays it.

Fourth, request the provisional VAT invoice, then pay the assessed VAT and record the deed within 180 days. Notify the Chief Valuation Officer promptly, and claim the foreign owner-occupied rate if you qualify.

Fifth, price insurance before you commit, including the hurricane deductible and cover for storm surge and flooding. Finally, take tax advice at home, because investing in the Bahamas does not end tax duties elsewhere.

Sources: Tax rules from the Department of Inland Revenue, the Official Gazette and PwC; exchange control and the peg from the Central Bank of The Bahamas; landholding and residency law from the Bahamas statute database, UNCTAD and the Legal 500; funds and digital assets from the Securities Commission; election, budget, tourism, growth, hurricane and tax-list facts from the Nassau Guardian, the Tribune, the Ministry of Tourism, the IMF, the IDB, the World Bank and the Council of the EU. All accessed 25 September 2026.

What Is Not Known

Whether new taxes will follow is not known. The IMF says the government needs extra measures to cut debt to its 50%-of-GDP target by 2030/31. No personal income tax has been announced.

How the July 2026 property-tax reform will work in practice is not yet clear. The first bills under the foreign owner-occupied class are still to come. It is not known how disputed classifications will be settled, or how often the new power of sale will be used.

The published commercial property-tax schedule and older consolidated versions of the statute do not match on the top rate. Owners of foreign-held rental homes should ask the Department of Inland Revenue for their own assessment rather than rely on a table.

The outcome of the EU’s October 2026 review of its tax list is not known. Nor can anyone forecast the next major hurricane, or how insurance premiums in the islands will move after it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do foreigners pay income tax when investing in the Bahamas?

No. The Bahamas levies no personal income tax, no capital-gains tax and no inheritance or gift tax. It relies instead on VAT, charged at a standard rate of 10%, and on property tax. Home countries may still tax their residents or citizens, as the United States does on worldwide income.

How much VAT does a foreigner pay when buying property in the Bahamas?

Non-Bahamian buyers pay VAT of 10% of the property’s value, so a US$1 million house carries US$100,000. A provisional VAT invoice must be obtained before signing, and the assessed VAT must be paid within 180 days. Mortgages attract VAT of 1% of the amount secured.

Do foreigners need a permit to buy property in the Bahamas?

A first home for personal use needs only a Certificate of Registration from the Investments Board, obtained after closing. A permit is needed before closing for a second property or an investment or commercial purchase. It is also needed for undeveloped land giving two or more contiguous acres, and each document costs US$1,000.

How much property tax does a foreign homeowner pay in the Bahamas?

From 1 July 2026, permit-holding foreigners who live in their home pay 0.625% on value up to US$1 million. Above that the rate is 1%, capped at US$200,000 a year. Most other foreign-owned homes are taxed as commercial property, listed at 0.75% to 1.5%.

How much must I invest for permanent residence in the Bahamas?

Since 1 January 2025, economic permanent residence requires at least US$1 million, held for at least ten years. It can be Bahamian real estate or Central Bank zero-coupon bonds, and the earlier minimum was US$750,000. Buying at the threshold opens an application, not an automatic right.

Can I take my money out of the Bahamas when I sell?

Yes, if the purchase was funded with foreign currency and documented. The Central Bank grants Approved Investment Status, which guarantees the right to repatriate sale proceeds and rental income on application. Since 2019, commercial banks can sell foreign currency to repatriate residential sale proceeds.

World.title: Is Nicaragua Safe for Expats in 2026? Crime, Politics and Daily Reality
World.content:
GUIDES · NICARAGUA

Key Facts — What it is A standing safety guide for foreigners living in or moving to Nicaragua. The country has about 7 million people and is slightly smaller than Wisconsin.

— Who it’s for Expats, retirees, remote workers and long-stay visitors from the US, Canada, the UK and Europe.

— The rules Foreigners may not take part in politics. Drones are banned, and photographing government buildings or police can bring penalties.

— Why it matters The US State Department rates Nicaragua Level 3, “reconsider travel”, and warns of wrongful detention of US nationals.

— The catch Street crime looks moderate for Central America, but official data cannot be checked. For foreigners, the state is often the larger risk.

— What is still open A reform passed on first reading on 1 September 2026 would lengthen terms to seven years. Its final vote is due from 18 January 2027.

Is Nicaragua safe for expats in 2026? Street crime is moderate by regional standards, but speech, photos and politics carry risks most newcomers do not expect.

For foreigners, safety in Nicaragua has two parts. Everyday crime appears moderate by Central American standards, though the data are opaque. Political risk, from phone searches to expulsions, has grown steadily since 2018.

Official crime data versus independent estimates

Nicaragua’s National Police present the country as one of the safest in the region. At their anniversary event on 25 September 2025, police chief Francisco Díaz put the homicide rate at 5 per 100,000 people.

That rate covered September 2024 to August 2025, according to 100% Noticias, an exiled news outlet. Díaz also said 97.5 percent of reported crimes were minor.

In a country of about 7 million people, a rate of 5 means roughly 350 killings a year. InSight Crime put Costa Rica at 16.8 and Honduras at 23.2 per 100,000 in 2025.

The difficulty is checking the claim. InSight Crime, a research group that tracks organised crime, said Nicaragua did not answer its request for official 2025 data. It found no reliable homicide data for the year.

Independent tallies fill part of the gap. Despacho 505, an exiled newsroom, compiled 98 weekly police bulletins from 2025 and counted 4,827 crimes that police class as “high danger”.

About two-thirds were robberies. The same bulletins listed 337 violent deaths, which, if complete, would be roughly in line with the official rate.

Despacho 505 found that reported serious crime rose about fivefold in the second half of 2025. The rise followed the release of 9,900 prisoners during the year under a “family coexistence” benefit.

Undercounting shows up elsewhere. ContraData, a monitor run by La Lupa Feminista and Despacho 505, documented 54 violent deaths of women in 2025. Authorities classed only 11 of them as femicides.

Perceptions are mixed. In Gallup’s 2025 Global Safety Report, based on 2024 interviews, 63 percent of Nicaraguans said they felt safe walking alone at night. The figure was 53 percent in Costa Rica and 71 percent in the United States.

Hagamos Democracia, an exiled civic group, runs a remote quarterly survey of 400 people. In its June 2026 round, about eight in ten said they had noticed state surveillance, and 83 percent said insecurity had risen in three months. Answers in a closely watched society need care.

What the US, UK and Canadian advisories say

The US State Department rates Nicaragua at Level 3 of 4, “reconsider travel”, in an advisory issued on 14 May 2026. It cites crime, health, wrongful detention and arbitrary enforcement of local laws.

Washington has determined that US nationals face a serious risk of wrongful detention by the Nicaraguan government. It says some US citizens have been detained for several weeks or more, and some have faced exit bans without a fair and transparent process.

The advisory lists groups the government has targeted. They include NGO workers, academics, business representatives, missionaries, journalists and current or former US government employees.

It also warns that officials may search phones, computers and social media for anti-government content. Property, including land, homes and cash, may be seized without warning or legal justification.

Canada’s advice, last updated on 29 July 2026, says “exercise a high degree of caution”, the second of its four levels. It cites the political situation, possible unrest and crime.

Ottawa tells Canadians to avoid political activity and not to discuss politics in public, online or on social media. It notes that Nicaraguan law bans political activity by foreigners.

Britain’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) does not use numbered levels. Its guidance says foreigners can be arrested, detained or deported for joining a protest or a political meeting.

Using Nicaragua’s blue-and-white flag or colours in a protest or campaign can also lead to arrest. Britain has no embassy in Nicaragua, so help comes from its embassy in San José, Costa Rica.

How politics has reshaped safety since 2018

The turning point came in April 2018, when protests against social security reforms spread nationwide. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR), an Organization of American States body, counted 355 deaths by July 2019.

Since then, the government of Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo has jailed or exiled opponents and closed independent media. The State Department says more than 5,600 non-governmental organisations (NGOs) have been shut since 2018.

For scale, the exiled newspaper Confidencial counted 7,227 NGOs operating up to 2017. By August 2024, more than 70 percent had been closed, on its tally.

A constitutional reform, Law 1234, took effect on 18 February 2025. It made Ortega and Murillo, who are married, joint “co-presidents” and lengthened the term from five to six years.

The reform lets the presidency “coordinate” the legislature, the courts and the electoral body, the US Library of Congress noted. Elections once due in late 2026 moved to late 2027.

On 1 September 2026, the National Assembly gave first approval to further changes. They would stretch terms to seven years, move the vote to 2028 and bar so-called “traitors to the homeland” from running.

A second vote is due from 18 January 2027. Until then, the six-year terms and the 2027 election timetable formally stand. Yet in a speech on 19 July 2026, Ortega said Nicaragua would hold no more elections.

Stripping citizenship has become a signature tool. The UN Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua has documented 452 people deprived of nationality by court order since February 2023.

They include 222 political prisoners expelled to the United States in February 2023 and 135 expelled to Guatemala in September 2024. The experts also documented 318 Nicaraguans refused entry to their own country between June 2018 and August 2025.

Since 16 January 2026, a further amendment ends dual nationality in most cases. Nicaraguans who acquire another citizenship now lose their Nicaraguan one.

The US Embassy says the change is not meant to be retroactive. The State Department says some people who held both US and Nicaraguan citizenship have had the Nicaraguan one revoked.

Nicaragua also left the UN Human Rights Council in February 2025, according to the US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF). It announced exits from UNESCO, the UN refugee agency and the International Organization for Migration the same year.

Risks specific to foreigners: drones, cameras, phones and church

Drones are the clearest legal trap. The FCDO says Law 1230, introduced in December 2024, bans owning and flying drones and requires owners to hand them in.

US guidance adds that customs will seize drones. Officers may also seize cameras, video equipment, binoculars and even gaming consoles, with no guarantee of return.

Bird-watching and other wildlife observation need advance approval, the State Department says. Public photography is restricted, especially of government buildings and police activity.

On 2 July 2026, a 19-year-old French student filmed a short video near El Carmen, the Ortega-Murillo compound in Managua. Police checked his phone, found the clip on Instagram and questioned him for more than 11 hours.

He was then expelled to Costa Rica, Confidencial and 100% Noticias reported. He said he was denied a lawyer and contact with the French embassy.

Social media is watched. US guidance says immigration officers review posts for political content, and critical posts can lead to investigation, expulsion or refusal of entry.

The government has also revoked foreigners’ permanent residency over actions or expressions it considers political. Independent journalists are not allowed in Nicaragua, the State Department says.

The cathedral in León at sunset; public processions have been widely restricted since 2018 (Photo: Adam Jones, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)
