Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Religious activity carries its own risk. USCIRF, an independent US federal commission, says 309 religious figures had been forced out, expelled or barred by February 2026.

Researcher Martha Patricia Molina counted more than 16,500 banned processions and religious acts from 2018 to August 2025. Bishop Rolando Álvarez was sentenced to more than 26 years in 2023 and expelled to the Vatican in January 2024.

Church trips, missions and medical brigades need advance permission from Nicaragua’s foreign ministry, US guidance says. Even approved visits can be cancelled without warning.

USCIRF also noted reports in late 2025 that travellers had been barred from bringing Bibles into the country.

Health, hurricanes and volcanoes

Medical care is the risk many foreigners underestimate. The State Department says comprehensive care exists only in Managua, which has one hospital accredited by Joint Commission International, a US-based body.

Public hospitals are understaffed, and evacuation to the United States may be the only option in serious cases. Evacuations are expensive and often not covered by standard insurance.

Mosquito-borne dengue, Zika and chikungunya are common, as are typhoid and leptospirosis. Tap water is generally not safe to drink.

Hurricane season normally runs from June to November, and the rainy season from May to November brings floods. The Caribbean coast has taken the strongest recent hits.

In November 2020, Hurricanes Eta and Iota struck the northern Caribbean coast as Category 4 storms less than two weeks apart. The US National Hurricane Center put Iota’s landfall about 15 miles south of Eta’s.

Gas rises from the crater of Masaya volcano, near Managua (Photo: Adalberto Hernandez Vega, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Volcanoes line the Pacific side of the country. The FCDO lists San Cristóbal, Masaya, Cerro Negro, Telica and Concepción on Ometepe Island among the active ones.

Local guides are required for most volcano hikes, including on Ometepe, US guidance says. Earthquakes are also a risk.

Pacific beaches have strong currents, few lifeguards and a record of drownings. The US warns that even experienced swimmers are at risk.

Granada, San Juan del Sur, León, Managua and the Caribbean coast

Managua, the capital, concentrates both risk and services. Canada lists Mercado Oriental, Jorge Dimitrov and Ciudad Belén among neighbourhoods with very high levels of assault and robbery.

US government staff may not visit Mercado Oriental, the national baseball stadium, casinos or strip clubs. They may not use taxis, moto-taxis or public transport, and may use only the Ray ride-hailing app.

Granada, the colonial city on Lake Nicaragua, is one of the main tourist centres. US staff may drive after dark on the Carretera Masaya between Managua and Granada, an exception to their night-driving ban.

Granada’s main risks are those US and Canadian advice flags for tourist areas. They are pickpocketing, bag snatching and theft from cars.

The bay at San Juan del Sur on the Pacific coast (Photo: Lubi nuñez, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

San Juan del Sur lies near the Costa Rican border. Canada flags property crime in remote Pacific beach communities, and US guidance reports sexual assaults on Americans in beach resorts.

Buyers there should check whether land lies within 15 kilometres (about 9 miles) of a border. A law passed on 5 August 2025 made that strip “border territory” subject to seizure, the State Department says.

León is a university city in the north-west. Its department recorded more than 20 deaths in the 2018 crackdown, according to the IACHR. Today Canada lists its poorer neighbourhoods among areas with frequent house and car burglaries.

The Caribbean coast is a different world. Most roads there are unpaved, and the US says the region’s isolation limits the embassy’s ability to help.

The Corn Islands have no forensic doctors, so victims of violent crime must travel to Bluefields for examinations. The nearest hyperbaric chamber for divers is in Puerto Cabezas.

Further north, the IACHR reported in October 2025 on armed settler attacks against Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities. It counted at least three large-scale attacks between 2020 and 2024.

Practical safety advice for living in Nicaragua

Clean your devices before you travel. US guidance advises deleting sensitive photos, posts and comments that could be seen as controversial.

Leave the drone at home, and think twice about long lenses and binoculars. Avoid filming police, government buildings and official events.

Stay out of politics entirely, online and offline. Avoid protests, crowds and blue-and-white political symbols, and keep a low profile.

Carry valid identity documents at all times; Nicaraguan law requires foreigners to do so, the US Embassy says. Dual nationals should carry both passports and leave on the one they entered with.

The US embassy may be denied consular access to detained dual US-Nicaraguan nationals. That makes a check-in plan with family more important.

US citizens pay US$10 in cash for a tourist entry stamp valid for up to 90 days. Passports need six months’ validity, and you need an onward or return ticket.

Use radio-dispatched or authorised taxis with red plates, as the FCDO advises, and never one called by a stranger. Express kidnappings, in which victims are forced to withdraw cash, have occurred.

Avoid driving at night outside cities. Since 17 June 2025, national speed limits are 50 km/h (31 mph) for most vehicles and 40 km/h (25 mph) for motorcycles, US guidance says. Drivers in fatal crashes are held for at least 48 hours.

The State Department describes the córdoba as fixed against the dollar. The Central Bank of Nicaragua’s official rate was 36.6243 córdobas per US dollar on 22 September 2026. The open.er-api.com service quoted 36.83 on 25 September.

ATMs can be unreliable, so keep some cash, and avoid street money changers, whom the FCDO links to muggings. US dollars are sometimes accepted.

Enrol with your embassy and buy insurance that covers medical evacuation. In an emergency, dial 118 for police and 128 for an ambulance.

So, is Nicaragua safe? Canada notes that foreigners are rarely targeted by violent crime. The larger risk is arbitrary action by the state, which no precaution fully removes.

Sources: Travel advice from the US State Department and US Embassy in Managua, the UK FCDO and the Government of Canada; laws from Nicaragua’s National Assembly and official gazette; the exchange rate from the Central Bank of Nicaragua; human rights findings from the UN Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua, the IACHR and USCIRF; crime data from the National Police as reported, InSight Crime, Despacho 505, ContraData and Gallup; hurricane data from the US National Hurricane Center; population from the World Bank. All accessed 25 September 2026.

What Is Not Known

The true level of crime is not known. Nicaragua publishes no transparent homicide dataset, and InSight Crime found no reliable figures for 2025. Weekly police bulletins cover only what the police choose to report.

Police announced the rate of 5 at their anniversary event in September 2025. They have not published a statistical yearbook since 2021, Confidencial reported in September 2026. Any new figure will face the same problem: it cannot be checked against disaggregated data.

How the dual-nationality ban will be enforced is not clear. The US Embassy says it is not meant to be retroactive, but the State Department says procedures remain unclear.

The seven-year reform still needs a second vote from 18 January 2027. The governing Sandinista party controls the assembly, but the outcome is not certain. How the ban on “traitors” standing for office will be applied is not known.

No public list shows who faces an entry or exit ban. The UN experts say the real number of people refused entry is likely far higher than the 318 they documented.

How a handover from Ortega, now 80, to Murillo would affect security is not known. Under the 2025 constitution, if one co-president leaves office, the other completes the term.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Nicaragua safe for expats in 2026?

Street crime is moderate by Central American standards, though official data cannot be verified. Police put the homicide rate at 5 per 100,000 for September 2024 to August 2025. The bigger risk for foreigners is political: the US rates Nicaragua Level 3 and warns of wrongful detention, phone searches and expulsions.

What travel advisory level does the US give Nicaragua?

The US State Department rates Nicaragua Level 3, reconsider travel, in an advisory issued on 14 May 2026. It cites crime, health, wrongful detention and arbitrary enforcement of local laws. Canada says exercise a high degree of caution, and the UK warns that foreigners can be arrested or deported for political activity.

Can I bring a drone or take photos in Nicaragua?

Do not bring a drone: Law 1230, introduced in December 2024, bans owning and flying them, and customs will seize them. Photography of government buildings and police is restricted. A French student was expelled in July 2026 after filming near the Ortega-Murillo compound in Managua.

Is Nicaragua safer than Costa Rica?

On official homicide figures, yes: Nicaragua’s police claim 5 per 100,000, while InSight Crime put Costa Rica at 16.8 in 2025. But Nicaragua’s figures cannot be independently checked. In Gallup’s 2025 report, 63 percent of Nicaraguans felt safe walking alone at night, against 53 percent in Costa Rica.

Which parts of Nicaragua need extra care?

Canada lists several Managua neighbourhoods, including Mercado Oriental, for very high levels of assault and robbery. Remote Pacific beach communities see property crime and dangerous currents. The Caribbean coast is isolated, with limited embassy help, and took two Category 4 hurricanes in November 2020.

Can dual US-Nicaraguan citizens travel safely?

Since 16 January 2026, Nicaraguans who acquire another citizenship lose their Nicaraguan one in most cases. The US embassy may be denied consular access to detained dual nationals. Dual nationals should carry both passports and leave on the one they entered with.

World.title: Police visit 40 homes as search continues for missing officer Kenyon Barrow
World.content:
Police visit 40 homes as search continues for missing officer Kenyon Barrow

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in Orange Walk have stepped up community outreach efforts as the search continues for missing police officer Kenyon Barrow.

On Wednesday, September 23, officers attached to the Orange Walk Formation conducted Meet and Greet operations in Guinea Grass Village and the Black Water Creek area.

Police say the main purpose of the operations was to gather information that could assist in locating Barrow, while also strengthening relations with residents in both communities.

The operations were led by senior police officers, including NRC Senior Superintendent Alejandro Cowo, Officer Commanding Orange Walk ASP Armando Dubon, Deputy Officer Commanding Operations Luis Quixaj and Deputy Officer Commanding Trial Farm Inspector David Cal.

Other staff officers, Community Policing Unit personnel and Volunteer Special Constables also took part.

Police say a total of 40 residences were visited during the two operations.

Residents reportedly welcomed the officers and expressed appreciation for the effort to engage with the community while gathering information related to the missing officer.

Barrow was previously reported missing from Orange Walk, and police continue to seek information that could help determine his whereabouts.

World.title: Wet Friday ahead as rain and thunderstorms spread across Belize
World.content:
Wet Friday ahead as rain and thunderstorms spread across Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Friday could turn wet across several parts of Belize as showers and thunderstorms spread from coastal areas into the rest of the country.

The morning forecast from the National Meteorological Service says moist and unstable conditions continue over the area.

Rainfall activity will initially be concentrated along the coast and offshore, where a few showers, thunderstorms and periods of light rain are expected.

By midday, however, showers and thunderstorms are forecast to develop around the country.

Inland areas will see the hottest temperatures today, reaching around 92 degrees Fahrenheit, while coastal communities can expect highs near 85 degrees. Temperatures in the hills will peak near 78 degrees.

Conditions should improve somewhat tonight, with generally isolated showers and thunderstorms.

Looking ahead to Saturday, forecasters expect cloudy periods and mostly isolated showers or thunderstorms, although coastal areas could see additional activity during the morning. Southern Belize has a higher chance for showers Saturday night.

Forecasters are also tracking Tropical Storm Fay and Tropical Storm Gonzalo in the Atlantic, but both systems are currently no threat to Belize.

World.title: International News: Barbados PM calls for inclusive global rules to govern Artificial Intelligence
World.content:
International News: Barbados PM calls for inclusive global rules to govern Artificial Intelligence

By Zoila Palma: Barbados Prime Minister Mia Amor Mottley has called for globally agreed rules governing artificial intelligence (AI), stressing that regulations must not be shaped solely by a handful of powerful countries and technology companies.

Addressing the General Debate of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), Mottley said every State affected by AI should have the opportunity to help shape the rules governing its development and use. “A technology that will affect every State must be governed by the rules that every State has had the opportunity to shape,” she stated.

Mottley acknowledged AI’s potential to improve healthcare, predict disasters, strengthen agriculture, and expand access to education and public services.

However, she warned that the technology could also reproduce discrimination, increase surveillance, and accelerate the spread of false information beyond the ability of institutions to respond effectively.

Mottley stressed that AI governance should not depend solely on voluntary corporate practices or decisions made by technologically advanced States.

She called for an inclusive international framework that protects human dignity, maintains meaningful human oversight, and ensures the benefits of AI are shared equitably among countries.

World.title: Guatemalan Defense Ministry says “operations are conducted with adherence to international framework”
World.content:
Guatemalan Defense Ministry says “operations are conducted with adherence to international framework”

By Zoila Palma: Following reports that on Thursday evening, a Guatemalan Air Force aircraft was tracked flying over Belizean territory and made several passes near Lighthouse Reef Atoll, the Guatemalan Ministry of National Defense has issued a statement.

“In response to reports circulated on Thursday, September 24, in Belizean media and on social networks regarding an alleged overflight by a Guatemalan military aircraft in the Lighthouse Reef Atoll area and near Caye Caulker, the Ministry of National Defense of the Republic of Guatemala addresses the public and the international community to reaffirm its institutional position:

All activities and operations of the Guatemalan Army are conducted with strict adherence to the national and international legal framework.

The institution acts with professionalism, discipline, and transparency, in fulfillment of its constitutional mission to serve the Nation and with full respect for human rights,” the statement said.

In addition, it noted that the “Ministry of National Defense works in coordination with State institutions, in accordance with the law.”

The Guatemalan Ministry of National Defense reiterated that its actions are governed, at all times, by respect for the law and by service to Guatemala.

World.title: PM Briceño meets OPEC Fund CEO at UN General Assembly, discusses future development projects
World.content:
PM Briceño meets OPEC Fund CEO at UN General Assembly, discusses future development projects

By Zoila Palma: Today, Prime Minister John Briceño held discussions with the OPEC Fund for International Development on potential future projects during his participation in the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

The meeting took place on the margins of the 81st United Nations General Assembly, being held from September 22 to 28, 2026, at the United Nations Headquarters in New York City.

Briceño said the discussion focused on opportunities for future projects and expressed his intention to advance those opportunities into concrete development initiatives. “I look forward to continuing the conversation and turning opportunities into tangible progress,” he stated.

World.title: Cordel Hyde to colleagues: “Power is temporary, it’s fleeting”
World.content:
Cordel Hyde to colleagues: “Power is temporary, it’s fleeting”

By Zoila Palma: Deputy Prime Minister Cordel Hyde is calling on the Government to make sacrifices, review its allowances, and address internal challenges, warning that leaders must remain connected to the realities facing Belizeans.

Hyde said Government officials must demonstrate that they understand the struggles of the people by making adjustments to their own benefits and spending.

“I think we as a Government have to tighten our own belts, have to make some sacrifices, have to look at our own allowances too, because we can’t be living one way and have the people living another way,” he stated.

Hyde also acknowledged that the People’s United Party (PUP) faces challenges and must take steps to strengthen itself. “I think that we have to face the reality, and the reality is that we aren’t this sleek running machine that we were as a party a year and a half ago when we were winning elections by record margins,” he said.

“We have some issues. We have to look inside ourselves and try to renew ourselves, try to rejuvenate ourselves, try to refresh ourselves, try to recalibrate and get ourselves back on track and remember where we came from,” he added.

“We have to understand that power is temporary, it’s fleeting even, it doesn’t last forever,” he reminded.

The Deputy Prime Minister also cautioned political leaders against becoming disconnected through the influence of power.

“But the minute you get carried away with your power and you think you’re God’s gift to the world, some of the people help you too—they fluff you up, they blow you up, they make you feel like all is well, and is not well,” Hyde said.

World.title: Cordel Hyde: “We have to be honest with our people”
World.content:
Cordel Hyde: “We have to be honest with our people”

By Zoila Palma: Deputy Prime Minister Cordel Hyde says that the PUP’s blue machine must work harder than ever before heading into the 2027 municipal elections.

“I was never good at predicting stuff. What I can say is that we have to be cautious, we have to work harder than we’ve ever been before. We have to be honest with our people, we have to take care of our people, we have to do right by our people, we can’t take anything for granted,” Hyde told 7news Belize.

Hyde says that this municipal election will be interesting.

“It’s going to be the first real test for this Government since 2025 in an environment that’s not what we are used to. So we’re going to have to be better than we’ve been, but we have the talent, we have the capability, we know what we need to do it’s about getting together and getting that done,” Hyde added.

World.title: Belize represented at 4th Climate Mobility Summit in New York
World.content:
Belize represented at 4th Climate Mobility Summit in New York

By Zoila Palma: Belize was represented at the 4th Climate Mobility Summit in New York, September 22–24, 2026, with the participation of Orlando Habet, Minister of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management.

The Summit brought together governments, experts and other stakeholders to advance practical solutions to the human impacts of climate change — including sea-level rise, flooding, drought and climate-related displacement.

For Belize, these discussions have real and lasting significance.

“Climate change can affect our coastal communities, homes, livelihoods, food security, cultural heritage and natural resources. The Summit’s focus on strengthening local adaptation, protecting the “right to stay,” and supporting safe and dignified mobility speaks directly to the need to build resilience and protect Belizean communities,” the Ministry said.

Through Belize’s participation, the country continues to contribute to the global conversation on climate resilience, adaptation and the protection of communities in the face of a changing climate.

World.title: KC principal responds to viral video of student being held over railing
World.content:
Kingston College Principal Dave Myrie speaking at morning devotion on Monday, March 31, 2025 as the school celebrated its 36th Boys’ Champs title. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Kingston College (KC) has launched an investigation after a video surfaced online showing a student being held by colleagues over a railing before falling.

In an official statement dated September 23, Principal Dave Myrie said the school’s administration and Board of Management are aware of the matter and are conducting a “thorough investigation” into the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Myrie said, however, that no student was injured.

“The School Administration and the Board of Management are aware of the matter and are currently conducting a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident,” Myrie said in the statement.

He assured parents, guardians, students and members of the wider KC community that the matter was being taken seriously and would be addressed in accordance with the school’s established policies and procedures.

The principal also reiterated the school’s commitment to maintaining what he described as a safe, disciplined and supportive environment for its students.

KC has also appealed to members of the school community to refrain from sharing or reposting the video.

According to Myrie, further circulation could unnecessarily compromise the privacy, dignity and welfare of the young students involved.

“Any further information considered appropriate will be communicated through the School’s official channels,” the statement said.

Myrie has served as principal of Kingston College since 2012.

– Howard Walker

World.title: Court walkout looms
World.content:
Defence attorneys staging a ‘silent protest’ outside the Supreme Court on King Street in downtown Kingston on Wednesday demanding that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 and its impact on “justice, due process and the rule of law” be taken on board for reform. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Defence attorneys have been placed on alert to pull their services from the island’s courts for an entire week, starting next Monday, a move that will deal a significant blow to the Michaelmas term which began just over a week ago.

The lawyers arrived at the decision after a meeting on Thursday with Justice Minister Delroy Chuck which they say failed to produce any meaningful plans to reform the 2022 Firearms Act.

The emergency meeting was called following Wednesday’s ‘silent protest’ outside the Supreme Court on King Street in downtown Kingston, where members of the Jamaican Bar Association, the Advocates Association in collaboration with Bar associations across the island, armed with placards, demanded that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 and its impact on “justice, due process and the rule of law” be taken on board for reform.

Some hours later, Chuck indicated that he would be meeting with representatives of the bodies to hear their concerns.

However, following those discussions, defence attorney Tamika Harris, a member of the Bar Council of the Jamaican Bar Association and chair of its Criminal Practice and Procedure Subcommittee, who was a key figure behind the protest, told the Jamaica Observer that the meeting amounted to little less than an exercise in futility.

“The minister could not give a timeline as to when anything would be taken to the legislature, and he has asked for the discussion to be placed in writing but before [the Act was passed] the Bar Association… made a submission to Parliament. We are not asking for anything different, so it’s not like our argument is new,” Harris stated.

“The meeting, in my mind, was an opportunity for us to say the same things we have already said, but we have not gotten any response from the minister to, for example, say when he will go to Parliament [with proposed amendments]. I know everything takes time, but I did not get any idea of a plan to put in action. So the minister didn’t confirm that he was going to put a plan in action, so there is no resolution,” Harris declared.

As such, she said attorneys will be moving to action the next stage of their protest.

“He was very courteous and he listened. He expressed that he understood our concerns, but he did not go any further to say exactly if they were going to be dealt with and when, so there is nothing. I am aware he has already been presented with similar arguments by the director of public prosecutions and even the chief justice. I am going to ask my members to withdraw our services,” Harris told the Observer.

“We are going to use the opportunity, perhaps, to do quick education. The public needs to be aware that we are not saying legislation must be weak on persons who use firearms to terrorise our Jamaican citizens, we are not saying the legislation needs to be weak; we are saying that the legislation is to be fair and cognisant that not every case is the same,” Harris said.

The protests come just over a week after the justice minister’s comments at the Annual Assize Service of the judiciary. Chuck said, while the mandatory minimum sentences contained in the provision were being reviewed because of widespread concerns, “The security forces and a number of my colleagues feel that the Act is working and it is bringing down murders and shootings.

“It is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country, and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms. But it is under consideration,” Chuck said.

The comments triggered furious commentary from several quarters.

A week later members of Jamaica’s legal profession met on Saturday, September 19 to consider what they described as “the operation and impact of the Act, particularly its mandatory sentencing provisions and the restrictions placed on judicial discretion”.

In a statement issued following that meeting, the attorneys said, “The legal profession supports strong and effective laws to combat gun violence and punish those who use illegal firearms to murder, rob, terrorise and intimidate our citizens. Our concern is not with strong penalties. Our concern is with a sentencing regime that does not adequately allow judges to distinguish between offenders, offences, and individual circumstances.”

The Act, which prescribes a mandatory 15-year sentence for specified violations, took effect in November 2022 and, among other things, provides penalties ranging from 15 years to life imprisonment for possession of illegal weapons. It establishes a dual regime — distinguishing between prohibited weapons or unregulated firearms and connected activities, and firearms that are duly authorised or registered.

According to the advocates, their September 19 meeting “identified several areas of serious concern, including the restriction of judicial discretion; the proportionality of mandatory minimum sentences in individual cases; the diminished incentive for early guilty pleas; the resulting increase in matters proceeding to trial and pressure on an already burdened criminal justice system; the treatment of imitation firearms; and the consequences of certain provisions for licensed firearm holders”.

“The legal profession is calling for urgent amendments to the Act, including consideration of an ‘exceptional circumstances’ provision allowing judges appropriate discretion in deserving cases, meaningful sentencing incentives for early guilty pleas, reform of the certificate regime, and a review of the provisions governing imitation firearms and licensed firearm holders. The profession also calls for urgent, structured consultation with the Government, Opposition, Parliament, the judiciary and other relevant stakeholders on the proposed amendments”, the attorneys said in that statement.

World.title: Christiana clampdown
World.content:
Vendors on Wildman Street in Christiana on Thursday (Photos: Kasey Williams)

CHRISTIANA, Manchester — Mandeville Mayor Donovan Mitchell says, effective today, there will be a clampdown on unapproved buildings and illegal vending, as part of enforcement activities in the south-central town of Christiana.

“Yesterday (Wednesday) I came into Christiana and as the chairman of the local Board of Health I spent about five hours walking the streets of Christiana. I visited the abattoir. I visited the market. I visited the transportation centre. I looked at some businesses [and] buildings going up. I know at the council meeting early this month I made a statement and some people are up in arms and all of that… What is happening in the parish will not continue,” he said on Thursday while addressing the launch of Sam Fo Meats mobile application on Wildman Street in Christiana.

“I said it yesterday (Wednesday) to my team that Wildman Street, please be prepared, because I am going to be changing the entire look of Wildman Street. There will absolutely be no selling on the street. I am warning the businesses that are putting their sewage and grey water into our water channels to stop and stop before tomorrow [Friday] morning, because a team from the public health service will be coming out and we are going to make sure it cannot continue,” added Mitchell.

He pointed to the public safety concerns and hazards of waste water flowing on the busy commercial street.

“You cannot be walking on the street and all you are seeing is grey water. Businesses can’t build their buildings and put their grey water on the street. What about our children, the elderly? You are walking and miss your step in soap water and you break your leg and the first thing is they call the parish council,” said Mitchell, who chairs the Manchester Municipal Corporation.

“I am warning people who are building houses without plans from the Manchester Municipal Corporation. I am not holding bar; you have to do better. When a building collapses because you have not done the correct thing, who is the first person you blame? Government. Where was the Government when you were building? Not around, because you put zinc all around your place and you do what you have to do and when you are finished you open up the zinc and you see a building there that has not gone through the proper channel,” added Mitchell.

Pertaining to the Christiana abattoir, Mitchell said he is contemplating closing it for renovations.

“We are having some problems and I will tell you that maybe, based on the letters I am getting from the health services, I may have to close it even temporarily to make sure that things go right. I am warning, since I am in Christiana, that things are not going to be the same in Christiana. There has to be some changes,” declared Mitchell.

World.title: Skippa in int’l spotlight
World.content:
Dancehall artiste Skippa was named as one to watch by Jamaica Observer at the start of 2026 .

When the Jamaica Observer named Skippa one of its artistes to watch at the start of 2026, the prediction came with the expectation that the young dancehall artiste’s momentum was worth keeping an eye on. What has followed, however, stretches well beyond even his own expectations.

There was the touring, the growing audiences, the songs steadily finding new listeners, and, perhaps most significantly, recognition from one of the music industry’s most established brands — Billboard.

Still, as the artiste himself revealed, 2026 has so far surpassed his wildest imagination.

“We had goals around touring and growing the music, but everything kind of surpassed what we had in mind. The amount of shows, the places we’ve been received, the people connecting with the music in places we didn’t necessarily expect, and then Billboard on top of that — it’s been crazy,” he shared. “We’re grateful for all of it, because you can set goals, but sometimes the reality goes way beyond what you planned for.”

Speaking to the Splash, the entertainer said that, although he has been putting in the work, he was taken aback when he was named by Billboard as a Caribbean Rising Star. He admitted that the honour caught him completely off guard and that he had to resist getting swept up in the whirlwind that the moment ushered in.

“Honestly, I was taken aback. I’m not really the type to overreact, so I was just there trying to take in the moment,” he said. “Billboard recognising me as a Caribbean Rising Star, in a room with so many people who have been doing this at the highest level, that’s crazy. I’m grateful, for real, and it’s something I’ll always remember.”

For an artiste whose career has accelerated considerably in recent years, the recognition represents another marker in a journey that appears to be moving faster than he anticipated. Billboard may have just caught up to Skippa’s burgeoning career, but the proverbial writing was on the wall since the latter part of last year.

By December 2025, YouTube year-end statistics showed that the entertainer had already emerged as Jamaica’s third-most-viewed artiste on the platform, behind Chronic Law and Vybz Kartel, with approximately 79.9 million views. His numbers remained consistent in 2026, with the artiste repeatedly placing multiple songs among Jamaica’s most-streamed records.

Still, he remains humble, crediting his chart success to his loyal fan base rather than to a secret creative formula.

“I wouldn’t say I figured out some formula, because I think what really sets my work apart is that people just relate to me. I’m being myself and making music from my own experience and perspective, and people see themselves in that,” he said.

That connection, he believes, matters more than the numbers themselves — or any ‘trending list’ he may or may not find himself on.

“I don’t chase whatever trend is happening just because it’s working for somebody else. I just try to make good music and stay authentic, and the people decide what they want to run with,” he said.

It is a philosophy that has become increasingly important as the numbers have grown.

For Skippa, there is a difference between having a hit song and building something that can last.

“Consistency, for sure. I think that’s one of the biggest things,” he said. “You can have one song that catches fire, but building a career is different. You have to keep showing up, keep making music, keep performing, keep connecting with the people, and keep growing.”

With that mindset, the entertainer shared that he is looking at his recent success as motivation to go even further, rather than being tricked into believing he has somehow arrived.

“To come into this space and, in such a short time, see my name alongside artistes who have been doing this for years, that’s a big thing. It’s definitely something I’m grateful for and amazed by,” he said. “But I don’t look at it like I’ve arrived and that’s it. It just makes me appreciate the journey even more and motivates me to keep working.”

The entertainer sought to acknowledge the machinery working for his good behind the scenes. Naming his manager, Cristina; engineer, producer and DJ Travis; Chargie Records; Solitary Muzic; and Bankroller, among others, as people who have contributed to his progress, Skippa expressed that, “Everybody played their part, so when I’m on that stage accepting something like Billboard Rising Star, I know it’s not just about me.”

The prediction made by the Observer at the beginning of the year has taken on a life of its own. Having lived up to the ‘one to watch’ status, Skippa is now ready to take things to the next level as he cements his place among dancehall’s best.

World.title: GOV’T QUERIES WINDALCO SALE
World.content:
The entrance to Windalco’s Ewarton Works plant in Clarendon

THE Government says it has received no notice that UC Rusal plans to sell Windalco and is seeking answers from the Russian company’s parent after a report that it has begun looking for buyers.

Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Mining Floyd Green told the Jamaica Observer that checks with Rusal’s local team had produced no information about a possible sale.

“Government has no record or notification any such plans and checks with the local UC Rusal team have indicated that they have no information or correspondence on that matter. We will be reaching out to the parent company regarding the unsubstantiated reports,” Green said.

Bloomberg reported Tuesday that Rusal had begun sounding out potential buyers for Windalco in Jamaica and its bauxite operation in Guyana. It cited people familiar with the matter, but said the plans were at an early stage and a sale might not happen. Rusal declined to comment to Bloomberg.

The report has surfaced at a difficult time for Jamaica’s bauxite and alumina trade. New figures from the Statistical Institute of Jamaica show that mining and quarrying export earnings fell 46.4 per cent to US$179.7 million in the first five months of 2026, down from US$335.3 million a year earlier. Alumina accounted for most of that fall. Export earnings in the industry dropped 47.9 per cent to US$149.8 million, while bauxite earnings fell 44.3 per cent to US$22.9 million.

Those figures cover the industry as a whole rather than Windalco’s sales. They do, however, show why any question about the future of a major alumina producer will draw attention from workers, suppliers, and the communities around its operations.

Meanwhile, Green pointed to Windalco’s recent spending as evidence that work on the ground is continuing.

“Windalco just completed a major haul road investment and are mining a new area,” he told the

Business Week.

The haul road in St Ann cost about US$29 million and opened access to more high-quality ore, Green told Parliament in May. The investment does not settle whether Rusal might consider selling the business, but it raises an obvious question about what its parent company intends to do with the Jamaican assets.

Windalco is Rusal’s remaining alumina business in Jamaica after the Russian company sold Alpart in 2016. It owns the operating Ewarton alumina refinery in St Catherine, bauxite mines, and the Port Esquivel shipping facility; its Kirkvine refinery has been mothballed since 2009. Rusal acquired the Government’s last stake in Windalco in 2014, making it the sole owner.

— Karena Bennet

World.title: SMART PLAY
World.content:
SPEID... we’ll do what we have to do in the right moments (Photo: AFP)

JAMAICA’S Reggae Boyz will be in action at the National Stadium tonight, hosting Guatemala in their Concacaf Nations League A opener at 7:00 pm. Interim head coach Rudolph Speid says the main goal for his team is to play smart, adapt, and do the basics well.

“It’s a performance where we do everything correctly as the needs arise,” Speid said during a pre-match press conference on Thursday morning. “What we have tried to do is to talk about adaptability. So, whatever needs to be done, we’ll be doing it. We’re going to try to play properly — we’ll do what we have to do in the right moments.”

Speid, who was in charge on an interim basis for the World Cup play-offs in Mexico last March, and the Unity Cup in London in May, returned on an interim basis last month but he has had only three days of training with the squad in this international window. He dismissed concerns about the short preparation window and questions about his own coaching future.

“It is what it is; we have three days in training so we just made the best use of it,” Speid said. “That [my future] is not important at the moment. What is important is that we try and win these four games.”

While Speid focuses on tactical execution, tonight carries deep personal significance for midfielder Courtney Clarke.

The Walsall midfielder grew up in the community of Hazard in May Pen. After showing his capabilities to overseas fans during the Unity Cup, tonight marks his first opportunity to play a senior international match on home soil in front of his family.

“I’d say I’m more than ready now; I’ve been waiting for a while,” Clarke said. “The Unity Cup gave me the confidence to show the Jamaican fans in England [what I can do]. Now I’m going to be on home soil and show everybody. Everybody’s been working harder, pushing everybody and the goal is to get it done.”

For Clarke, lining up at “The Office” is a milestone moment in his career, and one he hopes to mark with a win.

Addressing the team’s recent lack of goals is another primary focus for Speid. Instead of changing the entire tactical system, he wants his players to move better off the ball.

“Usually, when you’re not scoring goals, it’s usually the movements that are the problem,” Speid said. “So we have been working on that and we hope that with better movements from the attackers, we’ll be able to score goals.”

Jamaica will be without winger Leon Bailey due to an ankle injury. He has been replaced by Jahmarie Nolan. Speid sees Bailey’s absence as an opportunity for younger wide players like Renaldo Cephas, Kaheim Dixon, and Tyreece Campbell to step up.

“Jamaica has a lot of talented players so once Leon is not available, it gives another player an opportunity to come into the team,” Speid said. “There are a lot of players champing at the bit. So, while it’s bad in one sense, it’s still good for us to expose other players.”

Jamaica has extra motivation tonight after losing 1-0 to Guatemala in their last official meeting at the Concacaf Gold Cup last year under previous head coach Steve McClaren. Óscar Santis scored the winner in that match.

Speid respects Guatemala’s playing style but says his team is ready for the challenge.

“We recognise that they’re a tough team, they like to play with the ball at their feet,” Speid said. “So they have some strengths, but we’re aware of what those strengths are.”

Speid says the squad is focused on getting the right result tonight.

“They’re very motivated,” he said. “It’s a new-look squad, but I think we have the right players here to go forward.”

Squad

Goalkeepers

Andre Blake (captain), Shaquan Davis, Amal Knight

Defenders

Ronaldo Webster, Christopher Ainsworth, Joel Latibeaudiere, Tayvon Gray, Richard King, Damion Lowe, Miguel Freckleton

Midfielders

Isaac Hayden, Kasey Palmer, Courtney Clarke, Karoy Anderson, Dwayne Atkinson, Leon Bailey, Brandon Cover

Forwards

Bailey-Tye Cadamarteri, Javon East, Renaldo Cephas, Tyreece Campbell, Rumarn Burrell, Kaheim Dixon, Andre Brooks

World.title: Hyundai Jamaica goes elite
World.content:
Hyundai Jamaica’s launched its Palisade Elite Club programme on September 11. (Photo: Rory Daley)

Magna Motors, local dealers for the Hyundai line of vehicles, launched its Palisade Elite Club on Friday, September 11, at the official residence of the Mexican Ambassador to Jamaica Roberto Canseco Martínez in Cherry Garden, St Andrew.

“The Palisade Elite Club is something really special, and it’s a nice package for our customers who are interested in the 2026 Palisade. There are so many benefits, as we want to take care of our customers beyond buying a vehicle,” Carla Hollingsworth, marketing manager, Magna Motors, told the

Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

Purchasers of a 2026 Hyundai Palisade, the brand’s flagship model, will be immediately enrolled in this programme that boasts a large number of free benefits. Beyond the initial welcome package, Palisade Elite Club members receive a loaner vehicle during servicing with a dedicated service manager, premium detailing, airport concierge service that includes complimentary transfers twice a year, vehicle buy-back at a guaranteed value, and five years of service coverage. Non-vehicle related extras include airport lounge access.

The three-row premium SUV that is the Palisade is available in two trims, diesel and hybrid; both have all-wheel drive as standard.

“The Palisade Elite Club just makes sense for Hyundai Jamaica as we are a value-added brand globally. This is our way of stepping up that bar for our Hyundai Elite customers,” said Hollingsworth.

World.title: ‘I did not trip’: Dr Gabrielle Henry speaks on terrifying fall in new interview
World.content:
Miss Universe Jamaica 2025 Dr Gabrielle Henry .

Former Miss Universe Jamaica Dr Gabrielle Henry says moments before her serious and traumatic fall during the Miss Universe 2025 competition, she had simply been following instructions given to her by organisers.

“I stopped when I was told to stop, I looked at the cameras and then when I was instructed to go I turned to the left, which I was instructed to do,” she told Good Morning America (GMA), recalling the November 19, 2025 incident publicly for the first time, almost a year later.

At home, the video of her tumble generated shock and concern for the pageant queen, with Jamaicans offering prayers and well wishes.

The fall upended Henry’s life, shattering her dreams of representing Jamaica, she explained.

Henry’s disappointment was shared by her countrymen and was compounded by a series of prior shocks, including the Reggae Boyz’ failure to qualify for the World Cup and the passage of Hurricane Melissa.

“The devil may try to sabotage, but God’s purpose prevails! Get well soon, Gabby! We’re rooting for you to come back stronger and conquer the finals,” one user had posted under the Miss Universe Jamaica statement on Instagram.

Henry told GMA that after the fall, she was completely confused and disoriented, repeatedly blacking out for days.

“I have no recollection of the fall; I just know that the bottom of that hole was a concrete base, the first memory I have is that of waking up to my mother who was looking down on me. It was the first time I have ever seen my mother look so concerned, as soon as I saw my mom I blacked out again.” she shared.

When she regained consciousness fully, she was told she had received an intracranial haemorrhage and facial and back injuries.

“[A] brain injury is one of the most traumatising things; I would not wish it on my worst enemy. There is almost an out-of-body experience… it took me so long to get back to that place where I said, ‘This is MY body,’” Henry said in the report.

The doctor described the road to recovery as long and challenging, marked by sleepless nights and severe pain.

When asked who was to blame for the accident, she emphasised that she had not tripped and the fall could absolutely have been avoided.

“Proper measures should have and could have been put in place, it was the responsibility of those who had organised the stage who had put in the lighting to ensure that the protective mechanisms were also there,” she stressed.

Her comments align with allegations in a lawsuit she has filed against Miss Universe Organisation alleging that she was following rehearsed choreography when she fell into the unmarked hole.

READ: Dr Gabrielle Henry sues Miss Universe organisation over 2025 fall

The organisation in the wake of the lawsuit, has said they covered all of Gabrielle’s medical expenses in Thailand and “stood by her”.

The doctor confirmed that the pageant organisers had indeed supported her in the initial stages, including in Thailand however: “Following my return to Jamaica, I have not had much feedback from them as it pertains to covering my medical expenses which are still ongoing.”

The doctor is hoping to get back to practising ophthalmology eventually but noted that she has a long recovery ahead of her.

World.title: Pope Leo calls for dialogue as France’s populist forces eye power
World.content:
The pope named no politician or party. But his defense of diversity and religious freedom lands as Le Pen’s National Rally campaigns against immigration ahead of a presidential election she hopes to win for the first time.

“This dialogue is all the more urgent in the context of present-day France, where the people of differing cultural and religious backgrounds are called to live together,” the pontiff continued.

Standing in front of French government members and church dignitaries, the pope also argued against pushing religion out of public life, weeks after the National Rally said it was in favor of banning the Muslim headscarf. “Righteous secularism doesn’t mean excluding religion from public spaces,” he said.

Macron said the pope brought “hope” to France and praised his work on artificial intelligence and human dignity.

The papal visit will take Leo from the Élysée to UNESCO, Notre-Dame Cathedral and a youth vigil at the Stade de France. He will celebrate Mass on Saturday, expected to gather 600,000 people on the Champs-Elysées in Paris.

French politics have become deeply polarized in recent years, with the far-right National Rally and the far-left France Unbowed gaining popularity, just as traditional parties struggle to attract voters after a decade of Macron’s presidency.

World.title: Zelenskyy warns $27B funding gap could leave Ukraine short of weapons
World.content:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky (R) and High Representative of the European Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas (L) attend a joint press-conference following talks in Kyiv on October 13, 2025. | Sergei Supinsky/AFP via Getty Images

The president said he received a positive and constructive response from the EU during his diplomatic talks this week.

KYIV — Ukraine needs to secure $27 billion to plug a hole in its defense budget in the next two months or risk being unable to buy weapons early next year, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters in a WhatsApp chat Friday.

“Most of this money is for our drones, missiles, and supplies for our warriors. About a third of this money, perhaps even a little more, is for drones for January, February, and March. And if we do not order and pay for them in October and November, we will face serious challenges in January and February,” Zelenskyy said.

The president added that covering the deficit was a top topic of his negotiations with European partners: “I am urging the European Commission to provide the second tranche of the €90 billion [loan] sooner. Because, once again, we must have the necessary drones and missiles for January and February.”

World.title: Burnham plans first Berlin visit for talks with Merz
World.content:
Burnham took office on July 20 after replacing Keir Starmer, whose government had come under growing pressure following electoral losses, internal Labour Party disputes and weak public support. Starmer’s departure capped a turbulent final period in office in which domestic political problems increasingly dominated his government’s attention.

The change in leadership came less than a year after Starmer and Merz had made a major push to bring Britain and Germany closer.

The two governments signed the Kensington Treaty in July 2025. It laid out plans for closer work across defense and security, economic ties, transport and migration.

Defense has become one of the strongest parts of the relationship. Britain and Germany signed the Trinity House Agreement in October 2024, creating a framework for much closer military and defense-industrial cooperation. Since then, they have expanded work on joint weapons projects and military coordination while remaining major European supporters of Ukraine.

Burnham now has the chance to give those efforts new political momentum while setting his own approach to Europe. He entered Downing Street promising an intense domestic focus, but has since embarked on a diplomatic blitz, including meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy along with France's President Emmanuel Macron and U.S. President Donald Trump.

While Burnham is enjoying an early bout of optimism about his leadership, he will meet a German government facing significant domestic pressure.

Merz’s Christian Democrats suffered sharp losses in two state elections this month, while the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has gained support nationally. POLITICO’s Poll of Polls puts the AfD at 28 percent, ahead of the Christian Democrats at 20 percent.

For both governments, the October meeting offers an early opportunity to show that the closer relationship built over the past two years can continue under new political leadership in London.

World.title: Von der Leyen ally slams EU Commission’s AI response
World.content:
The enforcement of the EU's 2024 AI Act, which mandates that companies take measures to avoid losing control of their models, "is not on the level [where] we would like to have it," he added.

The comments shine the spotlight on the European Commission's Artificial Intelligence Office, which was put in charge of enforcing the AI Act in August.

Voss also said the Commission's overall response to the fast pace of technological developments is lagging, singling out von der Leyen's State of the Union last week.

"The Commission ... also the State of the Union is not ambitious enough regarding digital developments," said Voss, who is a member of the German Christian Democratic CDU, to which von der Leyen belongs.

One area where Voss sees a need for further regulation is liability of AI companies when their technology does damage. "What has been wrong from the beginning of this mandate is not to think about liability of AI," he said. "This can have an effect on every company."

POLITICO reported Monday that other European Parliament members have floated a proposal to add product liability provisions to address gaps in the AI Act.

World.title: Pope’s artificial intelligence guru admits he doesn’t use AI
World.content:
Pressed on whether he had any principled objection to the technology, he declared, “I’m quite willing and happy to learn,” he added. “I feel it’s my moral duty also to use it so that I have personal experience, and I hope it helps me with my work.”

Speaking on the fringes of Axel Springer’s WELT AI Summit in Berlin, Czerny called on European politicians and bishops to respond more clearly to warnings about the risks of frontier AI models forfeiting human control and oversight.

“There should be a dialogue between the bishops and the European governments to express the concern of the population to handle this with openness and with creativity … Otherwise, we will say five months or five years from now, ‘Oh, I felt there was a disaster coming, but there was nothing I could do.’”

The Roman Catholic Church is stepping up involvement in recent discussions over the future of AI. Paolo Benanti, the Vatican’s adviser on AI, attended a meeting of tech executives convened by King Charles III in Scotland last week to discuss the opportunities and risks surrounding the technology.

Anne McElvoy is a Global Reporter for the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.

World.title: Deutschland und Spanien zetteln Papierkrieg zu „Made in Europe“-Auslegung an
World.content:
In der EU geht es um Aufträge, die einen erheblichen Teil der Wirtschaftsleistung ausmachen. Von Windparks bis hin zu Stahl und Zement für den Bau von Autobahnen und U-Bahnen.

Deutschland, das Exportkraftzentrum der Union, dringt auf eine breiter angelegte „Made with Europe“-Definition. Dies entspricht auch weitgehend dem ursprünglichen Vorschlag der Kommission. Er sieht die Aufnahme von Partnern vor, die Freihandels- oder Beschaffungsabkommen mit der EU geschlossen haben oder einer Zollunion mit der Union angehören. Der Kreis könnte bis zu 80 Länder umfassen.

„Deutschland lehnt Protektionismus und Diskriminierung ab“, heißt es in dem deutschen Papier. „Die EU muss ein verlässlicher Partner für ihre Freihandelspartner bleiben und ihren rechtlichen Verpflichtungen nachkommen.“ Außerdem wird darin eine „Opt-in“-Möglichkeit gefordert, um Staaten einzubeziehen, die EU-Firmen eine entsprechende Behandlung gewähren.

Dem deutschen Papier haben sich bisher keine anderen EU-Länder angeschlossen. Frankreich, die zweitgrößte Volkswirtschaft der Union, dringt wie Spanien in die entgegengesetzte Richtung und plädiert für einen restriktiveren Ansatz.

Der französische Industrieminister Sébastien Martin bestritt zwar nicht, dass Europa gegenüber Handelspartnern offen bleiben müsse, betonte jedoch, dass öffentliches Geld in die Produktion in Europa fließen müsse.

„Auch in Zukunft wird es möglich sein, Produkte zu haben, bei denen ein Teil der Wertschöpfung aus anderen Ländern stammt, aber die Produktion muss in Europa stattfinden, damit sie für öffentliche Fördermittel infrage kommen“, sagte Martin bei seiner Ankunft zur Sitzung am Donnerstag in Brüssel.

World.title: 2027 : LE BAROMÈTRE DU REJET
World.content:
Tondelier et Mélenchon en tête

A ce stade de la campagne, c’est… Marine Tondelier qui remporte la palme du rejet, talonnée par Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Pas moins de 81% des sondés situent en effet entre 0 et 3 les chances qu’ils votent un jour pour la candidate Ecologiste. Ils sont 73% à en dire de même pour l’Insoumis, et même 98% à 100% chez les catégories de la population “réfractaires”, “autoritaires”, “anti-assistanat”, “traditionnalistes”, ou encore “libéraux”, selon la classification de Cluster 17.

Une différence majeure, toutefois, entre les deux principaux épouvantails de notre classement : là où seuls 9% de personnes interrogées jugent qu’il y a une probabilité forte ou très forte (entre 7 et 10) qu’ils glissent “un jour” un bulletin dans l’urne pour Tondelier, ils sont 19% à se voir probablement ou très probablement voter pour l’Insoumis en chef — soit l’équivalent des intentions de vote en sa faveur pour le premier tour de la présidentielle, à ce stade de la campagne et telles que mesurées par Cluster 17. Le socle de ceux qui adhèrent positivement aux propositions du candidat Mélenchon est donc nettement plus important. Et c’est particulièrement notable chez les jeunes : 42% des 18-34 ans jugent probables ou très probables (entre 7 et 10) les chances qu’ils votent pour l’Insoumis.

A noter : le fort rejet suscité dans une partie de la population par Marine Tondelier, notamment “dans tout l’espace conservateur”, a beaucoup à voir, selon Jean-Yves Dormagen, avec le “problème d’image” de son parti : “Les Verts sont très clivants sur les questions culturelles et sociétales, et l’écologie est devenue clivante aussi. Ils sont perçus comme très radicaux, promigrations, et ultraprogressistes”, note-t-il, soulignant que cette structure d’image est comparable à celle des Insoumis.

Le Pen et Philippe : même rejet

Autres enseignements majeurs de notre baromètre pour la présidentielle : les candidats les plus centraux ne sont pas en reste quand il s’agit de rejet. Les Français sont respectivement 68%, 72% et 66% à juger faible ou nulle la probabilité qu’ils votent pour Edouard Philippe, Gabriel Attal et Raphaël Glucksmann dans les temps à venir, et 69% pour le candidat des Républicains Bruno Retailleau. Et c’est bien Marine Le Pen qui est la moins rejetée : ils ne sont “que” 62% à déclarer que la probabilité qu’ils votent pour elle est faible ou nulle, contre 30% à l’envisager sérieusement (probabilité forte ou très forte, estimée entre 7 et 10).

Encore un peu plus dans le détail : 56% des personnes sondées jugent strictement impossible de voter pour Marine Le Pen (soit une note de 0 sur 10 ou une déclaration explicite de l’exclure), à touche-touche avec Edouard Philippe (55%), et à peine pire que Raphaël Glucksmann (53%). Ils sont en revanche respectivement 68% et 66% à l’exclure tout aussi catégoriquement quand il s’agit de Marine Tondelier et Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

La peur ou le rejet de l’Insoumis s’explique en partie dans le détail des traits d’image des candidats : Mélenchon est ainsi celui qui se voit le plus reprocher “un risque de dérive autoritaire” — le risque est estimé à 6,7 sur 10 en moyenne — devant Marine Le Pen, pour qui ce sujet est toutefois aussi un point faible (risque estimé à 5,6 sur 10 en moyenne).

World.title: Four suspects held over murder of Dominican singer Julián Oro Duro's wife
World.content:
The National Police of the Dominican Republic has identified the four suspects in the attack on the home of merengue singer Gilberto Julián Sarante, known as Julián Oro Duro. In the incident, his wife, 60-year-old Zeneida Socorro Castillo, was killed and the singer was seriously injured. All four suspects are already in custody.

 

The men arrested are Phillips Michael Tejeda Vásquez; Juan Carlos Hernández García, also known as Peña; Kevin Dariel Germán Troncoso, known as Yandel, aged 23; and 18-year-old Lawrence Mark Liranzo Marcos, nicknamed Chiquito. The latter was arrested after an intensive police manhunt. According to investigators, the four had professional or trusted links to the singer’s entourage.

Tejeda Vásquez worked as an air-conditioning technician and carried out private jobs at properties owned by Julián Oro Duro. The investigation indicates that he allegedly contacted the other suspects. Liranzo Marcos, meanwhile, knew the family and worked at a villa the singer was having built in Guerra.

The attack took place on 21 September, when the artist returned to his home in Brisa Oriental VI, in Santo Domingo Este, Dominican Republic, and was ambushed by the assailants after his wife had been held for hours. According to investigators, Castillo is believed to have been tortured for several hours before she was killed.

The singer suffered traumatic brain injuries in the assault and is still recovering. The Police and the Public Prosecutor’s Office are continuing to gather evidence about the crime. The case has provoked deep shock across the Dominican Republic.

World.title: Deep mining for memories: Greece opens digital archive to preserve Serifos ironworks history
World.content:
Serifos is one of the most beautiful islands in the Cyclades. Behind its major tourism development lies a history that most people know nothing about. The island was an important mining centre as far back as antiquity. Its subsoil is rich mainly in haematite and magnetite, with the result that to this day half of Serifos is perforated with galleries and shafts after many years of mining.

 

In the south-west, mainly at Mega Livadi and Koutalas, visitors can still see rusted rails, machinery, tools, wagons and loading piers. These are the visible traces of the intensive mining activity that shaped the island until the mid-20th century.

Mega Livadi Νίκος Κοκολάκης © Μουσείο Κυκλαδικής Τέχνης

In more recent times, iron ore extraction began in 1870 and became more systematic from 1885 onwards. Annual production often reached 200,000 tonnes. Mining was not only a livelihood for locals; many others arrived from different parts of Greece to work on the island.

In 1963, the mines closed for good, forcing most workers to migrate and change profession. The mining sites were abandoned. Their story, however, remains deeply etched in the soul and identity of the islanders.

To highlight and preserve these memories, the Friends of Serifos Association launched the project "The living history of the mines of Serifos", with the support of the Cycladic Identity initiative of the Museum of Cycladic Art. The research, interviews and documentation of material lasted a year. The result is a journey into the past, a moving exploration of residents' memories and the history of the mines, captured in a printed and a digital album.

Mega Livadi Νίκος Κοκολάκης © Μουσείο Κυκλαδικής Τέχνης

Digital underground

The digital archive (source in Greek)contains more than 250 photographs, rare documents, press clippings from the period and 10 first-hand testimonies by miners and their descendants who are still alive. This was deemed necessary because for decades the history of the Serifos mines survived mainly through the oral accounts of those who had lived and worked there.

As generations pass, these testimonies had to be recorded before they disappeared forever. At the same time, information panels with QR codes were installed at the mining sites, allowing visitors to read the miners' interviews on the spot.

Earlier this month, the Friends of the Cultural Heritage and Environment of Serifos Association presented the project to local residents, organised a round-table discussion with miners and their descendants, and held a guided tour of the mining sites at Mega Livadi, led by Thodoris G. Livanios.

The bust of Konstantinos Speras at Mega Livadi Νίκος Κοκολάκης © Μουσείο Κυκλαδικής Τέχνης

Katerina Papathoma, Vice-President of the Friends of Serifos Association, was the Programme Manager. Although she is not originally from the island, she has been living here for years and has grown deeply attached to it.

_"_The aim of the Friends of Serifos Association is twofold. First, to save and preserve this living history of the mines of Serifos. This was done through recordings and live interviews given to us by the miners and their descendants on the island. The second aim is that we want to share this story. The fact is that even we who live here in Serifos do not really know this history," explained Papathoma.

"I realised this when all the material was brought together and I saw that many aspects of this place's history are completely unknown. So first we ourselves have to learn, to answer questions we may have and to understand what happened with the mines.

"The second reason is to have a structured body of information so we can pass it on to young people. It is the young who will very soon be called on to deal with Serifos's issues. They need to know these places in order to become attached to them and, if possible, to protect them."

Miners' strife

Miners at the end of the 19th century. (Αρχείο Εθνικού Ιστορικού Μουσείου)

Serifos was the largest mining centre in Greece after Lavrio. The mines at Mega Livadi are a listed historic site. This was where the bloody miners' strike of 1916 took place. They demanded the introduction of the eight-hour working day and more dignified working conditions from their employers, the German company Grohmann.

The uprising was universal. It was driven by starvation wages, punishing working hours, appalling living conditions and the total lack of safety measures, which often led to deaths and crippling injuries.

The strike ended in bloodshed, during which four strikers lost their lives (Th. Kouzoupis, M. Zoilis, M. Mitrofanis, I. Protopappas) and two members of the gendarmerie were also killed (Ch. Chrysanthou and I. Triantafyllou). Konstantinos Speras (1893–1943) was the leading figure in the strike. Born in Serifos, he became a key figure in Greece's workers' and trade union movement.

Loading at the old wooden pier on the eastern side of Mega Livadi, 1890–1893. (Οικογενειακό Αρχείο Άννας Γρώμαν)

The Municipality of Serifos has for several years been trying to turn the area at Mega Livadi into an open-air mining museum that will showcase the history of the mines, the area's unique identity and offer a different kind of development for this abandoned region.

Konstantinos Revintis**,** The mayor of Serifos, spoke to Euronews at the site of the strike: "We are standing in the historic place where the miners' strike for the first eight-hour working day and for better working conditions took place, on 21 August 1916. It is a historic site that we want to highlight by creating here an open-air mining museum that will tell the story without a voice, simply through traces.

"Everything that still exists here must be restored. We have formed several partnerships with various bodies of recognised standing that have the necessary technical and management expertise, such as the National Technical University of Athens, the University of the Aegean, the Hellenic Society for the Environment and Cultural Heritage, Europa Nostra, the World Monuments Fund, the World Monuments Watch and other organisations. The Mega Livadi Association is a local body that shows particular sensitivity on this issue.

Mine at Mega Livadi Γιώργος Μητρόπουλος

"And of course, we as the Municipality are playing the leading role. If the Ministry of Culture can support us, that would be ideal, as well as the Ministry of Finance, because we are in a coastal zone here," said Revintis. "Our aim is to complete this project and return the site to public use so that people can visit it and so it can become an attraction, both for permanent residents and for visitors."

The project "The living history of the mines of Serifos" was funded by Cycladic Identity, an important initiative run by the Museum of Cycladic Art since 2022.

Its goal is to safeguard the intangible cultural heritage that has shaped the island's history over the centuries. To date, the museum has supported 26 projects in total on 15 Cycladic islands and will soon announce ten more for 2027:

Mine at Mega Livadi Γιώργος Μητρόπουλος

"The Cycladic Identity initiative is essentially our concrete way of saying thank you to the islands. In practice, we support organisations active on the Cycladic islands in the fields of culture, biodiversity and intangible cultural heritage," explained Theano Agalloglou, Project Manager of the Cycladic Identity initiative at the Museum of Cycladic Art.

"We want to engage as many residents as possible. We want them to feel proud of their unique cultural and natural heritage, but also to raise their awareness. We believe it is extremely important that the oral testimonies of the miners, or 'Metalliotes' as they were called on the island, are documented, digitised and preserved as a legacy for the new generation," added Agalloglou.

The project and the album were presented at the Theatre of the Serifos Association in Chora. There, former miners and descendants of mining families shared their stories and memories with the audience.

The presentation at the Theatre of the Serifos Association Νίκος Κοκολάκης © Μουσείο Κυκλαδικής Τέχνης

The testimony of Andreas Livanios (Katsafouris)

_"_I went to work in the mines around 1956–57. I was still a child. I went because at that time everyone, the whole of Serifos, worked in the mines. The mine meant great hardship, because those from Mega Livadi and Koutalas lived nearby. I am from Kallitsos, in the north. To leave home and reach Mega Livadi, it took us three hours on foot. We had to get up at 2 in the morning, get ready and leave at about twenty to three so that we would be at the worksite at ten to six or a quarter to six. If we arrived at one minute past six, we were sent to the office and lost the day's pay.

"It was exhausting because it was night and there was no road. We walked without light, in the cold and rain, along a path through the fields. I worked on compressors that pumped air. I went in the morning because these compressors ran on dynamite. I would put a small stick of dynamite inside, tap the detonator with a hammer and the machine would start up.

"What was left from the mines was only damage and hardship. They have eaten away all the guts of Serifos. There are galleries in the mountains where, if you go in, you get lost. Even now, when I think about it, I can hardly breathe. All the wealth left this place. Nothing was left for the island, which could have become a little Paris if the resources had been used properly."

Chora from the north in a picture postcard, circa 1965. (Συλλογή ΑΣΓ)

The testimony of Alexandros Livanios

"On both my mother's and my father's side, they were miners. My mother's father survived, although he was very seriously injured. He spent a couple of years in hospital but pulled through. He survived and even kept all his limbs, but for two years he had lost his mind. My other grandfather on my father's side, Alexandros Klaos, was killed. His body is still inside a mine at Aspros Kavos. My father never met his own father. My grandmother was pregnant with him when her husband was killed. There is no mining family in Serifos that does not have either someone injured or someone dead.

"The mines were both a blessing and a curse for the island. They kept people here, because mining was the main occupation and farming was a sideline. These people worked from night to night in the mines. Only Sundays were left for them to go and work their fields. Usually it was the woman who replaced the man because he was tied up with work. If you think that he had to leave from Chora and walk two hours to Mega Livadi, he had to get up in the middle of the night and return again at night.

"The school at Mega Livadi had 150 children when I was a pupil there. Gradually it was deserted and became a necropolis. In winter there are almost no residents at all. After the mines closed, there was both internal and external migration. I went to sea. I started out as a lathe operator and then went into the maritime sector because the pay was better, much better."

Koutalas, general view from the sea, 1961. (Συλλογή Α. Ζ. Φραγκίσκου, 1961-1965. Αρχείο Εργαστηρίου Αστικού Περιβάλλοντος Εθνικού Μετσόβιου Πολυτεχνείου)

The testimony of Thodoris G. Livanios

"I am an amateur researcher and folklorist. I have recorded dozens of people who worked in the mines and are unfortunately no longer with us, including people who experienced the 1916 strike. These are unique testimonies that I keep in my archive.

"We are children of miners, children of workers. We are descendants of the victims, not of the German exploiters. I have countless memories, because I experienced a lot in the mines both as a child and later through recording powerful testimonies that, unfortunately, have not yet been fully used. I have made several documentaries, television and radio programmes, and I have documented the popular culture of Serifos.

"Serifos is an empty shell. It was exploited by the Grohmanns and the successive employers who extracted the ore, drank the workers' sweat, drank the workers' blood and, in the end, left them unpaid."
