World.title: ‘Sunlight salary’: Exactly how much solar panels knock off your energy bills – even under grey skies
World.content:
Britain may be famous for grey skies and rainy days, but its sunshine could still help residents shave more than €1,000 a year off household electricity bills.

 

An analysis of more than 15 million UK homes by solar software company GreenSketch estimates that an optimised rooftop solar and battery system could save the average household around €1,100 a year – what the company calls a ‘sunlight salary’.

Even in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, the average savings topped €930.

The findings show that household savings depend on more than sunshine alone. Electricity prices, the angle of your roof, when you use power, battery storage and payments for electricity sent back to the grid are all important factors.

Grey skies aren’t a barrier to solar power

Researchers used satellite imagery to model individual homes, accounting for the slope of rooftops as well as their orientation, local electricity use and hourly solar generation.

Southwest Wales had the highest average estimated savings at around €1,160 a year, followed by southeast England at about €1,150. In Northern Ireland, the best returns were found in the east rather than the south, which GreenSketch says shows that local weather and geography can affect solar generation as much as geolocation.

Those figures challenge the idea that solar panels only make financial sense in sunnier places. Although they generate more electricity in direct sunlight, solar panels still produce power on overcast days – good news for Europe’s less sunny stretches.

Solar can also cover the cost of installment relatively quickly. The Energy Saving Trust – an independent UK energy advice organisation – estimates that a typical system can pay for itself in 10 to 12 years.

Europe has barely tapped its rooftop potential

The UK findings point to similar potential elsewhere around Europe.

If solar panels don’t need Mediterranean sunshine to cut electricity bills – especially when paired with batteries that let households store power generated during the day and use it later – they could make financial sense far beyond southern Europe.

A Joint Research Centre (JRC) study published earlier this year found that solar panels on rooftops could meet 40 per cent of the EU’s long-term electricity needs by 2050.

In Finland and Denmark, non-residential roofs alone could provide at least 95 per cent of the solar capacity targeted for 2030.

Still, just one in ten European rooftops has solar panels, according to the JRC, leaving enormous room for further expansion.

World.title: Obesity and overweight cost European economies billions of euros a year, industry says
World.content:
Beyond the health impact, obesity and high body mass index (BMI) pose a growing burden for European economies, costing billions of euros annually through direct and indirect costs, according to a new pharmaceutical industry report.

 

The total annual costs represent 0.7% to 1.4% of national GDP across Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Ireland, Greece, Romania and the United Kingdom, the countries analysed in the study conducted by the Office of Health Economics (OHE) for the pharmaceutical lobby EFPIA.

“Tackling obesity is vital for protecting citizens' health and wellbeing, safeguarding our European health systems and ensuring sustainable growth in Europe,” said Nathalie Moll, director general at the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries (EFPIA), which financed the report.

As of 2024, 26% of adults in Europe were living with obesity, defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or more, and an additional 30% were living with overweight, a situation that is expected to worsen. It is estimated that half of the world’s adult population will be living with overweight or obesity by 2035.

In Europe, the prevalence of overweight and obesity in adults has increased by 22%, while obesity alone has risen by more than 75% relative to 1990 levels.

How much money are countries spending?

Both obesity and overweight come at a high cost across Europe. Compared with other major areas of public spending, the report found that the economic burden of elevated BMI as a share of GDP is comparable to what some countries spend on housing and defence.

The estimated annual economic burden ranges from €2.5 billion in Romania to €55.2 billion in Germany. Total annual economic costs reach €43.2 billion in the UK, with Spain, Italy, and France each incurring around €20.0 billion.

As a percentage of GDP, costs attributable to elevated BMI range from 0.7% in Romania to 1.4% in Greece and the UK.

For Germany (1.3%), Spain (1.2%) and Ireland (1.1%), the share of their domestic economy attributable to elevated BMI exceeds the countries’ defence spending.

These translate into per capita costs ranging from €131 per Romanian resident to €662 per German resident.

A combination of direct and indirect costs

Obesity and overweight are linked to 278,000 deaths and the loss of 8 million years of healthy life across the eight countries analysed in the study alone.

Besides being a health problem in its own right, obesity is also a risk factor for non-communicable diseases, including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, fatty liver disease, cancers, neurological disorders, chronic respiratory diseases and digestive disorders.

Costs derived from these conditions — also known as “direct costs” — amounted to €100.4 billion, with Germany accounting for the largest share, at €30 billion.

However, the report found a substantial additional share of costs indirectly linked to these conditions, known as “indirect costs”. These include losses from absenteeism, economic inactivity, informal care and premature mortality.

What can be done?

The report's findings show that historical approaches to prevention and management "have not had the desired impact".

“An urgent shift in perception, prevention, diagnosis and treatment is required to improve outcomes, reduce the burden of costs on health services, boost economic productivity and societal resilience,” Moll said.

The report provides recommendations to address the health and economic challenges posed by obesity and elevated BMI, ranging from recognising obesity as a disease and not just a risk factor to improving access to prevention and treatment.

World.title: Small businesses in rural France bears the brunt of energy crisis triggered by Iran war
World.content:
France's rural communities are feeling the full force of the global energy crisis sparked by the war in Iran. Almost 21 million people — nearly a third of the French population — live in the countryside, which covers around 90% of the country's landmass.

 

In Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, a town of around 6,000 people in the northern Oise department, rising energy prices are being felt even in the local bakery.

Kevin Luce bakes his bread in two heating oil-fired ovens — a fuel that was once cost-effective but has become increasingly expensive. "At the outset it was a good deal: an oil-fired oven was cheaper to run than an electric one, until the price went up by 50%," he said.

His last delivery, two days ago, came to 2,200 euros for 1,200 litres. Six months earlier, he had paid 2,100 euros for 2,000 litres. The difference is being absorbed directly by the business.

"All this excessive spending on energy is money we are losing. It's wages we can't take, pay rises we can't give our employees, investments we can't make," Luce said.

Small businesses forced to cut back

Food truck owner Martial Realland has taken a different approach — he has stopped refilling his oil tank altogether. "Last year I had 1,500 litres delivered. It cost me 1,600 euros. Now, at 1.80 or 1.90 euros a litre, it's almost double. So I'm not getting any delivered," he said.

Realland has also begun turning down jobs that involve long distances. "Ever since I was born there have always been crises. But this is no longer bearable," he said.

The surge in energy costs is reviving memories of the gilets jaunes movement, which erupted in autumn 2018 after a rise in fuel taxes. The protest gained its strongest momentum in rural and outer-suburban areas — the same communities now bearing the heaviest burden of the current crisis.

World.title: From Croatia without waste: “truly circular” process offers hazardous chemicals a second life
World.content:
Equipped with air-filtering masks, workers at a recycling plant in Ivanić-Grad, Croatia, recycle ethanol, benzene or acetones, and thinners to dilute paints. These and other used solvents come from the food packaging, pharmaceutical or automotive industries. They are full of hazardous substances.

 

Polluted solvents prior to the purification process © Euronews

A complex process removes all their residues and turns contaminated solvents into clean ones, ready to be re-used.

“This is the contaminated solvent that we are taking from the machine and into the distillator. We are distilling it, and for the result we are getting the clean solvent that is used to further production. Clean as a whistle”, explains Mario Želježnjak, Production Supervisor at Premifab Ltd as he shows us the different technologies at an unassuming plant recently inaugurated.

Mario Želježnjak, Production Supervisor at Premifab Ltd © Euronews

Along with water and other impurities, the resulting waste is basically sludge that is used to produce energy that feeds the recycling facilities. “Everything is burned inside a rotary kiln and turned into harmless ash,” explains Mario. This ash can subsequently be used as a construction material.

Partially funded by the European Union, the clean-tech company claims to recycle around three million kilograms of used solvents annually—a 90% recycling rate for the contaminated raw material sent by its clients. Facing stiff competition from other major industry players in Germany, France, Spain, and Italy, the company must offer efficiency and versatility, explains its business development director, Igor Podravac.

Igor Podravac is the company´s Business Development Director © Euronews

“We have a lot of high demanding customers from pharmaceutical, automotive, paint industry,food packaging industry also. After they pollute a material and it is no longer usable for a second treatment, they send this material to us,” he explains while showing us the work done workers. “We are accepting the material, analysing the material, purifying the material and after all the parameters are checked, we return that material into the same production line to get a closed loop circular economy in real life.”

The first step starts at the company´s laboratory. Samples of used solvents are here first analysed to determine if and how they can safely and effectively be recycled. Very different parameters, including temperature, pressure or energy balance must be considered. “Maybe the distillation yield is too low, so it's not really feasible, both material-wise and financial-wise. And on the other hand, if we have lots of distillation residue remaining, that we cannot do anything about it, we opt not to use that material at all,.”, explains Silvija Petković, Quality Control Director & Laboratory Manager. “The specificity within the solvents is their flammability. So they're all flammable liquids, and we need to take all the precautionary measures in order not to burn anything, not to light anything up,” she adds.

Silvija Petković works as Quality Control Director & Laboratory Manager © Euronews

After the distillation, and prior to sending the now clean solvents back to the clients, quality control checks are enforced again.

“This one does not conform because of the precipitation, so this one cannot go to the customer. So, this sample is going to stay here, and we need to do further filtration,” Silvija, explains to our camera while holding one sample. “This one is okay, no precipitation, whatsoever. It can be closed and sealed and put into the truck,”after checking a second, much transparent sample.

The approved recovered solvents are shipped to the clients in special containers. We follow one such delivery with Nikola Gojavić, a driver at the company. “This cargo is unique because it’s in a liquid state and is highly explosive. Great care is required during loading and transport, so specialised drivers are needed—it’s quite a challenging job,” he tells us while driving.

Driver Nikola Gojavić handles and transports hazardous chemicals © Euronews

“The driver must be a specialist because, in the event of an accident or any incident, they must remain composed and be trained to carry out the necessary procedures.”

The cargo we follow brings back recovered solvents to a family business called Rotoplast. Each year, it manufactures approximately 5,000 tonnes of packaging and labelling for the food, energy and pet product industries. Solvents are used here to dissolve inks in the printing processes.

“It is important to us that our products, along with being highly effective from a production point of view, are also environmentally sustainable,” says Production Director Antun Čengić. “In cooperation with Premifab, we collect all our waste in a safe way, we transport it to their location, so that they can process it and return it to us as a new resource. With this, we reduce the costs of production.”

The company was founded in 1975 and currently employs 260 staff. Solvents are among the many recycled products that are reused here, claims the CEO, Blaženko Marić.

Blaženko Marić, Chief Executive Officer at Rotoplast. The company reuses purified solvents © Euronews

“80% of materials, it's possible to use like this. We would like to move to mono materials. For all materials, for all customers. This is the plan for the next few years, to be completely phase out materials which are unrecyclable,” he explains.

Premifab claims to see a significant demand in Europe for this type of recycling services © Euronews

Igor Podravac, its business development director, says their turnover has grown “approximately 20 to 25% per year” since they started operations, in December 2014. The company claims that, compared to primary production, recovered solvents generate up to 10 times less CO2 emissions.

World.title: Hungary dramatically cuts EU defence loan request under new government
World.content:
Hungarian authorities have informed Brussels that they intend to limit their request for an EU defence loan to €5.4 billion under the EU’s Security Action For Europe (SAFE) programme, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed on Friday.

 

The latest figure is less than half the €16.4 billion originally requested by former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.

The original proposal was contested by Orbán’s successor, Péter Magyar, who took office in April. It is understood that Magyar wanted to reassess the original proposal over alleged corruption risks linked to the previous government.

“We were always very clear with the new incoming Hungarian authorities and government that they would be able to take stock of the current situation, and they have now decided to take less than what we initially allocated to Hungary,” Regnier added.

Meanwhile, the size of Italy’s SAFE defence loan was also confirmed on Friday, with Regnier stating that Italy has formally requested €8 billion under the programme.

This is also roughly half of the €14.9 billion originally anticipated by the government of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

The announcement comes after terse negotiations between Brussels and Rome over the allocation, which was never formally finalised but nevertheless caused consternation between the two capitals.

The SAFE low-interest loan scheme was launched by Brussels last year to strengthen defence industries and military readiness across the bloc in response to the threat posed by Russia.

The programme has a total funding envelope of €150 billion, which is to be distributed among 19 member states.

SAFE forms part of the Commission’s Readiness 2030 plan, which aims to mobilise up to €800 billion in additional defence spending by the end of the decade. It places a particular focus on boosting the procurement of priority defence products.

Under the programme, at least 65% of the value of the weapon system being acquired must be sourced from an EU member state, Ukraine, or a country belonging to the European Economic Area or European Free Trade Association.

The remaining 35% may be sourced from any third country.

World.title: Podcast: Pope in secular France, vultures and farmers, first divorce law
World.content:
With its strong commitment to secularism, France is not an obvious place for Pope Leo XIV to stage an appearance, but his visit is drawing interest from Catholics and non-Catholics alike. After nearly disappearing from France, vultures are making a comeback, but their return has created new tensions with farmers. And France's revolutionary first divorce law from 1792.

Advertising

Some 800,000 people have signed up to see Pope Leo XIV on his first official visit to France, a secular country where the Catholic faith no longer dominates. Francois Mabille, head of the Geopolitical Observatory of Religion at the French Institute for International and Strategic Affairs, looks at why France is of interest to the Vatican, and young people of different religions talk about what Pope Leo means to them. (Listen @0'00)

Vultures all but disappeared from France by the 1940s as people sought to eradicate the scavenger birds. A programme to reintroduce the four European vulture species to the Grands Causses plateaux in the southern Massif Central has been sucessful – so successful that some farmers say there are now too many. We visit a vulture feeding station to explore the close relationship between vultures and agriculture, and the tensions that arise with the return of wild species. (Listen @20'00)

In 1792, France introduced one of Europe’s first and most liberal divorce laws, as part of a broader revolutionary effort to enact liberté, egalité et fraternité in the family itself. (Listen @14'00)

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: 'Lithuanian skies are NATO skies': DW interview with Lithuania's prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius
World.content:
In a DW interview, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius discusses threats to Lithuania from Russia and Belarus, NATO's need for stronger air defense and why military spending alone cannot ensure security.

Lithuania is on NATO's eastern flank, bordering Belarus and Russia's Kaliningrad region. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, security has become one of the country’s central political priorities.

The 42-year-old Mindaugas Sinkevicius recently took over as prime minister and also leads Lithuania's Social Democratic Party, a moderate center-left political force. In an exclusive interview with DW, he said he is concerned by the growing popularity of populist and far-right parties across Europe, particularly in Western Europe. But he also argues that the picture is more complicated, pointing to Social Democratic governments in several European countries and signs of renewed support for the center-left elsewhere.

For Lithuania, the war in Ukraine is closely connected to its own security. The country has experienced a series of incidents involving drones, instrumentalized migration and weather balloons entering its territory from Belarus. Sinkevicius says these developments have contributed to a broader sense of insecurity across Europe.

"As politicians, we have to tell society the truth," he said. He identifies air defense as Lithuania's most urgent security priority.

"Lithuania's airspace is NATO’s common airspace. Lithuanian skies are NATO skies," he said. "If Lithuanian skies are safe, then NATO’s skies are largely protected as well."

Drone incidents in Lithuania and beyond

He said Lithuania is seeking greater solidarity from its allies. The threat goes beyond its national borders as a series of incidents involving drones have affected other European countries as well.

Sinkevicius stressed that NATO membership does not mean Lithuania can simply rely on its allies. Collective defense, he argues, works only when individual members are prepared to contribute.

"Of course, there is Article 5. Of course, there is collective defense," he said. "But at the same time, we need to do certain things ourselves, rather than relying solely on our partners, neighbors and alliances."

For Lithuania, this means strengthening its own deterrence capabilities while continuing to work through NATO and regional partnerships. He also pointed to the Nordic-Baltic Eight, or NB8, as an important framework for cooperation between the countries of Northern Europe and the Baltic states.

National security climbs the national agenda

He rejected the idea that European countries should choose between traditional military equipment and newer technologies such as drones.

"Sometimes we see these issues being pitted against each other: drones versus tanks," he said. "I say we need both."

But for the Lithuanian prime minister, military equipment only goes so far. "Neither drones nor tanks will protect us if society does not feel safe, if people do not feel a connection with the state," he said.

For Sinkevicius, that connection is linked to social policy as well as defense. He argues that a state must also support people who are unemployed, ill or otherwise vulnerable.

The argument reflects a broader challenge for Sinkevicius as leader of Lithuania’s Social Democratic Party. Traditionally, Social Democrats have focused more on social policy, education and healthcare than on defense. Russia's war against Ukraine has changed the political environment, forcing center-left governments in Europe to place national security much higher on their agendas.

Sinkevicius says the challenge is to increase defense capabilities without abandoning the principles of social democracy.

'We will continue to support Ukraine'

Sinkevicius recently travelled to Lutsk and Kyiv, where he met Ukrainian political leaders. Lithuania has committed to allocating at least 0.25% of its GDP annually to support Ukraine. According to figures cited by the Ukrainian side, Lithuania's support in recent years has amounted to around 0.3% of GDP.

The prime minister acknowledges that some degree of war fatigue exists in Europe. But he says European societies should consider the scale of what Ukrainians have experienced.

"I sometimes ask myself: if we Europeans feel tired, then what must Ukrainian society be feeling?" he said.

Sinkevicius also points to the key role of Western European countries, particularly Germany, in maintaining support for Ukraine.

"Support and assistance must continue," he said. "Because if the Western front, figuratively speaking, weakens and falters, then on the eastern front — where Russia is fighting Ukraine — the risk of failure increases."

Edited by Jess Smee

World.title: India news: Protests against election chief escalate as Gandhi, Cockroach party allege 'rigged' vote
World.content:
Protesters from various groups gathered in Delhi on Friday demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, amid a growing controversy over reported differences within the Election Commission of India (ECI).



The protest followed an investigation published by The Indian Express on September 23, which reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally raised objections at least 14 times over a 10-month period to decisions concerning electoral rolls and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process. The report said some of the decisions had been taken without their knowledge.



The Election Commission, however, has rejected the suggestion of an internal breakdown, saying that differences expressed through internal notes are part of the normal decision-making process and that the final decisions of the three-member Commission were unanimous.



On Thursday, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) gave Gyanesh Kumar 48 hours to resign and warned that it would launch a nationwide agitation, including a second protest at Jantar Mantar, if he did not step down.



On Friday, CPI(ML) Liberation leader Dipankar Bhattacharya, AISA leader Neha Bora — who had gone on hunger strike during the first Jantar Mantar protest — senior advocate Prashant Bhushan and activist Yogendra Yadav joined the demonstration.



The Delhi Police had heavily barricaded the area around Jantar Mantar and did not allow protesters to enter the designated protest site. Several activists were detained within minutes of arriving at the spot.



Speaking to DW, Neha Bora accused the Election Commission of “stealing votes” and acting against democracy. She demanded Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation and said the protesters would continue their movement.



Dipankar Bhattacharya told DW that the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) should be scrapped and that fresh elections should be held in several states.

Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar is facing pressure to resign as demonstrations intensify Image: Abiraj Kumar Arulgnanakumar/DW

World.title: Pope Leo XIV criticizes AI, assisted dying on France arrival
World.content:
The pope has landed in Paris for a four-day trip. Received by President Emmanuel Macron, Leo warned about the risks of AI and criticized France's limited legalization of assisted dying.

Pope Leo XIV arrived for a four-day visit to France on Friday, the first official papal visit to the strictly secular country in 18 years.

Leo, the spiritual leader of the some 1.4 billion Catholics worldwide, was greeted at Paris' Orly Airport by French President Emmanuel Macron and will be in the country until Monday.

What did Pope Leo say alongside Macron at the Elysee Palace?

In remarks delivered at the Elysee Palace, Leo on Friday underscored opposition to assisted dying initiatives just two months after France created a legal right ‌to ⁠die ⁠for those with incurable illnesses.

Though he did ​not specifically mention France's new law, the pontiff criticized ​what ‌he called "profit-driven ventures" such as surrogacy and assisted dying.

"I firmly reiterate that the protection ‌of ​the right to life constitutes the indispensable foundation of every other human right," the pope said in an address to Macron and other French politicians.

"I am concerned at times by those trends ⁠in ​society that risk turning science and ​technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the ​trade in human organs ‌or the possibility of arranging one's own death," he said.

Pope Leo also delivered an urgent warning regarding the development of artificial intelligence.

"If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a 'paradise of machines' invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment," he said.

What else in on the pope's itinerary in France?

The papal itinerary has Leo meeting Macron at the Elysee Palace, speaking at UNESCO headquarters, leading Vespers at Notre Dame Cathedral and celebrating Mass for an estimated 80,000 young people at the Stade de France national stadium on Friday.

On Saturday, he is scheduled to celebrate Mass for another 600,000 at Place de la Concorde on the Avenue des Champs-Elysees before departing for Lourdes, a famous Catholic pilgrimage site located near France's Spanish border.

On Monday, Leo will travel to Metz, near the German border, where he will deliver a speech entitled: "To the roots of Europe for peace and unity." Macron will introduce Leo at the event and has invited fellow leaders across the EU to join him in attendance.

Pope speaks of press freedom, peace on flight amid White House exclusion furor

While traveling to France, US-born Leo was asked by a CNN reporter for his thoughts on US President Donald Trump's attempts to ban news outlets from covering him.

"I am very happy that here, you are all welcome," he told reporters.

Leo, who was forced to fly home alone after plane trouble on a recent trip to Spain, took the opportunity to apologize to his press pool.

Speaking to reporters at the back of his plane on Friday, Leo said, "I want to apologize personally for an incident, that I had nothing to do with, but which I know left a number of you unhappy with the fact that we couldn't have the flight back together back to Rome."

He further told reporters he was coming to France as "a pilgrim for peace" in a time of war.

Leo, a tireless critic of the wars in Ukraine, Iran and elsewhere, said "It is a message which at this time, as we all may know, is particularly important."

Pope Leo calls for sincere dialogue to tackle global crises To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AI, Church sexual abuse also on the agenda

Leo had already tipped his hat on his plans to address global concerns regarding so-called artificial intelligence (AI) and the "new dangers" it presents to "security and international peace" during his discussions with Macron.

Speaking at the Vatican prior to departure on Thursday, Leo had said leaders must "govern wisely" when dealing with the new technology, which he says raises questions about the very essence of what it means to be human.

Leo has taken a keen interest in AI, writing his first papal encyclical — published this May and entitled "Magnificent Humanity" — on the issue.

Pope Leo warns about risks of artificial intelligence To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The pope is also seeking to repair the Catholic Church's standing in France, where opinions grew particularly bleak in 2021 following the publication of a report documenting seven decades of abuse — impacting 330,000 French children — by clergy and lay leaders.

Leo will meet victims of church abuse during the trip.
