World.title: Hotline for Foreigners in Czechia: Tips to Save Time and Frustration
World.content:
Reaching the Client Centre for residence-related questions in Czechia requires patience.

More than 2,000 calls are received every day, so some waiting time is unavoidable.

However, you can significantly reduce your waiting time by calling during less busy hours, which are published through the authority’s official channels.



It is also worth having your identification document number ready before calling. This can speed up the process, particularly if you are calling to book an appointment.

Those who do not want to wait on the phone can use other ways to get in touch. Answers to many common questions are available in the Frequently Asked Questions section of the Information Portal for Foreigners (ipc.gov.cz).

If your matter is not urgent or your question is more complicated, you can also contact the centre by email at [email protected].

The current status of your application can be checked online using the dedicated service on the same portal.

When it comes to appointments, most bookings can be made through your personal account on the Information Portal for Foreigners.

You only need to book by phone in three cases: to provide biometric data, to inspect your case file, or to collect a residence card as an EU citizen.

World.title: Czech President Warns NATO Allies May Need to Shoot Down Russian Aircraft
World.content:
Czech President Petr Pavel has warned that NATO may eventually need to shoot down Russian aircraft or drones that deliberately violate the alliance’s airspace.

Speaking to Fox News Digital in New York during the U.N. General Assembly, Pavel said Russia was testing NATO’s readiness and could interpret continued restraint as a sign of weakness.

“There might be the time when we will have to shoot down some of these planes or unmanned vehicles that are testing our readiness,” Pavel said.



Pavel said the alliance needs to distinguish between accidental airspace violations and deliberate incursions in which an aircraft ignores warnings to leave.

“If it is deliberate and the violator doesn’t respond to our measures, then we will have to act, because otherwise Russia simply would push further on,” he said.

His comments came after a series of incidents involving Russian aircraft and drones near NATO territory.

On Wednesday, a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace after crossing from the Kaliningrad region. According to Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command, the helicopter travelled around 300 metres into Polish territory and remained there for 42 seconds.

On Thursday, Romania also scrambled two F-16 fighter jets after an unidentified aerial target entered its airspace from the direction of Ukraine. The object later crashed near the country’s border with Ukraine, with no casualties reported.

Pavel said Russia’s actions reminded him of incidents during his time at NATO, when Russian aircraft repeatedly tested the responses of allied forces.

“They are, on one hand, provoking. On the other, testing what will our reaction be,” he said.

In a speech to the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, Pavel said Russia’s “aggressive posture poses a direct threat to European security” and warned that the risks were increasing.

The Czech president also questioned whether Russia was genuinely prepared to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine. He said Moscow would need to agree to a ceasefire before entering meaningful negotiations without conditions.

World.title: New Sports Complex Opens in Prague’s Riegrovy Sady
World.content:
A new sports complex has opened in Riegrovy Sady, giving residents of Prague 2 access to a refurbished court, parkour equipment, a climbing wall and an outdoor fitness area.

The facility, next to the TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady building, was officially opened Tuesday afternoon. The renovation and installation of new equipment cost CZK 8.7 million, excluding VAT.



The site is intended for people of different ages and can be used for several sports. The refurbished court is suitable for football and basketball, while the new equipment includes a parkour area, climbing wall and a small fitness zone.

The project forms part of the district’s longer-term plans for Riegrovy Sady. Officials said the upper section of the park has lacked sufficient space for outdoor sports and exercise.

The sports area occupies land that until last year was used by two unauthorized structures, the Ice Magic ice sculpture exhibition and the Containall sports and cultural center.

The district is also considering a much larger project for the site. A multifunctional hall for sports and cultural events could eventually replace the current outdoor facility.

Petr Janů, deputy chairman of TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady, previously said the goal was to create a building designed to remain in place for decades or longer.

The project is still at an early stage. Prague 2 plans to discuss the design with local residents, heritage authorities and Prague’s Institute of Planning and Development. An architectural competition is also expected to be held.

World.title: Prague Taxi Drivers Could Be Tested on Czech and Local Geography
World.content:
Prague taxi drivers could soon be required to demonstrate their knowledge of Czech and the city’s geography.

The Chamber of Deputies approved the change on Wednesday as part of an amendment to the Road Traffic Act. The legislation does not automatically introduce testing in Prague or other Czech cities. Instead, it would give municipalities the authority to impose such requirements.



Under the amendment, municipalities could test taxi drivers on their legal rights and obligations, their Czech language skills to the extent necessary for the job, and their knowledge of locations within the municipality that are relevant to taxi services.

The bill now goes to the Senate.

What the new rules could mean for taxi drivers

The issue has been debated in Prague for some time, particularly as the taxi industry has changed with the rapid growth of app-based services.

Pirate Party leader Zdeněk Hřib introduced a more detailed proposal in May. That version included specific provisions defining what drivers could be required to know and what would fall outside the scope of the tests.

For example, the proposal said drivers should not be expected to demonstrate encyclopedic knowledge of Prague’s landmarks. Transport Minister Ivan Bednárik of the SPD, however, argued that the Pirate Party’s proposal had legal shortcomings.

A shorter amendment submitted by ANO MP Patrik Nacher ultimately became the version approved by the Chamber of Deputies.

Supporters of the change say taxi driving has increasingly become a profession with few formal qualification requirements beyond holding a driving licence.

The explanatory report accompanying the legislation argues that the sector has attracted foreign workers who may have limited knowledge of Czech, local traffic rules and the city in which they operate.

Critics, meanwhile, have raised concerns about the potential impact on fares. They argue that additional requirements could increase the cost of entering the profession and eventually lead to higher prices for passengers.

No English requirement in the legislation

The approved amendment refers specifically to knowledge of the Czech language. It does not introduce an English-language requirement, even though some taxi drivers in Prague also have limited English skills.

The legislation would apply to taxi drivers regardless of whether they operate independently or through digital platforms such as Uber and Bolt.

Foreign nationals make up roughly half of Prague’s registered taxi drivers, reflecting the sector’s long-standing reliance on foreign workers and recently arrived migrants.

World.title: More Than 250 People Fall Ill in Salmonella Outbreak at Prague School
World.content:
More than 240 children and 10 adults have developed gastrointestinal symptoms in connection with a suspected Salmonella outbreak at a school in Prague’s Újezd nad Lesy district.

Masaryk Elementary School, which has around 1,100 pupils, is being temporarily closed while health authorities investigate the source of the infection. The school’s kitchen and cafeteria will also undergo thorough disinfection.



Salmonella has so far been confirmed by laboratory tests in four children, according to Petra Batok, a spokesperson for the Prague Public Health Authority. Officials are continuing to investigate how the infection entered the school.

The first cases were reported earlier this week. The largest number of illnesses has been recorded among upper-level pupils and children attending Montessori classes. Classes for those groups were cancelled on Wednesday, while all pupils have been given Thursday and Friday off.

Food samples taken from the school cafeteria have been sent for laboratory testing, with results expected on Friday.

The final number of people affected is not yet known. Health officials are collecting additional information through questionnaires completed by parents and adults who visited the cafeteria.

The Prague public health authorities have described the incident as an epidemic.

Prague emergency services have received 55 calls from people reporting gastrointestinal symptoms in connection with the outbreak.

Twenty patients were transported to hospitals for treatment, while another 24 were examined and treated without being admitted. The remaining people received medical advice by telephone.

Salmonellosis is usually contracted by consuming contaminated food. Common sources include eggs, insufficiently cooked meat, unpasteurized milk and foods containing raw or unpasteurized eggs. Symptoms generally appear between 13 and 36 hours after infection.

World.title: Prague Metro and Tram Disruptions Planned for September 28 Weekend
World.content:
Prague commuters should expect changes to metro and tram services from Saturday, September 26, through Monday, September 28, as maintenance work affects Metro Line C and tram routes in Libeň.

Metro Line C will be suspended between Pražského povstání and Chodov for the entire long weekend. Trains will continue running between Letňany and Pražského povstání, while the southern section between Chodov and Háje will operate as a shuttle service.



Four stations will be affected by the closure: Pankrác, Budějovická, Kačerov and Roztyly. Passengers can use replacement bus XC, which will run between Pražského povstání and Chodov via all four stations.

Hundreds of railway sleepers to be replaced

The closure will allow Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) workers to replace several hundred wooden sleepers with concrete ones.

Once the work is completed, around 17,000 of the approximately 20,000 original sleepers between Florenc and Kačerov will have been replaced.

DPP said the work is scheduled during long weekends because the materials used to secure the new sleepers need more time to harden than a standard weekend allows.

Tram services suspended in Libeň

Tram services will also be disrupted between Palmovka and Ke Stírce from early Saturday morning until 6 p.m. Monday.

Several lines will operate on modified routes. Tram 3 will run via Těšnov, Vltavská, Strossmayerovo náměstí, Výstaviště, Nádraží Holešovice, Hercovka, Ke Stírce, Kobylisy and Ládví before terminating at Sídliště Ďáblice.

Line 10 will run from Palmovka via Balabenka and Arena Libeň jih to Nádraží Libeň, while lines 24 and 95 will terminate at Palmovka.

Replacement bus X3 will operate during the day between Palmovka, Bulovka, Ke Stírce and Kobylisy. Night service will be provided by bus X95, which will continue to Vozovna Kobylisy.

Passengers using Prague public transport over the long weekend should allow extra travel time and check the latest DPP information before travelling.

World.title: Czech Man Jailed 13 Days After Protest on Moscow’s Red Square
World.content:
A judge at Moscow’s Tverskoy District Court sentenced a Czech man to 13 days in jail on Tuesday for staging a protest on Red Square.

Identified as Michal Plamenek, the man was arrested for holding up a sign in English next to Lenin’s Mausoleum on Sunday afternoon, the court’s press service said in a statement.



No details were provided as to what was written on Plamenek’s sign, but the court press service said a judge ruled that the inscription was “aimed at discrediting the Russian Armed Forces.”

Police officers arrested Plamenek because Red Square directly adjoins the Kremlin, where protests are banned. He allegedly refused to listen to a request by officers to accompany them to a police station and resisted arrest.

A judge found Plamenek guilty on three separate administrative counts of discrediting the Russian military, violating protest rules and disobeying a police officer.

He was also fined a total of 60,000 roubles, around CZK 15,000.

The Czech Foreign Ministry said its embassy in Moscow has been providing the detained man with consular assistance from the outset. It declined to comment further because of the sensitivity of the case.

World.title: Energy efficiency and financing to shape the future of Hungary’s construction industry
World.content:
Where is the Hungary’s construction industry heading in a changing economic and energy landscape? The Building Future – Autumn Construction Industry Forum sought to answer this question by bringing together key players from the construction, logistics, electrical engineering and finance sectors. Held on 24 September at the Aquaworld Resort Budapest, the large-scale professional forum focused on the current challenges facing the sectors, the future of construction, energy efficiency and financing opportunities. Organised by the HAD Group, which looks back on a history of more than 30 years, the event focused not merely on assessing the current situation, but on exploring possible future directions and the business opportunities inherent in collaboration.

The central theme of the event was to identify sustainable and effective responses to the sector’s challenges. The event was opened by Ernő Hadnagy, owner and managing director of the HAD Group, who spoke candidly in his address about the challenges of recent years and the transformation of the group, emphasising the importance of professional collaboration and collective thinking in a changing market environment.

“Our group is a bit like a toolbox: each tool is a separate item that does its job on its own, but its true strength becomes apparent when, for a complex project, you don’t have to scour five different places for the tools you need, because the entire set is right at your fingertips. For us, this ecosystem is built around the property development and construction value chain.” – pointed out Ernő Hadnagy, owner and managing director of HAD Group. In his opening address, he emphasised that the aim of the Building Future event is not to sell, but to initiate an open professional dialogue with market players, where the future can be built together by combining each other’s capabilities.

Hungary’s construction industry.

Hungary’s construction industry: a united force from separate paths

“Previously, the companies belonging to this group performed excellently, but they operated side by side, each on their own path. It was this realisation that actually gave rise to the HAD Group. Until then, we’d merely been toying with the name, but it was this breakthrough in our way of thinking that shaped us into a true group of companies. Within this framework, it is teamwork that enables our outstanding staff to achieve extraordinary results together. We seek partnerships, joint ventures and opportunities where we can complement each other’s capabilities. Over the years, we have learnt that in today’s market, it is no longer lone warriors who shape the future. By joining forces, we can achieve so much more.” – said Tamás Nagy, Business Development Director at HAD Group.

If you missed it – Hungary new home VAT 2027: developers and buyers brace for a costly shift

Macroeconomic challenges and financial strategies

The specialist presentations that opened the event placed the sector’s prospects within a broader macroeconomic and international context. Zoltán Pogátsa, an economist, analysed developments in the global and domestic economic landscape, whilst Mariann Trippon, Senior Analyst at CIB Bank, drew attention in her presentation to the accelerating pace of change, the importance of technological adaptation and the need to manage economic uncertainties. The expert outlined the impact of geopolitical tensions – developments in energy prices and transport routes – and domestic macroeconomic indicators on the investment environment.

The forum’s financial panel discussion addressed key issues in financing, with banking and finance experts covering topics ranging from the current situation and outlook for the property and construction sectors – from the current situation and outlook for these markets, through the financeability of projects, to how construction companies are assessed by banks. The discussion also covered the types of projects banks consider financeable, the factors that make a contractor financeable in the long term, and the role that subsidised and guaranteed schemes – including the SZKP, EXIM and MFB programmes – can play in financing investments and SMEs. The experts agreed that, alongside increasingly stringent banking requirements, ESG criteria and energy efficiency now represent direct business value and a financing advantage.

Construction crisis or efficiency revolution?

Bence Bolfán, managing director of HAD Consulting, analysed the outlook for the Hungarian construction industry between 2026 and 2028 and the key market trends for the coming period in his presentation entitled ‘The future of the construction industry after 2026 – crisis, stagnation or renewed growth?’. He pointed out that the downturn stems primarily from a weakening of investment demand, whilst productivity, financial stability and the quality of project preparation will become increasingly important in the coming period. “It is possible to create value even in a difficult market,” emphasised Bence Bolfán, managing director of HAD Consulting.

In the round-table discussion that followed, key players in the construction market examined how current market challenges can be translated into concrete professional and business actions, and what technological, organisational and attitudinal changes are needed to set the construction industry on a more efficient course. The discussion therefore focused not only on identifying the challenges, but also on possible responses and action. “It is not enough to talk about the challenges facing the construction industry – we must take action.” – emphasised István Derczó, founder and owner of Weinberg 93 Kft.

Energy has become the new building material

The main theme of the afternoon session was the relationship between energy management and the construction industry. Attila Holoda, energy expert and managing director of Aurora Energy Kft., pointed out in his presentation that the price of energy and the costs of carbon dioxide emissions run through the entire construction value chain – from materials production to construction. Among other things, he emphasised that energy is no longer merely an operating cost (OPEX), but one of the most fundamental parameters in the design and life-cycle costs (LLC) of buildings.

“The cost of energy runs through the entire construction value chain, the extent of whose impact is determined by the chosen technology, the contract and the method of cost allocation. Thus, the cost of energy may already be reflected in the price of materials. Energy is no longer an overhead cost, but a design parameter.” – said Attila Holoda, Managing Director of Aurora Energy Kft., in his presentation.

The subsequent panel discussion on energy examined how energy is becoming a key business factor in the design and operation of buildings. The experts sought to answer how energy-related decisions can be made as early as the design phase that will reduce operating costs in the long term, increase the value of properties and improve the competitiveness of businesses. Key topics included the energy modernisation of the existing building stock, the business opportunities offered by smart building technologies, and the economic aspects of energy independence: the return on investment for solar panel systems, energy storage, electric vehicle fleets and power purchase agreements (PPAs). One important lesson from the discussion was that energy investments are no longer solely about sustainability: with proper planning, they can become cost-saving, value-creating and long-term business decisions. A key factor in this is ensuring that planning, technical and construction considerations are integrated from the very start of the project. This comprehensive approach is well illustrated by the way the HAD Group operates; drawing on the specialist expertise within the group, it is able to support its partners throughout the entire process, from design through technical solutions to construction.

Trust as a countermeasure to bureaucracy: the role of neurobiology in team performance

The professional session of the event concluded with a presentation by neurobiologist Máté Szász, which focused on the physical and mental performance of decision-makers and employees, as well as the role of health awareness.

“Trust fuelled by oxytocin reduces bureaucracy and uncertainty, and the resulting cost savings can lead to up to double the team performance and soaring levels of collaboration.” – emphasised neurobiologist Máté Szász in his presentation, who argued that the relationship between brain function and performance is also determined by the data we take in: “Information affects our bodies just as much as food does. You can become overfed, pathologically emaciated, and if it goes bad, it can even be toxic. It really does matter what ‘diet’ you put your brain on!”

The Building Future – Autumn Construction Industry Forum concluded, in addition to the specialist presentations, with intensive networking and test-drive opportunities, reinforcing the event’s main motto: “The future is built on cooperation.”

World.title: A little piece of home: a glimpse into the life of the Filipino community in Budapest
World.content:
On a warm afternoon in May, a simple gathering on Margaret Island had slowly turned into a small Filipino feast. We were there for a friend’s birthday. Around the picnic blankets were the usual signs of a celebration: cake, drinks, bags of snacks, and people taking photos for their Instagram. There was also champorado, the chocolate rice porridge many Filipinos grow up eating, and lumpia, thin and crispy fried spring rolls filled with meat and vegetables. More food appeared as people arrived, and much of it was cooked at home and brought along to share.

Written by Kate Berbano

Not everyone at the picnic was Filipino. Some of our international friends were curious about the food and wanted to try it, so plates were passed around, and explanations followed. Soon, it became the kind of gathering I had grown up recognising, where everyone insists that everyone else should eat. It also brought to mind a familiar Filipino dilemma: when only one piece of lumpia is left, somehow nobody wants to be the person who takes it.

The setting was unmistakably Budapest. We were sitting on Margitsziget, in the middle of the Danube, surrounded by other groups enjoying one of the city’s favourite green spaces. The Philippines is thousands of kilometres away, but over my first year in Hungary, I had started noticing little pieces of home like this scattered across the city.

Source: Kate Berbano

Little pieces of the Philippines

I felt it again one afternoon when I walked into Pinoy Basket, a Filipino grocery shop in Budapest, and almost immediately heard a cheerful “Magandang hapon po”, or “Good afternoon.” Inside were flavours and products familiar from home, the sort of things that might barely warrant a second glance in a supermarket in Manila but suddenly carry more meaning when found in Hungary.

Eleaverne Shayne Ruebe, president of the Association of Filipino Students in Hungary (AFSHu), describes the feeling simply: “Sometimes, it’s really the small things that make you feel at home.” Food is part of it, but so are singing, jokes, gestures, and familiar expressions. “When we’re in the Philippines, we don’t really stop and think about being Filipino or about our culture because it’s simply everywhere,” Ruebe said.

Living abroad changes that. Ruebe said Filipinos can suddenly find themselves representing their culture as friends become curious about their food, traditions, and language. The familiar becomes more noticeable when it is no longer everywhere.

What’s next? Explainer: Hungary’s guest worker ban takes effect, but foreign workers can still arrive under stricter rules

A church filled with familiar voices

I noticed this most strongly after I began attending the Filipino Sunday Mass at the Inner City Franciscan Church on Ferenciek tere shortly after arriving in Hungary last year.

The church is often packed, sometimes leaving people standing at the back. The Mass is celebrated in Filipino, familiar hymns fill the church, and the choir has the kind of voices that can make you stop what you are doing just to listen. During the sign of peace, people turn to greet one another, even when they have never met before.

Fr. Phoebie Romero Fababair, the Filipino Franciscan priest serving the community, said this connection extends beyond Sunday worship in Budapest. Tagalog Masses are also organised in different parts of Hungary, where churches have often been filled with Filipinos. For Fababair, the Church also has a role when people are adjusting to life far from home. “The Church is not merely a structure or a building, but is, above all, the people themselves,” he said.

Whena Matillano is one of the Filipinos who found community there. A factory worker who has lived in Hungary for almost four years, she said the Hungarian winter was difficult when she first arrived. Homesickness was harder, particularly missing her family and children in the Philippines.

For about two years, Matillano said she frequently cried because she missed them. In August 2025, she joined the Filipino church choir. “Mas gumaan ang lahat,” she said in Tagalog. “Everything became lighter.”

Matillano now joins Fr. Phoebie and other community members when they travel for Masses outside Budapest. She said the friends she has made through the community have helped her cope with homesickness, stress, and anxiety.

Source: Ghanie Linatoc

Making a home in Hungary

The community extends well beyond the church. There are groups such as the Mabuhay Filipino Community and Bayanihan Filipino Association that organise cultural and social gatherings, while AFSHu opens a network for Filipino students. Last December, Mabuhay and Bayanihan each held Paskong Pinoy, or Filipino Christmas, celebrations, which brought together workers, students, families, community leaders and Hungarian friends.

The Philippine Embassy in Hungary provides another meeting point. Independence Day brings Filipinos together each June, while this year’s Fiesta sa Nayon gathered community members from across Hungary alongside Hungarian and international guests. The Embassy’s Labor Office near Parliament also provides support to Filipino workers.

Although Budapest is at the centre of this story, Filipino communities have also developed in cities including Debrecen, Pécs and Szeged. Recent Philippine Embassy figures put the Filipino population in Hungary at at least 15,000.

Source: Philippine Embassy in Hungary

For Ruebe, being part of that community does not mean remaining within it. She said Filipino students also build relationships with Hungarians and other international students, learning from different cultures while remaining connected to their own. I have seen that exchange in my own university life. At Corvinus University of Budapest’s Cultural Day, I wore my best Filipiniana, traditional Filipino clothing that felt far less ordinary when worn thousands of kilometres from the country it represents. Around us, Filipino food and culture were being shared with Hungarian and international students.

However, building a life in Hungary also means taking part in the traditions here. On 20 August, I stood among the crowds at Batthyány tér as Budapest celebrated Hungary’s national day. Among the thousands waiting for the fireworks and light display over the Danube were groups of Filipinos, some holding phones and selfie sticks above the crowd to record the spectacle. At one point, I watched a group look after a companion who had become dizzy and nauseous in the crush of people. It was a small scene, easily missed among the thousands gathered along the river.

Over the past year, I have come to recognise the Filipino community in Budapest through moments like these: a Sunday Mass at Ferenciek tere, a “Magandang hapon po” inside a grocery shop, a Filipiniana worn to university, fireworks watched over the Danube, and food passed around a picnic blanket on Margaret Island.

None recreates the Philippines exactly as it was left behind. Instead, they are pieces of it carried into a life being built somewhere new. When Filipinos gather around food, though, there is always the possibility of one familiar dilemma: a single piece of lumpia left on the plate, and everyone suddenly becoming too polite to take it.

World.title: Record-breaking investments are pouring into Europe – here’s where the billions are going
World.content:
More than $51 billion in venture capital investment flowed into Europe in the first six months of 2026, whilst a record number of funding rounds worth over $1 billion were finalised in the first quarter of the year. Alongside AI, robotics, autonomous transport, fintech and energy, defence technologies and biotechnology are also attracting increasing attention from investors.

Record number of billion-dollar deals already in the first quarter

According to KPMG’s analysis , Europe’s venture capital market continues to benefit from its geographical and sectoral diversity, with investment activity well distributed across countries and industries. The strength of the market is particularly well illustrated by the fact that in the first quarter of 2026, six European companies raised at least $1 billion in funding – a higher figure than ever before. Of the six transactions, three were in the United Kingdom, two in Germany and one in France.

Among the largest European deals were the US$2 billion round for the British AI technology firm Nscale, the US$1.8 billion round for the German robotics firm Neura Robotics, the US$1.5 billion round for the British autonomous vehicle technology firm Wayve, the US$1.2 billion round for the German fintech firm Cloover, the French AI technology firm Advanced Machine Intelligence raising $1 billion, and the British energy technology firm Kraken Technologies raising $1 billion.

These billion-dollar funding rounds clearly demonstrate that investor interest is no longer concentrated on a single technology sector: alongside AI and robotics, autonomous transport, fintech and energy also featured amongst the largest transactions.

What’s next? Investment in Hungary: the next question is not where capital comes from, but how long it stays

AI remains the driving force behind investment

Interest continued to grow in the second quarter: the British firm Ineffable Intelligence raised $1.1 billion, one of the largest early-stage funding rounds in Europe to date. This record-breaking investment also indicates that investors are willing to risk extremely large sums even in the early stages of a company’s life cycle in pursuit of the growth opportunities offered by AI.

Alongside AI, the biotechnology sector is also attracting increasing attention from investors. This is clearly illustrated by the $2.1 billion funding round secured by Isomorphic Labs, another UK-based company specialising in AI-driven pharmaceutical research, which was one of the largest European transactions in the first half of the year. The convergence of artificial intelligence and healthcare innovations is likely to continue to attract significant investor interest in Europe in the coming years.

Defence technology is one of the fastest-growing sectors

Alongside AI, defence technology and dual-use technologies (which can be applied for both civilian and military purposes) have also become increasingly sought-after in Europe.

According to KPMG, defence technology has seen spectacular growth in Europe over the past two years, with investor interest ranging from drone technology and satellites to secure communications and cyber solutions. In the second quarter, Aura Aero, a French developer of dual-use hybrid-electric aircraft, raised $392 million in funding.

KPMG states that, due to geopolitical tensions and European countries’ efforts to develop their sovereign defence capabilities, defence technology is likely to remain a key investment area in the coming period.

Robotics, autonomous transport and energy are also attracting investors

Among the largest transactions of the first half of the year were several sectors which, alongside AI, demonstrate the broadening of the European technology ecosystem.

German firm Neura Robotics’ $1.8 billion funding round signals strong investor interest in robotics, whilst British firm Wayve’s $1.5 billion round has taken funding in autonomous transport to a new level. In the energy technology sector, Germany’s Cloover raised $1.2 billion, whilst the UK’s Kraken Technologies raised $1 billion.

According to KPMG, within the UK’s energy sector, the focus has been particularly on infrastructure solutions that offer a response to growing energy demand, such as power generation, battery storage or energy efficiency technologies.

Europe remained attractive to major investors

The European venture capital market had an exceptionally strong first half of 2026: according to data from KPMG Private Enterprise Venture Pulse, European companies raised $25.7 billion in venture capital in the first quarter, followed by a further $25.6 billion in the second, meaning that a total of approximately $51.3 billion flowed into the continent’s start-up and scale-up ecosystem over the first six months.

World.title: Parliamentary immunity: a loophole for politicians, or a shield against arbitrary power?
World.content:
The debate has flared up after prosecutors requested the lifting of the immunity of Péter Magyar and two Fidesz MPs. But is parliamentary immunity still necessary at all?

The timing of the request from the Office of the Prosecutor General was enough to set Hungarian public life buzzing. The immunity of three MPs was requested on the very same day, even though one case concerns a missing mobile phone, while the other two involve alleged financial damage worth billions of forints.

So what exactly are these three cases about?

Three cases, three very different allegations

The differences between the three cases are obvious at first glance.

According to prosecutors, in Péter Magyar’s case, proceedings should continue over a suspected theft. The prosecution alleges that in June 2024, at the Ötkert nightclub in Budapest, Magyar took a man’s mobile phone and subsequently threw the device into the Danube.

The allegations involving Miklós Seszták and Balázs Hankó are of an entirely different scale.

Seszták is facing suspicions of accepting a bribe in connection with his official duties, while Hankó is suspected of breach of fiduciary duty causing particularly significant financial damage. According to the prosecution, the case linked to Seszták involves more than HUF 11 billion in unlawful advantage.

Is a crime only a crime when it involves billions?

Magyar’s case therefore pales in comparison with the other two in purely financial terms.

But that does not make it legally irrelevant. Theft is a criminal offence under Hungary’s Criminal Code, and one that can be prosecuted by the state.

The real question, then, is not whether we consider one case more serious than another. It is whether smaller offences should effectively be overlooked simply because someone else is accused of committing a much larger one.

And, of course, the mobile-phone case did not begin yesterday.

Proceedings over the incident were already being considered when Magyar was still a Member of the European Parliament. Hungarian authorities asked the European Parliament to waive his immunity, but in a decision adopted in October 2025, the EP declined to grant the request.

Magyar moves to seize the initiative

Magyar has once again sought to take control of the political narrative. Alongside his unusually sharp attack on the Office of the Prosecutor General, he quickly put forward his own proposal: parliamentary immunity should be abolished in cases involving offences prosecuted by the state.

At first sight, the proposal may look like a major political move. Political analyst Gábor Török has pointed out, however, that its practical impact might be considerably smaller than it appears, since Parliament has generally lifted MPs’ immunity in cases involving publicly prosecuted offences.

But there is an important detail that can easily get lost in the political argument.

Parliamentary immunity is not only about whether Parliament ultimately allows an MP to be prosecuted.

It is also about what happens before that decision is made.

For an ordinary citizen, certain immediate investigative measures and coercive measures may be available to the authorities. In the case of an MP, however, parliamentary authorisation may be required.

This means that immunity can provide more than a symbolic shield. It can give a politician time, information and a degree of procedural protection. An MP may have an opportunity to prepare for proceedings rather than being caught completely off guard by a search of their home or another coercive measure.

What happens to MPs without immunity?

The arguments on the other side, however, are not without merit either.

The original purpose of parliamentary immunity was precisely to protect MPs from politically motivated prosecution and to safeguard the independence of the legislature. That is why modern democracies do not generally treat immunity simply as a personal privilege for politicians.

The real question, therefore, is not whether the issue is about Péter Magyar or Fidesz.

Nor is it a question of HUF 11 billion versus a mobile phone.

The fundamental issue is where to draw the line between protecting elected representatives from political abuse of state power and giving politicians special protection during criminal proceedings.

That line matters regardless of who happens to be in government, who sits in opposition and whose name appears in a prosecutor’s request.

After all, parliamentary immunity was not created to put politicians above the law. Its purpose was to ensure that the law could not simply be turned into a political weapon against them.

The difficult part is deciding where one protection ends and the other begins.

As we wrote on Wednesday, PM Péter Magyar accuses prosecutors of ‘protecting mobsters’ in escalating immunity row.

World.title: Revolut Hungary set to enter ATM market – what will change for customers?
World.content:
Revolut Hungary could soon become a much more visible part of the country’s banking infrastructure, as the fintech company is expected to join Hungary’s ATM deployment programme. The change could eventually bring hundreds of new cash machines, although customers should not expect an immediate transformation in cash withdrawals.

Hungary’s ATM network shrank slightly in the second quarter of 2026 despite regulations designed to expand access to cash. According to Bankmonitor, however, the decline is likely to be temporary, with Revolut expected to become involved in the nationwide expansion of cash machines.

The number of ATMs in Hungary stood at 5,688 at the end of the first quarter of 2026, before falling by 29 to 5,659 at the end of the second quarter. The decrease was particularly noticeable in and around Budapest.

Further expansion is nevertheless expected. By the end of 2026, settlements with more than 500 inhabitants are required to have at least one ATM.

Why Revolut Hungary may have to install ATMs

A customer is using the ATM at Revolut Hungary. Source: despositphotos.com

Hungarian rules require payment service providers whose issued bank cards account for at least 1% of the market to operate a minimum number of ATMs. The machines must also be distributed geographically, meaning providers cannot simply concentrate them in Budapest and other major cities.

Revolut has around two million customers in Hungary, according to Bankmonitor, putting it comfortably above the relevant threshold. Until recently, however, the company was not considered a domestic payment service provider for the purposes of the requirement.

That changed after Revolut established a Hungarian branch and began migrating existing Hungarian customers to it in May 2026.

Bankmonitor reports that the National Bank of Hungary (MNB) has confirmed that Revolut will have to participate in the ATM installation programme in the future. As a result, the central bank could require the company to install several hundred machines from next year.

For foreign residents, this is significant because Revolut is widely used as an alternative to traditional Hungarian banks, particularly by customers who frequently make international payments or hold several currencies.

If you missed it: You can run to Revolut, but you can’t hide: Debt collectors can now freeze Hungarian accounts

What changes for Revolut customers?

For now, very little.

Determining Revolut’s precise ATM quota and installing the machines will take time, meaning the current cash withdrawal options available to customers are not expected to change in the short term.

According to Bankmonitor, Revolut cards are still treated as foreign-issued cards for ATM withdrawals. This is important because some Hungarian banks charge an additional fee when customers use Revolut cards.

At present, Erste ATMs charge HUF 1,200 (approximately EUR 3.30) and OTP ATMs HUF 1,999 (around EUR 5.50) for withdrawals made with Revolut cards, Bankmonitor reports. Other Hungarian banks do not currently impose this particular additional fee. Euro conversions are approximate and based on an exchange rate of roughly HUF 366 to EUR 1 on 25 September 2026.

The arrival of Revolut’s own ATMs could therefore give customers another option for accessing cash. It remains unclear, however, exactly how the machines will operate or what fee structure Revolut will apply.

Bankmonitor also notes that, over the longer term, the costs of installing and operating a sizeable ATM network could potentially be reflected in Revolut’s pricing in some form.

Revolut Hungary enters a changing cash market

The expansion comes at an unusual time for Hungary’s payment market. The government and central bank have introduced several measures intended to preserve access to cash, including mandatory ATM coverage in smaller settlements.

At the same time, Hungarians are increasingly turning to electronic payments.

According to MNB data cited by Bankmonitor, electronic transactions reached a record share in 2025, accounting for 50% of payments compared with cash transactions. Bank transfers are also becoming cheaper: 48% of retail transfers were free in 2025, compared with 37% in 2023.

Hungary has also doubled the monthly limit for certain free cash withdrawals to HUF 300,000 (approximately EUR 820).

The expected arrival of Revolut ATMs therefore comes as two trends develop simultaneously: authorities are working to guarantee nationwide access to physical cash, while consumers continue moving towards cards and digital payments.

For Revolut Hungary customers, the immediate impact will be limited. In the longer term, however, the company’s entry into the Hungarian ATM market could expand withdrawal options and make Revolut an increasingly physical presence in a market where it has so far operated primarily as a digital banking service.

As we wrote earlier, Revolut launches Hungarian bank accounts.

World.title: Where Japan fits in Hungary’s changing ties with Asia
World.content:
While much of Hungary’s recent foreign-policy attention has focused closer to home, its relationships across Asia have continued to develop in parallel. China and South Korea have become increasingly visible through major investment projects, particularly in electric vehicles, batteries and manufacturing. Meanwhile, Japan, one of Hungary’s longest-standing Asian partners, has remained a quieter presence.

Written by Kate Berbano

Earlier this month, Japan and the Visegrád Four held their first foreign ministers’ meeting in five years near Bratislava, Slovakia. Hungarian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán joined her Czech, Polish and Slovak counterparts in talks with Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi. Their discussions centered on science and technology, artificial intelligence, economic security and connectivity.

Japan and the Visegrád Four held their first foreign ministers’ meeting in five years near Bratislava, Slovakia. Source: Facebook

Still, Japan’s role in Hungary has continued to evolve. The Japan External Trade Organization’s Budapest office, or JETRO Budapest, and historian Dr. Umemura Yuko provide different perspectives on what has changed, and where the relationship may be heading next.

A relationship built before the boom

Hungary’s relationship with Japan reaches much further back than the current expansion of Asian investment in Central Europe. According to Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, their formal ties stretch back to 1869, while diplomatic relations were restored in 1959 after the disruption caused by the Second World War and the Cold War. Japan later supported Hungary during its transition towards democracy and a market economy, while Japanese companies were among the early foreign investors to establish operations in the country.

For historian Dr. Umemura Yuko, that longer history still matters. “Among Asian countries, Hungary has the longest history of exchanges with Japan, so that tradition already exists,” she said in written responses translated from Japanese.

Umemura also pointed to periods of close cultural ties before the Second World War, saying that this background still contributes to a sense of familiarity between the two countries.

Daily News Hungary has followed that relationship before. In a 2024 interview with Japanese Ambassador Hikariko Ono, the ambassador highlighted Japan’s long-standing economic presence in Hungary and emphasised areas such as digital transformation, green technologies and start-ups as possible directions for deeper cooperation.

Two years later, Japan’s presence is already well established. The question now is what that presence looks like in its next phase.

Japanese investment is changing in character

According to JETRO Budapest, around 195 Japanese-affiliated companies currently operate in Hungary, employing approximately 30,000 people. Around 53 are manufacturers, while others are active in trading, logistics, IT and business services. Many long-established firms, including Suzuki, Denso and Ibiden, have become closely integrated into Hungarian and European supply chains.

JETRO sees the bigger change in the way Japanese companies are investing today. “The most significant change is not necessarily the sectors in which Japanese companies operate, but the way they invest.”

During the 1990s and 2000s, Japanese investment in Hungary was often associated with large greenfield manufacturing projects aimed at supplying European markets. More recent investment, according to JETRO, has increasingly centred on expanding existing operations and strengthening companies’ positions within European value chains.

One recent example is Hodogaya Chemical’s acquisition of Framochem in Kazincbarcika, which JETRO points to as part of a bigger move towards building on existing operations rather than starting from scratch. That type of investment attracts less attention than a newly announced multibillion-euro factory, but it reflects a relationship that has moved beyond its first stage.

China and South Korea move to the forefront

Japan’s lower profile also reflects the growing weight of China and South Korea in Hungary. Daily News Hungary’s recent interview with China’s ambassador explored its expanding ambitions in areas including robotics and artificial intelligence, while South Korean Ambassador Chul-min Park told DNH in June that Hungary was developing from an investment destination into a partner in innovation and research.

Umemura sees Japan’s quieter profile partly through that economic change. “Japan is gradually becoming unable to compete with China’s growth and economic strength, so I think it is only natural that Chinese expansion into Hungary is now much greater than Japan’s,” she said. She added that “Japanese manufacturing is no longer as active in expanding overseas as it was in the past.”

At the same time, she does not see the broader relationship as weakening. She pointed to the continued popularity of Japanese studies, manga, anime and Japanese food in Hungary, noting that the university department where she taught remained highly popular.

Less about volume, more about quality

Looking ahead, JETRO Budapest expects Japan-Hungary economic relations to be shaped “less by volume and more by quality.”

“In addition to traditional investment projects, we see growing opportunities for collaboration between companies, universities, research institutes, startups and business support organizations in both countries.”

Umemura also sees an imbalance in how well the two countries know each other. “When it comes to Hungary in Japan, there is still far too little information and knowledge,” she said. For JETRO, the next stage is similarly about widening those connections: “Ultimately, the greatest potential lies not only in new investment projects, but also in creating more connections between Japanese and Hungarian companies, institutions and entrepreneurs.”

China and South Korea may command more of the newest investment headlines, but Japan’s place in Hungary now rests on something harder to build quickly: depth.

World.title: Hungarian president Baka challenges UN over double standards and Ukraine
World.content:
Hungarian President Andras Baka warned Thursday that the UN faces a “crisis of trust,” saying the organization too often fails to act when powerful countries and their allies violate international rules.

According to Anadolu, Baka told the UN General Assembly that “no country should be above the law” and rejected applying different standards depending on the country involved.

“We cannot have one rule for our friends and another for others,” he said.

“But the answer is not to turn away from the United Nations. We need it, and we need it to work,” he added, saying the organization must be able to act, treat members fairly and apply the same principles to everyone.

Turning to Ukraine, Baka condemned Russia’s war as a violation of the UN Charter and international law, and reaffirmed Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.

He said diplomacy should end the fighting, but stressed that any lasting peace must respect Ukraine’s sovereignty.

Hungarian President Baka addresses the UN General Assembly in New York. Source: FB

“If taking territory by force becomes an accepted way of settling disputes, every smaller country will have reasons to worry about its own future,” he warned.

As we wrote earlier about Hungarian immunity rights, prosecutors seek suspension for PM Magyar and two former Fidesz ministers

On the Middle East, the president urged full respect for international humanitarian law and for humanitarian assistance to reach those in need “safely and without interruption,” referring to Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.

“Israelis and Palestinians must be able to live in security and dignity,” he said, as he urged a lasting peace.

On migration, Baka said Hungary would fight irregular migration and criminal networks profiting from it, while respecting human dignity and refugee protections, and support development that gives people opportunities to build their futures.

Why it matters

Baka’s speech places Hungary directly in some of the most difficult debates facing the UN: Russia’s war against Ukraine, the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and the credibility of international law. His warning against double standards is particularly significant for smaller countries, which depend heavily on international rules to protect sovereignty and territorial integrity. By arguing that the same principles must apply regardless of a country’s power or alliances, Baka framed the UN’s “crisis of trust” as more than an institutional problem: if rules are enforced selectively, confidence in the international system itself risks being weakened. At the same time, his remarks underline Hungary’s stated support for Ukraine’s internationally recognised borders while calling for diplomacy to end the war.

World.title: Fresh details emerge in Fidesz’s internal war over money: did this ruin Orbán and his party?
World.content:
There was agreement within Fidesz that Hungary needed a satellite system usable for both mass communications and military purposes if the country was to gain an advantage in the competition between nations in the 21st century. Where they very much did not agree was on precisely who should receive this fat, multi-hundred-billion-forint investment.

Entering the space industry would have come at a huge cost

Under the leadership of Orsolya Ferencz, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade worked for years on a plan for a Hungarian satellite system, Direkt36 reports on Telex. The idea was not to build a single device but to develop a system comprising several satellites, which would have served civilian purposes – such as communications and broadcasting – alongside military objectives. The project would have been kept under state control for national security reasons, with costs estimated at around 250 billion forints.

Orbán liked the idea, yet someone else got the project

In autumn 2023, Ferencz presented the plans to Viktor Orbán at the Karmelita. According to Direkt36’s sources, it was then that the prime minister truly recognised the strategic importance of a Hungarian satellite system of his own, and thanked Ferencz for the presentation. Not long afterwards, however, there was a twist: Orbán decided that the system would be built not directly by the state, but by 4iG. From January 2024, oversight of space industry development was also transferred from the foreign ministry to the Ministry of National Economy, led by Marton Nagy.

The Ministry of National Economy subsequently signed three contracts with 4iG. Their combined value is €2.36 billion, or roughly 850 billion forints, which the state would have paid out over about a decade and a half for satellite services. The company already received an advance of around 49 billion forints in 2025.

Some of the necessary expertise reached 4iG only later

According to Direkt36, 4iG did not yet possess serious space technology experience at that point. The company established a separate space industry subsidiary in February 2024, and around the same time acquired a 45 per cent stake in Remred, which already had space industry expertise.

4iG then began to emphasise that, through Remred, it had gained significant aerospace engineering know-how. In other words, the company did not enter the centre of the project as a player with fully developed satellite manufacturing capabilities: it began to build and acquire much of the capacity required in parallel with taking over the project. On the basis of the Direkt36 article, it appears that Orbán and his circle deliberately shaped matters so that, in the end, someone could be made to look suitable for carrying out such a project.

If you missed: Orbán-era business ‘mothership’ 4iG under scrutiny as PM Magyar speaks of graft and overpricing

Were financial conflicts also behind the collapse?

Orsolya Ferencz and her team were unhappy that the mega-deal would be handled not by the state but by an external player, and the former would-be Budapest mayor, envisioned as a “space commissioner”, became increasingly isolated. After the defeat, she turned into one of the sharpest critics of the Fidesz system and of Orbán himself.

Many believe that financial disputes of this kind were partly responsible for Fidesz’s collapse in the 12 April election. Orban’s party has remained at a low ebb since, although the latest Median poll shows it gaining 3 percentage points; Tisza’s support remains overwhelming, at 54 per cent among the entire population and 64 per cent among certain party voters. According to Peter Magyar, this would translate into a 160-seat majority in the 199-seat parliament if an election were held this coming Sunday.

Former government’s last hit is a HUF 1.3 trillion deal with Orbán-affiliated company, documents show

World.title: Serbia Sees First TV Debate Between Ruling Party and Student List
World.content:
Serbia’s first election debate ahead of October 25 polls aired on TV on Thursday night, pitting former prime minister and current speaker Ana Brnabic – third on the government’s “Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia” list – against Mirjana Nikolic, Rector of the University of Arts in Belgrade and a candidate on the rival “Student List – Students Win”.

The debate on the N1 TV channel was supposed to focus on education but quickly expanded into a wider confrontation over the anti-government student movement, the media, universities and the overall political situation.

Nikolic said she was initially apprehensive about debating a senior ruling-party official but welcomed the chance to present the Student List’s programme.

She said her previous meetings with Brnabic at parliament’s Education Committee had been marked by confrontation, adding that the televised debate offered a chance for both sides to present their programmes.

The appearance was notable because ruling SNS officials have largely avoided N1 during previous election campaigns and Brnabic last appeared in 2017.

“To be honest, I was not particularly happy to come to N1 this time either, given the way your television station has, over the past ten years, engaged in what I see as the dehumanisation of my President and my friend,” Brnabic said.

She accused N1 of having spread false information but said she had agreed to appear after Vucic encouraged her to give the television station “a chance”, following its change of management.

The debate quickly became heated, including an exchange over Nikolic’s alleged refusal to shake Brnabic’s hand.

The candidates also clashed over the student-led university blockades. Brnabic said students had been discriminated against “thanks to the Student List and the blockades”, while Nikolic accused her of promoting a misleading narrative about the protests and about how universities functioned.

On education, Brnabic defended the SNS record in government, pointing to higher teachers’ salaries, increased education spending and investment in science and technology infrastructure.

Nikolic challenged the figures, arguing that nominal salary increases did not necessarily mean education workers were better off, and questioned delays to university infrastructure projects.

She also criticised Brnabic’s understanding of Serbia’s education system, telling her: “As a professor, I have to tell you – Ana, you failed, you failed the exam.”

Nikolic said the Student List advocated free education, equal opportunities for students and teachers and the modernisation of the education system.

The debate was the first in a series of thematic election debates announced by N1 ahead of the October 25 parliamentary election.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czechia Restricts Rules for Russian Diplomats Travelling
World.content:
Sikorski confronts Lavrov as tensions rise; Russian helicopter enters Polish airspace

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski used a UN Security Council meeting on Wednesday to deliver a direct message to his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov: that after more than four years of full-scale war, Russia had failed to achieve its central objectives in Ukraine, and lacked the economic weight to outlast the countries supporting Kyiv. “You have been trying to conquer Donbas for over 12 years and Kyiv for over four,” Sikorski said. Ukraine, he noted, has only one-tenth of Russia’s GDP. But Poland alone has almost half Russia’s GDP, while Europe has roughly 10 times as much and NATO 25 times as much. “You can still kill a lot of people, but you cannot win,” Sikorski said. “You can stop this imperial war of choice at any time.” He ended by addressing Lavrov personally: “Sergey, I know you’re listening. Tell your boss: enough is enough.”

Hours before Sikorski spoke in New York, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter flying from the Kaliningrad region crossed into Polish airspace north of Braniewo at 11:08 on Wednesday. According to Poland’s Operational Command, it penetrated about 300 metres into Polish territory and remained there for 42 seconds. Warsaw scrambled fighter jets and raised the readiness of its ground-based defences. The Operational Command said the flight pattern suggested Moscow was again probing Poland’s ability to respond. The pressure continued on Thursday morning, this time from attacks inside Ukraine. PM Donald Tusk said Russian strikes close to the Polish border forced authorities to evacuate the border crossings at Hrubieszow and Dorohusk. “Just as we were talking, Ukraine was attacked again near the Polish border,” Tusk said during a meeting with Bulgarian PM Rumen Radev. He warned that “autumn and winter may be critical”.

The incidents come as Warsaw is seeking stronger security guarantees from Washington and dealing with an unexpected hitch in talks over a permanent US military presence. Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz had been due to meet his US counterpart Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Wednesday, with a permanent US Army base in Poland among the expected topics. The visit was cancelled at Washington’s urgent request, officially because of a scheduling conflict connected with Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US. No replacement date has been announced. The timing caused unease in Warsaw. Onet reported, citing unnamed government sources, that some Polish officials suspect Hegseth may be seeking to slow discussions on the permanent base. Subsequent reporting, however, indicated that the Pentagon initially tried merely to change the meeting’s time before cancelling it, suggesting the explanation may be less straightforward. The uncertainty comes days after Donald Trump said “significant progress” had been made towards establishing a US Army base in Poland and suggested its location could soon be announced.

World.title: Fading Away: Sicily’s Ancient Albanian Community Fears its Identity Risks Erasure
World.content:
Piana degli Albanesi sits among the fertile mountains of western Sicily, overlooking farmland and a lake whose waters have receded dramatically.

Its Arbereshe name is “Hora e Arbereshevet”, or, “Town of the Arbereshe”, the only one among the several other Italian towns to maintain a distinct name connected to the ethnic group that inhabits it.

The word “Hora”, explains Mayor Rosario Petta, as he walks through the town’s cobbled streets, is an old Albanian word for a town or homeland that is no longer commonly used in modern Albanian.

In Piana, however, the name is everywhere. It appears on street signs, public buildings and local businesses, a reminder that this is not simply a Sicilian town with an unusual history. It is the centre of one of Italy’s most important ethnolinguistic communities.

Petta says that in Albania, the Arbereshe are almost mythical figures –reminders of a version of Albania that disappeared centuries ago but still exists in these communities.

There is a strange historical relationship between the two sides.

The people of Piana look towards Albania as the ancestral land from which their communities emerged. Meanwhile, in Albania, the Arbereshe represent a living connection to an older version of Albanian language and culture that they can no longer experience in their homeland.

But the community in Piana is shrinking.

Over the past five years, according to Petta, the town has lost more than 20 per cent of its population. Its official population is now below 6,000, although the actual number of people living there is believed to be lower.

“The more people we lose, the more our ancient heritage is threatened,” Petta said.

The reasons are familiar across rural southern Italy: limited employment, young people leaving for larger cities or abroad, and the decline of traditional agriculture.

In Piana, climate change is adding another layer to the crisis.

The olive groves around Piana are increasingly exposed to drought, extreme temperatures and wildfires.

In 2023, wildfires destroyed several hectares of land around the town. The water crisis is also affecting farmers directly.

“We have felt the water crisis a lot and it is reflected in the quantity, quality and timing of our produce,” Claudio said.

Harvests have been brought forward as summers become longer and hotter. Trees are showing signs of stress that were previously unusual.

“The summer season is longer,” he added. “This year the grape harvesting season came earlier because of weather changes.”

The climate crisis, therefore, threatens more than individual farms. Agriculture has historically been one of the ways Arbereshe communities have remained rooted in their villages and integrated within Italian and Sicilian society. If farming becomes economically unsustainable, one of the remaining reasons for younger people to stay also disappears.

The Scalia siblings are trying to make agriculture part of the solution.

Their company was established in 2022, building on an olive grove planted in 1998. Their aim is to combine modern agricultural practices with the cultural heritage of Piana.

Their products are organic, with the longer-term ambition of securing territorial recognition such as the IGP designation. Alongside olive oil, they produce honey and other agricultural products, including plums.

The names of their products pay homage to their Arbereshe heritage. One of them, “Filari”, refers to the rows of olive trees while evoking “fili d’oro”, the golden threads used in traditional Arbereshe clothing.

The point is to make the connection between agriculture and culture more visible.

“Few people invest in agriculture and innovation in these historical times,” Claudio Scalia said. “Those who do struggle to live exclusively from it these days. To keep our farming culture alive, we are also taking on other jobs to financially sustain ourselves in a more stable way.”

Children no longer speak the language

World.title: Bringing the Balkans into Schengen: a Win-Win Scenario for Europe
World.content:
How would all this work? The member states would ask the Commission to prepare a roadmap of criteria: the Schengen acquis.

That means external border control, visa policy, the Schengen Information System, police cooperation and data protection – reinforced by rule-of-law conditions.

The Commission would report on progress every six months, and once a country met all the criteria, the member states would have to give their consent in the Council.

Reforms and the closer cooperation they bring can strengthen security rather than weaken it. When the Schengen area grew from 15 to 24 members in 2007, Germany’s then Interior Minister, Wolfgang Schauble, said: “We will have a gain in security, not a loss.”

The main argument against admitting Western Balkan countries has recently evaporated. For over a decade, several EU interior ministers saw the Western Balkan borders as a brake on irregular migrants and asylum seekers heading from Turkey and Greece into central Europe.

The admission of Bulgaria and Romania to the Schengen area in 2025 overturned that. Why would anyone on that route cross several tightly controlled borders when they could travel from Greece through Bulgaria and Romania to Hungary and Austria without ever leaving the Schengen area?

Reforms and eventual membership would meanwhile help to stabilise the region’s most fragile states – Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Kosovo, where Bosniaks, Serbs and Albanians live on both sides of the borders. As EU membership has receded into the distant future, the dangerous narratives of the late 1980s, that led to the wars of the 1990s, are returning, and with them ideas of redrawing borders along ethnic lines (floated by the presidents of Serbia and Kosovo in 2018).

The recent state funeral in Belgrade for Bosnian Serb wartime military commander Ratko Mladic, convicted of committing genocide in Srebrenica, is only the latest reminder of that.

It is precisely because these forces are gaining ground that the EU needs a stronger counter-offer. Schengen could be one. It does not move borders but makes them invisible, as they are between France and Germany, or Lithuania and Poland.

But you cannot make a border invisible before its status is settled, and the line between Serbia and Kosovo is the very thing being fought over. Settling it would become the price of a prize that’s within reach. It is a far stronger incentive than EU membership, which is at least a decade away.

Several countries already belong to Schengen but not the EU: Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein. Unlike with earlier Schengen enlargements, this time no new external borders would be required. Surrounded by Schengen members, the borders of the Western Balkan countries could simply be collapsed inwards.

Offering such a roadmap would cost the EU little, and only serious reformers would ever join. Yet the process alone would hand the EU influence and win back some of its lost credibility. More importantly still, it would offer the Balkans something better than more quarrels over where lines should run. Borders would no longer matter.

Kristof Bender is Deputy Chairman of the European Stability Initiative (ESI).

A German version of this article first appeared in the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ).

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: Mr Who? Professor in Race Against Time to Convince Serbia’s Undecided Voters
World.content:
On one hand, Ilija Srdanovic’s greatest asset might be his lack of political baggage. On the other, his obscurity may prove a hindrance.

With the 56-year-old medical professor from Novi Sad, northern Serbia, now the figurehead of a grassroots movement to unseat Serbia’s ruling party and president, voters will give their verdict on October 25.

Largely unknown to the wider Serbian public until this month, Srdanovic has been thrust into the spotlight, his every move and utterance picked over by tabloids and pro-government broadcasters.

Srdanovic hails from the city where 16 people were crushed to death in November 2024 when a concrete canopy at a newly renovated railway station collapsed, triggering an outpouring of anger and frustration at what many Serbs say is the mismanagement, corner-cutting and corruption that has flourished during 14 years of rule by the Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, and President Aleksandar Vucic.

Chosen by the students who took up the call for change, Srdanovic finds himself effectively going head-to-head with Vucic, a seasoned politician and, his critics say, an autocrat in the mould of Viktor Orban.

World.title: Bosnia Dismisses Two Soldiers for Glorifying Ratko Mladic
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Bosnia’s Defence Minister Zukan Helez at a military ceremony in Sarajevo, December 2023. Photo: EPA/FEHIM DEMIR.

Bosnia’s Defence Minister Zukan Helez on Thursday officially signed the dismissal papers of two soldiers following an internal probe into “ethno-nationalist misconduct” within the Armed Forces.

The two were part of a broader group of 37 military personnel Helez reported to the Prosecutor’s Office of Bosnia and Herzegovina this month for activities that glorified the late Bosnian Serb warlord Ratko Mladic.

Mladic died last month in a UN jail in The Netherlands, aged 84, while serving a prison sentence for genocide and other wartime crimes, and was buried with military honours in Belgrade, Serbia.

“While I am the Minister of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there will be absolutely no tolerance for the glorification of war criminals within the Armed Forces,” Helez stated, following the dismissals.

“Our military must remain an institution of ultimate trust for every single citizen – an organisation that firmly respects victims, legal frameworks, and the values of long-term peace,” he added.

Out of the 37 initial complaints about the glorification of Mladic by servicemen, ten cases have been qualified as criminal offences and forwarded to state prosecutors along with supporting evidence.

The remaining cases have been redirected to the judiciary to determine whether deeper criminal responsibility exists under domestic laws.

Under Bosnia’s criminal code, the public denial of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes established by binding international and domestic courts is illegal. Guilty verdicts incur a prison sentence of up to five years.

World.title: Here’s How the New Zagreb Pedestrian Zone Will Look
World.content:
September the 25th, 2026 – The brand new Zagreb pedestrian zone has been presented as part of European Mobility Week.

Zagreb’s city administration has emphasised that the presented solution retains hospitality terraces as an important part of the social life of the Lower Town, but provides for their uniform design and better integration into the public space. Poslovni reports that three years after the temporary arrangement of the pedestrian zone in Masarykova Street, the City of Zagreb has presented the project for its permanent and comprehensive arrangement that covers Masarykova and Teslina streets as well as parts of Preradovićeva and Gajeva up to Berislavićeva Street.

The project envisages uniform paving of the entire space, divided into a pedestrian zone and a calmed traffic zone between Republic of Croatia Square and Gundulićeva Street, as well as the formation of new public focal points at key intersections and points within the zone. Special emphasis has been placed on the greening of the space. The planting of around 50 new trees connected into a continuous tree line between the two arms of the Green Horseshoe is planned, along with additional green surfaces, urban furniture, drinking water fountains and spaces for rest. The project also includes new bicycle parking, zones for short-term stopping and delivery, as well as a series of measures that improve accessibility for persons with disabilities and the safety of all users of the space.

a unique and well connected pedestrian zone in the heart of zagreb

The conceptual design was prepared by the Institute for Spatial Planning of the City of Zagreb, and an extensive participatory process included citizens, residents, business users and experts of various profiles, it was announced on Thursday from the Office of Zagreb Mayor Tomislav Tomašević.

Zagreb Deputy Mayor Luka Korlaet said that by arranging the pedestrian zone they are creating a complete public space intended for safer and higher-quality pedestrian movement, staying, socialising and public events. It is especially important, he says, that they are connecting the existing pedestrian spaces and expanding the pedestrian zone on the northern arms of the Green Horseshoe, from Republic of Croatia Square to Zrinjevac. In this way they are creating a unique, connected and passable pedestrian whole in the very centre of Zagreb, Korlaet emphasised.

Director of the Institute for Spatial Planning Nikša Božić said that an interdisciplinary team of the Institute worked on the project, which brought together architects, landscape architects, traffic experts and other collaborators.

“It is particularly important to us that through the preparation of the conceptual design we built on the tradition of arranging public spaces that the Institute developed in previous decades, participating in projects such as the arrangement of Jurišićeva and Draškovićeva streets, the Stock Exchange Square and other important city locations,” Božić said.

what are the top priorities?

He noted that in preparing the solution the Institute took into account the collected views, proposals and needs of citizens as well as the results of expert analyses of the space and its development potentials.

The results of a survey fully completed by around 3,400 citizens showed that 88.4 percent of participants support the comprehensive arrangement of the space. The temporary arrangement was rated as positive or extremely positive by 76 percent of respondents, while 72 percent of them supported the expansion of the pedestrian zone to Teslina and Gajeva streets. As the most important priorities citizens highlighted more greenery, benches and spaces for staying, as well as better organisation of traffic and delivery.
