World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Heavy rain disrupts travel, raises flood and landslide risks across Nepal
World.content:
Heavy rain disrupts travel, raises flood and landslide risks across Nepal

Roads reopen in Taplejung but night travel is restricted in several districts, while rising river levels, damaged homes and snowfall affect communities across the country

World.title: Storm menaces Japan after highest cyclone tally since 1966
World.content:
A tropical cyclone brewing in the Philippine Sea is set to intensify over the weekend and take aim at Okinawa, the latest storm to menace Japan in a busier-than-normal season.

Tropical Storm Surigae is currently 791 kilometers south-southeast of Okinawa, packing top sustained winds of 74 kilometers per hour, according to the U.S. Joint Typhoon Warning Center. It’s forecast to intensify into a typhoon by Sunday, and strengthen to the equivalent of a Category 1 hurricane as it makes its closest approach to Okinawa on Monday, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.

The tropical cyclone is the 11th system to approach Japan since June, above the historical norm of around 9 for the period, JMA data show. It follows an exceptionally active August, which saw 10 tropical cyclones form in the west Pacific basin — the highest number since 1966, according to the JMA.

Surigae also comes barely a week after Typhoon Dujuan hit Tokyo and surrounding areas with torrential rain, leaving at least nine dead and causing an estimated ¥5.7 billion ($36 million) in economic losses, according to preliminary estimates by Weathernews.

Fueling the abnormally active storm season this year is a “chain-reaction triggered by the El Nino background,” said Takahisa Nishikawa, a senior meteorologist at Atmospheric G2.

A strong El Nino expands a warm ocean pool across the Pacific, he said, triggering a number of changes in winds and clouds that eventually create a “steady conveyor belt” of what are known as tropical easterly waves — atmospheric ripples that pulse across the tropics, bringing rain and thunderstorms, which in turn spawn tropical cyclones.

“Most storms through mid-August formed directly from these atmospheric ripples,” Nishikawa said, citing JMA analysis.

After passing south of Okinawa early next week, Surigae is expected to continue tracking northeast toward Japan’s main island, according to Weathernews, although the forecast remains uncertain.

World.title: Japan regulator is boosting scrutiny of AI data center financing
World.content:
Japan’s Financial Services Agency is stepping up its scrutiny of financing for AI data centers by the country’s biggest banks and life insurers, as major financial institutions increase their exposure to the rapidly expanding sector.

The regulator will examine areas including the lenders’ risk-management frameworks, according to a senior FSA official, who asked not to be named. The official said he’s talking about data center projects mainly in the United States.

In its policy priorities announced earlier this month, the agency identified project finance — including that for data centers — as an area for enhanced monitoring, along with lending to the domestic real estate sector.

Regulators around the world have been increasing their focus on financing for data centers and other AI-related infrastructure. The European Central Bank examined the risks faced by banks in the region from the artificial intelligence industry, Bloomberg reported in February. In Asia, Singapore’s central bank has warned that uncertainty over sustaining massive AI investments is a key challenge for global growth and financial markets.

The FSA has no intention of discouraging financing to AI data centers, which it sees as a growth sector, the official said. Still, regulator needs to pay closer attention to the risks surrounding such lending, citing uncertainty over whether hyperscalers can generate adequate returns on their massive spending, as well as the debate over the rapid pace of development and its safety.

World.title: Japan growth minister says economy has exited reflationary phase
World.content:
Japan no longer needs a reflationary policy of aggressive monetary easing and nimble fiscal spending, according to Growth Strategy Minister Minoru Kiuchi, one of the Cabinet’s most aggressive reflationists.

“The era of ‘Abenomics-style’ reflationary policies — which involved aggressively easing monetary policy and taking a flexible approach to fiscal policy — is over,” Kiuchi said at a press conference on Friday.

He also noted that Japan is no longer in “an era of monetary easing,” but has entered a phase in which prices are gradually rising and interest rates are climbing.

Kiuchi’s comments follow renewed weakness in the yen and further gains in government bond yields this week. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama separately said that U.S. President Donald Trump had conveyed his concern over the yen during his meeting with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi earlier this week.

The salvo of comments by senior officials on Friday gave the impression that the government was looking to shore up the currency and reassure investors concerned about Takaichi’s spending plans. The yen gained after Katayama’s comments to briefly hit ¥158.33 against the dollar, but still remains close to levels that could spur Tokyo to intervene in the currency market again.

The remarks by Kiuchi echo recent comments by U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Bessent has urged Japan to move away from the reflationary policies associated with Abenomics, the economic strategy initiated by the late Prime Minister Shinzo Abe.

Kiuchi sought to draw a distinction between Abenomics and the current policy mix under Takaichi, while reiterating the government’s position that Japan has yet to decisively emerge from deflation.

“If you view Abenomics and Sanae-nomics as essentially the same thing, I would appreciate it if you could understand my remarks to mean that the latter is not reflationary policy,” he said. “I understand that we have not yet fully escaped deflation.”

Kiuchi was retained in a cabinet reshuffle last week. That helped signal policy continuity for Takaichi’s administration, but it also kept fueling the view among some market analysts that the government is still looking to pursue a loose fiscal policy while trying to slow down interest rate hikes by the Bank of Japan.

The BOJ raised its policy rate last week at a meeting attended by Kiuchi. Bessent has strongly hinted at the need for the BOJ to raise interest rates to help the yen find an appropriate level.

World.title: The unmaking of Friday Night Plans
World.content:
What the hell happened to Friday Night Plans? When she first appeared in the late 2010s, the Tokyo-based singer (who just goes by her first name, Masumi) seemed like a notable new exponent of the sleek, R&B-inflected sound that had emerged in the wake of the city pop revival earlier that decade, typified by artists such as Wonk , Iri and Sirup.

Her 2018 cover version of Mariya Takeuchi’s “Plastic Love” (over 28 million YouTube views and counting) was so assured that it got a thumbs-up from the song’s creator. “Honda,” released the following year, even managed to make product placement sound cool. Masumi’s nonchalant bilingual vocals and preference for appearing with her face partially obscured only added to the mystique.

World.title: Say where? Japanese towns use self-deprecating humor for tourism boost
World.content:
Japanese municipalities are turning their low name recognition into tourism promotion opportunities, using self-deprecating jokes to attract attention.

The Akita prefectural government’s tourism strategy division launched a campaign from May to July this year to distribute accommodation coupons under a catchy slogan, “Akita Prefecture: Still Unnoticed.”

The northeastern prefecture has struggled with its low name recognition despite its rich tourist attractions, including the Shirakami-Sanchi mountain range, a UNESCO World Heritage site, which also straddles Aomori Prefecture, and the Akita Kanto Festival, a traditional summer event in August.

In June, the number of overnight stays in Akita totaled 339,100, up 34.4% from a year earlier, marking the highest growth rate nationwide, according to the Japan Tourism Agency’s statistics.

“The campaign appears to have had an effect,” a prefectural government official said.

The city of Kusatsu in Shiga Prefecture, aims to raise its name recognition by promoting itself as “Kusatsu without onsen hot springs,” setting itself apart from the town of Kusatsu in Gunma Prefecture, one of the country’s leading hot spring resorts.

Last year, the city’s tourism and products association released a mascot character named “Onsen Dorobou,” a thief who steals hot spring water from all over Japan to turn Lake Biwa in Shiga into a hot spring. The character attracted widespread attention, leading to its appearance at the Kusatsu onsen festival in Gunma in August.

A poster for a tourism campaign launched by Akita Prefecture, playing on the prefecture’s low name recognition with the tagline, “Akita Prefecture: Still Unnoticed.” | Akita Prefecture / via Jiji

“It may seem like self-deprecation, but we hope it will provide an opportunity for people to learn about the charm of Kusatsu,” Kana Sakamoto, 29, an official of the tourism and products association said.

Among Japan’s 47 prefectures, Tottori became the only one without a Matsuya gyūdon beef-on-rice restaurant after Matsuya Foods Holdings opened an outlet in Izumo, Shimane Prefecture, this spring.

The prefectural character, “Toripy,” posted on X, “I don’t care about it at all!” Even so, the attached photo shows him sitting at a desk with a fan bearing the slogan “Come here!” The post drew attention and recorded more than 800,000 page views.

In April, the Tottori prefectural government launched a campaign using the hashtag “#If Matsuya comes to Tottori” to solicit collaborative menus using ingredients produced in the prefecture on its X account.

“We don’t take it negatively that we became the last prefecture, but we want to make it positive and convey our charm,” said Saki Nakagaki, 35, an official of the prefecture’s public relations division, who organized the campaign.

World.title: Why Russia’s Potemkin election actually matters
World.content:
In what must be the world’s least surprising election result, parties loyal to President Vladimir Putin have made a clean sweep in elections to Russia’s parliament, the State Duma.

There’s little purpose to parsing who won what share of the vote; the point is that opponents of Putin and his war were either jailed, dead, in exile or banned from running. As a democratic exercise, this signified nothing — but it was an important moment nonetheless.

Putin’s approach to this conflict has changed. Where he once felt he had time to wait until Ukraine and its backers faltered, he now wants the war over quickly and on his terms. So what mattered to the career KGB agent and his like-minded officials this month was not that the election would let Russians pass judgment on his plans, but rather that it should help ensure public acquiescence to the demands for greater sacrifice he will soon make.

World.title: Xi calls for U.S. to ‘oppose’ Taiwan independence as Trump hails China as WWII ally
World.content:
Chinese leader Xi Jinping has used a high-profile summit with Donald Trump to urge the United States to formally “oppose” Taiwan independence, delivering one of his most explicit calls for the U.S. president to shift Washington’s stance toward Taipei.

Xi’s comments during their summit in Washington on Thursday came as Trump hailed the two superpowers’ “common interests” that he said had “even made us allies in World War II” — remarks likely to raise eyebrows in Tokyo, a U.S. ally currently embroiled in a festering dispute with Beijing and facing pressure from Trump on both trade and defense issues.

“China hopes the U.S. side will adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence,’ and handle the Taiwan question with prudence to lay a solid foundation for bilateral strategic cooperation and the development of China-U.S. ties,” Xi told Trump at the White House in remarks published by the Chinese Foreign Ministry.

World.title: The notion that sanctions work is an illusion
World.content:
When governments impose economic sanctions, like the “economic D-Day” U.S. President Donald Trump is now imposing on Iran, they portray them as a precision instrument — a scalpel rather than a sword — capable of pressuring ruling elites while sparing ordinary citizens.

That narrative has been used to justify some of the most sweeping acts of economic coercion in modern history. The only problem is that the central premise is untrue.

The case against sanctions is not merely strategic — that they rarely achieve their stated foreign-policy objectives — but also moral. Sanctions, particularly financial ones, do not fall equally on a population. They fall hardest on those least able to bear them: low-income, wage-dependent and publicly employed people. Thus, anyone who claims to care about the ethics of coercive statecraft must confront its distributional realities with the same rigor applied to questions of military tactics.

World.title: Whistle-blower Jason Poon and wife charged over HK$6 million Covid-19 loan fraud
World.content:
Hong Kong businessman Jason Poon Chuk-hung and his wife have been charged with defrauding a government financing scheme for businesses out of HK$6 million during the Covid-19 pandemic, the South China Morning Post has learned.

A source said on Friday that construction businessman Poon, 56, and his 54-year-old wife, both out on bail, had been charged with conspiracy to defraud and money laundering and would appear at Kowloon Court on Monday.

Poon, director of mask manufacturer Lockill Biochemical, his wife Chu Shui-fong and four company employees were arrested in March.

The SCMP previously reported that police intelligence suggested a surgical mask manufacturer had allegedly defrauded HSBC out of HK$6 million via the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme during the pandemic.

World.title: Police arrest 3 over HK$70,000 Jellycat claw machine shop theft
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested three men suspected of using crowbars to steal popular Jellycat dolls and other plush toys worth about HK$70,000 (US$8,923) from a claw machine shop to resell them.

The force on Friday said it received a report in the early hours of September 17 that two thieves had broken into an unstaffed claw machine shop in Tai Wai.

The shop owner had offered a HK$100,000 reward on social media to catch the thieves after the crime.

“They used a crowbar to pry open two claw machines and stole nearly 100 plush toys valued at around HK$70,000,” said Inspector Chan Wai-chi of the Sha Tin district anti-triad section.

World.title: Opening hours cut short as large crowds at lantern display spark safety fears
World.content:
Hong Kong tourism authorities have cut short the opening hours of a lantern display at Victoria Park in Causeway Bay out of public safety concerns after large crowds flocked there to celebrate the Mid-Autumn Festival.

“In light of the large number of visitors and in the interest of public safety and order, entry queues of the ‘World Lantern Boulevard’ will be closed shortly,” the Hong Kong Tourism Board said at around 9pm on Friday.

“All lantern installations at the International Lantern Spectacular will remain on display until October 4. Members of the public and visitors are encouraged to visit at an alternative time.”

The board later said no one would be allowed to join the queue from 10pm.

World.title: HK Electric to cut fuel charge for first time in 4 months as CLP raises rate
World.content:
HK Electric customers are set to pay less for electricity in October after the Hong Kong supplier cut its fuel charge for the first time in four months, but it warned that international energy prices remained volatile.

CLP Power , the city’s other electricity supplier, will raise its energy prices next month.

HK Electric, which mainly supplies Hong Kong Island and Lamma Island, said on Friday that its fuel clause charge would fall by 1.4 HK cents to 59.3 cents per kilowatt hour (kWh) in October.

The charge, a component of the overall tariff, is adjusted monthly to reflect the actual cost of fuel used for power generation.

World.title: Hong Kong teacher jailed for 3 years for molesting pupil during free tutoring
World.content:
A Hong Kong teacher clinically evaluated as a paedophile has been jailed for three years for molesting a primary school pupil and taking intimate pictures of the child and another boy during volunteer tutoring.

Deputy District Judge Ko Wai-hung on Friday sentenced the 31-year-old, who earlier admitted to sexually abusing a student in his Yuen Long flat between January 2022 and July 2024. The pupil was aged nine when the first assault took place.

The defendant, a maths teacher who was identified in court by his initials CWH, also abused a six-year-old pupil in November 2024.

World.title: Dog rescuers vow to microchip after charges, decry punishing ‘those trying to help’
World.content:
Hong Kong animal welfare activists say they will forge ahead with microchipping stray dogs despite the heightened legal risk after authorities charged an advocate who engaged in the practice during an investigation into the death of a cyclist.

The advocates argued that charging dog rescuers was counterproductive and renewed their calls to implement a comprehensive “trap, neuter, release” programme, while the government said allegations it engaged in “convenience culling” were untrue.

The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) has also said that sterilisation alone was not enough to eliminate the public safety risk posed by unowned and uncontrolled dogs.

The department late on Thursday announced it had concluded a joint dog capture operation in Yuen Long following the suspected fatal mauling of a 27-year-old cyclist.

World.title: Asia-Pacific hotels a ‘most compelling’ investment amid travel growth, flat supply: CBRE
World.content:
Investor appetite for hotel assets increased in Hong Kong and the wider Asia-Pacific region in the first half of the year as consumers showed growing eagerness to travel and constrained supply supported property values, according to CBRE.

The region netted US$8 billion of investment in the period, up 21 per cent from a year earlier, with Japan, mainland China and South Korea attracting the most activity, the property consultancy said in a report on Thursday.

“Hotels have become one of the most compelling real estate investment sectors in Asia-Pacific,” said Steve Carroll, head of hotels and hospitality for Asia-Pacific at CBRE. “Strong travel demand and limited new supply are supporting both operating performance and asset values.”

Higher borrowing costs could moderate investment activity in some markets during the second half of the year, Carroll said, adding that investor interest remained concentrated in markets with strong growth and positive supply-demand fundamentals.

World.title: Over 1,000 visitors flock to Po Pin Chau trail as Mid-Autumn Festival holiday begins
World.content:
More than 1,000 visitors flocked to one of Hong Kong’s most popular geological attractions on the morning of the Mid-Autumn Festival, putting a new real-name reservation system through its first major holiday test.

As mainland Chinese tourists began visiting the city for the long weekend, crowds were seen streaming towards the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail in Sai Kung under clear skies, despite the heat on Friday.

Many mainland visitors said they had discovered the scenic spot through social media and had travelled to Hong Kong specifically for day trips or short breaks.

World.title: Beijing Court Lets Widow Use Embryos Created With Late Husband
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019073/Beijing Court Lets Widow Use Embryos Created With Late Husband
World.content:
A Beijing court ordered a hospital to resume embryo-transfer treatment for a widow seeking to use two frozen embryos she and her husband created before his death.

On Sept. 22, Beijing’s Chaoyang District People’s Court disclosed details of the case while releasing its annual white paper on medical disputes. The court said it had ruled in favor of the woman, surnamed Zhang, who would be responsible for the related costs. It found that her request did not violate any law, the couple’s agreement, or ethical principles.

Zhang and her husband, Li, married in 2016 and later sought fertility treatment after she experienced repeated miscarriages and Li was diagnosed with secondary infertility. In 2019, the couple underwent treatment at a Beijing hospital’s reproductive center, where three embryos were frozen.

Li died of a brainstem hemorrhage in July of that year. Zhang later used one of the embryos and gave birth to a daughter, leaving two embryos remaining.

Years later, Zhang asked to use the two remaining embryos, but the hospital refused. It cited the difficulty of obtaining consent from her late husband, concerns that the request was linked to an inheritance dispute, a contract provision allowing the embryos to be destroyed if either spouse died, and the lack of approval from the hospital’s ethics committee.

Zhang said she was willing to assume all legal, ethical and moral responsibilities arising from the embryo transfer and any resulting childbirth. Zhang’s mother-in-law supported her decision, and Zhang later filed a lawsuit.

China’s regulations on human assisted reproductive technology, issued in the early 2000s, restrict access to such procedures to married couples and exclude single women.

The hospital argued that Zhang no longer met that requirement after her husband’s death, while Zhang argued that the embryos had been created during their marriage and that she should be allowed to proceed.

The Chaoyang court found that Zhang’s request did not violate the law, the couple’s agreement or ethical principles. It said there was no unresolved inheritance dispute, as Li’s estate had already been settled through notarization and a settlement agreement. The court also found that Zhang and Li had formed a clear, shared intention to have children before his death.

The judges said Zhang’s case differed from that of unmarried women seeking assisted reproductive treatment because the embryos had been created during her marriage. Having already helped Zhang complete one successful embryo transfer, the hospital could not later rely on restrictions on treatment for “single women” to deny access to the remaining embryos, the court said.

The court ordered the hospital to resume treatment, with Zhang responsible for related costs. It said Zhang was an independent rights holder under the embryo-transfer service contract. The judges said disputes involving assisted reproductive technology should balance legal limits, ethical considerations, family consensus and contractual obligations.

The court included the case in its annual white paper on medical disputes, describing it as an example of new legal questions arising from advances in assisted reproductive technology.

Editor: Apurva.

World.title: Spleen May Affect Cognitive Decline in Women, Says Chinese Study
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019063/Spleen May Affect Cognitive Decline in Women, Says Chinese Study
World.content:
Chinese scientists have identified a pathway connecting the spleen to the brain that may in part explain why women are more susceptible than men to cognitive decline as they age.

The study, published Sept. 18 in the peer-reviewed journal Neuron, was led by Ma Huan, vice dean of the School of Brain Science and Brain Medicine at Zhejiang University, in eastern China.

Existing literature shows that although women live on average longer than men, they are more susceptible to cognitive impairment from midlife onwards. Scientists have lacked a clear biological explanation for this phenomenon, attributing it until now primarily to estrogen.

The new research, however, has found that the spleen may influence brain aging through a pathway involving a gene on the X chromosome, which becomes more active in women as they age.

Using gene-expression data from 11 major organs in a preexisting database, the team found that beginning around age 40, signs of cellular senescence — when cells stop dividing and begin to malfunction — rose sharply in women’s brains and spleens, exceeding levels observed in men of the same age. A similar pattern was confirmed in naturally aging mice and in donor human brain tissue.

The researchers’ findings raise a key question: Is cognitive decline in part the result of the body sending a signal to the brain telling it to age?

In searching for that signal, the researchers identified miR-10a-5p, a microRNA — a type of gene expression regulator — whose levels rose in the spleens and brains of middle-aged female mice but not in their male counterparts.

The team then looked for proteins that regulate miR-10a-5p and discovered that RBMX, a protein encoded by a gene on the X chromosome, binds to, stabilizes, and allows the microRNA to accumulate. This process only occurred in female mice, as females carry two X chromosomes.

Next, the researchers injected mice with a compound to block miR-10a-5p, finding this lowered its levels in their brains, as did removing their spleens — indicating that the organ is a major source of the microRNA. Because the compound used does not efficiently cross the blood-brain barrier, the results imply that muting it elsewhere in the body may be enough to alter levels in the brain.

Once inside neurons in the brain, miR-10a-5p suppresses a protein called γCaMKII linked to calcium regulation within mitochondria — structures within the cell that generate its energy. When levels of this protein fall — which occurs during middle age in females — calcium signaling weakens and energy output declines, pushing neurons toward senescence. Restoring the protein in mice with reduced γCaMKII reversed these changes.

“We’ve tended to treat cognitive aging as something confined to the brain,” Qu Jing, the first author of the study, told Sixth Tone. “This work suggests the brain isn’t an isolated organ, and age-related changes in peripheral tissue may start shaping its condition much earlier than we assumed.”

The findings also suggest that because some of the brain’s miR-10a-5p originates elsewhere in the body, testing for it in patients’ blood could help assess brain-aging risk long before cognitive symptoms appear. Second, because reducing miR-10a-5p levels in the body affects the brain, it may be possible to protect against cognitive decline without developing a drug that crosses the blood-brain barrier.

“One important message from this work is that midlife isn’t just a stage where you wait for aging to happen, but a possible critical window for maintaining long-term brain health,” Qu said, adding that because the study points to a connection between the immune system and the brain, sustaining a well-functioning immune system may matter for cognitive health too.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.
