But the framework for success is there if they can stay the course and keep their litany of off-contract stars on the books. Are they lacking the size of a Whyte to match it with the best, after Finefeuiaki finished as the only Dolphins forward to surpass 100 running metres? Or is it a matter of starting games better, having developed a concerning habit of conceding the first points of a match despite winning eight games straight on two occasions throughout the campaign? Whatever it may be, there is plenty for the Dolphins to look towards, even with Kodi Nikorima, Jamayne Isaako, Jake Averillo and Ray Stone leaving the club.



“I don’t think we’ve hit our ceiling yet. I don’t think we’ve quite hit our absolute peak through the year, we’ve had patches of them and really good periods … we’re building consistency, learning how to win and win different ways, and that’s not something we’ve been able to do in previous years,” Woolf said. “I have no doubt we’re on the up as a squad; we’re a young squad getting better each year. We’ll be better again next year.”

World.title: Victim of Te Awamutu train incident was a young person
World.content:
A young person was the victim of a "tragic" train incident over the weekend, the Waipā District Council revealed.

The person died after the incident at Te Awamutu train stop on Sunday night.

Emergency services had rushed to the Waikato railway station around 6.20pm and said the person had "died at the scene".

The Waipā District Council said in a Facebook post it was young person that had a "tragic and untimely passing".

It also shared the details of a vigil to be held at Anchor Park in Te Awamutu on Sunday 11:30am.

"Everyone is welcome to attend and take a moment to remember, reflect and stand together.

"Our thoughts are with the whānau and all those affected at this difficult time."

Embedded content removed for printing https://www.facebook.com/WaipaDistrictCouncil/posts/pfbid02V7NAPEamf2r2yqUWjrcfqoUz8bZQiBxbQwmxPdZWbwoN9huy1tbvcYy9m6eFGn58l

A passenger, who RNZ agreed not to name, had said at the time it was something she would never forget.

"We weren't told what happened, but looking at the trauma of the bystanders... the trauma of staff, something I'll never forget."

She said she heard people yelling "stop" as the train left the station before it came to a halt.

The staff were extraordinary, she said, keeping passengers hydrated and informed as much as possible.

Senior Sergeant John McCarthy had previously said police were "providing support to whānau and those who acted immediately to try to help.

"Chief investigator of accidents Louise Cook said following the incident it had appointed a team of investigators who were now gathering evidence.

"Our investigators will focus initially on establishing what happened and identifying any evidence that could assist the inquiry. Our first priority is to gather evidence while it is available.

World.title: Marmite smears, live locusts to celebrate Orana Wildlife Park's 50th birthday
World.content:
Gibbons at Christchurch's Orana Wildlife Park have been treated to smears of Marmite and peanut butter on poles, and gift-wrapped boxes of cooked corn and live locusts, as part of the zoo's 50th birthday celebrations.

Festivities marking five decades since the park's opening on 25 September, 1976 came days after the cash-strapped park received a $1.2 million lifeline from ratepayers, with neighbouring councils also urged to chip in to secure its future.

Orana Wildlife Park chief executive Rachel Haydon said the zoo's drive-through safari, which ran from 1976-95, was still a big talking point.

"I do love people's stories of claw marks on the Cortina hood and things like that," she said. "Let's say, in our vision for our future, we are aiming to bring back a different version of a drive-through, so that still speaks to that nostalgia, but thinks about safety through a modern lens as well."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405604917112

Haydon said that different version of the drive-through would be part of a masterplan design, due be released in coming months, as the park grapples with financial difficulties.

An independent analysis by consultants BDO estimated a funding shortfall of $4.1 million for 2026/27 would increase to approximately $4.6-5.6 million each year for the following five years.

Earlier in September, park managers warned that the zoo might have to close without a cash injection.

On Wednesday Christchurch City Council agreed to contribute $1.2 million, as long as Orana approached other organisations for contributions, including neighbouring councils.

Haydon said Orana was grateful to the city council and had employed a fundraising and partnership manager.

"We have begun engagement with Selwyn and Waimakariri [District Councils]. No hard-and-fast plans yet, but we are organising times to hope to present and see what is possible."

Haydon said she understood councils faced tough funding decisions, but feedback showed that Orana park was valued by visitors.

Orana Wildlife Park celebrates its 50th anniversary. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"I'm blown away by the emails and words people have sent through to me and the team about what the park means to them," she said.

On Friday, London holidaymakers Ryan and Liz Simes paid a visit to Orana Wildlife Park, with three-year-old son Reuben.

Ryan Simes grew up in Christchurch and said it was a nostalgic trip back to the park, which he hoped can climb out of a financial hole.

"I'm sure there are plenty of billionaires in the country who could reduce their lifestyle by 0.001 percent and it would cover it for years to come," he said. "The government could probably take their hands out as well, instead of reducing everything for everyone."

A historic image of lions in the carpark of Orana Wildlife Park as it celebrates 50 years. ORANA WILDLIFE PARK / SUPPLIED

On a visit from Sheffield in the Selwyn district, Jess Herring was celebrating son Archie's third birthday. She was not opposed to other councils financially backing Orana Wildlife Park.

"We all learn a lot about conservation coming here and a lot of children don't get the opportunity see these animals otherwise," she said. "I've been coming since I was a little child.

"It's such an integral part of Christchurch and such a big attraction, it would be a shame to see it go."

World.title: Shane Jones backs NZ First's controversial New Plymouth candidate selection
World.content:
New Zealand First deputy leader Shane Jones is backing the party's controversial candidate selection for the New Plymouth electorate.

Murray Chong has served 13 years on the district council and is one of three rotating deputy mayors.

He's no stranger to the headlines.

Chong was kicked out of the chamber last year, after describing council's procurement policy as "racist", because it had a goal to improve partnerships with iwi, hapū and Māori businesses.

A vocal critic of Māori wards, he abstained in 2024, when council voted to retain its Māori ward, citing safety concerns.

Chong had previously defended the flying of a Confederate flag, widely regarded as a symbol associated with slavery and racial oppression in the United States, at an American car rally.

Jones was in New Plymouth on Friday, speaking to a campaign rally attended by about 300 supporters.

He said Chong was a long-term supporter of New Zealand First and the core policies it represented.

"We all know that he's got strong opinions, but hey, Shane Jones and Winston Peters have got strong opinions. Lined up against us, he's in the third form in terms of being opinionated, if opinionated is a bad thing.

"He's a very valuable member, very loyal to to the core elements that make up our party's identity and how we want to take our country back."

He said Chong's job would be to go out win votes based on the party's record and policies.

"I don't think people are going to totally make their decision on the basis of one or three colourful lapses.

"They're going to ask themselves how is this party going to contribute to a more cohesive nation, a better set of responses for cost of living and getting industry charged up again, and I can't think of a better person to be pro-industry in Taranaki than our candidate."

Chong said many of the controversies were a long time ago.

"I've learned a lot and I'm a very well respected councillor, which I've proved.

Murray Chong was named NZ First's candidate for New Plymouth. RNZ/Robin Martin

"I had twice as many votes as any of the other candidates last election, and I've been the highest-polling councillor for the last two elections, so I mustn't be that bad."

Chong stood for New Zealand First in 2017, before heading over to New Conservative in 2020.

He was excited to be back.

"Oh, it's good," he said. "I mean, at the end of the day, they hold true to my values and I've always stood for the same values based on their policies, compared to any other party."

Earlier, Jones apologised to the party's supporters for New Zealand First's role in the oil and gas exploration ban, which he said had "destroyed" the Taranaki economy.

"Bugger the climate, lets go for jobs," he said to loud applause.

Jones explained New Zealand First's position on a proposed LNG terminal was that during the heat of an election campaign was no time to sign up to such as deal.

His preference was the "re-emergence of indigenous gas", repeating his "drill, baby, drill" catchphrase, when pointing to recent government investment in exploration projects.

Jones promised to cut "red and green tape" and not let any "frog, lizard or hitherto unknown bat" get in the way of legitimate projects.

He wanted action on State Highway 3 at Awakino Gorge - which had been closed several times over the past year, due to weather events - indicating a complete new road similar to the Manawatū solution could be in order, but its expense would need to be kept in check.

Immigration settings needed a rejink, where the focus was on migrants New Zealand needed, rather than those that needed New Zealand, Jones said.

He labelled the India Free Trade deal as the "Indian free travel deal".

The New Zealand First deputy steered away from the controversy over the failed bid to mine vanadium on the seabed off the South Taranaki coast during his speech.

"Winston has told me not to upset the good people of Taranaki."

Following the meeting, Jones said mining the seafloor was still on its radar.

"I was disappointed that the panel seemed to take great glee in turning it down. The applicants obviously were unable to meet the threshold, but the party remains committed to the extraction and utilisation of seabed minerals as a policy plank of our party."

People leaving the meeting enjoyed what they heard. Jay liked the commitment to try and reboot local industry.

"Oh look, I definitely agree with the oil and gas. That's pretty pivotal for our community."

Stuart was impressed.

"I found it very inspiring and uplifting, mostly the getting rid of the woke nonsense that we've been subject to for the last several years."

Jones' approached resonated with Chris.

"Just getting us all back on track. The common sense and pragmatism and, yeah, getting back to the values that we grew up with."

Partner Roger also echoed her thoughts.

"The common sense, really. I mean, getting behind making some money, instead of all this bullshit that's going on.

World.title: Santana Minerals mining company offers $10m to protect lizards in Central Otago
World.content:
An Australian mining company is offering an additional $10 million to protect lizards in a bid to help get its Central Otago gold mine project approved.

Santana Minerals is seeking fast-track approval to build an open-cast mine in the Dunstan Mountains to target a $4.4 billion gold deposit.

The company initially proposed 81 hectare sanctuaries, but its evidence suggested the conservative lizard population growth in those areas would equate to about 13 percent of the number of killed or displaced lizards.

Legal submissions for the conservation director general this month said an estimated 590,000 protected lizards would be killed, as mine development proceeded under the company's revised proposal to manage lizard impacts.

The fast-track expert panel asked the company to consider creating a "substantially larger, better-sized exclusion fenced sanctuary".

In response, Santana offered to use the $10 million funding to build a 140-150 hectare pest exclusion fence, eradicate introduced pest mammals in the fenced area and maintain zero densities of targeted pests over 30 years for the benefit of Central Otago lizards.

It also proposed to increase the number of southern grass skink that could be salvaged and relocated from approximately 800 to 1800, and establish a dedicated relocation site or sites for them.

A few days earlier, on 21 September, the Department of Conservation provided legal submissions agreeing that killing hundreds of thousands of lizards was foreseeable, but challenged the idea that the scale of mortality was "not directly intended" or was "unavoidable".

"The applicant's own evidence confirms that the deaths of many thousands of lizards could be avoided and that the mortality envisaged is directly intended as a consequence of the [Bendigo-Ophir Gold Project] proceeding," the submission said.

The expert panel heard closing legal arguments, with Kā Rūnaka saying the company's evidence indicated the environmental and cultural impacts could not be adequately mitigated or avoided.

A Santana Minerals spokesperson said detailed responses to the submissions would be filed in due course.

The application has already been paused twice.

World.title: Search continues for Queenstown woman Erika Rodrigues Coelho
World.content:
The search continues in Queenstown for a 47-year-old Brazilian woman, who has not been seen or heard from since Friday, 18 September.

Erika Rodrigues Coelho's rental car was found at Skippers Saddle, near Coronet Peak, on Monday.

Police say search and rescue volunteers have carried out an extensive search of the surrounding area, with support from coastguard, drones and a helicopter.

Senior Sergeant John Fookes said the car - a white Toyota RAV4, with a black roof and registration RKM122 - was apparently parked at Skippers Saddle sometime during the afternoon or evening last Friday.

"Land Search and Rescue volunteers have spent hundreds of hours searching the Shotover, Devil's Creek and other nearby catchments, as well as points of interest and routes that could have been taken by Erika from where the vehicle was left," he said.

"Coastguard Queenstown's underwater drone has been used by one of their volunteers to search a mountain tarn [pond] near Skippers Saddle."

Police are asking the public to report any sightings of Erika since 18 September via 105 - or any information that could help find her.

Any sightings of Erika should be reported via 111, police said.

"We want to stress that even the smallest amount of information can make a huge difference to our investigation and finding Erika," a police spokesperson said.

World.title: Ministry investigating 'serious concerns' about Horowhenua College's leadership
World.content:
The Ministry of Education is investigating concerns raised at Horowhenua College in the lower North Island.

Stuff is reporting more than a dozen staff and community members have sent a letter to the ministry and Teaching Council raising "serious concerns" about leadership and governance at the college.

In July, teacher Asaria Saili - previously the language dean - was dismissed after an investigation upheld concerns regarding his conduct towards a student.

Horowhenua College presiding board member, Juliana Mansvelt declined an interview with RNZ, but in a statement said the school had not received any formal complaints directly.

Do you know more? Email mary.argue@rnz.co.nz

"We are aware that concerns have been raised with the Ministry of Education and are working with the Ministry while these matters are being looked into."

She said it would not be appropriate to comment further, but said the board took its responsibility to provide "a safe and healthy workplace, and to govern and oversee the school effectively, very seriously".

Mansvelt said the board regularly sought independent governance advice and if concerns were raised with the school, they would be managed through the complaints process.

She encouraged anyone with feedback or concerns to get in touch.

Teaching Council chair, Patrick Walsh confirmed it received a letter raising concerns on September 16, and that it was being considered through the council's statutory process.

"Where concerns are raised with us that fall outside our mandate, including concerns about school culture, leadership and governance, we pass those concerns on to the relevant agency, such as the Ministry of Education, to investigate.

"We will not be commenting on the contents of the letter, or on the detail or progress of any matter that may be before the Council, including allegations about individuals," he said.

In response to questions from RNZ, the ministry's acting director of education for Greater Wellington, Te Rangipai Renata, said ministry staff met with the college principal and the presiding member of the board on Wednesday.

"We are assessing the information provided and working through our usual processes.

"When concerns are raised, it is important that we establish the facts and give those involved an opportunity to respond before reaching any conclusions."

World.title: Eagles keep Dons winless, Dogs put Power on the brink
World.content:
Ella Roberts has celebrated her 50-game AFLW milestone in grand style, producing a typically brave effort as West Coast survived a frenetic Essendon comeback to post a 10-point win at Windy Hill.

The Eagles led by as much as 34 points during the third quarter of Friday's match and the margin was still 28 points at the final change, with Essendon scoring just two goals up until that moment.

But any thoughts of West Coast simply cruising to victory were extinguished as Essendon launched wave after wave of attack in the last quarter to put the Eagles under all sorts of pressure.

In the end, it was Essendon's missed chances that resulted in them falling just short, with the Bombers kicking 2.7 to 0.1 in the final quarter as West Coast clung on for the 6.9 (45) to 4.11 (35) win.

Roberts starred on her special day with 31 disposals, four clearances, one goal assist, nine tackles and 717m gained, while Jaide Britton kicked two goals and Amy Franklin kicked 1.3 and took six marks in a powerful display.

Maddy Prespakis (27 disposals, 466m gained) and Steph Wales (20 disposals, one goal) fought hard for the Bombers, who slumped to a 0–7 record.

West Coast started their season with four losses on the trot, but are now back in the finals mix at 3–4 following three consecutive wins.

Over at Whitten Oval, the Western Bulldogs improved to 5–2 with a 13-point win over lowly Port Adelaide (2–5).

Bulldogs forward Heidi Woodley was the star in the 10.2 (62) to 8.1 (49) win, kicking a career-high four goals from 18 disposals.

Ellie Hampson kicked three goals to go along with a goal assist in her Port debut, while Shineah Goody chipped in with two majors and Matilda Scholz had a huge day in the ruck with 22 disposals, 40 hit-outs and five clearances.

But the Bulldogs' deadly accurate return of 7.0 in the second half meant Port were never able to claw back the 13-point half-time deficit.

In the afternoon game at Princes Park, Carlton romped to a comfortable 11.10 (76) to 3.3 (21) win over Richmond.

Later, North Melbourne bounced back from their first AFLW loss in more than 1000 days, overcoming a horrid first quarter to hammer previously unbeaten Melbourne by 31 points.

Coming off a first defeat in 35 games, North overturned a 17-point quarter-time deficit to win 10.5 (65 to 5.4 (34) at Ikon Park on Friday.

With both teams now having a 7-1 win-loss record, victory lifted North above Melbourne into top spot on percentage.

AAP

World.title: 'Cynical' Freo coach bemoans how long AFL took with Neale reprieve
World.content:
Brisbane coach Chris Fagan doubted Lachie Neale would be cleared for the AFL grand final, as his "cynical" Fremantle counterpart Justin Longmuir took umbrage with the lengthy process.

But both coaches are happy with the end outcome, with Fagan declaring Neale's availability "good for footy".

The dual Brownlow Medal winner will feature in the premiership decider against Fremantle — his former club — at the MCG on Saturday after having a one-game ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan downgraded in a drama-filled hearing on Thursday.

Neale was instead fined $10,000 as the appeals board gave the four-time All Australian midfielder the ultimate reprieve due to having never previously been suspended in his decorated 320-game AFL career.

"I didn't think he would (get off)," Fagan told reporters on Friday.

"It was a bit like last year, I didn't think he was going to play last year until the day before the game when he got through a fitness test.

"So it's sort of history repeating itself, just in a different way. Good for footy I reckon but we were pretty much ready for him not to be playing, I must admit."

Brisbane swayed the appeals board that the tribunal had made an error of law in not considering the exceptional and compelling circumstances of Neale's past record.

Longmuir expected Neale to be cleared all along, although thought the decision would have come earlier in the week.

"I'm a bit cynical with these things. Sometimes I feel like that's the outcome that gets reached a little bit later than what I thought it would get reached," the Dockers coach said.

"We prepared for Brisbane's best and he's clearly in their best team. Even if he didn't play, we felt like someone else would have had to step up and they've got a lot of those 'someone else's' that are probably searching for midfield time."

Longmuir later added: "If players who have great records, who have contributed so much to our game, get a bit of leeway at certain times, I don't think that's a bad thing for the game".

Defender Noah Answerth, injured in Brisbane's qualifying final loss three weeks ago, was available and would have returned had Neale been suspended, but misses out.

"Coaches aren't supposed to have favourite players but he's (Answerth) one of mine," Fagan said.

The AFL's gut feel to Neale's gut punch leaves fans dazed and confused It was the AFL's Folarin Balogun moment, and the decision to let Lachie Neale play in the grand final has left many seeing red.

"If Lachie hadn't have played, Noah would have come into the team and Jaspa Fletcher would have pushed up onto a wing."

For the second year in a row, Neale has been the headline story of grand final week.

Last year, the 33-year-old famously overcame a calf injury that appeared season-ending to play a second-half super-sub role in the Lions' stunning demolition of Geelong.

Neale's fourth-straight grand final will almost certainly be his last for Brisbane, with a move to Collingwood looming in the off-season.

"Who says it's my last?" Neale replied to a question about his future.

With rain expected on Saturday, Neale will figure prominently as one of the Lions' best wet-weather players.

Brisbane take an unchanged team into the grand final as they attempt to become just the third side in the last 69 years to complete an AFL premiership three-peat.

And should they win, it would be the second three-peat in their history, following 2001-2003, and it would see them join Melbourne (1939-41 and 1955-57) as one of the only two teams to record the feat twice.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Fagan's future undecided as Lions focus on making grand final history
World.content:
Chris Fagan will again wait until after the grand final to confirm his future as he stands poised to join one of AFL coaching's most select clubs.

There has been speculation over the last few days about whether Saturday could be it for the two-time Brisbane premiership coach.

While Fagan said nothing had changed from the last couple of years — he will speak with Lions hierarchy once the season is over — the 65-year-old acknowledged on Friday that he had been in the role for a decade.

If Brisbane beats Fremantle on Saturday at the MCG, Fagan will become only the seventh VFL/AFL coach to mastermind a premiership three-peat.

"I'm only worried about the game tomorrow," Fagan said at the pre-game media conference.

"Every year, for the last two or three years, I've had a chat with our CEO and president about when's the right time for me to finish up.

"This is my 10th year, so I've been going for a while. I will get through this game and probably have the usual chat I've had every other year."

Chris Fagan has led the Lions to four straight grand finals. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Fagan's long-time confidant Leigh Matthews, who coached the Lions to their 2001-03 three-peat, and former Brisbane captain Jonathan Brown discussed Fagan's future earlier this week.

Brown suspected Fagan would want to try for four in a row if the Lions won. While Matthews said coaching was a lifestyle and Fagan might decide at some point he did not want to do it anymore.

"It's fair enough to speculate about it, but I honestly don't know right at this point in time whether I will keep going or not," Fagan said.

"I was like that last year and the year before, so we just have to work out the right time to go.

"It's not the big issue; we have to play a big game tomorrow."

Justin Longmuir says he is hoping to emulate Chris Fagan's long-term success. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

As Fagan and the Lions try to win another premiership, Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir and his team are looking to win the club's first flag.

Sitting next to Fagan, Longmuir said the goal was to make sure that whatever happened on Saturday, it was only the start of a successful Dockers era.

"I've thought about this moment for a number of years," Longmuir said about the prospect of Fremantle winning the premiership.

"It would fill me with great pride to be able to do that. But win or lose tomorrow, it's not the end of the journey.

"We want to create something that 'Fages' has created, where you're contending for a number of years."

AAP

World.title: Front-running Freo ready to claim first flag
World.content:
Football fans unite in glory, but the bonds of fandom are often forged in failure.

It is fair to say that Fremantle fans have suffered more than most since their club's entry to the AFL. It's also fair to say that, as a result, Dockers fans are some of the most passionate and dedicated in the league. It's why something like Wharfie Time is endearing instead of cheesy. The Purple Army is something to believe in.

The Fremantle experience has often been one of struggle. Struggling against the bigger brother in blue and yellow. Struggling against the tyranny of distance in a league based on the other side of the continent. Struggling against the weight of its own history.

The anchor is sometimes less a motif of their moniker and instead a weight tethering their expectations.

But this year everything seems different. This year Fremantle has led from the front, often without looking back.

Even as the pack came for the Dockers, they didn't fold under the pressure. Instead, they buckled down and somehow got better.

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition," Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir explained last week.

"So we all know what's on the line, but we've just got to make sure that we give our best at each moment, and the next moment's the most important one."

The Dockers showed a resilience often only attached to the best of teams. It's also one baked into the identity of their side.

Fremantle aren't just stocked with high-draft picks. The Dockers are also filled with players overlooked and discarded by others. Almost half of the side that will run out on Saturday fits into those categories, with a few rookies to boot. If these players had given up at the first rejection, they wouldn't be in the league.

More pertinently, Fremantle wouldn't be in the big dance without many of these names.

If Fremantle's fandom and side are somewhat unconventional, its success on the field is anything but. Like many successful teams of years' past, they have been built on a solid defensive base, with enough star power to shine through when needed. Like many great teams, they are more than the sum of their parts.

Like many great teams, they play their best footy when it matters most. Last week, Fremantle put together arguably the best quarter of its season to make the grand final.

"We played our best footy in the last quarter when everything was against us … I'm just so proud of everyone," captain Alex Pearce said in the immediate wake of last week's victory.

Thirteen years after their first grand final, the Dockers finally seem primed to break their premiership drought. In their way stands a side featuring the only remaining Fremantle player from that 2013 loss: Lachie Neale.

Strength in defence

Alex Pearce (right) is the lynchpin of a formidable defensive unit for Fremantle. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Often the leaders of a side dictate the identity and style of a side.

Led ably by captain and All-Australian Alex Pearce, Fremantle's backline may not be as star-studded as other defensive units around the league, but it is as sturdy as any. They scramble, hustle and fight through all four quarters. Regularly through the year teams fell away as the Dockers held strong.

The Dockers have had the league's most consistently good defence across all facets of the game. Some backlines drop their heads when the tide starts to turn — not Fremantle.

Fremantle excels at defending before danger begins. Its midfield works hard to prevent clean exits from stoppages and contests around the ground. Although the Dockers don't have the best clearance differential or ability to win ground balls in the mid-arc, they are exceptional at preventing opposition teams from scoring from these sources.

When they lose possession in their front half, the Dockers stay eager to get the ball in their hands. They are the best side in the league at winning the ball back in the middle third of the ground.

If the ball does end up inside their defensive 50, no side is better at repelling opposition forwards. Miserly is an understatement about how Fremantle defends. It is the biggest reason that the Dockers are still alive in season 2026.

When they win the ball back, they can turn on the jets and blow opposition sides away.

The cherry on top

Players such as Luke Jackson (left) and Shai Bolton (right) ensure Fremantle can beat teams offensively as well as defensively. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Few fans turn up to the footy for stout defence. It's the action at the other end that hypnotises.

Despite their defensive DNA, Freo are not lacking for weapons of their own. They turn defence into attack at the drop of a hat thanks to a plethora of creative players.

Fremantle can put on a show like few others when everything is firing, possessing the ability to pile goal after goal on the scoreboard. While their defence is often understated, their attack is anything but.

Few players generate more highlights than Shai Bolton, with the former Mark of the Year winner routinely getting Purple fans off the edge of their seats. Bolton isn't alone however.

The Dockers side is stocked with players that use the ball well.

Murphy Reid has quickly cemented himself as an attacking line breaker, while Caleb Serong, Jordan Clark and Corey Wagner gain ground with ease.

Luke Jackson also proves a challenge for any opponent as the most capable ruck at ground level in the league. Jackson has the most score involvements of any ruck this year.

The Dockers often attack in straight lines, and use the tallest timber in the league to their advantage.

But when sides like Sydney take those avenues away, Fremantle doesn't shy away from changing angles of attack and look laterally as well.

That ability to win aerial contests has another benefit. It tends to encourage opposition players to fly more often than they should, leaving Fremantle with an outnumber at ground level. That allows even more room for the ground gang to work in.

Up forward, the Dockers can beat you in any number of ways. The likes of Hye Amiss, Patrick Voss and Josh Treacy can take clunks and convert them into sure scores. At ground level, Michael Frederick, Isaiah Dudley and Shai Bolton regularly hit the scoreboard and strike fear into the hearts of opposition small defenders.

Their big men love a bomb from the top of the arc, but Freo don't tend to score a lot from out wide. That makes Hayden Young's preliminary final heroics all the more notable.

Perhaps Fremantle's biggest strength is their evenness across the board. Against Hawthorn it wasn't just the stars like Bolton and Luke Jackson that stood up late, but also players like Judd McVee and Frederick. It is clear that there's belief in this team, and dedication to a united cause.

The Final Challenge

Lachie Neale (centre) and the Brisbane Lions are standing between Fremantle and its maiden premiership. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Although Fremantle has been the best side across the year, it isn't coming into the grand final at the peak of its mid-season powers. The Dockers have won just three quarters in their three finals so far — a feat no other team has achieved before.

The Dockers have struggled late in the year when the ball has hit the deck against good sides, and some of the best midfields have overwhelmed their attacking midfield unit. These may sound like minor issues, but to win a grand final against the two-time defending champions, everything has to be on point.

But the Lions are a side that the Dockers have vanquished through the year. In round 12, the Dockers eased to a 25-point win in one of their most impressive wins of the year. The Dockers absorbed the Lions' clearance dominance while preventing them from getting the upper hand in the marking battle. Fremantle worked out a way to penetrate the Lions' whole ground defence, scoring a massive 52 points from their defensive half.

But it was also a Brisbane side that Longmuir acknowledged wasn't at their best coming into the game.

Fremantle got the better of Brisbane in the only meeting between the two sides during the home-and-away season this year. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman)

"We felt like there were some opportunities there. You know, Fages [Lions coach Chris Fagan] would come in here and say they're not in the greatest form," he said.

"I just don't want to be disrespectful with that because they've been in the last three grand finals."

Longmuir and Fagan both know that premierships aren't won in May. The early season Lions are vastly different to the side that Fremantle has to beat in the grand final.

But there's hope in the West that the result will be the same and that the Dockers three-decade drought will be over.

World.title: Retiring Dolphin lauded as one of NRL's toughest ahead of prelim final
World.content:
Ray Stone has claims to being the toughest man in the NRL.

Not that the Dolphins' warrior would care two hoots for the title as he nears retirement at the end of the 2026 season at the tender age of 29.

But there was a reason coach Kristian Woolf singled him out at last year's presentation night for playing the last six rounds with a broken hand and final 15 rounds with needles in both shoulders.

He had off-season shoulder surgery after pushing himself to play when the Dolphins had multiple forwards on the injured list.

Stone is one of those players who performs when busted. When fit and relatively injury-free, though, he is even more dangerous.

"There are a lot of tough men who play our game but he is in the top group," Woolf said.

"It is not just his toughness, it's his commitment to the team that I really admire.

"He is just a guy who refuses to let his teammates down. It doesn't matter if it is playing injured, he is making an effort on a kick-chase, getting into a tackle or a carry.

"I love his hit-ups off the kick-off. I get a kick out of watching those because he runs so hard. He is just committed to the team. That is what we are going to miss."

Stone has been linked to a boxing career but AAP understands he has obtained multiple tickets in trade areas and will only get in a ring if he sees fit. He can hold them up, as the saying goes.

Finals battle between an unstoppable force and an immovable object Brian To'o and Greg Marzhew have never met a rugby league problem they couldn't solve by running over it and now the two wrecking balls will go head-to-head with an NRL grand final berth on the line.

"It is probably based on family time for me," Stone said, when asked why he was calling time.

"The kids are getting a bit older and I am quite busy on weekends so I want to be a part of that."

Woolf wanted him on deck in 2027.

"I have spoken to him a number of times and asked if I could change his mind but he has got other things in life he wants to do," the coach said.

"I respect that about him. He knows what he wants. He has pushed himself through the pain."

Stone was the second player signed at the Dolphins after starting his NRL career at Parramatta, where he played 31 matches in five seasons. At the Dolphins, he has notched 81 games in four years.

Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf has tried his very best to convince Stone to play on next season.

"The reason I came up here was for opportunity," he said.

"I was in and out of first-grade at Parramatta where we had a strong team and I spoke to Wayne Bennett about coming here and he said I'd be more of a consistent first-grader."

The warhorse, who plays mostly off the bench, has scored eight tries for the Dolphins but, like an old-school footy player of the past, he doesn't smile after any.

"It's not something I stress about," Stone said, through gritted teeth.

"I like to leave all my celebrating until after the game when the boys have got the result."

The Dolphins have won 16 of their last 18 matches coming into Friday night's NRL preliminary final. (Getty Images: Matt King)

He's done plenty of that this year, with the Dolphins winning 16 of their last 18 matches ahead of the preliminary final against Sydney Roosters.

"This year I've been a lot healthier and the squad has too, which has definitely helped our middle rotation," Stone said.

"Last year, pretty much our whole starting pack was in rehab. The minutes have been distributed a lot more which has helped me stay healthy."

Woolf is just glad to have Stone in the team after he missed the early rounds with his shoulder recovery.

"We did miss him too. He is a small man in a big man's world who plays so tough," Woolf said.

"He is loved, respected and will be missed next year.

"He is going to leave a legacy that people don't realise. There are no discipline issues around Ray. He turns up and gets his job done every day of every week."

AAP

World.title: Brazil’s big-name squad meets mega hype from soccer fanatics
World.content:
As some of the world's most famous football players arrive in a city known for its love of another football code, soccer fans hope the hype might change people's minds.

The Brazilian soccer team landed in Townsville yesterday ahead of their friendly clash with the Socceroos tonight at North Queensland Stadium.

Legendary coach Carlo Ancelotti brought a squad of big names, including Vinícius Júnior and captain Marquinhos, whose combined yearly salaries are estimated at more than $55 million.

Brazilian superstar Vinícius Júnior met with fans in Townsville to sign autographs. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

For the city's small and vibrant Brazilian community, their arrival has been a cause for celebration.

Enthusiastic fans wore jerseys and held signs, screaming out to the star-studded team, after they touched down in Townsville.

"We love to party, we love dancing, and we like to cheer for our soccer team," Tatiane Pinheiro said.

"Very loud, very excited, everyone is going to be so excited to watch the game."

Football fanatics came from far and wide to welcome both the Brazil and Socceroos teams. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

The friendly match is one of two games in the series, with the other scheduled for Brisbane on September 29.

It will be the 12th time the Socceroos and Brazil have met since their first match-up in 1988.

Australia has beaten the five-time World Cup champions just once, in 2001.

But a lopsided head-to-head has not tainted the excitement in Townsville, which has been decked out in green and gold in anticipation of the international game.

Brazilian community fires up

Ms Pinheiro, a Townsville resident and Brazilian national, said she was excited to welcome crowds of Brazilians from around the country to her city.

Tatiane Pinheiro expects to meet Brazilian fans who have flown in from around the country. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

"Everyone that we know from other cities is coming to watch the big game," she said.

Organisers said more than half of the sell-out crowd of 25,000 were visitors from outside of Townsville.

Louise Monteiro (right) came with friends and family to greet the Brazilian team in her new hometown of Townsville. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Louise Monteiro and her family recently moved to Townsville, and she is originally from Brazil.

She said it was difficult for her to decide which team to support.

"I think I'll always support Brazil first," she said.

"If Socceroos play against another team, I'll be supporting Socceroos."

Socceroos vs Brazil, everything you need to know Everything you need to know as the youthful Socceroos take on a Brazil team on the rebuild under legendary coach Carlo Ancelotti in Queensland, with international friendlies in Townsville and Brisbane.

Townsville Brazilian community leader Ronie Reed said the occasion trumped every event she'd ever seen in Townsville.

She said the hype among her community had been building since the announcement, including gathering for pre-game events.

"The supporter part of Brazilian football is such a big thing," she said.

"All the Brazilians are so excited to go and support the team and just to be there."

Brazilian community leader Ronie Reed said the local community has been very excited about the game. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

Ms Reed has lived in Townsville for 14 years and organises many local events for the South American community, which is often made up of the many backpackers who visit North Queensland.

"We want to show our presence; we want to show the impact that we have," she said.

"We want everyone to know how good it is to have this community here."

The Brazilian team lined up for a photo in front of Cleveland Bay. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

A street party and festival in the city starts at 3pm, before entertainers and musicians lead the crowd to the stadium.

A different type of football

North Queensland Stadium is home to the NRL's North Queensland Cowboys, but soccer fan and local player Mark Gadzikwa hopes Brazil's appearance and performance at the stadium could help curb a "lack of interest" in the round-ball game.

Townsville resident Mark Gadzikwa is both a rugby league and soccer fan. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

"Brazil has always meant football; there's no better team to do it," he said.

" When you think of football, you think of Brazil. "

Anotida Sandengu has watched soccer since he was five, but this will be his first time watching a team as skilful as Brazil.

Mr Sandengu said he was surprised Townsville was chosen for the international match, which was announced after the World Cup in June.

Townsville locals Anotida Sandengu and Jobe Waring. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

"I wouldn't have called it; I remember I heard the news around the World Cup when everyone was watching soccer," he said.

"It was just really exciting. This is a once-in-a-lifetime event; it probably won't ever happen again." Brazil is the most successful team at the FIFA World Cup, having won five times.

The Socceroos last met Brazil for a friendly game in Melbourne in 2017, where they lost 4-0.

Kick-off in Townsville is 8pm.

World.title: Infantino calls for 'culture of dialogue' amid resignation calls
World.content:
FIFA's embattled president, Gianni Infantino, says he is committed to a fresh culture of openness at the football body that is "not about generating positive headlines".

Two months into a deep rift in global soccer over Infantino's now-dropped $4.2 billion ($6 billion) World Cup sell-off plan, he offered his critics this week an independent review of how FIFA is run and makes decisions.

"I have received positive messages about it from different parts of the world, and it is important that we keep listening to each other," he wrote in an Instagram post from Jeddah in Saudi Arabia, which is hosting the Arabian Gulf Cup.

Infantino will chair an October 15 meeting of the 37-member FIFA Council that will also be asked to approve consultation with the 211 member federations and six continental soccer bodies on "how to further strengthen FIFA's decision-making processes".

The 211 members already effectively own FIFA, a Switzerland-based not-for-profit that has at least $5 billion in cash reserves after a financially successful men's World Cup in North America.

FIFA's ruling council includes three vice presidents — European football leader Aleksander Ceferin, North America's Victor Montagliani and Asia's Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa — who have led opposition to Infantino during the furore over his proposal to create a commercial spin-off part-owned by investors fronted by Josh Kushner.

"There must be a culture of dialogue, of listening to each other and respecting one another," Infantino wrote on Thursday, local time, about the council meeting in Zurich. "This is not about generating positive headlines; it is about doing what is right for the game."

Infantino's presidency since 2016 has created most turmoil when proposing multi-billion-dollar commercial plans without fully consulting continental bodies like UEFA, which succeeded in stopping them.

Flying FIFA solo toward close ties to Trump

Gianni Infantino's close ties to Donald Trump have caused tension in the football world. (Getty Images: Chris Brunskill)

FIFA has often seemed an executive one-man leadership as Infantino built closer ties to US President Donald Trump around this year's World Cup. FIFA created a peace prize to award Trump last year and allowed United States striker Folarin Balogun to evade a mandatory ban at the tournament after intervention from the White House.

Infantino's secretive plan to sell at least 20 per cent of FIFA's commercial rights in a deal anchored by Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law, provoked the soccer body's biggest crisis since anti-corruption arrests in 2015 that led to trials in New York.

The 211 national federations were offered $20 million each to approve the creation of the FIFA Forward Enterprise subsidiary. UEFA, North America's CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation countered by saying FIFA could afford to give each federation a $10 million dividend just from its reserves.

Now Infantino, who faces an election challenge ahead of a March 18 vote by FIFA members in Morocco, insists he is ready to listen to soccer officials.

"I have never been more determined and committed in doing that," he wrote on Instagram.

"FIFA is always engaged. I am always engaged, and I want to hear how we can continue to grow football for the benefit of everybody, everywhere."

AP

World.title: Incredible catch helps South Africa beat Australia in one-day clash
World.content:
Mitch Marsh could not hide his dismay at how Australia capitulated tamely in their opening ODI in South Africa, who were helped to victory by an incredible catch by Marco Jansen that needs to be seen to be believed.

The Aussies ended up succumbing to a 67-run defeat to the disappointment of their stand-in skipper after a succession of cheap dismissals in a sorry run chase in Durban.

Marsh himself seemed to have laid the foundations for victory with his blistering opening knock of 60, but after he had perished needlessly to the spinning wiles of Kehav Maharaj, none of his team could cement the partnerships to get them anywhere near the hosts' 298-run target.

After watching the world champs collapse to 230 all out off just 41.2 overs, Marsh sighed: "I'm pretty disappointed. South Africa outplayed us. It was a good game of cricket, but we fell well short.

"We had our opportunities. I am probably going to sound like a broken record speaking about having partnerships in our batting, but we weren't able to form many tonight."

Mitchell Marsh got Australia's run chase off to a fast start with a rollicking knock of 60, but his departure was followed by a collapse. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan)

The South Africans had set a challenging target after being inserted by Marsh, compiling 8-297 thanks largely to a brilliant 112 from Matthew Breetzke and a spectacular 75 off 59 balls from pace-bowling all-rounder Jansen.

Marsh, standing in as skipper again for the rested Pat Cummins, then led from the front in response with his 36-ball pyrotechnics, which featured three sixes, one of which sailed for 104 metres over the dressing room roof at Kingsmead and landed at the roadside.

He shared a blistering opening stand of 90 in just 9.2 overs with Travis Head, but like Head (36), Cooper Connolly, who'd looked supreme in making 38, and Matt Renshaw (44), he got out to an airy shot when the Australians were up with the required rate and under no real pressure.

The superb spinning of the two slow left-armers Maharaj (4-20) and Bjorn Fortuin (2-34) soon put them under that pressure, though.

Discomfited, Josh Inglis got out to a poorly executed reverse sweep on the eighth ball he faced and Australia lost their last six wickets for just 54 to allow the Proteas to draw first blood in the three-match series.

The key moment may have been when Jansen took a sensational running, diving, one-handed catch in the outfield, stretching out his long telescopic arm to scoop up the ball just above the turf to get rid of key man Renshaw off Gerald Coetzee. It left Australia on 7-215, and there was no way back.

So, after the three-match sweep of the Zimbabwe series, this really did feel like a proper test of Australia with the defence of their 50-over World Cup in southern Africa just a year away.

The first part of the reconnaissance mission demonstrated just how much they still have to work on, and the weakness against spin was again shown up even while South Africa had five top-line pace bowlers sidelined through injury.

Matthew Breetzke's brilliant 112 off just 106 deliveries allowed South Africa to post a score of 8-297 in the first innings. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan)

Man-of-the-match could easily have been Jansen, with his one wicket, four catches and big-hitting or the superb 36-year-old veteran tweaker Maharaj, but batting at No.4, Breetzke's superb 106-ball knock, before being run out by Connolly, deservedly won the day.

All-rounder Jack Edwards had an uncomfortable debut — 0-56 off 10 overs, followed by scoring five off 15 balls — but there was encouragement again in the display of paceman Nathan Ellis, who, fresh from his outstanding series against Zimbabwe, was again the bowling pick with 3-57.

All-rounder Cameron Green, back in the side after missing the series against Zimbabwe as he recovered from a shoulder injury, had a poor day with the bat, falling for five while trying to belt Maharaj over cow corner and getting caught in the deep.

The opening loss has really put pressure on Australia to turn the series round at The Wanderers in Johannesburg on Sunday, when Cummins is set to be recalled. They haven't won a bilateral series against South Africa since 2014.

AAP

Tech.title: Cricut’s new compact crafter prints, cuts, and laminates stickers
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Cricut announced its first crafting machines with printing capabilities that are primarily designed as all-in-one solutions for turning photos and other images into pre-cut stickers. The Cricut StickerPix Print plus Cut and Cricut StickerPix Print are also two of the smallest machines in the company’s current lineup and seem ideal for those whose crafting aspirations may be limited by their available storage space.

The larger Cricut StickerPix Print plus Cut prints, laminates, and cuts stickers but leaves them on the larger for easier peeling. Image: Cricut

Starting at $299, the Cricut StickerPix Print plus Cut is the larger and more expensive of the two new machines and is also available as part of pricier bundles that include more consumables. It’s compatible with 4x7-inch sticker sheets and 4x6-inch photo paper and uses a dye-sublimation printing process that relies on heat instead of spraying ink for better color reproduction. Unlike Cricut’s larger crafting machines, these new offerings include a built-in lamination process making prints resistant to water, scratches, and fading over time.

The smaller and cheaper Cricut StickerPix Print lacks cutting abilities and relies on pre-cut sticker sheets. Image: Cricut

The smaller Cricut StickerPix Print starts at $169 and is also available as part of larger bundles. It carries forward most of the functionality of the larger model but without cutting capabilities. It instead prints directly to pre-cut sticker sheets with shapes that include circles, rectangles, and squares, but it can also be used to print 4x6 photos.

The biggest difference between the StickerPix Print plus Cut and Cricut’s larger machines is that it’s only capable of cutting through the top layer of a print, producing what are known as kiss-cut stickers that come out still attached toa larger sheet. Cricut’s other machines are capable of making die-cut stickers that are sliced right through the backing paper.

Tech.title: Gaming’s biggest horror series are more vital than ever
Tech.content:
For the third year in a row, I’ve been scared out of my wits by a new Silent Hill game. First it was the modern remake of Silent Hill 2, then the Japan-set spinoff Silent Hill F. Now I find myself slowly crawling through a quaint Scottish town in Silent Hill: Townfall, trying my best not to get brutally murdered by demonic creatures chasing me through the streets. It’s been a remarkable turnaround for a franchise that once seemed like it was on life support. And when you combine it with a strong run from Resident Evil across games and film, you have gaming’s two biggest horror franchises both at the height of their powers.

For Resident Evil, it’s been a steady buildup, but it really started with Resident Evil 7 nearly a decade ago. It jolted the series back to life with a first-person perspective that made its scares feel more visceral. Since then, Capcom has settled on an effective strategy of alternating between bottom-up remakes of classics like Resident Evil 4, and new spins on the formula, like the vampire-tinged Village. This has allowed the studio to be more experimental with the mainline titles; this year’s Requiem, for instance, was a bold attempt to merge two types of Resident Evil games together, mixing straight-up action with first-person terror.

Silent Hill has followed a similar trajectory, albeit on a smaller scale. After lying largely dormant following the 2015 cancellation of Silent Hills, a reboot led by Hideo Kojima and Guillermo del Toro, Konami signaled a return for the franchise with a series of announcements in 2022. Not everything has been a winner — a film came out earlier this year with little fanfare, and the less said about the bizarre interactive TV series Ascension the better — but when it comes to games Silent Hill has been on a roll. The Silent Hill 2 remake set the stage, introducing arguably the most beloved title in the series to a new audience, while Silent Hill F offered a freshly horrifying experience through its setting and more RPG-focused gameplay.

Townfall likewise expands the idea of what a Silent Hill game can be. It launches this week on the PS5 and PC, and is developed by Screen Burn, an indie studio known for games like Observation. You play as a man named Simon who arrives at a small Scottish town where it’s immediately evident something is wrong; it seems completely deserted and is shrouded in the classic Silent Hill fog. Oh yeah, and screeching creatures ripped out of Hellraiser stalk the streets. From there you have to figure out what actually happened, and try your best not to die at the hands of a mutated monstrosity.

What’s most notable about Townfall is how it plays. It has much in common with “walking simulator” games like Firewatch and Everybody’s Gone to the Rapture, where the experience is about exploring a space and uncovering a story organically. Here that means poking around in abandoned homes and medical centers, reading through files and listening to phone messages that reveal the extent of the town’s horrific history. The game then layers on more traditional horror elements.

There’s some light combat, but mostly there’s a big focus on stealth: to get where you need to go you’ll often have to sneak past unpredictable monsters, who hunt mindlessly while screeching and writhing in pain. This plays out a little like Alien: Isolation; you have a handheld device that tells you where enemies are, and you can hide in closets and sheds in hopes they don’t spot you. It’s incredibly scary, and still feels intrinsically like a Silent Hill game, despite the shifts in gameplay and setting.

The triumphant return of Resident Evil and Silent Hill is coming at a particularly exciting time for horror, with breakout successes at the box office and a promising wave of streaming series. The genre is having a moment — and despite being around for decades, both series are hitting a fresh stride at just the right time

Tech.title: Can Apple Home’s AI camera features outsmart Amazon’s and Google’s? I put them to the test
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

All the smart home news, reviews, and gadgets you need to know about

A few years back, I was at a beachside Easter egg hunt, watching my kids dash through sand dunes searching for sweet treats. My phone buzzed in my pocket; I ignored it. A moment later, it buzzed again. I pulled it out, glanced down, and saw a “motion detected” notification from my security camera. “Just my dog in the yard,” I thought, dismissing it.

As the colorful eggs piled up in the baskets, my phone kept buzzing. Reluctantly, I pulled it out again and saw several more “motion detected” alerts. I tried to load a video clip, but it just buffered endlessly.

AI-powered text descriptions paint the whole scene in a sentence.

When I returned home, I found my four pet chickens dead, killed by my small border terrier. Looking back over the camera footage, I saw that they had pushed open their coop door, which I, in a rush to get to the Easter festivities, hadn’t properly secured.

If instead of “motion detected,” that first notification had read “small dog chasing a chicken,” I would have raced back home and maybe saved them.

Today, that type of notification is possible. With AI-generated text descriptions, a short message describing what the camera saw can arrive almost instantly, well before a video feed loads, painting the whole scene in a sentence.

The surprise is that Apple is charging up to three times as much as its competition for the feature. Is it worth it? And are security cameras getting better at telling us about what actually matters?

You’d think no one can get past my door without me knowing about it.

I focused on how quickly each service sent the AI-powered notifications, how accurate and useful the descriptions were at telling me what happened, and how reliably it captured and notified me about activity. I also tested other AI-powered features each platform offers, including Apple’s ability to search and stitch together activity across multiple cameras, Ring’s Unusual Event that distinguished normal activity from out-of-the-ordinary events, and Google’s ability to trigger automations based on what a camera sees.

The AI features on all three platforms are a significant improvement over their basic smart alerts. It’s now easier to understand what’s happening at a glance and decide whether to react, and security cameras feel more useful and less annoying overall.

Ultimately, the real value of AI in cameras isn’t in describing what they see, but in using that knowledge to figure out what you actually need to know, and eventually what your home should do about it.

What Apple Intelligence provides, at what price

With Apple Intelligence, a compatible camera connected to Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video service can send you text descriptions through the Apple Home app: “A dog sat on the floor,” “a cat played in the room,” “someone delivered a package.”

It also enables natural-language video search, surfaces “noteworthy” events, stitches relevant clips together, and adds a reduce notifications feature that combines related events into a single alert that updates. This is in addition to the existing smart alerts, facial recognition, and 10 days of video storage available with HomeKit Secure Video.

Pricing is where it gets tricky. Apple Intelligence for Home is bundled into iCloud Plus: $10 a month covers one camera, $30 covers two, and $60 up to five (see sidebar). No tier supports more than five cameras.

By comparison, Google Home’s Nest cameras offer Gemini-powered text descriptions, video search, facial recognition, and a daily Home Brief digest — which summarizes the day’s activity in a short paragraph (sometimes with a fictional slant) — for $20 a month, covering unlimited cameras and 24/7 recording on wired models.

Amazon’s Ring also charges $20 a month for its AI text descriptions, video search, facial recognition, unusual events alerts, and clip recording on unlimited cameras, with 24/7 costing an extra $3 per camera on wired models. Ring has its own reduced notification option that rolls similar events from the same camera into one notification, such as “Brian is mowing the lawn.”

Apple says the least

Text descriptions are a game changer for security cameras. For me, getting an alert that says “A FedEx delivery person is walking on the lawn” rather than “person detected at front door” is the difference between getting up and going downstairs or carrying on working. But quality and accuracy vary wildly, even within a single provider.

Sometimes I get useful details, other times a few words that tell me almost nothing. Then there were the times when the descriptions were detailed, but laughably wrong: “A tennis serve simulator is rolling on the walkway,” “A gray hoverboard is driving on the pathway” — both misidentifications of a robot lawn mower.

Previous Next



1 / 3 I donned a Ghostface mask to see how the various AIs would react. Nest sent the most useful alert.

In my testing, text alerts from Google and Ring provided the most context and specificity, and Apple often didn’t try, saying “someone” rather than providing any detail. For example, it would say “someone is walking in the yard,” whereas Ring and Google provided more context: a delivery person is walking in the yard, a person in uniform, someone carrying a bag, and so on.

Apple was also the briefest. For example, when my cat was on the front porch, Apple said, “A cat sat on the porch.” Ring went with “A cat is standing on the pathway outside the porch.” Google Home told me which cat: “A black and white cat walks across the porch.”

All three identified delivery trucks, correctly flagging UPS and FedEx vehicles driving past, as well as delivery people approaching the door. Apple was the only one to ID the USPS van pulling up to my mailbox, although not consistently.

Google was the most descriptive with vehicles — “a light-colored car drives by on the street” or “a white van,” “a dark-colored SUV” — Apple and Ring mostly said “a vehicle drove by,” sometimes with a type (van, car, truck).

Apple’s reduce notifications feature combines several alerts into one. These were difficult to read and not terribly useful.

Apple’s descriptions were the hardest to digest at a glance, particularly the combined ones through reduce notifications. For example, “Someone seen. Someone carried a box” is clunky. Ring and Google merge the events more fluidly into “a person carried a box up the driveway.”

In fairness, Apple Intelligence in Home only officially launched this month, so I expect this to improve, but as things stand, Ring’s and Google’s are more useful and cost less.

Finicky facial recognition and alerts

For a doorbell camera, the real advantage of AI descriptions is knowing who’s there right away. All three offer facial recognition alongside the ability to spot a UPS driver or similar.

Ring was the most consistently accurate, identifying me every time I approached the door. Apple hedged its bets, sometimes identifying me, sometimes saying “Someone who may be Jennifer Pattison Tuohy,” and other times just “Someone.” Google got it right about half the time; the other half it thought I was my daughter’s best mate (a change from the UPS driver it pegged me as for most of last year).

Apple just wasn’t sure about me. Ring was the most accurate; Google was mostly accurate.

Text descriptions are more useful if they show up, and quickly. But on the doorbell camera I was testing, Apple’s often didn’t. Apple Home reliably alerted me when someone pressed the doorbell, and it recorded every event, but notifications about other motion events were inconsistent.

A potential issue here is that, unlike its competition, Apple doesn’t control the whole experience. HomeKit Secure Video only works with third-party hardware — there are no Apple cameras yet. I was using the G400, Aqara’s latest wired doorbell camera.

When I first set it up, alerts arrived in Apple Home with no issues, but at some point they stopped, and no amount of troubleshooting brought them back. However, alerts kept coming through in the Aqara app. I also still got doorbell ring alerts in the Home app, and notifications from other Aqara cameras continued to work.

The Google Nest doorbell captured everything and was consistently first to notify me of an event. Ring was also fast and mostly reliable; its notifications showed up just after Google’s, though I’d occasionally get “This video is unavailable” when trying to play back footage.

Reliability is Apple’s biggest fix, plus some innovation

The good news is that recording in HomeKit Secure Video has improved significantly with iOS 27. Apple said it completely rearchitected the system, which addresses a long-standing problem with missing clips.

I’ve noticed that cameras load faster, are more stable, and no longer miss recordings. An Eve outdoor camera that was almost always offline has been stable since the upgrade, and the Aqara Camera Hub G5 outdoor camera and G350 indoor camera have also been solid. The G400 doorbell camera has been the only problem child, with missing notifications, but it records consistently.

All the other HomeKit cameras I tested reliably sent alerts; only the Aqara doorbell camera had the issue, but even when I didn’t get alerts, I could use video search to find events.

Typing “When did the USPS truck come” in the Apple Home app pulled up every instance the Aqara doorbell spotted the mail delivery. In comparison, while the Nest Cam didn’t identify the USPS truck as often, its video search results contained more specifics, including an event where the mail person dropped off an Amazon package.

Of the three, Google’s video search was the most useful, followed by Ring’s, then Apple’s, which directly correlates with the amount of detail each provides in the text descriptions.

Apple has two features Ring and Google don’t offer. The first is clip stitching, where Apple Intelligence identifies someone or something on one camera, recognizes it again on another, understands these are related, and plays the sequence as a single video in the Home app. I haven’t found a real use for this so far, but it’s been fun for tracking my dog around the house when I’m out.

The second feature is bringing events that Apple judges important to the top of the search box. In the last two weeks, it’s only highlighted the trash pickup ━ I guess my life just isn’t that noteworthy.

Here’s where Ring wins

One of the biggest problems with security cameras is filtering out the important info from the sheer volume of everything they see. Even with AI notifications turned on, I still get a stream of alerts from Apple Home and Google Home. Some are more useful than they used to be, but overload is still an issue.

These are the only alerts Ring sent from the doorbell camera over an entire weekend when I had Unusual Event enabled. Apple’s noteworthy events is a similar concept, but it doesn’t send a specific alert instead just surfacing the clip to the top of your search page.

While Apple’s noteworthy events feature shows promise, Ring’s Unusual Event feature is the best solution I’ve seen. It learns what normal traffic looks like for each camera, then notifies you only when something isn’t normal. This summer, I cut my Ring notifications down from around 40 a day to just two or three.

Instead of getting an alert every time my cat is on my porch, I only get one when a raccoon or possum walks by. It doesn’t send alerts when my son comes home from school, but it does when he comes home at 2AM. The camera by my chicken coop no longer sends a series of notifications when someone is feeding them or collecting eggs — but it does alert me when I am out there at midnight with a flashlight to wrestle a snake.

What’s next: cameras that can act

The cats were a big fan of Google Home’s inability to tell them apart, as it meant more kibble. (This is not Smokey).

The natural progression here is automations triggered by the camera understanding what it sees. Turn on the sprinklers if there’s a raccoon in the backyard, but not if it’s just my dog. A cat at the back door broadcasts an alert through my smart speakers so someone can let them in. The trash truck rolling past without stopping sends an urgent notification to put the bins out before it comes back the other way.

This is where cameras move beyond being simply security devices to become intelligent smart-home sensors that can understand what’s happening and potentially act on it.

Google Home recently added the ability to trigger automations from camera alerts, although in my early testing, it’s not reliable enough.

I tried it with my three cats and a pet feeder using Google’s new Pet Memory feature. But instead of only dispensing food for one specific cat as I asked, it triggered every time it saw a cat. At least the cats were happy.

The problem is accuracy. When AI can’t reliably identify the subject, the automations can’t respond reliably. So, my earlier example of Apple accurately recognizing the USPS van half the time would mean any automation I set up to alert me the mail is here would only work half the time.

Today, Apple doesn’t have this capability, but if the rumors that the company is developing its own video doorbell and security camera are true, I would expect to see a feature like this come to Apple Home.

The privacy tradeoff

The smarter cameras become, the more they need to know about your home. For a system to understand what’s normal, it needs to learn who lives there, when they come and go, which pets are around, and which vehicles belong. This raises very real concerns around privacy and surveillance.

Ring has faced particular scrutiny over its cloud-based architecture and partnerships with law enforcement. Where Google and Apple can start with local processing, Ring processes all footage in the cloud by default.

There’s real benefit in a system knowing everything about my home — I’d just prefer to be the only one who knows it.

Last month, Ring announced an overhaul to that model, introducing a new default encryption system called TAKE. This rotates encryption keys for cloud-stored video and deletes Ring’s copy after 24 hours. Among other privacy protections, including no admin access, Ring says this means it can no longer hand over decrypted footage to the police. However, it can still be compelled to provide encrypted files.

With Apple’s standard HomeKit Secure Video, your home hub processes footage locally and encrypts it end-to-end before sending it to the cloud for storage. But adding Apple Intelligence changes that: Video summaries are now processed in the cloud using Apple’s Private Cloud Compute (PCC), where they are unencrypted for processing.

According to Apple, PCC writes the captions, sends them back, and then “permanently deletes the data from PCC.” Apple support docs also state that there is no admin access, and nothing identifies who the footage belongs to.

Google takes a similar approach to Apple, but without end-to-end encryption; footage is encrypted in transit and at rest. Gemini for Home-enabled Nest cameras can use some on-device processing, but the heavy work is done in the Gemini cloud, in line with Google Home’s privacy practices.

A big question for me is whether all this intelligence has to live on someone else’s computers. There’s real benefit in a system knowing everything about my home — I’d just prefer to be the only one who knows it. For privacy, security, and potentially speed, local AI processing and storage feels like the right answer. Manufacturers including Anker Eufy, Reolink, Ubiquiti UniFi, and UGreen already have or have announced products that do this.

With a new Apple TV, HomePod, and a possible smart display all rumored to be imminent, Apple’s next generation of hardware might shift more processing back into the house — which could mean paying less every month for the privilege.

When Ghostface is at my door, I want Apple Home to tell me.

Is Apple Intelligence worth it?

Based on my testing of the beta and the initial full release, Apple Intelligence in Home has brought substantial improvements, finally putting HomeKit Secure Video in contention with Ring and Google.

Whether it’s worth the price depends on how many cameras you own. If you have one — say, a video doorbell — Apple Intelligence is a reasonable deal at $10 a month if you also need 2TB of iCloud storage. You get competent descriptions, better video search, and Apple’s privacy position. Even with multiple cameras, you can get some benefit by enabling it on just one.

Next let’s make them better at telling us what actually matters.

However, if you want AI capabilities across your home, including clip stitching, the math gets bad fast. At five cameras, you’re paying $60 a month for Apple to tell you “a cat sat on the porch” or “a vehicle drove by.” The competition gives you more detailed descriptions on as many cameras as you own for $20 a month.

Today, you’re paying an Apple premium for less. But this is Apple’s first move, and I expect it to improve. AI has unlocked genuine utility here, making security cameras better at telling us what’s happening; next, let’s make them better at telling us what actually matters.

A few years ago, a “motion detected” alert wasn’t enough to tell me that my chickens were in trouble. Today, AI can tell me it’s a dog chasing a chicken. The next step is for it to understand that this is something I need to know right now and make sure I get that information quickly enough to act. Eventually, an intelligent home might actually be able to do something about it, too.

That’s the smart home I want. But we’re not there yet.

Photos and screenshots by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Tech.title: Insta360 conquered 360 cameras — now it’s eyeing glasses
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

But as Insta360 sells its 10 millionth camera and opens its first flagship US store in New York City’s Times Square, it’s thinking bigger than two hemispherical lenses on a stick. It’s looking to challenge Canon, Sony, Nikon, and Fujifilm by becoming a “top imaging camera company” or “even a tech company,” cofounder Max Richter tells me — and it’s experimentally building its own mirrorless cameras and smart glasses to get there.

Insta360, also known as Shadow Stone or Arashi Vision in its native China, isn’t targeting Meta’s AI glasses or DSLR-wielding professional photographers just yet. Nor is it trying to replace the smartphone camera in your pocket.

The Insta360 X6, on a selfie stick. Image: Insta360

“We don’t try to fight against the rise of the smartphone in photography and content creation,” says Richter. “We see that there’s an opportunity between smartphone users and professional cameras — a growing trend that people want to express themselves,” he adds.

He tells me that if Insta360 were to sell a pair of smart glasses, “we wouldn’t necessarily compete with companies on smart intelligent features.” It’d be about helping people conveniently capture high-quality images, not about an AI assistant on your face. And while that doesn’t sidestep the “pervert glasses” problem, I wonder if there’s room for Insta360 to go about it differently, with headgear that’s obviously a camera instead of covertly spying.

Though Insta360’s smart glasses ambitions haven’t been widely reported — I could only find one brief mention — founder JK Liu previously confirmed that two mirrorless cameras are already in development. One will have a shape that “you have never thought of before,” Liu told MyNavi News in August. (Liu reportedly became a billionaire when Insta360 went public last year.)

“When you think about mirrorless, for us it would really go into making it more convenient and making a camera that is really suited for a new generation of content creators, not necessarily what’s already out there on the market,” Richter tells The Verge.

If Insta360 does expand into those camera categories, they’ll just be the tip of the spear. The company has already been pushing into many other categories dominated by its Chinese rival DJI, including DJI-challenging drones, gimbals and gimbaled baby steadycams, and modular action cameras.

Insta360’s current camera lineup, not counting its drone and professional VR rigs. Image: Insta360
