Tech.title: I Tested Ninja’s CrushBoss, a $230 Blender That Chops, Dices, Minces and Mixes
Tech.content:
One of the biggest roadblocks for adding countertop appliances to your kitchen is storage. For folks with a small kitchen, myself included, the struggle often looks like a constant shuffle, trading one appliance for another in the pantry. This problem is less noticeable in larger kitchens, but you might end up with more clutter than you’d like.

This modestly sized blender does far more than blend. John Carlsen/CNET

Eventually, you need to decide if you’ll use an appliance often enough to justify getting it. In my case, I’m much more likely to choose a multipurpose product like an Instant Pot pressure cooker or an air fryer. Perhaps this is why I was excited to test out the Ninja CrushBoss, which combines a large blender, food processor and small smoothie blender into a single device. I spent the two weeks using a sample unit from Ninja in my kitchen, and I’m eager to share my thoughts.

Four appliances in one. Well, kind of

The main appeal of the Ninja CrushBoss is that it comes with three vessels: a 72-ounce blender pitcher, a 64-ounce food processor bowl and a 26-ounce smoothie tumbler.

CrushBoss isn’t Ninja’s first attempt at an all-in-one kitchen system, as the Ninja Detect, Ninja Professional Plus and Ninja Foodi Power Blender all attempt similar feats. What sets Ninja CrushBoss apart are the PrecisionDice and MultiBlade Disc attachments for the food processor bowl, plus a better smoothie tumbler design than previous models.

More from CNET

Similarly, the blender’s preset programs change depending on which vessel you attach to the 1850-watt base motor, with each program running automatically to achieve the desired results. You can rotate the outer ring of the small LCD screen to choose your setting, then make the final selection by pressing the top of the screen inward to click. It’s not a touchscreen, but it’s easy enough to use once you learn the controls.

Intelligent blending features, PrepIQ and SmoothSense, track the type and consistency of what you’re blending, but I didn’t notice a difference compared to the preset programs or custom speed controls. John Carlsen/CNET

There isn’t much that’s special about the large blender pitcher, which uses largely the same design as other standalone Ninja blenders. It comes with a single blade assembly and presets for mincing, small chopping and large chopping. The smoothie tumbler is similarly simple, with its small blade assembly supporting ice crushing, blending and smoothie presets. Compared to older tumblers, the Travel Tumbler’s main upgrade is a better carrying handle, flip-top lid and a large smoothie straw — it’s more like a Stanley cup than a NutriBullet personal blender.

Last, but not least, is the food processor, which has the most accessories, including a chopping blade, dough blade, MultiBlade Disc and the PrecisionDice assembly. Where the Ninja Detect’s food processor included reversible stainless steel discs, the MultiBlade attachment is largely plastic, with specific inserts depending on the model you choose. The model I tested came with inserts for thick slices, crinkle-cut slices and shredding — Ninja also sells inserts for thin slices, french fries and julienning.

While I understand that the plastic MultiBlade Disc and inserts reduce the amount of stainless steel in the package, I can’t help but wonder about their long-term durability compared to all-metal discs. John Carlsen/CNET

I call it a kind of four-in-one appliance because the smoothie tumbler’s main benefits are, naturally, smoother blending consistency than the large pitcher and greater travel portability with the included lid and smoothie straw. You can still use the large pitcher for family-size smoothies and anything too big for the other two vessels, so adding a blending function to each vessel is largely superfluous. Similarly, the dicing kit is hardly an appliance on its own, since you’ll see it on other food processor brands like KitchenAid and Breville.

How useful is the Ninja CrushBoss?

My Ninja CrushBoss tests were informal, so I mostly wanted to see whether it could handle a few tasks, like making salads, smoothies, processing cheese and chopping a few kinds of vegetables. I tested every attachment and accessory in the box, with most receiving multiple tests. John Carlsen/CNET

Of the three vessels, I spent the most time with the food processor. I used the PrecisionDice attachment to prepare a fruit salad, which went very smoothly and had no issues with mango, watermelon, strawberries and pineapple. I pureed some blackberries with the food processor’s chopping blade to add more texture to the salad, though the smoothie attachment was ultimately a better option for crushing the blackberry seeds.

Next, I swapped the dicing attachment for the MultiBlade and sliced potatoes and cucumbers with the normal and crinkle-cut attachments. Again, the results were very good. Things were a little less consistent when I processed carrots and cabbage with the shredder for a quick coleslaw, as some bits of each remained unprocessed between the blade and lid. The amount of unprocessed vegetables was minimal, so I tossed them into a bowl of ramen instead of manually chopping them for the coleslaw.

The point of the cheese test was to find the food processor’s limits, so I’m happy to report the motor safety cutoff and error messages worked as intended when I stressed the unit too much. John Carlsen/CNET

To give the food processor a proper workout, I brought out the cheddar cheese, which I put through the shredder, slicer and dicer. As you might suspect, the cheese worked best with the shredder, with very little waste and no clogs. The other two attachments are less suitable for cheese, with the slicing disc producing passable slices. However, I clogged the dicing tool when I tried to make cheese cubes. I ultimately succeeded with some tiny cubes, but I don’t recommend it.

The Best Blenders We Tested in 2026 See at CNET

While I didn’t use the dough blade attachment much, it seemed good for mixing bread dough into a state where I could knead it by hand. I ran three cycles using the dough preset — though I admit the last cycle was because I forgot to add an ingredient. One reason I finished by hand was that I could hear the motor straining a bit toward the end of the second and third cycles.

Even if I’m not 100% on board with using it for dense bread dough, the unit is plenty powerful for cookie dough and cake batter. John Carlsen/CNET

I suspect the CrushBoss can handle the job, as the manual says it can hold up to 2 pounds of dough and shut off if necessary, but it took only a minute of hand-kneading after processing to reach the consistency I wanted. My advice: Listen to your machine and avoid tasks that trigger the auto-shutoff too often. Fortunately, my testing didn’t surface any problems with the system’s durability.

Beyond the food processor bowl, little stood out about the blender pitcher and smoothie tumbler attachments. Each did well with various levels of blending, pureeing and ice crushing, but nothing so outstanding that my ancient Oster blender couldn’t also do. The biggest advantages over my modest blender are the pitcher’s size — even if it’s more than I need in my kitchen — and the tumbler’s portability. Ninja says CrushBoss isn’t suitable for hot blending, so you can’t safely use it with hot liquids.

The challenge of modular kitchen systems like Ninja CrushBoss

Somewhat paradoxically, the modular nature of the Ninja CrushBoss is also its biggest weakness — at least for me. John Carlsen/CNET

Although I’m happy that I don’t have to store three motorized bases for separate specialty appliances, all of Ninja’s vessels and attachments are bulky enough that they’d take up an entire shelf in my kitchen cabinets. There’s not really a safe way to store the extremely sharp food processor discs, so I ultimately kept them in a carrying case for a massage gun I threw out ages ago. Fortunately, you can safely store the largest blender blade assemblies in each vessel.

The other challenge is that while all of the attachments are dishwasher-safe, that only applies to the top rack. My older dishwasher’s top rack isn’t adjustable, so I can’t fit any of the vessels inside and I have to wash them all by hand. This isn’t a problem I experience with the glass jar of my Oster blender, or the slightly smaller vessel of the Tribest Backspin I tested in 2025. At least the other parts fit, which made cleanup much more manageable.

My point in calling these out isn’t to discourage anyone interested in the CrushBoss, but to note that storage space and dishwasher space still matter before you buy.

Should you buy the Ninja CrushBoss?

The CrushBoss’s value becomes more apparent as the amount of food increases. John Carlsen/CNET

As I used the Ninja CrushBoss 4-in-1, I kept coming back to one central question: “Who is this for?” Ultimately, it’s a harder question to answer than I thought. I have no problem recommending each function separately — blending, smoothies, dicing and food processing — because it seems to do all of these well enough.

For example, this particular setup should work well for two types of households: large families and meal preppers. I grew up in a large family, and having an appliance to prepare a huge amount of ingredients for every meal is a no-brainer. Another group that might benefit is the meal-prepper, regardless of household size.

Still, selling everything together in a single kit is excessive for someone like me, who has a small apartment. I have plenty of travel cups for smoothies and rarely need to process large amounts of food. Ninja thankfully offers various CrushBoss configurations and will most likely sell the attachments separately down the line, like with its older products. Personally, I’d love a configuration with only a large pitcher and food processor — I don’t need a smoothie tumbler.

At $320, the Ninja CrushBoss 4-in-1 costs about what you’d pay for separate Ninja appliances, but it is pricier than previous generations of Ninja’s modular kitchen systems, even without the dicing kit. This is a drop in the bucket compared to getting similar attachments for a Vitamix Ascent X. Despite my personal reservations, I think the Ninja CrushBoss 4-in-1 is a great idea, especially for folks looking to consolidate multiple specialty appliances into a single modular system. It taps into the reason why people love the classic KitchenAid stand mixer, and that’s a good thing.

Tech.title: These Lightweight Audio Memory-Recording Glasses Might Be Meta’s Next Step (and Apple’s)
Tech.content:
The multiple pairs of smart glasses prototypes I’m trying on are attractive, familiar and lightweight. They look normal, fit my face well and have no cameras. All they have on board is audio and microphone support. These Vonder smart glasses are all about listening to you as much as to others. And they can tell the difference.

Meta announced its own camera-free audio glasses this week, but Vonder, a company founded by execs from display glasses maker Viture, along with Guillaume Hamon, the chief brand officer, goes further. I met with Hamon and David Jiang, Viture’s CEO and co-founder, in New York a few weeks ago to learn about their new $299 to $399 glasses, which fit a wide range of eye prescriptions but also require a monthly paid AI subscription.

Viture’s frames look totally normal, are lightweight, and lack cameras. Scott Stein/CNET

Bone conduction inside

Viture’s tethered wearables are more like wearable monitors in glasses form with augmented-reality bells and whistles. Vonder has no displays and leans on extended battery life and a unique approach to audio technology, using bone conduction in the glasses to help with privacy to filter personal voice memos versus recording external voices in a room.

More from CNET

The onboard array of microphones can listen in on conversations and summarize them using AI, which then appears in a phone app or a web app. But the glasses don’t keep any audio recordings. Apple is doing something similar on its Apple Watches and iPhones later this year via Siri Recap. Meta, meanwhile, hasn’t gotten into the memory-recording audio space yet.

I wore Vonder’s glasses. They look good. Scott Stein/CNET

I found the bone conduction microphones in the glasses’ arms to be the most interesting feature, which can listen to your own voice even at a whisper. I hadn’t seen that idea before in the glasses I’ve worn. According to Jiang and Hamon, Vonder’s glasses can either record just your own voice for memos and personal notes or a conversation with others. The bone conduction microphones help differentiate between your voice and whoever you’re speaking to.

In conversation modes where the glasses are recording others, a small side LED light turns on after you press a recording button on the glasses’ arm. In personal modes, there’s no light.

Vonder’s memory graph becomes a mind map of related memories that’s cloud stored. I saw a demo on a laptop in the web app. Scott Stein/CNET

A memory assistant, for a monthly subscription

“The idea of Vonder is fashion-forward glasses that allow you to basically reduce your cognitive load and rely on Vonder as a second memory, almost, so you can stay in the flow of your life, your conversations and rely on Vonder to keep track of what matters,” Hamon tells me.

These glasses aren’t designed as phone replacements. “It’s utopic, I think, at this current stage, to ask people to ditch the phone,” Jiang says. Jiang’s other company, Viture, also uses glasses (display-enabled ones) as phone accessories, not self-contained face computers.

Vonder’s phone app and its discrete recording and microphone controls. Scott Stein/CNET

It’s also utopian – some would say dystopian – to imagine AI platforms as true memory extensions. That was how I tried to live for a month with a pendant called Looki, and it didn’t go well. I don’t know how Vonder’s Personal Memory Graph, its cloud and phone app-based AI system that pulls from OpenAI, Gemini and Claude models, will actually work in practice. Vonder’s AI service won’t directly log into those other AI services; it’ll draw from their AI models instead, similar to how AI glasses services like Rokid’s work.

Vonder’s AI services can also proactively summarize and brief, like it did for my name. Scott Stein/CNET

Vonder’s memory-mapping platform aims to be a safe place to store all your conversations and personal memos, creating a searchable mind map. Seeing an early preview of the software in a web browser, I was skeptical. Every company wants to be our collective memory now: How do we trust collecting those memories, though? Vonder’s pitch is also a subscription one: The required AI service is priced in tiers based on how much it’s used, from $5 to $30 a month. I don’t like the idea of subscription memories, not at all.

There are lots of good looking Vonder glasses styles I saw. Scott Stein/CNET

No cameras here

I do like how small Vonder’s glasses frames are, though, and how they’re styled. At 30 grams, they feel exactly like regular glasses and have flexible arms for a comfortable temple fit. They’re notably lighter than Meta’s smart glasses, which hover around 50 grams. They’re also lighter than the small Even Realities G2 glasses I wore earlier this year.

And Vonder’s leaning completely on audio at a time when the rest of the smart glasses industry may be seeing a similar pivot. With the ongoing backlash against smart glasses cameras, privacy features will be what Meta’s new glasses, and Google and Samsung’s, will be judged against. Meta’s already promising more private computing in the year ahead. How will Vonder measure up? And, with Meta now promising better battery life on its Ray-Ban Audio glasses, could audio-recording memory modes like these be on deck next? Or Apple, for that matter?

Vonder says its glasses will last over 16 hours on a single charge, even when recording continuously. They truly could be used all day. Apple’s promising all-day battery life in its upcoming Siri Recap recording mode, too. To do this, Vonder’s using a chipset also found in earbuds instead of a higher-end Qualcomm glasses-focused processor, making the glasses more power-efficient.

I won’t know more till I try a pair, but Vonder’s frames are the nicest-looking I’ve seen. Will the AI services be worth it, too? I expect a lot out of any device promising to extend my memory. I’m very protective about my memories, too, so we’ll see.

Tech.title: Planning a Fall Hike? Here’s How to Download a Map to Your iPhone
Tech.content:
PRODUCTION – 19 September 2026, Rhineland-Palatinate, Kordel: Hikers are walking along a trail in the woods. For many people, fall is the perfect time to get some exercise outdoors. Photo: Harald Tittel/dpa (Photo by Harald Tittel/picture alliance via Getty Images) Harald Tittel via Getty Images

Fall is here, and after a sweltering summer the weather is finally cooling down. Before it gets too cold out, you might be thinking about planning some outdoor activities for yourself and others to enjoy, and a hike is a great way to get outside and see the changing of the seasons. Before you step out the door, you should plan and map your hike on your iPhone, and download it to your device so you don’t get lost.

When Apple released iOS 18 in 2024, it made some improvements in your iPhone’s Maps app, including the ability to create a custom walking route. These can help keep you on track without needing additional maps or equipment. This feature can also tell you the distance of a route, as well as what your elevation is while you’re on the trail. If you’re in Denver, I imagine it just says, “Up there.”

Here’s how to create your own custom route in Apple Maps on your iPhone.

Make a custom route on Apple Maps

1. Open Maps.

2. Either tap the blue icon marking your current location or long-press near where you want to start your route to drop a pin.

3. Tap the three dots (…) across the bottom of your screen.

4. Tap Create a Custom Route.

From here you have to plot your route by tapping around your map. You can tap intersections and landmarks — like restaurants and shops — and the app will start mapping your route. You can also tap intersections and unmarked locations on your map for a more granular approach to creating your route.

You don’t have to tap a location near your last route point, either. After you tap Create a Custom Route, you can tap a location miles away and Maps will create a route for you. It’s important to note that if you tap a location miles away from where you start your route, Maps will find a path that doesn’t involve busting through walls like the Kool-Aid man. In that regard, creating a route is just like getting driving directions on Maps.

While creating your route, Maps will also give you three route options if you tap your original location: Reverse, Out & Back and Close Loop. Reverse flips your route so where you initially started is now where your route ends. Out & Back maps your route on top of itself so you start and end where you began in a single path. Close Loop also ends your route where you started but for routes that are circular in nature.

Maps makes it easy to close your loop or end your route. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Once you’ve created your route, tap Save Route and you’ll be asked to name your route. Then tap the blue check mark in the top right corner of the new menu. Maps will also download your custom route to your iPhone, so you won’t have to worry about losing reception, especially if you’re hiking out in the wilderness.

Where to find your custom route

After you’ve saved your custom route, it will be moved to your Library in Maps. Here’s how to access it.

1. Open Maps.

2. Tap your profile icon to the right of the search bar in Maps.

3. Tap Places.

4. Tap Routes.

5. Select the route you want to take.

You can find your routes here, in Maps. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

After selecting the route, Maps will pull it up on your map. If you’re near the start of your route, tap Go and your iPhone will give you directions along your route. If you’re not near the start of the route, you can tap Directions and Maps will show you how to get to the start of your route.

For more, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and why your battery might be draining faster after updating. You can also check out why the iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1.

Tech.title: Google’s AI Wants to Call Stores for You — Here Are the Problems With That
Tech.content:
Google on Thursday announced an expansion of its mobile Gemini AI capabilities, a new agentic feature built to handle everyday phone calls for you. Introverts of the world, rejoice — but also pay attention to the fine print, because there are limits to what Gemini can do for you.

This technology, which starts with a “@Call for me” prompt when using Gemini on your phone, is slowly rolling out to eligible users. Gemini could call a store to verify business hours or ask about product availability. With the right prompt, it could call a local restaurant and make a reservation for a specific time. Or it could ask about pricing for a specific service, such as dry cleaning a suit.

Gemini’s new feature is intentionally limited when it’s time to close the deal. It’s designed not to make any payments or share a credit card number, though it can share your name and contact information.

More from CNET

That means, for many tasks you may want Gemini to handle, you’ll have to follow along with a transcript or listen in to the call, then use the “take over” option to sub in for the AI and provide sensitive data. This limits how much time the call-for-me feature can really save.

CNET senior editor and mobile guru Michael Sorrentino has questions about the new feature.

“While I’d like to test this out, the real measure of this feature will be both its transparency of being an AI assistant and whether businesses themselves will be willing to talk to it,” he told me. “I’ve long enjoyed Pixel’s other Call Screening features and Hold For Me (feature) for skipping hold music, so seeing Google get Gemini involved isn’t surprising.”

A representative from Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Will businesses play along?

You’ll need the latest Google phone for these capabilities. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

Gemini will play an automated message to whoever takes your call, letting them know an AI is speaking, before launching into a conversation based on your prompt. But a lot depends on how the business responds.

Will there be a way for businesses to prioritize human calls over Gemini AI if they want to? What if a specific business location receives too many AI-generated calls and can’t reach human callers in a reasonable time?

Google is restricting this feature from using emergency services, but many service-related companies could still run into issues. And it’s unclear how the new call-for-me feature will handle voicemail recordings or phone wait times, which are common in busy shops and restaurants.

When someone answers a call, questions arise about how employees will manage an AI interaction. The process remains distinct from speaking with a human, and unanticipated contact may cause confusion among staff. Organizations receiving a high volume of AI-generated calls will likely need to implement new operational guidelines to manage these interactions. While blocking Gemini calls is possible through an opt-out process, the availability of this feature for all companies isn’t clear. I also want to see how well the Gemini feature responds to a business that asks you to call back.

Finally, the calling feature has daily limits, though Google doesn’t specify how many calls you can make. This is probably to prevent overuse of Gemini’s energy-hungry features and to stop people from using it to make robocalls.

How do I get the call-for-me ability?

You’ll have to jump through several hoops to use this Gemini feature if you’re interested. First, you’ll need to be over 18 and have a Pixel 11 or later phone. The service is only available in the US and in English for now.

Next, you’ll need a Google AI subscription, which starts at $5 per month, and you’ll have to download the public beta of the Phone by Google app. Then you can update to the newest version of the Gemini app and use the @Call for me ability in a prompt.

Risks and issues

Google has set boundaries on the call feature, including restrictions about what sensitive data the AI can share. By design, it can’t provide data such as passwords or Social Security numbers. But that doesn’t mean it’s risk-free.

Google has confirmed that Gemini breached the security of three different companies this year without permission, raising questions about how easily the AI can slip past Google’s safeguards.

We’ll be testing this feature as soon as we can and will report back.

Tech.title: Nintendo Switch Owners: Update Your Firmware to Protect Against Security Exploit
Tech.content:
If you own an original Nintendo Switch, there’s a security exploit you will want to patch immediately, especially if you use the game console in public. Nintendo revealed the vulnerability on Sept. 10, shortly after the company released its latest 23.0.0 firmware update.

The vulnerability applies only to original Nintendo Switch owners who use the Send to Smartphone feature. This feature generates a QR code on the Switch that users can scan with a smartphone, allowing them to transfer game captures and screenshots directly to their phone.

The exploit also affects people playing Super Mario Kart: Home Circuit on the physical cartridge, as the game uses a QR code to establish a wireless link with nearby players.

More from CNET

Should someone else scan the QR code before you, they can connect their device to your Switch and use the connection to run unauthorized code on your Switch or steal information stored on the game console. Since your account information is stored on your Switch, that’s information you don’t want in the hands of someone else.

A Nintendo representative did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.

The exploit doesn’t affect the Nintendo Switch 2.

How to fix the problem

The fix is simple. Nintendo released update 23.0.0 on Sept. 9, which fixes the exploit. It’s recorded as CVE-2026-82079, which is “a stock-based buffer overflow vulnerability” that lets attackers within wireless range execute code. It only affects the original Switch on firmware versions older than 23.0.0.

To update your Nintendo Switch, head to System Settings > System > System Update to apply the update. Follow any additional on-screen prompts to install the update.

Nintendo says that those who can’t immediately update their firmware can avoid the issue by only using the Send to Smartphone feature at home, where attackers can’t see them, or by not playing Super Mario Kart: Home Circuit in public. The gaming giant also recommends not scanning any QR codes with any device that isn’t yours.

People who only play games at home are protected from this exploit and don’t have to worry about it.

Tech.title: How to Customize Your AI Tools, From ChatGPT to Gemini and Claude
Tech.content:
Hallucinating, sucking up and providing way too many bullet points and emoji in the response when you just asked a simple question: The sins of AI chat tools are many.

Spending precious moments searching for and refining prompts that will get you to the right answer in the way you want it delivered is one way to go, but there’s a more sophisticated, permanent method hiding in the depths of your favorite AI chat’s toolkit.

AI chat tools like ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Claude AI and others have options in their settings that serve as permanent instruction manuals for how they interact with you. Using these features can give the tools specific instructions that might lead to better outcomes and less frustration, but first, you have to find them.

More from CNET

Here’s how to customize your AI to give you the best responses in the way you want them.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Personalization settings

To access all of these personalization settings, start by clicking your username in the open chat window of most AI chat tools. You’ll find something in the settings list usually called “personalization” or “personal intelligence.” This is the starting point for all AI chat customizations — your command center for the best prompt results possible.

ChatGPT offers a range of options for customizing your experience with the tool, including how “warm” and “enthusiastic” the responses in your chats might be — aka, how much butt kissing you’d like in your interactions — as well as whether you want to nix emoji use altogether or how you’d like ChatGPT to refer to you in your sessions.

ChatGPT/Screenshot by CNET

Gemini’s version of this is called Personal Intelligence, and it offers a much more open-ended alternative to the toggle method in ChatGPT’s settings. You access it the same way, but instead of a list of options, in addition to providing custom instructions, Gemini operates only on custom instructions.

Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

Claude AI also allows you to pick a style of communication in the tool’s settings and add custom instructions for how Claude should build its responses to prompts.

Claude/Screenshot by CNET

Claude offers several custom setting capabilities, including chat fonts, voice styles and the option to provide specific instructions like ChatGPT and Gemini.

Setting the tone

Each AI chat tool has its own default voice, literally, and they can all be adjusted to suit your individual tastes.

In ChatGPT, the default is average “warmth,” and you can toggle the friendliness from bestie to fact-focused professional. Fiddling with the “enthusiasm” toggles offers a range from energized and excited to calm and neutral, and there’s even a switch that lets you up the ante on emoji or nix them outright.

Gemini and Claude are more self-guided and require you to come up with your own specialized set of instructions to specify what kind of tone you’d like the chats to take.

The test prompt

I started with a baseline setting across all three AI chats, focusing on responses within an area of expertise in which I am woefully underinformed, but which offers a chance for the AI tools to respond in a wide variety of ways: the video game EA Sports College Football.

Using the default settings, I entered the prompt, “What team should I manage in EA Sports College Football?” into each AI tool. The resulting advice differed in each chat, with fairly vanilla phrasing and varying lengths.

ChatGPT/Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

Claude/Screenshot by CNET

Using the same prompt, I bumped the warmth, enthusiasm and emoji use up to the max in ChatGPT, as well as setting the base style and tone to “quirky.” I used the same kind of tailoring for both Gemini and Claude.

ChatGPT’s friendlier output showed the most change in tone, and the tool even changed its recommendations for which team to go with in its response. Gemini, on the other hand, seemed to simply add some more adjectives and emojis to the same response, and Claude threw in a football emoji and narrowed the team pick down to Georgia.

Claude/Screenshot by CNET

ChatGPT/Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

Refining the responses

Once you’ve set up your instructions, the AI tools should be able to incorporate them immediately. You won’t need to start a fresh chat to get them up and running. Here’s how ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini performed when given their more specific marching orders.

I added some custom instructions to each AI tool that I hoped would address the biggest gripes users seem to have — too much butt kissing, making things up to fill in the blanks and using language that feels inhuman or reads like AI slop.

The instructions: Do not compliment the user. Do not tell the user they are “brilliant” or making a wonderful point, for example, in the chats. When presenting new information, always cite the source of that information in the chat, if available. Keep responses human – do not summarize points at the end of the responses.

Of the three tools, only Gemini fully followed the directions without prompting in the chat, providing a link to EA’s website with information about a specific team I mentioned and asked about.

ChatGPT cited a source, but it turned out to be user data (recalling my time as an ASU professor), and not any empirical information like player stats or metrics from the game. Only when asked directly to provide sources did it deploy a robust listing of links, saying, “You’re right to ask. I didn’t provide citations in that response, and I should have distinguished source game information from my own recommendation.”

Claude also relayed sources only after specific requests for them in the chat.

Claude/Screenshot by CNET

As for the anti-glazing instructions, I put those to the test in a very deliberate way, asking all three tools what they thought of my team pick and even dropping into the chat to say that I thought my selection was indeed brilliant. Only one of them really took the bait — Gemini — calling my choice in team “phenomenal,” when pressed for an opinion.

Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

ChatGPT and Claude, however, provided resounding confirmation of my choice based on my personal ties to the Sun Devils while keeping their digital lips miles away from my butt cheeks.

Which AI tool fares best with personalization picks?

The most human: If you’re looking for an AI chat tool to vent about your partner leaving the backdoor open or how annoying your parents’ FaceTime calls have become, then Gemini and ChatGPT might be the best bet.

In my testing, they both consistently offered the most personable tone and stayed solidly in the pocket of the most “human-like” responses. Both tools could be tweaked with toggles and specific instructions to reliably offer a sounding board that could appear to have a personality.

Least likely to hallucinate: If you’re looking for a purely analytical, fact-based experience, you’re best served by the settings and outcomes in ChatGPT. Although Gemini was the only AI chat tool that followed my explicit instructions to cite sources without being reminded in the chat on the first try, it subsequently dropped citing sources without being prompted, whereas ChatGPT provided a robust set of links after being reminded once.

Overall impressions: The AI chat tool that most closely followed my instructions and acted in the spirit of the exercise was ChatGPT. It might be the dedicated toggles meant to address the specific concerns around tone that people have complained about. It also might be a matter of opinion. But ChatGPT seemed to be the most coachable AI chat tool in the bunch.

Tech.title: Online CVS Shoppers Might Be Able to Cash In on a $20.5 Million Settlement
Tech.content:
Popular pharmacy chain CVS has been hit with a lawsuit that alleges the company sold data from customers who shopped on its websites (cvs.com and cvshealth.com) or the mobile app.

The lawsuit alleges that CVS disclosed private health information, browsing data and more from users to advertising company Criteo and other third parties, though the pharmacy denies any wrongdoing. It has settled to the tune of $20.5 million to avoid additional expenses by continuing the lawsuit and other business disruptions.

Email notifications (PDF) for potential class members were sent out earlier in September, but the deadline to submit the claim form is Nov. 16, 2026. If you’ve ever shopped on any of the CVS websites or mobile apps prior to July 27, 2026, you’re considered eligible to receive payment, but you must still submit a claim.

More from CNET

According to the official settlement website, customers who submit a claim without documentation may receive up to $5, and those who submit a claim with valid documentation of belonging to the class may receive up to $10, but the amount may be reduced depending on the number of valid claims submitted.

As is typical with class action lawsuits, potential class members may also opt out of the settlement. Opting out of the settlement will prevent payment, but will allow you to maintain your rights to directly sue the company yourself. The final date to opt out of the settlement is Nov. 1, 2026.

The final hearing is set to take place on Dec. 1, 2026, and if the court approves the settlement, payments will be issued 120 days after approval. Class members can be paid via check, PayPal, Venmo or Zelle.
